https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: My Family’s Dark, Hidden History With Institutionalization
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
My great-great-grandfather was the namesake of an infamous institution for the disabled. From long-neglected records of the property, the lives of forgotten people were uncovered.

On the Fernald campus. From left to right: Walter Jr, Walter Sr., Tom (the eventual father of Barbara and Winton), Helen (my great-grandmother), and Katherine.

There is a single name across the front of my family gravestone: FERNALD. A simple slab tucked beneath a low-hanging spruce, it would be easy to miss among the grand monuments and lush gardens surrounding it at Mount Auburn Cemetery in Cambridge, Massachusetts. But for many people in the state, the name it bears can still incite a shiver of terror. It was once invoked by teachers and parents as a threat to misbehaving children: “Keep it up and I’ll send you to the Fernald.”

The Walter E. Fernald State School and Hospital, known to locals as the Fernald, sits on a hill in Waltham, Massachusetts, a few miles down the road from my family’s plot. Now an abandoned heap of earth and brick, from its founding in 1848 until its closure in 2014, the Fernald was the oldest institution for intellectually and developmentally disabled people in the Western Hemisphere. For decades, thousands of disabled, neglected, or “behaviorally troubled” children were brought there; many never left. In the mid-20th century, it became one of the nation’s most infamous institutions after journalists, activists, and lawyers brought to light the squalid conditions inside the Fernald, its neglect of patients, and even the medical experimentation, sponsored by corporations like Quaker Oats, that took place there.

In the spring of 2024, I stood before the family stone as my grandma was being buried. She had died a year earlier, and her name was being added to a long list on the back of the stone which began with that of our patriarch: “Walter E. Fernald.” For 37 years, he was the superintendent of the institution that was then called the Massachusetts School for Idiotic and Feeble-Minded Youth. When he died, 100 years before his granddaughter did, flags flew at half-mast across the state, The Boston Globe wrote that his life inspired “something approaching to awe,” and the institution he had run took his name—an honor that ultimately cemented his dishonor.

My grandma had been the family archivist: Cabinets in her home office overflowed with yellowed newspaper clippings and family trees printed from her 1992 Macintosh. I never paid much attention when she extolled our Mayflower origins or showed me photographs of scowling ladies who were apparently related to me. But in September 2022, early in my senior year of college, while I was mapping out a thesis about my older brother’s hospitalizations with a brain illness, I remembered the occasional conversations I had had with her about her famous grandfather. A quick Google search sent a shock of shame up my spine—there were a slew of stories about abuse at the institution he had once run, but also damning information about the man himself. He was labeled a “eugenicist,” a “sterilizer,” a “monster.”

This revelation led me to drive up to my grandma’s nursing home in Northampton, Massachusetts, to ask her about him. Her health was declining at this point, but she was adamant that I had it all wrong: Walter Fernald was not a monster; he was a remarkable man who would visit every single resident each night before bedtime and taught service to others above all. She insisted that there were no “horror stories” to tell, no matter how much I “seem to want them.” I kept replaying that last point over in my head as I drove back to campus, past the fast fading leaves. Did I want them?

All I knew was that my obsession with Fernald’s legacy only grew. I was lucky that my grandma was such a fastidious record-keeper. I went through her archives, which had been tossed into bankers boxes and were sitting outside in the barn at her old house, and spoke to local historians, but I was only able to view a few of the tens of thousands of records belonging to Fernald that were held in the state’s archives. I could only access the small number that had the patient names redacted due to a draconian Massachusetts law that restricted access to institutional medical records indefinitely—rather than the standard 50 years as specified in the federal Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA). That meant that the Fernald records from 1848 were treated the same as those from 2014.

What I was able to uncover complicated both the condemnations of Walter Fernald that I found online and my grandma’s unequivocal praise. He was undoubtedly a fierce supporter of what was then a radical idea: that disabled children should be offered treatment and education rather than being abandoned or neglected by their families. Through his work at the institution and in local school districts, he created the foundations of what we now call special education. But while he was opposed to the practice of forcibly sterilizing residents, he promoted eugenicist ideas about their potential criminality and, for a period of his career, called for their lifelong segregation from the surrounding community. These ideas turned his Waltham institution into the archetype for a national state hospital system—hundreds of sister institutions were established from Maine to California that were designed to permanently warehouse the disabled under the guise of “public safety.” This system—now often forgotten, its abandoned institutions the backdrop to haunted houses or misremembered as asylums (which served the mentally ill and typically had short-term, rather than indefinite, stays)—was among the largest public investments in the country from the late 19th to the mid-20th century. At its peak in 1967, it held nearly 200,000 people, very often against their will; Walter Fernald was one of its original masterminds.

I never got to share what I had learned with my grandma. She died a couple months after my visit. Would she have been disappointed by who her grandfather really was? Vindicated? In denial? I only knew she would have been proud of me for trying to understand our family history. Now, as she was being interred beside Walter, I recognized all the names on the back of the stone. I knew the story. I remembered.

But as I stepped back from the gravestone, I felt my foot drop onto stone instead of grass. I looked down and saw I was standing on a barely visible mud-caked slab with a name I didn’t recognize: “Barbara M. Fernald 1921–1935.” I called to my mother, “Ma, who is this?” She came over and together we scraped the mud off with our soles. She didn’t know, perhaps a cousin of my grandmother’s who had died young. What had kept her name off the central stone? Beside Barbara’s stone I noticed an even smaller square with no words on it—a nameless grave.

Who was Barbara? Who lay beneath that bare slab? Soon after my grandmother’s funeral, Alex Green, a fellow researcher I had met through my work, contacted me. Alex, a lecturer in public policy at Harvard University who was then finishing a book about my great-great-grandfather, had commiserated with my struggles with the state’s exceptionally restrictive records law. He had sued the state to get access to records from Fernald that were over 100 years old and, in order to view them, agreed to have his notes checked each day to make sure he wasn’t recording confidential patient information. He was so frustrated by the obfuscation that he persuaded the Legislature to create a Special Commission on State Institutions to study, among other things, the state’s actions with regard to records and offer recommendations for ways to improve access to them. Signed into law in July 2022, the 15-person commission—the nation’s first disability rights-led human rights inquiry into the legacy of institutionalization—met for the first time in June 2023.

“This may be a bit of a shock,” he now told me, “but I am fairly certain Fernald had two grandchildren who died in institutions for children with intellectual disabilities.” He had come across offhand references to them in his research. Tom Fernald, my grandmother’s uncle, had two children who both had PKU, a now-treatable genetic condition that causes toxic buildup of the amino acid phenylalanine and leads to progressive brain damage. Barbara Fernald had died at age 13 at a private facility in Pennsylvania in March 1935. Her younger brother Winton had been admitted to Fernald’s sister school, the Wrentham State School, where he died at age 21 in June of 1946. That was all Alex had.

The private facility in Pennsylvania was long closed, and according to the local historical society, its records had almost certainly been destroyed or lost. But I knew Winton’s records must be out there, in some basement archive, but that the state was not going to give me access to them, even though I was related to him and he was long dead.

This restriction was not only absurd but hypocritical. I knew, despite the state’s supposed emphasis on protecting patients’ identities, that thousands of records from as recent as the 1990s had been left on the abandoned grounds of the Fernald for hordes of trespassers to steal and vandalize. I knew it because I’d seen the documents myself.

A couple months after my grandmother’s death, on a cold January morning in 2023, I sat in a car outside the metal gate leading to abandoned acres of the Fernald. I watched Bryan Parcival, a local photographer and Fernald historian I’d befriended through my research, jostle the gate’s lock. “If this doesn’t work we’ll have to hike on,” he said as he shook and twisted the key. With a sudden crack, the lock opened and fell to the ground. He pushed open the groaning gates and hopped back into the driver’s seat. “I got this key five years ago when the state had me take photos of this place. The guy who gave it to me, some maintenance man, died a few weeks later, so no one knows I have this.” He lifted the little silver key up to my face and smiled. “You ready?” he asked, and without waiting for my reply, he drove us past the “No Trespassing” signs and onto the property no one in my family had set foot on in decades.

I followed Bryan’s footsteps as he darted across the buckling wood floors into the Asylum building, which once served as the institution’s main hospital. Mountains of rusted wheelchairs lay crumpled on their sides beside wooden restraint chairs with thick black ropes. Spilling from cabinets was a stream of papers that lay beside books with broken spines, children’s drawings of butterflies, sheet music for “Ode to Joy,” forks, knives, and spoons. I picked up one of the loose papers, a patient record from 1995 titled “Psychotropic Medical Treatment Plan” with a person’s name, birthday, medications, symptoms, and a diagnosis of “chronic schizophrenia” clearly visible. It was one of thousands like it that dotted the floor.

Of course, the campus was technically off-limits. But in 2020 and 2021, the cameras Bryan had set up around the property recorded more than 5,300 incidents of trespassing, during which buildings were frequently damaged and records were stolen, urinated on, and graffitied. One video showed people shooting pornography in the abandoned library that had once housed one of the largest collections of disability literature in the nation. He shared all of this with the City of Waltham, which has owned the property since the institution’s closure. Nothing happened. A police spokesperson told me that they were unable to secure the property due to its size. Urban explorers shared their adventures openly on social media. A local teenager told me it was a rite of passage for kids in the city to visit the campus and that he personally had multiple boxes of patient records in his room that he had swiped. “Do you want to see them?” he asked.

I wrote an article in early 2024 for The Boston Globe about these blatant violations of both HIPAA and the state’s own more restrictive records law that had taken place with the knowledge of the state and the city. The Massachusetts Department of Developmental Services (DDS) blamed the state’s Division of Capital Asset Management and Maintenance (DCAMM) for failing to remove the records in 2014. The DCAMM responded by shifting the blame back to the DDS. Meanwhile, Waltham’s mayor stayed mum. The article changed little for the campus itself. Over the past two years, some of its oldest buildings have been destroyed by arson, and the town has opened a park on a corner of the property that includes miniature golf and a train. The state did remove thousands of records from the campus. According to Caitlin Ramos, the curator at the Massachusetts State Archives, they were extremely damaged and were ultimately all destroyed by the DDS.

But the article did have one major effect: People who were desperate to get some information about loved ones who had died at the Fernald began to reach out to me. One had heard that his sister had choked to death on peanut butter while she wasn’t being properly supervised, another wanted to track down a beloved aunt who had vanished during his childhood, and another had recently discovered that he had a cousin he had never been told about, and he wanted to find his unmarked grave and buy a proper headstone. The state had previously rebuffed them all, telling them it was to protect the privacy of the patients. What privacy was there on the moldy floors of the Fernald?

One of those who had been denied access was Susan Ruderman, a 64-year-old fifth-generation Bostonian who had long known that her mother, Betty, had a missing sibling. In January 1933, when Betty was 4, her half-brother didn’t come home after school. “Where’s Larry?” she recalled her older brother asking. Their mother turned to the two children and barked, “Never speak of him again!”

Despite her mother’s admonition, Betty occasionally mentioned her long-lost sibling to her daughter. In 2019, years after Betty’s death, Susan became concerned that she might be a carrier of PKU and decided to track down what happened to the lost boy, whose name was all she had to go by. Combing through the 1940 US Census, she found an entry for Lawrence Barry. He was listed as a resident of the Fernald. A request to the state archives for his records led to a typical bureaucratic response: She was told that she needed to hire a lawyer, go to court to prove lineage, and be appointed guardian of his estate. It was too much; she begrudgingly let Larry slip back into the well of silence where he’d sat for decades.

But in May 2025, the Special Commission on State Institutions that Alex had helped start and which he served as vice chair of, released its final report on the decades of mistreatment and disregard for records and graves at the Fernald and other state institutions. In response, in November of that year, Governor Maura Healey signed a law that opened the state’s institutional records to families and researchers 75 years after their creation or, if still held by the DDS or the Department of Mental Health, 50 years after the death of the patient. Alex estimates that 75 to 100 million formerly hidden records were found, received, and opened to the public and that more than 1,000 people have been able to access the story of their loved ones. (The state archive did not immediately keep track of access to institutional records under the new law, but between July 1 and October 13 of this year, 143 people received records; the vast majority are family members of former patients.) The new law also temporarily paused the destruction of documents, a de facto admission that the state had been destroying them. Massachusetts, once one of the most restrictive states for access to institutional records, overnight became one of the most transparent.

Susan made a new request and received Larry’s records within days. There was no evidence of PKU in Larry’s records, but what they did reveal was that he was admitted to the Fernald in 1933 at the age of 8 as a “neglected child,” and that he was determined to escape. A medical note dated November 17, 1933, a few months after he was brought to the Fernald, indicated that he was constantly getting into fights and sprinting from the campus into the surrounding neighborhoods. According to the records, after he was brought back on one occasion, he said, “[I’m] posted anyway, so what’s the use of being good?” The file documents years of constant escapes from wards, infirmaries, haylofts, and, once, from a bean patch on the school’s farm. He stole bikes, made it to train stations, and was caught by local residents and police in towns near and far. He was continually being brought back. His yearly files often ended with the same two sentences: “He had no visitors and no correspondence. Clothing is free.”

After an escape when he was 18, the institution gave up on tracking him down. The file continues with notes that the Fernald staff occasionally received phone calls reporting that he was in and out of prisons and other institutions. The final accessible record was from January 1951, when a Waltham police officer questioned a suspicious-looking man at the employee residence at the Fernald; the man claimed that he was a sailor from California and thought the place was a hotel. In fact, he was Larry Barry, returning to the place he hated so much that he’d escaped a hundred times but that was also the only home he’d ever known. The unnamed staff member who wrote the note told the police officer that Larry was not a patient anymore and “they were free to deal with him as they saw fit.” Larry was taken away by the police.

While many questions are left unanswered, Susan says this access was an unbelievable gift—an opportunity to finally get a glimpse of a family member who had been relegated to oblivion since that cold January day in 1933. She is determined to find out what happened to him after he was taken by the Waltham police in 1951, to find his grave, and, if necessary, give it a proper stone.

Just as it did for Susan and the dozens of other people who reached out to me for help, the change in the law meant I could access not only Walter Fernald’s records but also those of his grandson. Within a matter of days, I received Winton’s records from the DDS in an e-mail. It included his autopsy report, which gave him a mental age of 2 years and 10 months and a diagnosis of “imbecile,” a series of medical and psychological notes from his admission at the age of 1 to his death 20 years later, and two photos: one at age 7, standing in a field with a mischievous smile on his face, and another at age 20, in an oversize suit with a large white handkerchief protruding awkwardly from the chest pocket, staring grimly down against a black background. The records show that Winton was constantly shredding his clothes and, as he grew older, smashing his fists into windows. He often had to get stitches on his knuckles. He occasionally had visitors, but his parents, perhaps because of the trauma of institutionalizing two of their children, moved to Florida shortly after his birth and apparently rarely visited Massachusetts.

Wrentham was founded and run by one of Walter Fernald’s closest protégés, Dr. George Wallace. It is very likely that this is why Winton was brought there, and perhaps, though the records don’t reflect this, he received special attention because of his last name. But after Wallace’s sudden death in 1930, Wrentham, like most institutions in the period coinciding with the Great Depression and then the Second World War, had scant funding and dangerously few employees. One staff member per 50 residents was common. Whatever special attention he might have had was likely gone—it is no wonder he kept smashing his fist into windows.

In the final pages of his records, I found proof that Winton was indeed buried under that small stone square at the family plot at Mount Auburn. The files have no mention of his grandfather, the man who had bought that plot, whose name had been bestowed on the institution a few miles down the road, and who had helped create the very system of institutionalization in which his grandson had died. No, it just says Winton died with his mother at his bedside, that he was cremated and buried beside his sister, Barbara, laid to rest 10 years earlier. Unlike her, he did not get a name.

These records cannot do much. Written in the institution’s removed hand, they cannot truly tell his experience, what he was like, what he thought or felt or desired. His life was just one drop in a great ocean of forgotten lives. But is that so special? Despite our best attempts to archive the past, to keep the records from rotting, from potter’s fields to Mount Auburn, from institutions to families, isn’t forgetting the one inevitable thing?

But even so, why do I keep looking at the sad photographs of this faraway boy? What do I want from these “horror stories”? Why do I keep reading and rereading the records, especially returning to the rare moments when he speaks? Such as the January 3, 1941, examination in which he kept repeating, “So glad I’m going home” and “I hate this damn dump.” Or on November 12, 1935, when he kept begging the nurse, “Turn light on, Miss. It’s dark, Miss.” The game, the report says, was an “obsession with him and it was practically impossible to get him to stop.” He jumped up and down and up and down, flicking the light on and off and on and off, answering questions at random, until he finally declared, “No more.”

The filmmaker discusses military pollution, her reporting in Hawai’i, and why the climate and antiwar movements belong together.

What would climate politics look like if it put the military at the center of the conversation? In her documentary Earth’s Greatest Enemy, Abby Martin examines the environmental costs of US power, from its dependence on fossil fuels to the contamination left behind at military bases.

Those costs reach service members and their families as well as the communities around them. At Red Hill in Oʻahu, fuel releases in 2021 contaminated drinking water supplied by the Navy. At Camp Lejeune in North Carolina, another contamination exposed personnel to chemicals associated with increased risks of cancer.

Abby Martin: The film covers not just emissions but the maintenance of the military arsenal coupled with legacy contamination and the further militarization and expansion of the military, and what that actually does to our drinking water, to our air. Seeing the ecocidal destruction in Iran and Gaza, it becomes really clear what’s going on.

SC: You’ve said we have to look at the military as the institution keeping fossil fuel infrastructure in place through brutality and violence. Can you speak to that?

AM: The climate community has rightfully looked at fossil fuel infrastructure. But those companies have a military that works on their behalf. The US military is basically the enforcement arm of global capitalism. The military has always been a force for extractive industries to maintain its own force around the world.

National security has always explicitly been about fossil fuels and securing and maintaining access to those fossil fuels. When you look at all of the bases around the world, where are they? They’re where the main arteries of capital flow. It’s controlling the supply chain and the arteries of capital. That expanse necessitates the continuous growth and pillaging and plundering of all the resources on Earth, just to maintain itself.

SC: Most of this film was made under the Biden administration. What keeps this level of violence in place no matter who’s in power?

AM: The film is important because it’s a time capsule of the Biden administration. It exemplifies the status quo and what has been deemed normal by the ruling class, by the global elites. That’s really important and instructive because it has gotten so bad.

Trump has taken it to such a new level, but we have to go back and realize Trump is not an anomaly. Trump is an extension of the system that incubated this. He’s a natural consequence of what has been normalized and allowed. When we don’t hold criminals to account, when we let this impunity reign, coupled with the wanton environmental destruction, this is what we get.

SC: What do you wish people understood about the cost of war for the people sent to carry it out?

AM: I see it firsthand. Everyone in the military is a victim of this machine. They’re a victim of propaganda too. We are all being harmed by this. But what it’s doing to service members, it’s killing them too.

SC: If military dominance relies on fossil fuels, what does that mean for the possibility of a real energy transition?

AM: We can’t have an energy transition with a global military empire. It’s not going to be allowed. You see people in the film telling me that point-blank.

The problem is you can’t green a global military empire that essentially runs on oil. That is oil, oil, oil. You even heard major generals tell me it’s a pipe dream. We need oil.

AM: [Jet fuel] seeped into the drinking water wells used by military families. These antiquated, rotting storage tanks sat right above Oʻahu’s main aquifer. The military decided to build storage tanks of oil right on top of it. Why?

The Red Hill disaster is one part of what the military has done to Hawai’i. A lot of Americans have no idea that Hawai’i was a sovereign country that had its own government up until the late 1800s.

SC: You got access to RIMPAC, the Rim of the Pacific naval exercise. What did you witness there?

AM: The scale and scope of these exercises are massive. They sink a ship. They love doing that. They will destroy a ship and let it sink to the bottom of the ocean. They do this as the grand finale, I guess, at the end of the exercises.

They use Hawai’i as not only a dumping ground but as a playground for themselves. They have a good time. They treat the island as expendable. They’re blowing stuff up, patting themselves on the back, pumping fists.

SC: How the hell are you getting into RIMPAC and these industry and military events? A quick Google search would show you’re Abby Martin, the anti-imperialist.

AM: There is a contradictory narrative throughout the film. On one hand, the military is this very secretive institution. They don’t grant you any access. But on the other hand, they’re dumb. They don’t Google you.

They don’t do their research. I’m applying to get into these spaces and I’m like, I’m Abigail Martin. They’re like, “Come on in, Sis.” I thought I was going to be beating down other journalists at RIMPAC because it’s such a huge event.

I lived in DC for several years. I know how it works. It’s access, access, access. You don’t want to step on the toes of not being able to get back into these spaces. So you play the game. I go into these spaces knowing that I will never go back. You have one shot to get it right.

I’m not special. I do the bare minimum of what a journalist should do. My question is, where’s everyone else?

SC: Where are the pressure points? What are some tangible things you want to see?

AM: There are incremental steps that can be taken now. There’s the big vision of what ultimately needs to happen to have a habitable planet that we can all survive on. And there are things that need to happen right now that are completely feasible and that are actually being proposed.

The military budget continues to grow and grow and grow. It needs to be completely cut in half right now.

There’s been so much movement with the encampments and the demand for accountability of what weapons systems and contractors are invested in universities.

Banding together, building big tents and broad coalitions and stopping these things in their tracks. That’s possible. There’s so much that we can do, but I think we have to decommission this global military empire and we have to force accountability mechanisms to make the remediation happen. We have to force the military to clean up their mess.

SC: I keep thinking about the 1960s and ’70s and the rise of anti-imperialism at the height of the Vietnam War. What will it take to see our society rise up in that way?

AM: We’re in the infancy stages of organizing and mass education. I feel like we’re getting back to that foundational understanding that capitalism is driving a lot of this. That’s why Gaza has been such a fundamental moment of awakening for so many people, understanding the mechanism and the structure of why these things are happening.

We have to be anti-imperialists. We have to be internationalists, and we have to have solidarity with all oppressed people in the Global South and understand how their oppression is our oppression. It’s all intrinsically tied together.

As an advocacy journalist, I create media to agitate. I try to use propaganda in a way that’s slapping you across the face with the truth, but not to paralyze you, to empower you. Education, action, community, building organizations that have the understanding of what we’re talking about, because we can’t make a dent in the environmental space if we don’t address the elephant in the room.

We’re not going to fight them militarily. We have to speak in the language that they speak: capital flow, withholding our labor, strikes, understanding how labor is essential. During Occupy Wall Street, that shut down the ports. It was the most beautiful day of my life because I saw the power of all of these people coming together and I understood how it could be stopped.

We can’t ever let this system prevent us from imagining something different, from realizing that we have the power and the agency to do something else. This movie is just one tool in the arsenal to give us a fighting chance.

In this week’s Elie v. US, our justice correspondent breaks down the real message of the attacks on Ilhan Omar. Plus: the anti-trans case that will come for us all.

Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN) speaks during a campaign rally for Wisconsin Gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong.

I do not think the national media, members of Congress, or people in general are sufficiently outraged over what is happening to Representative Ilhan Omar. The feds have broken into her house and subpoenaed and harassed her family. They have stolen her laptop, notebooks, and phone. They took her passport. They are said to be “building a case” for denaturalization and deportation.

Omar is a literal refugee: Her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was 8. She spent years at a refugee camp in Kenya before her family was resettled in the United States. Since then, she has become a naturalized US citizen and the first African refugee ever to be elected to Congress. It is precisely because her success defeats the white-supremacist narrative pushed by the Trump administration and the white-wing media that she is being threatened and hunted by this administration.

It would be easy to focus on the hypocrisy of the administration’s attacks on her. The South African–born Elon Musk and the Slovenian Melania Trump both came to this country under dodgier immigration circumstances than most people, including Omar, and Musk has been accused of working illegally in the United States.

It would also be easy to focus on the sketchiness of the timing of the attacks. The Department of Justice is not supposed to take public action on politically sensitive cases within 60 days of an election. The violation of this norm—when James Comey revived the “but her e-mails” nonsense just a few days before the 2016 election—has already benefited Trump once. It would seem the Republicans are hoping for a similar result by invading Omar’s home and forcing everyone to talk about it less than a month before the midterms.

Still, for me at least, the hypocrisy and sketchiness of this smear campaign fails to capture what’s happening here. A political figure, supported by the people, is facing exile from the country because the white-supremacist rulers running the joint can’t get rid of her any other way. The attack on Omar should be viewed as an attack on every immigrant, every person of color, and every outspoken activist in this country. The Trump administration is saying that no matter who you are, they, the white people in charge, can make you disappear.

It is racist. It is fascist. It is disgusting. It is something all of us should stand against.

Ilhan Omar is the physical embodiment of the idea—the dream—that you can start with nothing in this country and not only make a life for yourself but also lift up others on your way. In contrast, the people doing this to her represent the very worst this country has to offer: the idea that no matter what you have, the white man can take it from you whenever he feels like it.

One of the things I desperately try to explain to self-identified liberals who nonetheless feel “uncomfortable” with trans issues is that there is no way to carve transgender individuals out of the protective shield of our equal protection laws but leave everyone else alone. To be clear, I hate that people want to exclude trans people from the grant of equal treatment and opportunity, but even putting my moral disagreement aside, trans people simply can’t be excluded if you want everyone else to have those rights. If you take away rights from trans people, the same legal justifications can and will be used to take away rights from someone else. In the fight against the (cis-heteronormative white) man, we are truly all in this together.

The Supreme Court agreed to hear a case that will put all of this into stark relief. It’s called Trump v. Kingdom, and it’s nominally about Trump’s executive order preventing the Bureau of Prisons from using federal funds to support gender-affirming care. Now, I am well aware that among the people who still watch television ads, some of the Democratic ones feel they were hurt by Trump’s ads saying Kamala Harris is for “they/them, not you.” Harris had said that she supported gender-affirming care for people who rely on the state for their healthcare, including people who are in prison.

The whole thing was called a Harris “blunder.” Incarcerated transgender people are probably the very first people Democrats would nominate to be thrown under the bus, and “moderate” Democrats would further advocate running the bus back over them a couple of times for good measure.

Since the 2024 campaign, many Democrats, including some who are asking to lead the party, have done just that by adopting bigoted positions on trans issues. But those anti-trans positions aren’t just harmless campaign rhetoric. They can have real, disastrous legal consequences for trans people—and for everybody.

We’re about to see some of those consequences at the Supreme Court. As Ian Millhiser explains in this article, when you look at the Kingdom case, you quickly see that it’s not just about denying gender-affirming care to people in prison; it’s about denying medical care more broadly to people in prison, regardless of their trans status. That’s because once you open the door to politicians, instead of doctors, making decisions about what kind of medical care a person can receive, you open Pandora’s box. The Eighth Amendment does not say: “Excessive bail shall not be required, nor excessive fines imposed, nor cruel and unusual punishments inflicted… except to trans people because fuck ’em.” Once you say that the Eighth Amendment doesn’t apply to some prisoners in some situations, the list of people who can be denied human rights only grows. The Kingdom case could be used to deny people in prison the right to psychiatric care, prenatal care, preventive medicine, and even aspirin if the Trump administration decides that “criminals” don’t “deserve” pain medication.

And if you still somehow believe that what applies to people in prison doesn’t affect the rest of us, I’ll remind you that we are, at heart, talking about medical care supported by federal funds. The logic used against trans prisoners in Kingdom could easily be ported over to people who rely on Medicare and Medicaid, to say nothing of those in the US Army or federal employees.

I defend trans rights because it is the right thing to do. But if you are a Democrat who can’t figure out the right thing to do, you should at least be motivated by rational self-interest. Trans rights are human rights, and if you give them up, the damage will not be localized to people you can’t bother to care about.

Football Coach Brian Flores is engaged in long-running litigation against the National Football League. Flores is a superb sideline tactician; nobody disagrees with that. But he also happens to be Black. He was the head coach of the Miami Dolphins from 2019 to 2022, leading the (very bad) team to a 24–25 record, at which point he happened to be fired.

Flores sued the Dolphins, alleging racial discrimination. When he couldn’t get another head coaching job, he sued the NFL. And then he sued the Dolphins again for retaliating against him, by bad-mouthing him to other teams, because of his initial lawsuit. Flores is currently the defensive coordinator for the Minnesota Vikings but he’s still not a head coach (for those unfamiliar with the sport, defensive coordinator is like a deputy coach), despite being very successful with the Vikings.

Flores’s lawsuits (which have been joined by two other Black coaches from around the league) are still in the discovery phase, but this week the closest thing you will see to a “smoking gun” in this kind of employment dispute was made public by the judge overseeing the cases.

It’s a document drafted by Korn Ferry, a search firm many NFL teams use when trying to find their next head coach. Flores had applied to become the Las Vegas Raiders head coach, and Korn Ferry produced a one-page memo listing Flores’s “pros and cons.” The document was produced in part through conversations with the Miami Dolphins organization, and it is explosive. Under cons, it lists things like “chip on his shoulder,” says his personality is “unpredictable,” and that he “needs someone strong at the top to reign [sic] in some of his worst behavior.” One Dolphins executive allegedly said Flores was the “worst hire we ever made”—an objectively untrue fact based on his record, and a pretty good indication of illegal retaliation against a former employee. Taken together, these all read like racist dog whistles: The angry Black man cannot be trusted without a white guy in charge holding his leash.

But it’s actually under the “pros” section where the racism swallowed the whistle and left me gasping on the floor. The search firm wrote: “Polished and a good presenter despite growing up in Brownsville, Brooklyn (same as Mike Tyson). He was able to build a strong friendship with a billionaire’s son which gave him opportunities to socialize and learn how to build relationships with white-collar and upper-class individuals.”

These people wrote down, as a compliment, that “despite” growing up in a Black neighborhood, which happens to be the same neighborhood that a convicted rapist (and millions and millions of other people) grew up in, Flores made a rich friend who gave him “opportunities to socialize” and learn how to talk to “white-collar” folks. ’Cause, I guess, without the literal billionaire nepo-baby guiding him like Jane Goodall out of the mists, Flores would just grunt and beat his chest around “upper-class individuals,” completely unable to make polite conversation, and steal their good silverware… or something.

I must also point out that this document was prepared in 2024, years after Flores had already sued the NFL for discrimination. Korn Ferry put this down in writing after the man had sued the league for stuff like the statements memorialized in this document!

Flores did not get the Raiders job, by the way. Instead, they hired a white man, whom they then fired, before hiring the current white man who runs the team.

Many of you may remember Colin Kaepernick, the Black quarterback who was blackballed by the NFL for kneeling during the national anthem in protest against police brutality. There are many differences between the Kaepernick situation and the Flores lawsuit, but a key one to think about is that Flores is a coach, not a player. Unlike players, who have a limited shelf-life when they’re actually good enough to play professional football, Flores can coach for a long, long time. And he’s frankly too good of a coach to be ignored, because even if he gets drummed out of the NFL for having the gall to defend himself from racism, he can always be a top-level coach in college. He can be a thorn in the NFL’s side for exactly as long as he wants to be. The NFL is going to have to reckon with Flores.

I want Flores to get all the money, and then get another head coaching opportunity. The team that hires him will become my favorite team. Because I am not a wizard-level football strategist. But I know this is how they talk about me, as well. This is how they talk about all of us.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Where Is the Outrage Over Trump’s Racist Targeting of Ilhan Omar?
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The establishment press and some Democrats are strangely mute over the president’s flagrant abuse of the legal system.

Donald Trump has long fantasized about deporting Representative Ilhan Omar. In 2019, Trump lashed out against Omar and her congressional colleagues Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Rashida Tlaib, and Ayanna Pressley—all left-wing Democrats and women of color and part of the “Squad.” Deploying a familiar xenophobic jibe, Trump taunted, “Why don’t they go back and help fix the totally broken and crime infested places from which they came.” For three of the Squad, Trump’s threat was vile but empty: Ocasio-Cortez, Tlaib, and Pressley were all born in the United States.

But for Omar, Trump’s words carried a direct intent of harm. Omar was born in Somalia, came to the United States at age 8 as a refugee, and was eventually granted citizenship at age 17 in 2000. On Thursday, The Washington Post reported that in 2019, the same year Trump was telling Omar to “go back” to where she came from, his administration ordered immigration officials to comb through her personal records to find evidence of fraud that could lead to her removal from the US. This fishing expedition came up empty-handed.

Never one to be defeated by a mere lack of evidence, Trump has persisted in calling for Omar’s deportation ever since—calls that have ramped up over the last year. In January, he said Omar should be sent “back to Somalia,” a call he repeated the following month. In March, Vice President JD Vance joined in, bluntly declaring, without evidence, that Omar “definitely committed immigration fraud.”

There are ample reasons why Omar has been one of Trump’s favorite punching bags. As a leading leftist in Congress, she is a natural antagonist. But, more importantly, as a fearless Somali American woman, she excites all the passions of racism, xenophobia, and misogyny that animate Trump and his MAGA movement.

Given the long history of Trump’s vendetta against Omar, it was ultimately not surprising when the Department of Homeland Security raided her home this week in search of evidence of immigration fraud, a move that The Wall Street Journal reports is motivated by a goal of stripping her of her citizenship.

The campaign against Omar stinks to high heaven of partisanship and bigotry. It is also part of a larger pattern of Trump’s weaponization of law enforcement to punish perceived enemies. As The New Yorker documented recently, Trump’s persecutions have done immense harm to the Department of Justice:

Numerous attorneys have been pushed out or fired after refusing to prosecute such Trump enemies as the former F.B.I. director James Comey and the New York attorney general Letitia James. When these vindictive prosecutions eventually fell under scrutiny in courtrooms, they didn’t fare well. It is extremely rare for grand juries to dismiss charges brought by federal prosecutors, but the case against James, who was accused of committing mortgage fraud, has been rejected twice. Indictments of James and Comey were initially secured by Lindsey Halligan, a lawyer and a former beauty-pageant contestant whom Trump had appointed as the U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, even though she’d had no experience as a prosecutor. But a magistrate judge subsequently reprimanded her for a “disturbing pattern of profound investigative missteps,” including repeatedly misstating the law to grand jurors. Another judge then dismissed both cases, ruling that Halligan had been appointed unlawfully.

But there’s a striking fact that sets the malicious prosecution apart: Unlike earlier victims of Trump’s lawless abuse of the justice system, Omar isn’t getting a full-throated defense from the political and media elite.

Omar does have people fighting on her side. As my Nation colleague John Nichols reports, she remains popular with her constituents in Minnesota, and the state’s Democratic Party has rallied to her side. House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries decried Trump’s “vile personal attacks” and the fact that Trump’s “violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.” Even former Republican representative Marjorie Taylor Greene was critical of Trump. In a post on X.com, Greene asked how “pretending to get ready to deport Ilhan Omar is going to bring gas down under $2, make health insurance freaking affordable, make a family’s weekly grocery bill make sense, and stop sending our beloved military off to fight for another fucking foreign war???”

Greene’s pointed rebuke of Trump stands in sharp contrast to Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer, who in the five days since the raid has yet to say one word in defense of Omar.

Schumer’s silence is hardly surprising. Because Omar has been outspoken in her criticism of Israel and the Israel lobby, establishment Democrats such as Schumer have often kept their distance from her.

Omar’s criticism of Israel and her larger anti-war stance are overwhelmingly popular with Democratic Party voters and have majority support with the general public. According to a recent poll by Project 270, 67 percent of the public want to end overseas war, and 51 percent believe Israel has committed genocide in Gaza (as against 29 percent who deny that genocide has occurred). But these positions are less popular with the political and media elite.

Other victims of Trump’s wrath have been turned into media heroes. But Omar is being treated differently. Writing in The Intercept, Adam Johnson drew a pointed contrast between the Omar raid and the August 2025 raid on the home of John Bolton, Trump’s former national security adviser turned critic.

The very day of the Bolton raid, we saw scathing editorials from the New York Times, Washington Post, and Wall Street Journal. Over the next week, each of these newspapers also published separate pieces from their opinion staff opposing the raid, casting doubt on its legitimacy, and otherwise leveling outrage at the obvious power grab. The raid was explicitly condemned in Politico, The New Yorker, and The Atlantic, which published four different indignant columns.

The raid on Omar’s home has thus far received zero of the above media interventions. No editorials, no opinion columns in the Times, Post, or Journal; no preening in The New Yorker or Politico or Atlantic about the erosion of “rule of law.” The Atlantic did run an article on the Omar raid but it was equivocal and Both Sides in its tone…

As Johnson notes, the reason for the difference in treatment is simply one of identity: Omar is a critic of the establishment, while Bolton is a fixture of the national security state.

On his Unpopular Front Substack, John Ganz also noted that the response to the Omar raid has been “muted” and “tepid.” He suspected the reason might be complacency, due to the “repeated failure of this regime to prosecute its enemies.” But Ganz rightly notes that the attack on Omar is one of the most disturbing events of Trump’s presidency, since it upturns the core principles of liberal democracy:

[T]he attack on citizenship itself is both the very essence of the Trump movement and its most dangerous feature. From birtherism to the stolen-election myth, Trumpism can be understood as the notion that some Americans are not really Americans, that their political rights are illegitimate, and that the nation must be purged of these interlopers.

Ganz is right to highlight the dangers of Trump’s actions. One could add that there is a dual threat: Trump’s subversion of liberal democracy is aided and abetted by an establishment that is so committed to fending off outsiders that it can’t be bothered to defend Ilhan Omar at this crucial moment.

Jeet Heer is a national affairs correspondent for The Nation and host of the weekly Nation podcast, The Time of Monsters. He also pens the monthly column “Morbid Symptoms.” The author of In Love with Art: Francoise Mouly’s Adventures in Comics with Art Spiegelman (2013) and Sweet Lechery: Reviews, Essays and Profiles (2014), Heer has written for numerous publications, including The New Yorker, The Paris Review, Virginia Quarterly Review, The American Prospect, The Guardian, The New Republic, and The Boston Globe.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: Smoke and Mirrors: The Right's Latest Attacks Against Trans People
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
The MAGA movement is redoubling its attacks on trans healthcare in an attempt to win votes this November.

In the final weeks of the 2024 election, the refrain “Kamala is for They/Them, Trump is for You” blared from TVs in the battleground states during NFL and college-football games. Seeking to capitalize on voters’ frustrations after several years of inflation, the campaign ad warned that a Harris presidency would mean government-funded transition surgeries for children and migrants amid soaring food and housing costs for Americans.

This wasn’t the first time that the MAGA movement concocted a blend of populist resentment and anti-trans sentiment. That summer, Trump posted a video on social media in which he pledged to “investigate Big Pharma and the big hospital networks to determine whether they have deliberately covered up horrific long-term side effects of sex transitions in order to get rich at the expense of vulnerable patients.”

Since retaking office, the president has made good on that promise. The Department of Justice has issued subpoenas to doctors and clinics providing gender-identity care to children, while the Trump administration has moved to implement an executive order directing the Department of Health and Human Services and the DOJ to investigate and restrict such care. More recently, the federal health bureaucracy issued a report, “Wolves in White Coats: How Doctors and Hospitals Pushed and Profited From the Fraud of ‘Gender Medicine,’” alleging potentially fraudulent insurance-coding practices in gender-affirming care for minors. If the Trump regime and its allies cannot credibly run on a record of economic success, at the very least they might direct voters’ attention to someone else who, they claim, has been picking taxpayers’ pockets.

For a document that is ostensibly about healthcare, the provenance of its authors—mainly conservative women’s groups and Christian policy shops—is striking. Its most decorated author, May Mailman, is a veteran of the first Trump administration’s immigration team who returned to the White House to orchestrate the 2025 executive order “Defending Women From Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government.” Its few medical experts are Quentin Van Meter, the former president of the fringe American College of Pediatricians, which broke away from the prestigious American Academy of Pediatrics over the latter’s support of adoption rights for gay and lesbian parents, and Eithan Haim, who previously collaborated with the conservative activist Christopher Rufo to expose Texas Children’s Hospital’s defiance of the state’s criminalization of trans healthcare as potential child abuse. (Haim had been previously indicted for accessing that data under false pretenses, but the case was dropped one week into Trump’s second term).

The report itself presents what one could call a trans-exceptionalist view of the US healthcare system’s flaws. That is, it portrays the real deficiencies of a highly privatized approach to care as a problem of “ideological capture” and radical transgender activism rather than one of marketized medicine. It attempts to shock readers with sensationalized language about the “unique and lifelong revenue streams” that “sex-rejecting procedures” afford providers. Those relatively low-paid and prestige-hungry pediatricians, the report’s authors claim, stumbled upon a “strategic area of growth” in gender-affirming care, one that greedy “elite” hospital administrators were more than happy to encourage.

There is truth but far more fiction in this account of trans medicine. While medical transition does indeed require the persistent use of hormonal medications, these are often available as cheap generics. Yet the report explicitly alleges that pediatric gender-medicine programs generated substantial revenue and created groups of “captive patients” requiring long-term care. There is limited evidence, in the report or elsewhere, that leaders of hospitals consider gender-identity clinics, with their tiny patient populations, to be an especially lucrative “growth area.”

At its worst, “Wolves in White Coats” takes real problems in healthcare billing and attributes them to providers of trans care. The authors make a scandal of how some providers used creative diagnostic codes to convince insurers to pay for medically necessary treatment. For instance, the report alleges that a physician might diagnose a patient with an “unspecified endocrine disorder” rather than gender dysphoria, or file claims for adolescents with a diagnosis of “precocious puberty.” In the eyes of the Trump administration, however, these acts of clever compassion are nothing more than fraud, a violation of the False Claims Act that should be met with punishment.

The report also cites recent high-profile instances of actual systematic fraud in the Medicare Advantage system that resulted in $90 million settlements with the DOJ. These cases have nothing to do with trans medicine, but they have everything to do with the Trump administration’s support for this privatized form of Medicare—one that creates an incentive for this exact kind of con. By paying “risk-adjusted” higher rates to insurers based on the health of enrollees, Medicare Advantage basically invites its partners in the insurance industry to manipulate patient records. Unlike these insurers, however, trans-healthcare providers are not taking liberties with diagnostic codes to make anyone rich; they’re simply trying to get their patients much-needed care in a system that often withholds everything from hormones to cancer drugs.

Although Republican elites have benefited politically from the myth that a marauding gender-identity industry has been preying on unsuspecting children and their parents, they did not invent this conspiracy theory. One of the first influential articulations of the idea came in 2018, from the little-known blogger Jennifer Bilek, writing in The Federalist. Bilek described a cabal of gay, trans, and Jewish billionaires, including George Soros and Jennifer Pritzker, along with major pharmaceutical companies and Silicon Valley types, who had constructed a medical-industrial complex rivaling the military’s own sprawling network of government-subsidized firms. Over the next few years, this idea gained traction among gender-critical feminists and Christian fundamentalists before a slightly tamer version was adopted by think tanks like the Heritage Foundation and the Manhattan Institute.

In the summer of 2022, as inflation hit a 40-year high and the Democrats’ ambitious Build Back Better economic plan lay dead in the Senate, an influential conservative group put the gender-identity-industry trope to work. That August, the American Principles Project unveiled its “Top 25 Threats to the American Family” report, led by Senators Marco Rubio and Josh Hawley and featuring contributions from JD Vance, Heritage president Kevin Roberts, and others who became leaders in the second Trump administration. Although the American Principles Project had failed in its earlier attempts to mobilize anti-trans messaging for Republican politicians—its strategists were largely responsible for the first slew of gender-affirming care state bans that at first failed to do much better than the then-losing issue of trans bathroom bills—this new populist branding showed promise.

Straying from the GOP’s typical pro-business rhetoric, the American Principles Project took on Google, Amazon, and BlackRock as well as “special-interest groups” like the Chamber of Commerce and Big Pharma. Special ire was reserved for AbbVie, the manufacturer of puberty-suppressing medications, which was compared to the corrupt Tammany Hall political machine. “Woke” Silicon Valley moguls were also blamed for their role in broadcasting social-media content that allegedly spread gender dysphoria like a social contagion, eventually sending those confused children to specialists who were more than happy to sell them surgical salves.

This message ultimately resonated with many Americans, drawing as it did from a growing suspicion of Big Pharma and Big Tech in the post-pandemic era. Vaccine skeptics like Steve Bannon hosted Bilek to complain about the “transhumanist” machinations of trans-healthcare providers, while Make America Healthy Again leader Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and podcasters like Joe Rogan demonized gender clinicians and public-health officials alike. Just in time for Trump’s adoption of the conspiracy theory, the American Principles Project published its “Gender Industrial Complex” report in 2024, documenting a purported $4.4 billion market in hormones and surgeries—which might sound scandalous without the context that US healthcare spending runs in the trillions. No matter though—27 states and the federal government have now restricted best practices in medicine, spurred on by horror stories about a rapacious transition industry that cares for little more than insurance reimbursements and out-of-pocket surgical expenses.

This election season, Republicans are hoping that the anti-trans sentiment that propelled Trump back into office still has momentum. In Texas, the president’s handpicked candidate Ken Paxton has made such attacks central to his Senate race against Democratic nominee James Talarico. Resorting to schoolyard-bullying tactics, Paxton has referred to his opponent as “low-T Talarico” and “Six-Gender Jimmy”—barbs that conflate Talarico’s support for trans rights with a supposed masculinity deficit. Trump advisor Stephen Miller has gone as far as transvestigating Talarico with a backhanded celebration of the “first transgender senate candidate.”

Even more brazenly, the American Principles Project has been running a pro-Paxton ad that loops Talarico into the gender-identity-industry conspiracy. Borrowing from President Lyndon B. Johnson’s famous 1964 “Daisy” campaign ad, which cautioned against Republican nominee Barry Goldwater’s trigger-happy attitude toward the country’s nuclear arsenal, the video depicts an innocent young white girl who—according to an AI-generated LBJ voice-over—is at risk of a “trans industry [that] preys on confused children.” Although the ad begins with the familiar flowery field where the girl counts each petal that she delicately pulls from a daisy, the scene quickly shifts to a hospital gurney, over which a masked and scrubbed-in Talarico hovers. The child, now donning an anesthetic face mask, continues to count down as the disembodied LBJ tells us of the surgeries that will soon be forced upon her. And yet another Paxton-aligned PAC is currently airing an ad that warns “Talarico is for They/Them, Not You.”

Beyond Texas, these fears have also moved into intra-GOP battles over the party’s future. This was most visible in Kentucky, where the isolationist US Representative Thomas Massie fought against the Trump-endorsed Ed Gallrein in what became the most expensive House primary race in history. In one ad, a pro-Massie PAC directed attention to the fact that his rival, whom he called “woke Eddie,” was funded by the billionaire hedge-fund manager Paul Singer, a Republican known for his iconoclastic support of LGBTQ causes as well as his donations to the Israel lobby AIPAC. Combining those elements, the ad foregrounds Singer’s visage as a rainbow Star of David rises behind him while the voice-over denounces Singer as a “far-left trans-activist billionaire” member of the “LGBTQ mafia.” In conflating Singer’s Jewish heritage with his political support for Israel and trans rights, the ad recaptures the earliest fringe critics of the gender identity industry who were never shy about centering Soros in their narrative.

Elsewhere, Groyper-aligned candidates and their media champions like Tucker Carlson are harnessing due outrage against Israel, Silicon Valley, and the affordability crisis to push these and other scapegoating narratives into the political mainstream. Perhaps no one is more aware of this message’s electoral potential than Vice President J.D. Vance who co-authored the original American Principles Project report against the gender identity industry and later broadcast the conspiracy on Joe Rogan’s podcast during the final weeks of the 2024 election. Today, Vance is getting heat from within the party for his “America First” style approach to Israel and his willingness to blaspheme the GOP’s holy trinity of Reagan, Thatcher, and the Wall Street Journal, if that is what it takes to ascend to the presidency two years from now.

And yet those conservatives who are most eager to denounce Big Pharma and specific features of our privatized healthcare system are also the least likely to do anything about them. Instead, they’ve cut Medicaid and refused to extend the Affordable Care Act’s tax credits. And lest liberals remain off the hook, their failure to reckon with inequality and their complicity with the forces that keep both the healthcare industry and the country’s megadonor-driven politics intact are also to blame. After all, “Kamala is for They/Them, Trump is for You” worked because the Democratic Party’s botched economic agenda fueled the idea that trans rights are incompatible with the public good. Until something is done about the ugly truths of private power, there will be plenty of those who are drawn to these conspiratorial untruths.

Joanna Wuest is an assistant professor of women's, gender, and sexuality studies at Stony Brook University.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: Progressives Are Backing Puerto Rican Independence. It’s About Time.
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
More and more leftists are concluding that statehood for the island is not enough.

A video of New York congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier advocating for Puerto Rican independence.

Something is changing in the political conversation about Puerto Rico. In recent months, major leaders and organizations on the American left have explicitly signaled their support for the island’s independence.

On September 23, to mark the 158th anniversary of the Grito de Lares freedom revolt, future congressman Chris Rabb joined his Puerto Rican constituents in Philadelphia and declared, “I support Puerto Rican independence. Puerto Rico has the right to be a free, sovereign, and independent nation.”

Rabb, who will almost certainly get elected to the US House of Representatives from Pennsylvania’s 3rd district, joined other influential progressives who have come out for Puerto Rico’s freedom. Earlier this year another general election shoo-in, Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York, called for an inclusive Puerto Rican self-determination process. She added: “I also support independence for the Puerto Rican people. Because after 128 years, it’s the least the people on the island deserve.”

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has also weighed in. In June, on the eve of the National Puerto Rican Day Parade, Mamdani gave Puerto Rican independence a poetic shoutout:

“This weekend, the boricuas of our city will don bright colors, sing songs of freedom, and wave a flag that was once made illegal by the United States government. There will be joy…as well as the bittersweet knowledge of an independence that has too long been denied.”

Notably, support for sovereignty is rising among political leaders outside of Puerto Rican bastions like New York and Pennsylvania. Former Missouri representative Cori Bush and fellow Missouri Democratic primary candidate Hartzell Gray came out in support for Puerto Rican sovereignty. So did Julie Gonzales, who gave John Hickenlooper a scare in the Democratic primary for US Senate in Colorado. (Full disclosure: My organization, Boricuas Unidos en la Diáspora, which advocates for Puerto Rican independence, endorsed all three of those candidates.)

Some of these candidates are adopting the institutional position of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), which recently reaffirmed its long-standing commitment to Puerto Rico’s decolonization and independence.

The explicit support for independence is a welcome change from the American progressive movement, which has historically been far too silent on Puerto Rico’s colonial status. But it is not without controversy. Avila Chevalier’s statement, for example, was celebrated in some corners but panned in others—not just by centrist liberals but also by more than a few fellow leftists.

Some insist that Puerto Rico should instead be granted statehood as a matter of inclusion and equality. But that amounts to an endorsement of annexation. Puerto Rico is a nation that was invaded by the United States in a war of expansion and has been held as a colony for over a century. Statehood would reward the US for its imperialist misadventures by allowing it to permanently keep a land it took by force. Colonies should be liberated, not subsumed by the empire that claimed them. Statehood would also accelerate the assimilation of the Puerto Rican people and the displacement from our homeland, as American remote workers and retirees flock to their new warm-weather state.

Other progressives contend none of that matters because Puerto Ricans don’t seem to want independence, and have instead consistently voted for statehood. The full picture is not so simple. While Puerto Rican sovereignty was historically a hyper-minority position, that’s no longer the case. In the 2024 Puerto Rican status plebiscite, more than 40 percent of voters chose one of the two sovereign options for Puerto Rico: full independence or sovereignty in free association with the United States. The latter would make Puerto Rico an independent country that has a bilateral compact with the US.

Moreover, because Congress has never made these votes legally binding or acted on their results, the plebiscites have served as informal polls more than actual elections. And because the last six plebiscites have been held by the ruling pro-statehood party on the island, which decides what’s on the ballot and gets to put its thumb on the scale, hundreds of thousands of Puerto Ricans boycott the votes.

In short, these local plebiscites have not been legitimate instruments of Puerto Rican “self-determination,” which is a foundational tenet of international law that demands “an informed democratic process, impartially conducted.” No Puerto Rico status vote has met that standard.

That said, there is no denying that statehood has significant support among Puerto Ricans—perhaps more than sovereignty. That is to be expected after more than 125 years of political repression that once heavily targeted the Puerto Rican independence movement, and of colonial economic dependence that has led many Puerto Ricans to believe they have no choice but to rely on the United States.

But progressives should be well used to taking political positions on ideological grounds regardless of how well they poll. The history of liberation and justice for oppressed peoples is the history of once unpopular ideas that, in time, came to be seen as obviously righteous. Americans should support Puerto Rican independence not because it is popular, but because it is just.

By far, however, the most common rebuttal to support for independence is that Americans shouldn’t take a position at all. This has been the tried-and-true talking point of the political establishment for decades: that it’s “up to the Puerto Rican people” and therefore inappropriate—even outright imperialist—for anyone outside the island to have a say.

That is a noble sentiment that seeks to center the voices of Puerto Ricans. But it is both morally incongruous and divorced from American political reality. First, the duty to decolonize Puerto Rico should rightfully fall on the colonizer, not on the colonized. Saying that it’s all up to Puerto Ricans passes the buck, and it implicitly blames a colonized people for their continued subordination.

Second, there are already plenty of non–Puerto Ricans deciding the island’s future: the members of the United States Congress—and, by extension, their voters and constituents in the United States.

It is Congress that has declined to make any Puerto Rican status plebiscite legally binding. It is Congress that has failed to act on the results, year after year, even when statehood has won admittedly controversial victories at the ballot box. It is Congress that has neglected to establish some other decolonization process by which Puerto Ricans might change the status quo; and Congress that must ultimately legislate to either admit Puerto Rico as a state or initiate a transition to sovereignty.

Why has none of that happened? Because as long as Puerto Ricans might choose statehood, Congress won’t let us choose at all. Republicans are convinced that Puerto Ricans would reliably elect Democrats, so they’re viciously opposed to it. These days, President Trump can’t go two days without asserting that Puerto Rican statehood would “destroy” the United States. And Democrats are too divided or disinterested in statehood to expend the massive political capital it would take to overcome GOP opposition.

As with the statehood movement for Washington, DC, there is no way for Puerto Rican statehood to get 60 votes in the US Senate. In theory, Democrats could end the filibuster and ram through statehood on a party line. But there is a reason they haven’t already: Eliminating the filibuster would enable the next Republican-controlled Senate to enact a nightmarish right-wing agenda.

And if the island becomes the 51st state through a wholly partisan Democratic effort, its people are likely to be treated with dangerous disdain by MAGA Republicans who would see Puerto Ricans as illegitimate Americans

The strident opposition to statehood doesn’t just sink the prospects of adding Puerto Rico to the Union. It acts as a poison pill in every legislative proposal to address the island’s status. Any effort to “let the Puerto Rican people decide” is ultimately undone by the fact that Congress will not approve any bill that includes all potential status options and might therefore force US lawmakers to admit the island as the 51st state. Puerto Rican self-determination dies on the floor of the US Senate.

In the face of that political reality, progressives must offer Puerto Ricans more than a nod at “the will of the people” and a shrug when, decade after decade, those people remain colonized. We must build a movement around a political future for Puerto Rico that is both just and viable in Washington, DC.

And we need not fear that it will result in Americans’ unilaterally imposing their views on the Puerto Rican people. There is near-universal agreement that Puerto Ricans deserve a just, democratic, and inclusive decolonization process, and that the final choice will ultimately be ratified in a binding vote. But we won’t even get that far if we keep pretending that statehood might be on the table.

Leaders at the DSA, and politicians like Chris Rabb and Darializa Avila Chevalier, are stepping up to support the movement for Puerto Rico’s sovereignty. They must be joined by more candidates and elected officials who are committed to decolonization, and by millions of progressives who want their country to stop being an imperial power. Only by advocating for freedom can Puerto Ricans and Americans, together, end a colonial relationship that has lasted for more than a century.

Alberto C. Medina is the president of Boricuas Unidos en la Diáspora, a national organization of Puerto Ricans who advocate for decolonization and sovereignty. He writes regularly about Puerto Rico’s status on his Substack, Free Puerto Rico, and his book of the same name will be published in 2027 by The New Press.
