https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
When Operation Metro Surge went into high gear in January, the life of Ana (her name has been changed for her safety) underwent a profound crisis. While she is a US citizen, born in Minneapolis in 2006, she was well aware that she fit the ICE profile: a brown person living in a neighborhood of brown people. She notified her college that she would be taking off a semester, a setback to her ambition of becoming a physician. She had no choice. ICE was everywhere—stopping traffic, waiting for parents to pick up their children at school or daycare, watching at the mall, small businesses, markets, parks.

Her father, who is undocumented, was working at a restaurant when ICE agents entered and interrogated the manager: “Where are the immigrant workers?” Her father called home. “If you don’t hear from me or if I don’t come home, it’s because ICE agents are in the restaurant,” Ana remembers him whispering. He slipped out the back door and never returned. He made it home and did not leave the house for four months. Ana’s mother, who works the graveyard shift cleaning offices, stayed home as well. They were terrified.

One morning, an ICE agent, dressed in what looked like an Amazon deliveryman’s uniform, banged on the front door. Her parents remained still and did not answer. They heard him trying to break into the garage. He left, but his attempted intrusion sent a shudder through the family. “They wouldn’t even take out the trash,” says Ana.

During this period, Ana was busy around the clock. She took and picked up her two younger siblings at school daily. She bought the family groceries, medicines, and other necessities. Their family’s small savings were dwindling fast. Even today, debts from that time are still owed.

Her family was not alone. Ana’s mission extended to six other families, fulfilling their needs as well. She checked Facebook posts daily to know where, and where not, to go. Many Hispanic households in the neighborhood were in hiding at home, including one with a pregnant woman in dire need of doctor visits, trips also undertaken by Ana.

The killing of Renée Good, on January 7, sent a shock wave through the community. The message was clear: No one was safe. After the killing, Ana recalls thinking, “I could only imagine what they would do to me.” News of a toddler used as bait to lure his parents from their home added to the pervasive atmosphere of fear.

Ana’s father’s best friend—“like an uncle to me”—also undocumented, was picked up by ICE in January and put in detention. Later, he related his harrowing experience there, like so many stories told about ICE detention facilities across the country. He told of being held for six weeks in a cell with 30 men, one sink, and one toilet. The meals were inedible, disgusting. Finally he self-deported to Mexico, “dropped in the middle of nowhere,” as he told Ana’s father. All his belongings were left behind. His earnings from work had supported his family back home in Mexico for decades. His life, like so many, was consumed by hard work and family.

Not one immigrant Ana’s family knew had a criminal record. In fact, according to The New York Times, October 10, 2026, “Homeland Security data shows that arrests of people with no criminal record soared over the summer.” This essential fact went largely unnoticed. National Public Radio’s On the Media program reported on October 9, 2026, that “coverage of ICE has decreased since the spring, while the agency’s operations have quietly surged.”

The stress at Ana’s house was overwhelming. Her father could not stop crying, telling her he felt he had put the family in danger. “He could not stop apologizing,” she says. Today, months later, Ana’s mother still incessantly hears the whistles observers blew to warn of the presence of Operation Metro Surge agents.

Ana continued a 9-to-5 job at a retail shop. The family needed money, and her earnings were keeping them afloat—barely. Her mother insisted Ana carry not just her passport but her birth certificate, too.

On one occasion, when Ana was driving, she stopped behind a car where two Hispanic men were being extricated by ICE agents and handcuffed. She could see that the men spoke no English. She rolled down her window, offering to help translate, and an ICE agent started to pull out his gun, looking directly at her. She froze, raised the window, and waited for the ICE vehicle to leave.

Sandy Hood was in touch with her daughter, Leah, in early January, after the shooting of Good. Leah Hood teaches English as a second language at a college in the Twin Cities. Nearly all of her 25 students, a majority of them Hispanic, failed to turn up after the Christmas break. She understood. Operation Metro Surge was at full throttle, and Hispanic residents of Minneapolis, whether they were undocumented, green-card holders, or even US citizens, were staying home if they possibly could. They were learning by word of mouth and social media about the intensity of the ICE presence in their city—initially 3,000 agents acting with a presidential mandate to capture thousands of immigrants and process them for deportation.

Sandy’s husband is a sixth-generation Iowa farmer, now growing corn and feed. Sandy retired as a high school history teacher in the nearby town of Independence, population 5,000. There were just a few Hispanic students in her classes over the years. Nevertheless, what her daughter was relating profoundly affected her. “I believe in justice and treating people kindly. This feels like a leap backward into the 1950s,” she says.

After the shooting of Good, Sandy and her husband decided to drive up to Minneapolis to assist their daughter in her efforts on behalf of immigrants besieged by ICE. They stayed for a month and later two additional weeks delivering groceries, “rice and beans and fruit.” Sandy says, “They were so humble and thankful.” Once, in a trailer court, she observed severe poverty and “school-aged kids not in school.” She learned that many had no heat, “layering up instead.” Both she and Leah handed out winter clothing.

Leah recalled a few years back when armed Proud Boys showed up at a school board meeting. They were “intimidating and scary.” That incident had stayed in her mind, in stark contrast to her experience with the Hispanics she taught—some teens, mostly adults. Their decency was apparent; her respect for their desire to learn and be part of the community was profound.

By the end of February, Leah had handed out her entire life savings—desperately needed cash to housebound immigrants to pay rents, utility bills, and other necessities. Like Ana, she delivered food and medicines to immigrants, took their children to and from school, and accompanied them to doctor visits.

Leah showed no hesitation in joining in the civil disobedience in the streets. “It was remarkable to stand up to an authoritarian force. We are regular, everyday people who had to be involved.”

By March, Leah was exhausted. The ICE patrols no longer at the school remain “vivid memories.” “People were beaten and kidnapped,” she says. Some students were deported.

After the killings of Renée Good and Alex Pretti, Leah says, “We came out of our houses and we stood face to face against these agents and we said, ‘Not here!’ I understand that what happened here is of historic importance.”

ICE agents remain in Minneapolis. Reports of immigrant disappearances continue. Minnesota’s economy has felt the effects. According to the Immigration Research Initiative, “the level of employment among US-born workers is 25,000 lower than it would have been [without Operation Metro Surge].”

In mid-September, Ana noticed that ICE activity had returned to her neighborhood. Still, Ana’s mother had to go back to work. The family was drowning in debt. Ana drove her to the 1 am shift cleaning offices and picked her up at 6 am. “She would pray before going to work.”

“Voting is our way out of this,” Leah says. “This is the most critical election in my lifetime.” She is an election judge, a city-appointed citizen working as a volunteer to “help ensure that the process of voting is lawful, smooth and fair.” Voting is sacred to her.

Sandy says it was a “terrible shame” that Iowa turned over voter lists to the US Department of Justice. “I’m nervous about GOP cheating, not accepting the results if it doesn’t go their way.”

“It’s crucial for people to go out there and vote,” says Ana, who has yet to go back to school. Instead, she is working the phones, telling people that their vote counts. Intensive calling starts October 27, and she’s on board.

It’s a familiar line in the midterms: Anti-trans attacks are a “distraction” from “kitchen-table” issues. That sends a chilling message about whose rights are worth fighting for.

In a world dominated by neoliberal market fundamentalism, “socialism” is what will make a more moderate, regulated form of capitalism work for most people.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Gina Hinojosa Is Showing Democrats How to Run Against Republican Grifters
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The Democratic gubernatorial candidate has closed the gap in Texas by focusing relentlessly on Greg Abbott’s corruption.

Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa (D-TX) speaks during an education town hall at a local community center on October 10, 2026, in Cypress, Texas.

If Texas Democrats end their three-decade-long electoral losing streak this year, it will be because they have figured out new ways to “do” politics.

That’s been much noted with regard to this year’s US Senate contest in the state, where Democrat James Talarico has upended political calculations with a scripture-quoting, economic populist challenge to the state’s billionaire-based politics and the scandal-plagued Republican who exemplifies it. If Talarico defeats his Republican opponent Ken Paxton, the result could give the Democrats control of not just the Senate but—should their party win a US House majority—control of Congress for the last two years of Donald Trump’s second presidential term.

It would also be a breakthrough of historic consequence for Texas Democrats, who have not had a member of their party sitting in the Senate for 33 years—since appointed Democratic incumbent Robert Krueger was swept out of office after having won just 33 percent of the vote in a 1993 special election.

But the Senate race is not the only one in which Texas Democrats could experience a renewal that is of both state and national significance.

The last time that a Democrat was elected as governor of Texas, George Herbert Walker Bush was the president of the United States, Margaret Thatcher was finishing her tenure as prime minister of the United Kingdom, and Mikhail Gorbachev was the general secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. The year was 1990, and the winner of the Texas gubernatorial race was Ann Richards, a sharp-tongued populist who upended conservatives on both sides of the political aisle.

Richards lost reelection to George W. Bush amid the Republican wave of 1994, and—despite ritual predictions that “this could be the year Texas turns blue,” no Democrat has come close to winning the governorship—or any statewide office—in three decades.

But, in a striking measure of sinking Republican fortunes this fall, Texas could actually turn blue in 2026—not just in the Senate contest but also in races for statehouse posts.

While Texas Democrats have had to live on hope for a long time, this year they have poll numbers, deep dissatisfaction with Republican governance, and an energized, diverse, and growing base of supporters on their side.

State Representative Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat from Austin, has narrowly led incumbent Republican Governor Greg Abbott—who has been in power since 2015 and was, until relatively recently, seen as a shoo-in for a fourth consecutive term—in several recent polls. The race is still very much “a toss-up,” but the latest University of Texas/Texas Politics Project survey points to “a clear partisan enthusiasm gap favoring Democrats.” And this week, the editorial boards of the state’s largest newspapers have endorsed Hinojosa. The San Antonio Express-News did so with a jab at the incumbent, declaring, “After 12 years in office, it’s clear that Abbott has come to take Texans’ votes for granted. It’s time for someone who will alter that trajectory in a positive, inclusive way. To meet that challenge, we recommend Hinojosa for governor.” The Houston Chronicle hailed Hinojosa as “smart, pragmatic and resourceful,” while the Austin American-Statesman announced, “Texans deserve a leader who will work to uplift the many, not the few. Hinojosa is ready to bring that change.”

That’s high praise for a candidate who began her campaign against Abbott, the most entrenched major Republican official in Texas history, as an uphill climb. The Republican has held statewide office for almost 24 consecutive years, first as attorney general and then as governor. He enjoys universal name recognition and massive support from powerful donors tied to corporate special interests and the state’s many billionaires. But Hinojosa built her campaign around a compelling message. The American Dream, she suggested, was slipping away from Texans. “As Governor, I’ll put it back on the table with a short, simple agenda, because the plan should be as plain as the promise: save Texas schools, put money in your pocket, and end the Greg Abbott Corruption Tax.”

Most Texans, like most Americans, may be new to the idea of a “corruption tax.” But it is a notion that Democrats would be wise to add to their lexicon—especially in the way that Hinojosa’s camp describes it. “[The] Greg Abbott Corruption Tax has taken taxpayer dollars from hardworking Texans while they struggle with their neighborhood schools closing, data centers flooding their communities, and the rising costs of gas, groceries, utilities, and healthcare,” argues the campaign. Specifically, explains Hinojosa, Abbott’s decades of campaign fundraising from millionaires and billionaires have cost Texas taxpayers a fortune.

Billboards paid for by the Hinojosa campaign have reminded voters that, for instance:

To keep the corruption issue front and center in the minds of voters, Hinojosa proposes to direct the legislature to approve a one-time “Corruption Tax Refund” that would send $1,500 checks to every household in the state. “Greg Abbott has hoarded $27 billion in taxpayer money into the Rainy Day Fund—money that belongs to Texans—while families struggle to pay their bills,” explains the Hinojosa campaign. “No Texas politician has ever hoarded taxpayer dollars like this—and it’s time Texans get that money back. It is fiscally irresponsible for the government—that money should be working in our economy.”

Hinojosa’s camp says, “The Rainy Day Fund needs about a $10 billion balance to be fiscally responsible according to experts, so Gina will direct the legislature to return the other $17 billion to Texas families in the form of a $1,500 refund—because Gina knows your money should work for you, not sit idle in Austin.”

The refund proposal is part of a broader populist platform, in which Hinojosa proposes to “save public schools” by addressing one of the issues highlighted on those “Greg Abbott Corruption Tax” billboards. Focusing on the Republican governor’s support for school vouchers, Hinojosa’s campaign argues that

Greg Abbott’s voucher scam was never about helping kids—it’s a payout for the privileged. After accepting more than $12 million in donations from out-of-state billionaire Jeff Yass, Abbott funneled $1 billion into the voucher program, redirecting money from 5.5 million public school kids to instead serve his rich donors. Today, 70% of voucher applications are from families who already have their kids in private school, and private schools retain the power to keep everyone else out.”

What Hinojosa is doing is transformational for Texas, and for the rest of the United States. She is not just making an issue of corruption. She is showing Democrats how to talk about it in ways that connect with voters. At the start of her campaign, she promised to take on Abbott by calling out “his failures and his grift.” It’s working.

John Nichols is the executive editor of The Nation. He previously served as the magazine’s national affairs correspondent and Washington correspondent. Nichols has written, cowritten, or edited over a dozen books on topics ranging from histories of American socialism and the Democratic Party to analyses of US and global media systems. His latest, cowritten with Senator Bernie Sanders, is the New York Times bestseller It's OK to Be Angry About Capitalism.

https://www.thenation.com/article/enviro.title: Trump Is Making Deals With Big Oil
https://www.thenation.com/article/enviro.text:
Democrats and the press should be paying attention to how this pay-to-play behavior relates to the midterms

President Donald Trump stands alongside Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Dan Caine at an April press conference on the Iran War.

With the US midterm elections less than three weeks away, is it any surprise that corruption has emerged as voters’ top concern? “Corrupt” was the adjective most often chosen when registered voters were asked for a single word to describe President Donald Trump, according to a survey conducted in September by The Economist and the market research firm YouGov, with 53 percent of respondents calling Trump corrupt and only 23 percent saying he is “honest.” A Pew Research Center poll in early October found that nearly seven in 10, or 69 percent, of Americans are “not confident” that Trump keeps his business interests separate from his presidential decisions.

Americans can thank diligent investigative reporting for alerting them to much of Trump, his family, and aides’ self-dealings. For example, The Washington Post has reported that Trump’s sons, Don Jr. and Eric, were investors in 15 companies that “collectively generated at least $3.2 billion in direct government business since the sons invested and an additional $3.1 billion in future contract options.” And on Tuesday, in a rare retreat, the White House asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign as US ambassador to Greece after a Wall Street Journal investigation revealed that Guilfoyle promised political favors to a Trump donor if he would quietly pay off her $100,000 American Express credit card bill.

Throughout the history of modern polling, voters have usually ranked the economy (or its proxies, such as “the cost of living”) as their top issue. Now, linking corruption with the cost of living, “Democrats Are Making Corruption Messaging a Pocketbook Issue,” a recent Politico headline declared. The Democrats’ claim, The New York Times reported, “that rampant corruption in Congress and the administration is directly costing average citizens who are paying more for necessities like groceries, gas, and medicin.”

Both Democrats and the press however are so far overlooking one of the most overt and consequential examples of Trump’s pay-to-play behavior. On May 24, 2024, Josh Dawsey and Maxine Joselow of The Washington Post published a blockbuster exposé, reporting that Trump privately told a group of oil company CEOs they should donate $1 billion to his 2024 presidential campaign: It would be a good “deal” for the industry, Trump reportedly said, because of the tax and regulation benefits they would receive if he returned to the Oval Office.

Specifically, Trump reportedly said he would reverse the Biden administration’s pause on new liquified natural gas export permits, approve more drilling for oil in the Gulf of Mexico and Alaska, and roll back environmental regulations that the industry didn’t like, including electric vehicle purchasing mandates and vehicle emissions limits. Hawley and Joselow then published a follow-up, reporting that Trump also promised to soften Federal Trade Commission scrutiny of industry mergers and acquisitions.

Two and a half years later, his administration has delivered on each of these promises and then some. The Brennan Center has published a well-documented summary of Trump’s assault on climate policy—including his administration’s repeal of the “endangerment finding” that has granted the federal government the authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions—that connects the dots between Trump’s actions and the many billions of dollars the oil industry has reaped as a result, including the millions of dollars that benefit oil executives individually.

What makes all this relevant to the midterm elections—beyond the fact that the leader of the Republican Party is directly implicated—is that many of Trump’s accomplishments were only possible because of rubber-stamp support from Republicans in Congress. Now, those same Republicans must face the voters. How will they explain themselves?

To be clear, Democrats don’t get a pass here; corruption has been part of politics forever, and one of the press’s central obligations is to expose and hold its perpetrators to account, whoever they may be. That requires following the facts where they lead. But it also requires challenging the practice, still common among old-school newsrooms, of false equivalence—or of portraying both sides as equally culpable for a given transgression for fear that an accurate portrayal would look like “taking sides.” If most of the facts point in one direction, our reporting should have the integrity and courage to say so.

Most voters don’t have access to directly question candidates seeking their votes. It’s our job as journalists to ask questions on their behalf so they can make informed decisions about their leaders.

Corruption is understandably a hot issue these days. Meanwhile, new scientific analysis from the nonprofit Climate Central shows that every congressional district in the country is hotter than it was in 1970, thanks to climate change. No surprise, then, that polling also shows that the vast majority of people want their government to take stronger climate action. Journalism that connects those dots—accurately and fairly, and without pulling any punches—is a true public service.

Mark Hertsgaard is the author of eight books that have been translated into a total of 16 languages, including Big Red’s Mercy: The Shooting of Deborah Cotton and a Story of Race in America and A Day In the Life: The Music and Artistry of the Beatles. He is executive director of the global journalism collaboration Covering Climate Now and the environment correspondent for The Nation.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: Is Blockbuster Video the Answer to Our Digital Privacy Woes?
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
The Supreme Court is weighing whether a 1988 video-store law can be used to protect our digital privacy.

The Supreme Court heard oral arguments on Wednesday in Salazar v. Paramount Global, a case about digital privacy. Well, it should be a case about digital privacy, but it is actually about whether a law passed in 1988 to regulate (not making this up) Blockbuster Video can be used to protect us from prying, data-hungry tech giants. Which… is asinine. It is absurd that a law meant to protect people who rented Emmanuelle IV represents our best chance to get stronger data privacy regulations in the year 2026. And yet, here we are.

This issue starts at the beginning of the modern Supreme Court, which most people date to the confirmation hearing of Robert H. Bork. Bork was a very bad, very racist man who was nonetheless nominated by Republicans to the Supreme Court. Stopping his confirmation became an all-hands-on-deck proposition for many Democrats and people of conscience. That effort included doing anything possible to smear the man (which was unnecessary, in my opinion, because his public record was damning enough), and that somehow led to the clerk at Bork’s local Blockbuster video testifying about Bork’s viewing habits. (For our younger readers: Blockbuster was a store where people would go to rent video tapes of movies, and stores were physical places where goods or services could be exchanged for money, and goods and services were things people could afford to buy before Trump started a trade war as well as a war-war for no reason.)

Bork’s video rental history was pedestrian and unexciting, but the fact that his viewing history became public knowledge freaked out a lot of politicians. (I can’t imagine why. I’m sure Denny Hastert’s private video rentals were totally normal and cool.) In response, Congress passed a whole-ass law to prevent their (I mean “our”) video rental histories from being outed: The Video Privacy Protection Act (VPPA). The law prohibits “video tape service providers” from disclosing personal information about any customer.

As I mentioned, all of this happened in 1988. We have to use a DeLorean to fast-forward through multiple technological revolutions to get all the way to 2022 and a man named Michael Salazar, who is the named plaintiff in this case. Salazar was a subscriber to the newsletter for a sports website called 247Sports. The site is owned by Paramount. Salazar viewed free videos that were embedded or linked to parts of the newsletter. The information about which videos Salazar viewed was shared by Paramount with Facebook, without Salazar’s consent. Salazar filed a class-action lawsuit arguing that Paramount’s disclosure of his personal data violated the VPPA and he was entitled to damages. Salazar’s case was dismissed by lower courts based on various theories, including that 247Sports is not a “video tape service provider,” and Salazar appealed to the Supreme Court.

The problem here is obvious: There is no law exactly like the VPPA that applies to “the Internet.” Nor is Blockbuster Video particularly like “the Internet.” Nevertheless, people have or should have a reasonable expectation of privacy in their video viewing history. The VPPA seems to stand for the principle that your personal viewing history should remain private.

Is it a stretch to apply the VPPA to modern Internet habits? Sure. Of course it is. But the foundational regulations of the internet itself are merely stretched from regulations we applied to books or newspapers. Everybody reading this article is protected from Kash Patel’s thought police under the same framework that applies to reading a newspaper article. It makes sense that everybody who clicks on a video linked to this article is protected under the same framework that protected people who went to the video store right after school on Fridays to pick a movie before all the good ones were out of stock.

Much of the discussion during Supreme Court arguments centered on the definition of “video tape service provider.” What makes a store, or a website, or a newsletter, a video tape service provider? Justice Clarence Thomas suggested that stores have to provide a physical product—like an actual VHS cassette or DVD—to be covered by the VPPA. In a world of streaming services, such a narrow definition would render the VPPA functionally obsolete. Other justices rejected that ribbon-thin reading, instead focusing on whether the business of the store has to be dedicated primarily to providing videos—a standard that would encompass, say, Netflix, but little else.

Republican super-lawyer Paul Clement, arguing on behalf of Paramount (because of course he was), kept pushing the most wild hypothetical scenario. He kept bringing up Chick-fil-A, arguing that a person who watches a video provided by Chick-fil-A should not be protected by the VPPA, because Chick-fil-A is clearly not a “video tape service provider.” Literally nobody disagreed with him, not even the lawyer for Salazar, Joshua Hammack, but Clement kept harping on about Chick-fil-A—so much that I began to suspect the homophobic chicken shop paid him for product placement at a Supreme Court hearing.

The problem with most of the hypotheticals raised during the arguments (not just Clement’s) is that they served to distract from the core reason for this law, rather than illuminate it. Nobody really cares if Facebook knows I’m watching college sports recruiting videos (which is what 247Sports actually serves) or if a congressional confirmation committee knows that I watch deep-dive retrospectives on Star Trek: The Next Generation. What we all care about is porn. People do not want their porn video habits available for public disclosure (or their lack of porn habits, which I’d find even more disturbing, but maybe that’s just me). People are worried about their streaming porn getting out there in public, just like they were in 1988 when the VPPA was passed. We’d all be better off if we just admitted what we are actually talking about and worked to keep private what we all instinctively want to keep private.

Amazingly, Justice Elena Kagan went there. Her hypothetical was not about chicken sandwiches or video cassettes. Instead, Kagan imagined a judge who watched “sketchy videos” with “lots of women wrestling” and feared “embarrassment.” She said that was the “paradigmatic” VPPA case.

Kagan’s solution to the real problem was really simple. She said Paramount has two choices to avoid liability under the VPPA: gaining people’s consent or stop selling people’s data, “take your pick.”

This has to be the right answer. Not selling data should be the default, unless you obtain consent to do so (and we can go to the mattresses later about what constitutes “informed consent”). And that standard should apply to anybody who serves you a video, whether it’s part of their core business or not. Consent or GTFO. Why is this such a difficult concept for some people to understand?

Even alleged attempted rapist Brett Kavanaugh said that obtaining consent would be “a very easy solution,” though Kavanaugh [wait for it] seemed to be perplexed about how internet companies would actually go about obtaining consent. Kagan shot back that we give our consent to “hundreds” of these companies every day, and referenced the “accept all cookies” prompts that are ubiquitous.

Clement would not accept consent as a solution. He said that requiring companies to obtain consent would force everything behind a paywall. This argument is facially untrue, but even if it were true, it should have no bearing on how we protect our privacy.

Kavanaugh said something else—and this comment boded well for Salazar: “We are a textualist court, but not a literalist court.” Now, in real time, I disregarded this statement because it’s a dirty lie: This court is happy to get hyper-literal when it comes to deporting immigrants, sentencing people to death, or getting rid of affirmative action. But when this statement is taken with the rest of the arguments, it might mean that Kavanaugh is at least open to reading the VPPA as applying to more than a literal Blockbuster Video and nothing else. Add to that the fact that Chief Justice John Roberts and Neil Gorsuch were particularly quiet during the arguments, and I can just about talk myself into a win for Salazar and a ruling that forces Paramount to offer a bare minimum pop-up consent form to subscribers before selling your data to Facebook. One must always assume that this Supreme Court is going to side with the biggest business in the room (which is Paramount, in this case), but I’m saying there’s a chance in this case. People, especially Republicans, do weird things once porn gets involved.

Still, the most simple, effective, and best solution would be for Congress to write a new law that protects people’s digital privacy in this century. Trying to graft digital privacy rights onto a Blockbuster Video law is fundamentally stupid.

We shouldn’t have to wait for one of these guys (and it’s going to be a guy) to be headed to a confirmation hearing to realize that it’s probably a bad thing for OnlyFans to sell their viewing history to the National Enquirer. Updating laws so that they actually make sense, textually and literally, should be the job of Congress, not the Supreme Court.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: The Saudi Phase of the Iran War Signals More Chaos to Come
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
The conflict that Donald Trump has repeatedly proclaimed an unequivocal American victory keeps spiraling out of control.

Flames rise above a state-owned Aramco oil facility attacked under unclear circumstances outside Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, earlier this month.

The Houthis, an Iranian ally vying for control of war-torn Yemen, hit the headquarters of the Saudi state oil company Aramco in Dharan on Tuesday night. That attack came just days after they fired ballistic missiles into the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, killing 12 and further puncturing the regime’s carefully cultivated image of competence amid a sea of instability. These market-rattling attacks unfolded just weeks after an Iraq-based militia struck and damaged a critical east-west Saudi oil pipeline.

This sudden demonstration of Saudi Arabia’s vulnerability is the latest bout of regional fallout from President Donald Trump’s impulsive and failed war against Iran. The conflict hasn’t accomplished any of Trump’s war aims—to the extent that he’s able to articulate them—but it is clearly destabilizing the entire Persian Gulf region, with consequences that will extend far beyond the time horizon of the upcoming midterm elections or even this disastrous presidency. And if Trump can’t bring himself to somehow come to terms with an emboldened Tehran, it’s far from clear that the chaos now enveloping the Gulf can be stopped at its frontiers.

Riyadh is under siege from all directions in what amounts to a dizzying reversal of fortune. Just a year ago, Saudi Arabia was riding high, having greased enough palms inside the Trump family syndicate to ensure that the kingdom wouldn’t be the target of confiscatory tariffs or some other sudden spasm of incoherent, late-night rage from the president himself.

Meanwhile, the kingdom’s longtime rivals in Tehran were on their heels, having allowed the joint Israeli-American 12-Day War in the summer of 2025 to degrade Iran’s nuclear program and military readiness without any meaningful retaliation. Riyadh also had significant leverage to deploy, given that Trump was desperate for the Saudis to abandon the Palestinian cause, join the Abraham Accords, and come to a diplomatic accord with Israel.

Today, the Saudis’ decades-long security and development strategy is in deep crisis, thanks to an American war that Riyadh very much egged on. There’s never been any reason to support America’s alliance with the corrupt, despotic Saudi regime. But the sudden unraveling of the Saudi economy would have knock-on effects that would be unpleasant for everyone. And it’s now clear that the shortage of critical munitions plaguing the US military extends to regional allies who seem to be close to defenseless against missile and drone strikes.

The fact that the Houthis, who control barely a third of one of the poorest countries on Earth, can almost effortlessly bring a wealthy, advanced society like Saudi Arabia to its knees with the flick of a switch is genuinely unnerving. It suggests, among other things, that no structure in the Gulf region that doesn’t have its own battery of Patriot missiles is safe from attacks from Iran and its allies. This is but the most recent indication that Trump’s repeated claims to have obliterated Iran’s military-industrial base are utterly unfounded.

Iran is not a puppeteer of the Houthis, but Houthi forces are more than willing to play the part of chaos agent in Tehran’s quest to cleave the Gulf Arab monarchies from their security alliance with the United States. That maneuver is calculated to tighten the economic vise on Trump, which would further the Houthis’ ambitions to secure the permanent eviction of Saudi forces from Yemeni territory as part of the settlement.

The Iranians are, in effect, trying to supplant America’s dominant position in the regional balance of power by making the US military response look shambolic and inadequate. So far, they’re succeeding. Iran is acting as an entity that, in Charles Tilly’s famous description of European state transformation, “produces both the danger and, at a price, the shield against it”—-in other words, a protection racket.

This leaves the Saudis and other Gulf monarchies in a bind. Rather than banking on a distant, unreliable ally in Washington that’s tailing off into imperial madness, they are being asked to accept Iranian hegemony in the Gulf at gunpoint in exchange for peace. If they ever want their reputations as slick oases of oligarchic capitalism back, they may have to do exactly that.

A turn toward the Iranians would of course mean relinquishing decades of close collaboration with the still-powerful United States—and it might be too fraught and costly for the kingdom to consider seriously. But at minimum, Iran has punctured the myth of American supremacy in the region and made it very uncomfortable for the Gulf monarchies to simply return to their prior security strategies if and when the war ends.

Today, risks abound where none appeared to exist eight months ago. Repeated attacks on soft Saudi targets raise the prospect of virtually unlimited mayhem—including bombing attacks on data centers, pipelines, airports, and the target-rich environments where the Gulf’s premier cities have erected their gleaming vertical palaces. This isn’t the first time that Tehran or its allies have targeted Saudi infrastructure, but it is their first effort to use air strikes as part of a concerted strategy to drive the United States out of the region.

And the airport attack is just the latest in a series of setbacks and humiliations for the vaunted American military. It followed up last week’s fiasco in which the United States had to evacuate a dozen B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford airbase in the United Kingdom in light of a terrorist threat. Exactly what spooked the Pentagon enough to prompt this rushed and embarrassing withdrawal has yet to be revealed.

America’s network of military bases in the Gulf is also in ruins. The high-cost, around-the-clock effort to steward oil out of the Strait of Hormuz is working for now, but it is neither sustainable nor capable of achieving a return to the prewar status quo in the Strait. At best, it’s an attempt at economic triage disconnected from any plausible theory of victory.

Clearly, Trump and the war planners in Pete Hegseth’s Pentagon never seriously reckoned with the possibility that Iran would emerge from a months-long aerial pummeling with not only its regime intact but also the capability to strike targets far and wide around the region. In any functional administration capable of experiencing and acting on shame, Hegseth would have resigned months ago. Instead, he has accepted zero responsibility for the deepening quagmire and still spends most of his time on political photo-ops and his deranged crusade to drive any career military officials capable of independent thought out of their jobs.

Even today, the administration is committed to what looks like an unworkable strategy of waiting for the Iranian government to collapse under the weight of the US naval blockade and economic sanctions. That’s merely a variation on a strategy that has failed for 25 years to bring about the regime change that America wants in Iran. Instead, as Narjes Bajoghli and Vali Nasr wrote recently in Foreign Affairs, it is Iran suddenly dreaming of “evicting U.S. forces from the Persian Gulf, forcing Washington to remove all its sanctions, and getting the United States to accept that Iran is a great power.”

George W. Bush’s ill-advised invasion of Iraq in 2003 ultimately led to a host of negative, unforeseen consequences, including the rise of ISIS and the destabilization of multiple countries in the Middle East. Now Trump’s own unforced Middle East blunder has set into motion a chain of events that the United States seems both unable to control and uninterested in comprehending. The Houthis certainly won’t be the last player to use the security vacuum created by America’s bumbling war to achieve its own goals.

It’s astonishing that after a quarter century dominated by ruinously expensive and tragic overreach in the Middle East, the United States has had to once again learn that it cannot remake distant societies with the blunt instrument of military force. And now the lesson looks to be more costly than ever.

David Faris is a professor of political science at Roosevelt University and the author of It’s Time to Fight Dirty: How Democrats Can Build a Lasting Majority in American Politics. His writing has appeared in Slate, The Week, The Washington Post, The New Republic, and Washington Monthly. You can find him on Bluesky at @davidfaris.bluesky.social.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Michael Bloomberg spends $80m on Democrats as Trump moves $400m to Republican candidates
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Billionaire ex-mayor of New York City is focusing funds on House races to help Democrats retake majority in midterms

The billionaire Michael Bloomberg will spend $80m to help Democratic candidates in the midterm elections, US media reported on Tuesday, a significant infusion of cash for a party that has recently struggled with fundraising as it seeks to win control of Congress.

The reported donations came as Donald Trump announced on Tuesday he intended to spend a total of $400m to aid Republican candidates, with $300m already disbursed.

The New York Times reports that Bloomberg made the contributions in September and October, and is particularly focused on Democrats running to flip the US House of Representatives, which Republicans currently control by a historically small margin. The goal, Bloomberg’s political adviser Howard Wolfson told the Times, is to ensure that a Democratic majority is greater than just the 218 seats needed to win control of the chamber.

“The difference between 221 and 230, in terms of the House majority, really matters,” Wolfson said.

One of the world’s richest men, Bloomberg, 84, served three terms as mayor of New York City, from 2002 to 2013. He was an independent then, but later registered as a Democrat, spending $80m to help the party in the 2018 midterms, during Trump’s first term, then made a well-funded but unsuccessful bid for the party’s presidential nomination in 2020.

Among his donations this year are $24m to Everytown for Gun Safety, a group he cofounded that is spending on Democratic candidates in the lower chamber, and $16m to the House Majority Pac, which is connected to the House minority leader, Hakeem Jeffries.

Democrats believe they are favored to take back the House this year, though they’ve acknowledged trailing Republicans in fundraising. Besides Trump’s money, Republicans are being aided by the president’s ally Elon Musk, who has spent $366m on conservative groups and campaigns so far.

Democrats also believe they have a shot at netting the four seats necessary to retake control of the Senate, though analysts believe it could go either way.

Control of either chamber would allow Democrats to block Trump’s legislative agenda and more effectively investigate his administration. If they win a majority in the Senate, the party’s lawmakers could also reject his nominees for the supreme court and other federal judicial positions.

Bloomberg has donated $2.5m to a Super Pac backing James Talarico, the Democratic candidate in Texas’s US Senate race, as well as a Super Pac backing the re-election campaign of the New York governor, Kathy Hochul, and the campaigns of several Democratic gubernatorial candidates, the Times reported.

Asked how effective Bloomberg believed the money would be, Wolfson said: “He is of the view that resources matter in campaigns.” He added that the billionaire “expects a result”.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Robinson sparks 23-0 run as Pistons stun Celtics in NBA season opener
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Duncan Robinson scored 15 of his 21 points in the fourth quarter as the Detroit Pistons reeled off 23 unanswered points to beat the visiting Boston Celtics 121-113 in the NBA’s regular-season opener on Tuesday afternoon.

Jalen Duren and Cade Cunningham scored 22 points apiece for the Pistons, who led the Eastern Conference with 60 wins last season.

Javonte Green came off the bench to score 19 points in 18 minutes, while Ausar Thompson added 11 points, 11 rebounds and five assists.

Paul George scored a game-high 38 points on his Celtics debut. Payton Pritchard and Derrick White scored 17 points apiece, but Jayson Tatum was held to 13 points on six-for-23 shooting, although he contributed 11 assists.

The Celtics led by 13 at halftime thanks to a second-quarter surge. Detroit held a 39-35 advantage early in the quarter before Boston reeled off 15 unanswered points.

George scored the Celtics’ final eight points of the half as Boston took a 58-45 lead into the break.

George showed no signs of cooling off in the third quarter, hitting three three-pointers in a 52-second span to give Boston their biggest lead at 72-50.

Green entered the game shortly afterward to slow George down. He not only did that but also gave Detroit an offensive spark, scoring 11 points in the quarter, including three three-pointers, as the Pistons pulled within three in the closing seconds.

George opened the fourth quarter with a layup to give Boston a 90-82 lead. The Celtics soon stretched their advantage to 12 points, but Detroit began another comeback, sparked by a three-point play from Thompson.

Robinson scored 11 straight points to pull the Pistons within one at 99-98. He then set up a three-pointer for Green before Duren converted a three-point play. Robinson hit another three-pointer with 5min 13sec remaining to put Detroit ahead 107-99.

Green capped the 23-0 run with another three-pointer, extending the Pistons’ lead to 112-99 with 3min 33sec left.

Boston rallied to within four points, but Green made two free throws with 6.7 seconds remaining to seal Detroit’s opening-day victory.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: These Working-Class Populists Are Struggling to Win Over the Working Class
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
So far, the 2026 midterm elections are shaping up to be a Democratic wave. That’s obviously great for the party. But an election in which anyone with a “D” next to their name stands a good chance of winning doesn’t tell us all that much about which kinds of campaigns are best at reaching the working-class voters Democrats need to secure durable national majorities, rather than more fleeting ones that, like a wave, can recede as quickly as they appear.

Over the past decade, the party has steadily lost ground with working-class voters, and a growing number of commentators have argued that the way to win them back is to run working-class candidates on an economic populist message. We at the Center for Working-Class Politics, in partnership with The Nation and Nira Data, have been trying to test this question on the 2026 campaign trail. That’s why, last month, we launched the Economic Populist Tracker, in which we follow four working-class populist candidates running this year in places Donald Trump won in 2024—Dan Osborn, an independent running for Senate in Nebraska, and three House candidates, Brian Poindexter in Ohio’s Seventh Congressional District, Bob Brooks in Pennsylvania’s seventh, and Rebecca Cooke in Wisconsin’s third.

While three of the four candidates we’re tracking hold slim leads over their Republican opponents, in a wave year victories alone may not tell us much about whether the candidates’ working-class, economic populist appeals made any difference. Instead, we have to look at whether these candidates do better than a generic Democrat would in their districts.

Two months into our tracking, the answer is mixed. Cooke and Osborn (who, though he is technically rejecting the Democratic Party label, is running with the Nebraska Democratic Party’s support) are running a few points ahead of the Democratic Party, Poindexter is even, and Brooks is slightly behind. The two who are running ahead of the party label are doing it mainly thanks to their support among independents and Democrats—plus, in Osborn’s case, a small number of Republicans. Ironically, though, their edge over the party does not come from working-class voters: None of the four is yet doing measurably better than the party among voters without a college degree in households earning less than $100,000.

In our September survey, Osborn trailed GOP incumbent Pete Ricketts among likely voters by eight and a half points, compared with 10 points in August. Poindexter led Max Miller by five points (down from six in August), Brooks led Ryan Mackenzie by two points (up from one in August), and Cooke held a slight edge over Derrick Van Orden by two points (down from six in August). None of these figures changed by more than the margin of error.

But steady overall numbers can mask changes that may matter in the home stretch. Here is a brief look at how each race has developed.

Ohio’s seventh district. Poindexter still leads, but Republican voters are rallying to Miller, who was initially damaged by abuse accusations from his ex-wife (accusations he denies). Miller responded to his own scandal by dredging up a 1998 incident in which Poindexter, then 18, was arrested but never charged, and he seems to have won back some of his base. In September, more of the district’s Trump voters called Poindexter “too extreme” compared with other Democrats (27 percent, up from 13), and Miller’s support among Trump voters rose from 44 to 54 percent, mostly as undecided Trump voters came off the fence. Poindexter’s own support among Trump voters held steady at about 10 percent, and his overall lead remains essentially unchanged. But 44 percent of the seventh’s undecided likely voters are Republicans, while 23 percent are Democrats and 13 percent are independents. As the district’s Republican-leaning undecideds make up their minds, Poindexter’s lead could narrow to well within the margin of error.

Nebraska. Ricketts spent September portraying Osborn as a Democrat in disguise, calling him “Democrat Dan” about 40 times at their September 1 debate. The attacks, along with leaked recordings in which Osborn appeared to contradict his stated position on immigration and mocked a small-town Trump supporter, appear to have hurt Osborn’s standing with Republicans.

In a state Trump won by 20 points, Osborn cannot win without a sizable share of Republican votes. He won about one in eight Trump voters in his 2024 loss and likely needs closer to one in five; right now he has about 7 percent.

Among Nebraska’s Trump voters, the share calling Osborn “too extreme” in our September tracking rose from 27 to 42 percent, and among those with an opinion of him, the share with a favorable view fell from 21 to 13 percent. Undecided voters won’t close that gap on their own. Nebraska’s undecided likely voters are 44 percent Republican, 24 percent Democratic, and 14 percent independents. Even if undecided Democrats and independents break his way, Osborn would still trail unless he won over most of the undecided Republicans. His other option is Nebraskans who aren’t sure they will vote, a group about a fifth the size of the likely electorate. They are far less Republican than likely voters (29 percent, compared with 55 percent), so bringing them to the polls could help him.

Pennsylvania’s seventh district. Brooks is picking up steam among Democrats, and undecided voters lean in his favor. In September, his campaign put his working-class biography at the center of its messaging, including an ad featuring Brooks decked out in firefighter gear promising to “smoke out the billionaires and their lobbyists,” as well as the creation of a Latino outreach coalition, “Bombero Bob.” Brooks’s support among likely-voting Democrats rose from 63 to 72 percent as more Democrats became familiar with him, though small losses elsewhere kept his overall lead about the same. More working-class voters are also learning about Brooks’s working-class background: among voters with an opinion of the candidate, the share who say he did working-class work before politics rose from 46 to 60 percent—mostly among voters without a college degree, although that hasn’t yet produced an increase in support among non-college-educated voters in the district. Crucially, however, Pennsylvania’s seventh is the only one of the four races where undecided Democrats outnumber undecided Republicans, 36 to 27 percent, and another 18 percent of undecideds are independents. If each of these groups breaks the way voters in the same group have who’ve already made up their mind, Brooks’s lead would grow to about five points.

Wisconsin’s third district. This is the one race we’re tracking where the challenger appears to be losing ground with the Democratic base. It also shows that a working-class image can help Republicans as well as Democrats. Van Orden spent the month of September attacking Cooke’s working-class credentials, calling her a “phony” who “occasionally waits a table.” In August, Wisconsin voters were about equally likely to say that Cooke and Van Orden had done working-class work before politics; by September, 37 percent said so of Van Orden, a retired Navy SEAL, and 30 percent of Cooke. Over the same month, Cooke’s overall lead narrowed from six points to two. Wisconsin has the fewest undecided voters of the four races, and they are 31 percent Republican, 24 percent Democratic, and 16 percent independents who lean toward neither party. If they break the way decided voters in their party have, Cooke would still eke out a narrow lead.

Even if all four candidates win, however, it won’t be clear that their particular blend of working-class economic populism was the driving force. In a wave year, any other Democrat might have done just as well. To assess this, we compare each candidate’s support with which party the same voters say they will support in the 2028 presidential election. Brooks, for instance, trails the Democratic Party by about three points on this measure but still leads Mackenzie. What the comparison tells us is how much support each candidate is getting beyond the partisan lean of their districts.

Here the results are surprising. These candidates were recruited on the theory that working-class backgrounds and economic populist messages would help them pick up more working-class voters. Two of the four are indeed running ahead of a generic Democrat, but that additional support is coming from independents, Democrats and, in Osborn’s case, affluent college graduates, not from working-class voters.

Here again, little has changed between the two months. Cooke was about four points ahead of the party in both August and September, and Osborn about three points ahead in August and two in September. Poindexter matched the party in both months, and Brooks sat about three points behind. Because this picture has stayed roughly stable since August, below we combine our data for August and September to look more closely at which groups of voters are driving these differences.

Independents, who make up about one in 10 voters in each district, are the clearest source of the populists’ edge. Among them, Osborn outpaces the Democratic Party by about 21 points, Cooke by about 20 and Poindexter by about nine, while Brooks does no better. Put simply, if Cooke and Osborn did only as well as the party among these independents, much of their advantage would disappear: Cooke’s four-point edge over the party would shrink to about two points, and Osborn’s three-point edge to nearly zero.

The candidates differ most in their support among Democrats. Cooke does about eight points better than the party among 2024 Harris voters. Brooks lags the party by about nine points among Democrats. Because Democrats make up only about a third of his district’s voters, that shortfall works out to about three points overall, and since he is about even with the party among everyone else, it accounts for virtually his entire deficit relative to the party brand. Poindexter falls slightly short of the Democratic Party among Democrats, which offsets his gains among independents and leaves him even with the party overall.

Osborn is about six points behind the party among Democrats, but he makes that up elsewhere: He is the only one of the four who outperforms the Democratic brand among Trump voters, by about three points, and among people who voted for a third-party candidate in 2024, by about 13. The other three do about as well among Republicans as the Democratic Party.

Our findings on working-class voters are the most sobering for the economic populist theory of victory. Combining both months gives us enough respondents to split each district’s voters by education and household income as well as gender. None of the four candidates is measurably ahead of the party among voters without a college degree in households earning less than $100,000. Among this group, Cooke is about three points ahead, Osborn is even, and Poindexter and Brooks trail by about three to four points, all within the margin of error.

The candidates’ performance among working-class voters splits sharply by gender. Cooke does better with working-class women than with working-class men: Among women without a college degree in households earning less than $100,000, she is nearly eight points ahead of the party, while among men in the same group she is even. Brooks and Osborn show the reverse pattern: Brooks trails the party by about six points among women without a degree in lower-income households, and by about 10 points among lower-income women with a degree, while among working-class men he is about even with it. Osborn sits about four points below the party among women without a degree in lower-income households. His advantage comes instead from affluent voters: He outperforms the party by about 10 points among college graduates in households earning $100,000 or more, and by about 14 points among the men in that group. Poindexter’s differences among all these groups are small, generally within about three points of the party label.

Putting these pieces together, the populists who are running ahead of the Democratic Party are doing it mainly by winning independents who don’t lean toward either party, and by how effectively they inspire Democratic voters. But they are not outperforming the party with working-class voters: Among voters without a college degree in lower-income households, all four are doing about as well as a generic Democrat would, with the exception of Cooke’s strength among working-class women. Republicans make a difference only in Osborn’s race, where he is running a few points better than the party among Trump voters.

The populists outperforming their party are doing it mostly with independents who lean toward neither party. But winning in November depends on who is still undecided, and in every race most undecided voters are Democrats or Republicans, as independents who lean toward neither party make up only 13 to 18 percent of undecided voters. That makes undecided Democrats the most important target for the three House candidates. Brooks, whose undecided voters include more Democrats than Republicans, can grow his lead simply by becoming better known among the Democratic base. Poindexter and Cooke will need to hold on to undecided Democrats as well as independents to stay ahead as undecided Republicans settle on Miller and Van Orden.

Osborn is the only one of the four who cannot win without substantially more Republican support. For the three House candidates, the weeks until November 3 are likely to turn on Democrats who still aren’t familiar Brooks and Poindexter, working-class men in Cooke’s district as Van Orden claims the working-class mantle, and non-college-educated voters in Brooks’s district who now know he was a firefighter but haven’t yet moved into his column.

Each of the four economic populists we’re tracking has a real shot at victory in November. But even if they win, the bigger test for the theory of the case of progressive economic populism is whether they can deliver working-class votes above and beyond what any Democrat could in a highly favorable electoral context. That remains to be seen.

Methodology: The CWCP/Nira Data tracker interviewed 8,100 respondents from July 31 to August 25 and a separate sample of 9,510 from August 25 to September 24. Respondents were recruited through targeted online ads and assigned to districts by their self-reported zip code and county. Each sample is weighted to district demographics and 2024 presidential vote. Horse-race figures come from the September survey. Where we combine the two months to study smaller groups or small differences, we re-weight the combined sample. “Likely voters” say they will definitely or probably vote. In describing undecided voters, we count independents who lean toward a party as members of that party. In the September survey, the margin of error for each candidate’s share among likely voters ranges from about two and a half points in Wisconsin to four points in Ohio. We describe changes between August and September as changes only when they are larger than the margin of error, unless we say otherwise.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: How Congress Is  Cashing In on the AI Boom
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Roughly one in five members of Congress has household investments in the industry.

Congress has so far failed to regulate artificial intelligence, despite the increasingly dire warnings about the threats it poses. At the same time, lawmakers are profiting from the AI boom. Roughly one in five members of Congress has household investments in companies developing AI models or supplying the infrastructure behind it, according to our analysis of recent congressional financial disclosures.

At least 106 members of Congress, their spouses, or their dependent children hold stocks or other investments in AI developers, chipmakers, cloud-software providers, data-center companies, or specialized AI firms, the disclosures show. Members of Congress only disclose the value of their financial assets in broad ranges, but we calculated that as of September 17, the members’ AI investments are worth between $82.8 million and $325 million.

The holdings are concentrated in tech giants like Nvidia, Meta, and Alphabet. Six companies account for more than half of the value of AI assets held by lawmakers. But some lawmakers also hold and trade shares in smaller companies such as BigBear.ai and C3 AI, as well as in little-known private start-ups. At least 44 of the lawmakers who own shares in AI stocks serve on committees responsible for legislation on issues like AI safety, consumer protections, semiconductor policy, and trade with China. (There is no law limiting the ability of members to own stocks, even in the companies they oversee.)

One powerful legislator with money in AI development is House Republican Conference chair Lisa McClain of Michigan. Since December 2025, McClain’s spouse has purchased up to $515,000 worth of stock in four AI companies, including three private firms whose shares are not available on public exchanges. The buys included up to $250,000 of private stock in Elon Musk’s xAI in December 2025, just days before the Pentagon announced a major integration with the company.

Several other lawmakers’ households also hold stakes in private AI companies. Representative Anna Paulina Luna, a Florida Republican, disclosed that her spouse owns a 10 percent interest in Nokturnal AI, though the filing valued the stake at $1,000 or less. Nokturnal AI, a subsidiary of the defense firm OKSI, was tapped by the Pentagon in February for its “Drone Dominance” program. House Republican Policy Committee chair Kevin Hern of Oklahoma has family-related holdings of up to $3.8 million worth of stock in Amazon, Alphabet, semiconductor-equipment companies, and an AI-focused fund. Freshman Republican Representative Rob Bresnahan of Pennsylvania has up to $4.5 million of AI assets in his portfolio.

This is by no means a GOP-only trend. New Jersey Democratic Representative Josh Gottheimer’s household reports holdings valued between $8.5 million and $38 million across the AI supply chain, including developers like Microsoft, chip designers like Nvidia, chipmakers like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the equipment company Applied Materials, and the data-center infrastructure provider Vertiv. Gottheimer has been named cochair of the House Democratic Commission on Artificial Intelligence and the Innovation Economy, a panel that is developing the party’s AI policy and legislative agenda.

Another Democratic AI-stock buyer this year is California Representative Gil Cisneros, who made dozens of purchases worth up to $1.2 million in stocks, including Nvidia, Amazon, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), and TSMC. A member of the House Armed Services Committee, Cisneros also traded shares in the AI-powered defense contractors Palantir, Oracle, and Snowflake. And Representative April McClain Delaney, a Maryland Democrat who oversees AI as part of the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee, reported an interest valued at as much as $500,000 in the drug-development company Zephyr AI through a family trust.

The largest AI portfolio identified by Sludge, based on its maximum estimated value, belongs to the household of former House speaker Nancy Pelosi. Her husband, Paul, reported holdings in Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Nvidia, Broadcom, and the drug- discovery company Tempus AI worth between $28.4 million and $134.9 million. Throughout 2026, Paul Pelosi also purchased around $1.3 million to $2.6 million worth of Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia, and Tempus shares. And he has up to $12 million worth of shares in Bloom Energy, an AI energy- infrastructure firm supporting the growth of data centers.

The path for federal AI regulation runs through key congressional committees in which around one in five members owns shares in AI companies. The House Energy and Commerce Committee considers issues of data privacy and who pays for power-transmission lines to data centers, while the House Judiciary Committee oversees issues including copyright and antitrust matters. Each includes some 10 members who are currently invested in the AI industry, with stakes worth up to $9 million and $5 million, respectively. Congress’s next moves on AI could happen with lawmakers looking at their personal portfolios rather than the public interest.

David Moore is a cofounder of Sludge, an independent newsroom focused on money in politics. He is based in Brooklyn.

At first, I felt resistant to the idea of reading an Emily Brontë biography. After all, Brontë did not make herself the most approachable author—or person, for that matter. If you take Elizabeth Gaskell’s word for it, she was “never happy nor well but on the sweeping moors that gathered round her home—that hater of strangers, doomed to live amongst them.” Nobody knows what endowed her with such fierceness and strangeness or made her do what she did or write what she wrote. As someone who has read nearly everything she wrote that survives, I must confess that I didn’t really want to know. Brontë herself, after all, seems to have wanted her readers to know nothing about her, not even her real name.

In her new biography of the unknowable Emily, This Dark Night, Deborah Lutz doesn’t commit the prime biographical sin of trying to make Brontë too easy to understand or relate to. Instead, she asks more questions than she answers.

For this reason, while some readers may be frustrated by the paucity of new facts or explanations for why Emily was the way she was, for others (including this reader) this vagueness is the very reason for the book’s success. Weighing in at a mere 264 pages (before notes), This Dark Night is not the door-stopper that habitual readers of biography might be used to. The fact of the matter is that Brontë didn’t live very long (she died of tuberculosis at age 30), and very few traces of her short life remain. Much of what we “learn” here is speculation, gleaned from the poetry, prose, and fragments of writing—sometimes literal scraps as well as ﻿minuscule productions that Lutz calls “paper crafts”—that she left behind.

From these pieces, as well as those by her siblings Anne, Charlotte, and the good-for-nothing Branwell, Lutz imagines what Emily’s days would have been like. Born in 1818 to an Irish clergyman father and a mother who came from a wealthy Cornish merchant family, Emily had to grow up fast. While she was still a young child, she lost her mother and two older sisters, and over the next two decades her beloved remaining siblings moved away: Charlotte continued her schooling and became a disgruntled teacher, Branwell tried and failed at a variety of professions, and Anne found some success as a governess.

As a result, Emily became the de facto head of the Brontë household at the Haworth parsonage in Yorkshire. While her father, Patrick, was busy with his spiritual and intellectual pursuits as the parson of Haworth, Emily took on some of the domestic tasks of cooking and cleaning. Even after her siblings returned from their positions elsewhere, Emily remained the main caretaker of the family’s home.

Hedging language (such as would and may) predominates here, as Lutz tells us what life in the parsonage was like and describes Emily’s day-to-day tasks, which included “turning” clothes (reversing and restitching them so the less-worn sides faced outward), peeling potatoes, and feeding the dogs, as well as her role in the famous imaginative worlds of the Brontë siblings.

Lutz also has to rely on this hedging language when exploring Emily’s intellectual formation in these years. She makes the assumption that the Brontës’ mother, Maria, had “bluestocking ways” and likely read Mary Wollstonecraft based on her membership in various lending libraries, including the Penzance Ladies Book Club, which seems a little too easy, but otherwise sticks to what we can reasonably know or assume. She tells us about Emily’s attendance at church; her time spent in Keighley, where she borrowed books; and her famous wanderings on the moors with her siblings and her mastiff mix, Keeper.

To that end, Lutz wisely keeps out of the debate surrounding what Emily may or may not have done to get sent away to school at age 17. Emily and the other Brontës, Lutz reminds us, had a social existence in Haworth and in Yorkshire more generally. They weren’t, as is often depicted, merely hermits living alone on the heath.

The mythology of Emily as a free-range “moor nymph” was partly started by Charlotte in her editor’s preface to the posthumous second edition of Wuthering Heights. In her grief, and perhaps also because of an inability to communicate what Emily was really like, Charlotte depicted her genius sister as a kind of feral savant—a “native and nursling of the moors,” as she put it—who was somehow otherworldly.

Lutz seeks to remind us that this was not the case by returning Emily to the domestic sphere as well as the “wild workshop” of West Yorkshire that she loved so much. Her Emily is not some weird sprite haunting the landscape, but something even stranger: a real woman.

Emily was also a writer. With Charlotte and Anne, she wrote a series of poems that were published under their male pseudonyms: Ellis, Currer, and Acton Bell. Although there had been plans for Emily and Anne to publish their novels first (Wuthering Heights and Agnes Grey, respectively, which were published together in 1847), they did not appear until Charlotte’s hugely successful Jane Eyre came out separately, also in 1847.

Unlike Jane Eyre and Agnes Grey, Wuthering Heights does not tell the story of a poor governess making her way in the world. Instead it draws on the twisted tales of violence and drama that Emily had heard in her Yorkshire youth, as well as the stories of the bog bodies and other mysteries that pervaded the local landscape. There is nothing nice or educative about the novel; all of its characters, from the pain-wracked lovers, Cathy and Heathcliff, to the miserable servants who inhabit the Heights alongside them, are at best tortured, and at worst torturers themselves.

Ever since Wuthering Heights first appeared (also under the nom de plume Ellis Bell), it has brought out strong feelings, both good and bad, in its readers. According to Lutz, critics at the time largely agreed that the novel was “coarse, strange, disagreeable.” But as the years have gone on, many others have been drawn to it precisely for its strangeness.

One such reader, who found in Brontë an unsettlingly kindred spirit, was another unrelatable Emily, Emily Dickinson, who called her “gigantic” and wanted one of Brontë’s poems read at her funeral. One can only speculate about what drew one Emily to the other, but I fancy that at least part of it was their shared sense of estrangement. Both insisted on a certain distance between themselves and the world; they asked readers not to get closer to them but to remain at a remove.

This challenge—to be drawn into another’s writing but also to stand at some distance from them—persists today. In a post-theory world still laboring in the shadow of the New Critics, most graduate students in literature are taught that identification is the cardinal sin—that to identify with a character, or to identify the speaker of a poem as the author, is naïve. Yet as a teacher, I’ve noticed my undergraduate students using the word relate as though it were a prerequisite to being drawn toward a text rather than a pitfall to avoid. I think that sidestepping this shift—from seeing identification as an intellectual mistake to embracing it as a feelings-based relation—is at the core of how I approach Brontë’s life. I don’t want to view her simply as a cold and intellectual figure. But I also don’t want to relate to her; to the extent that I do, it shows me monstrous capabilities in myself.

The point is not to bring Emily Brontë down to earth by claiming (as the 2019 show Dickinson did to that later Emily) that she was just like us, all anachronistic feelings and hidden Sapphic longings, but to bring her down to an earth that was uniquely hers. Lutz’s book does just that. Her Emily is a thrillingly earthbound creature, as individual and ultimately as inaccessible as we all are. To think we know her or understand her would be reductive. But to realize that we don’t fully know or understand her is to realize that she is just like us.

After reading This Dark Night, I don’t feel like I really know Emily Brontë any better, but I do think I understand her world a bit better—her terroir, the environment she was steeped in and that infuses her verse and prose. Lutz does not try to explain Emily—rather, she leaves her where she wanted to be, on her own. Lutz doesn’t make her do anything; instead, she wonders often about how Emily might have found her eventual role as the keeper of the Haworth parsonage, but she is careful not to put words in her subject’s mouth.

We don’t learn much that’s new about Emily herself, but we do learn what it would have been like to be in her world. Anyone looking for easy answers to Wuthering Heights, a brutal and confusing book, or its strange author will be disappointed—but those readers for whom the mystery is the point will certainly be pleased.

Sarah Chihaya is the author of Bibliophobia, which was a finalist for the 2026 Pulitzer Prize, and a coauthor of The Ferrante Letters: An Experiment in Collective Criticism.
