https://jacobin.com/2026/10/fergie-chamb.title: Trump’s War on Palestine Comes for Fergie Chambers
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/fergie-chamb.text:
On Tuesday, September 22, the Spanish Council of Ministers refused to block a US extradition request for James “Fergie” Chambers, a prominent and wealthy leftist activist and donor. The council did not determine whether the US citizen and activist will be sent to the United States, but only whether the request would proceed in Spanish courts, who will then make the final determination. Chambers’s legal team, which includes a number of legendary human rights lawyers, have vowed they will argue before the courts that Chambers’s extradition is politically motivated; thus granting it would violate the US-Spanish extradition treaty.

The US indictment against the activist remains sealed, but Chambers’s lawyers have accused the US government of seeking to criminalize humanitarian aid to the Palestinian people, which has been a priority for Chambers to provide. The US extradition request has aroused considerable controversy within Spain. The electoral platform Sumar, a junior partner in Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist-led government, has opposed the extradition, as have a number of Spanish parliamentarians. They not only view the move as at odds with current Spanish government’s support for Palestine but as aiding the Trump administration as it seeks to internationalize its repression of pro-Palestinian voices.

The attacks on Chambers come at a pivotal time. For the last three years, as Israel has waged a genocidal war of annihilation in Gaza, Western governments have sought to shield the apartheid state from accountability by restricting their own citizens’ free speech rights. The United States has not been immune from this. It has escalated a long-standing trend of using its anti-terrorism laws and sanctions to target global support for the Palestinian cause.

After inheriting this assault on free speech, the Trump administration has sought to broaden its scope across the Left. And as the State Department has repeatedly made clear, this program is not to be limited to the United States domestically. It is in this context that the extradition request for Chambers must be understood.

Chambers is a self-described communist. He also is a former heir to the Cox cable family fortune. He divested from his family’s fortune, granting him $250 million. With this money, Chambers began funding left-wing groups. The multimillionaire garnered media attention, some of it highly inflammatory, over his role in supporting the Stop Cop City protesters, an Atlanta-based activist movement opposed to the building of the Atlanta Public Safety Training Center on a mix of environmental and anti–police militarization grounds.

The movement itself has faced heavy repression, with the state of Georgia bringing widely condemned charges against sixty-one supporters of the movement. According to Chambers, he donated a “couple of million dollars” to groups opposing the facility, as well as hundreds of thousands in bail support for those arrested. Chambers also funded the defense of a group of activists who vandalized Elbit Systems offices in New Hampshire, part of an international movement of direct actions against the Israeli weapons manufacturer.

Chambers’s funding of activist causes and his underlying radical politics did not go unnoticed by the US media. In 2023, Los Angeles Magazine ran an exclusive on Chambers under the headline “Heir to Cox Family Fortune: ‘I Chant Death to America Every Day.’” In 2024, Mother Jones ran a profile of Chambers’s support for Stop Cop City with the headline, “There’s a Communist Multimillionaire Fomenting Revolution in Atlanta.” Days later, Rolling Stone published its own piece, “Fergie Chambers Is Heir to One of America’s Richest Families — and Determined to See the U.S. Fall.”

Since Chambers’s arrest, Mother Jones has again written about him under the headline “Meet the Multi-Millionaire Pro-Hamas Activist Who Was Arrested in Spain.” (Shortly after October 7, 2023, Chambers tweeted “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’. There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for. No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done anything wrong. It’s simply genocide. Like it has been.”)

The fact that an heir to one of the largest fortunes in the United States is now funding very left-wing activism is certainly newsworthy. And while many of these headlines were clearly designed to draw readership, it does not appear these profiles misrepresented Chambers’s views or misquoted him.

But the attention to Chambers came at a time when the Right was increasingly targeting those who funded left-wing protest movements. As part of these efforts to stamp out political movements they disfavor, the Right has once again turned to an old rhetorical playbook, claiming such protests are not organic expressions of dissent but the sinister machinations of outside forces. While in the past the Communist Party has played the role of boogeyman, and today the nebulous “antifa” frequently also plays that role, significant focus has been placed on the role of funders as the supposed puppet masters inciting unrest in the United States. Attacking such funders is a clear strategy in Donald Trump’s National Security Presidential Memorandum-7 (NSPM-7).

Rhetorically, much of this attention has been devoted to the liberal, well-connected philanthropist, George Soros, and his son, Alex Soros. But in terms of the actual mechanics of repression, the targets have increasingly been individuals like Chambers, whose views are more outside the mainstream.

On Capitol Hill, Republicans, egged on by right-wing media, have engaged in a witch hunt reminiscent of the McCarthy era against Neville Roy Singham, even going as far as to subpoena a news outlet that received funding from him. Singham has been a left-wing activist for decades. A former member of the League of Revolutionary Black Workers, Singham started his own software company, which he sold in 2017 for $785 million. Singham is the husband of Code Pink founder Jodie Evans, and his philanthropy came under fire as part of a series of attempts to demonize the venerable antiwar group as agents of China. Singham currently resides in Shanghai, and critics have asserted without evidence that he is an unregistered agent of China in order to taint the activism he funds. Anyone familiar with the McCarthyite campaign against him will immediately note that parts of NSPM-7 clearly allude to him.

Fox News has played a significant role in fearmongering about Singham, so it is significant that in an article on Chambers’s arrest, the conservative outlet directly compared the two. In line with the Right’s growing narrative about US protests, the same article described Chambers as “bankrolling anti-cop, pro-Hamas communist revolution” and “years of financing anti-Israel and anti-West organizations and protests.” And while Chambers is certainly wealthy, unlike the Soroses, who fund mainstream causes and are close with powerful Democratic politicians, Chambers is certainly marginalized within US political life.

With both Chambers and Singham, a huge factor in the attacks on them are their support for the Palestinian cause. It is this support that has now directly placed Chambers in the crosshairs of the Trump Justice Department.

The US indictment against Chambers remains sealed, thus making it impossible to independently assess what the government is even alleging. According to his legal team and multiple media accounts, the indictment alleges money laundering in support of Hamas and “conspiracy to commit disorderly conduct.” The Grayzone, an independent media outlet focusing on US empire, claims to have viewed the sealed indictment. It describes the indictment as alleging “international money laundering. . . . with the intent to provide material support to and resources to foreign terrorist organizations.”

In 2023, Chambers moved to Tunisia, though he has since relocated to Ireland. The indictment focuses on wire transfers Chambers made from banks in his native United States to banks in his then–home country of Tunisia. According to The Grayzone’s Kit Klarenberg, while the indictment focuses on these transfers, the indictment offers no evidence Chambers gave money to any foreign terrorist organizations.

Chambers’s partner, Stella Schnabel, has publicly claimed the money was transferred as part of Chambers’s backing of Club Africain, a Tunisian soccer team, and youth soccer programs in the country. Chambers also has donated money to the Sameer Project, a humanitarian charity in Gaza. According to Middle East Eye, Chambers’s donation “helped establish a bakery in northern Gaza, complete a desalination plant and operate a free medical clinic.” Since Chambers’s arrest, Sameer has not paused its vitally needed humanitarian work.

Without having access to the indictment, or understanding the wider US government case, it is unclear what role this laudable humanitarian work plays in the United States’ case against Chambers. His lawyers and supporters have repeatedly brought it up in the context of the extradition. And the United States has a long history of criminalizing such humanitarian efforts, oftentimes working in tandem with Israeli intelligence to do so.

In one of the signature prosecutions of the post-9/11 war on terror, the US government put five leaders of the Holy Land Foundation for Relief and Development on trial. They were not accused of supporting the 9/11 attacks, al-Qaeda, or even any act of violence. Instead, the Bush administration argued that the bona fide humanitarian aid they had sent to the occupied Palestinian Territories had gone through Hamas-controlled social-welfare committees, something the charity disputed. After two trials, and with help from the recently passed Patriot Act and Israeli intelligence services, they were convicted. The prosecution made clear that even pure humanitarian aid can be dubbed support for terrorism by the US government.

Since Israel launched its genocidal war in Gaza, both the Biden and Trump administrations have escalated the use of this counterterrorism framework against Palestinian human rights advocacy. The Biden administration slapped Samidoun, a Palestinian prisoners’ rights group, with counterterrorism sanctions accusing them of being a sham charity. The Trump administration has continued this trend, including by sanctioning the organizers of the Freedom Flotilla on spurious claims that they are “terrorists.”

It has also escalated by now sanctioning human rights groups and officials not accused of terrorism but of helping the International Criminal Court in attempting to prosecute Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. False allegations of terrorism are no longer necessary; mere human rights advocacy is enough. Such sanctions have sweeping reach, as the US government considers coordinating advocacy with a sanctioned party a violation of the sanctions regime, meaning US citizens seeking to work with these human rights groups or international officials risk prison sentences under the International Emergency Economics Powers Act by doing so.

The Trump administration is also seeking the extradition of a Turkish national from the UK on claims that the charity he collected humanitarian aid for Gaza through was a “sham charity” on behalf of Hamas. In their press release announcing the request, the US Department of Justice explicitly thanked Israel’s domestic security service for their aid in the matter.

And, in addition to internationalizing its attacks on aid for Palestine, it is also internationalizing its attacks on the Left. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Stephen Miller hosted a bizarre international conference on left-wing terrorism and are now extending the mania for sanctions beyond Palestinian human rights advocates to what it dubs “far-left terrorism.” This includes counterterrorism sanctions placed on Autistici/Inventati, an Italian volunteer collective that provides encrypted email services to activists. According to the Trump administration, they provided these services to “Marxist, anarchist, and other left-wing extremist groups in the United States, Europe, and elsewhere.”

The United States’ extradition request has rightfully generated opposition. Sumar, whose members include the vice prime minister and labor minister, have opposed it, as have a number of leftist members of the Spanish parliament. Over 150 prominent international activists, including Greta Thunberg, signed a petition opposing it. In Spain, Chambers is represented by Baltasar Garzón, a prominent human rights lawyer who, as a judge, issued an arrest warrant for former Chilean dictator Augusto Pinochet.

The Left in the United States should also rise to the occasion and demand their government drop this extradition. Chambers has certainly been a polarizing figure on the US left, to put it mildly. Many on the Left disagree with many of his views, and Chambers has not been shy about voicing his own criticisms of the US left. But faced with political repression from a Trump administration hoping to both stamp out the Left and willing to aid Israel’s genocide in Gaza, such internal differences of opinion do not matter. The situation is urgent to stand against political repression, not just for Gaza but the entire international left. If the Trump administration succeeds in getting their hands on Chambers, it will set a dark precedent.

https://jacobin.com/2026/10/maine-collin.title: Susan Collins’s Record: Making Injured Workers’ Lives Harder
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/maine-collin.text:
Susan Collins has been the senator from Maine for twenty-nine years, during which time she’s received scrutiny for her coziness with corporate donors, her record on war with Iran, and her votes against lowering prescription drug prices, among other things. But one of the most impactful measures on Maine workers that she took happened well before she first went to Washington.

In an episode that’s little remembered today, in the late 1980s and early ’90s, Collins led the way on a set of reforms to Maine’s workers’ compensation system that saw the state government shut down for the first time in its history and led to major cuts to injured workers’ benefits. Appointed to the task by an insurance-industry-friendly Republican governor, Collins — then a state official who had never held elected office — ardently pursued the changes, openly appealing to the insurance industry to help push them through, and pushing for far-reaching cuts that were only prevented because Republicans lacked the numbers in the state legislature.

Collins has carved out a reputation as a moderate in the Senate, a reputation at odds with her tendency to vote in alignment with Donald Trump’s position more than 90 percent of the time. But as her early role in cutting benefits for injured Maine workers recalls, Collins has also had a long history as an ideologically driven servant of the business sector.

Though the workers’ comp reforms were the brainchild of, and set into motion by then-Governor John McKernan, Collins played a leading role. Reports at the time described her variously as “the administration’s point person on workers’ comp,” his “top advisor” on the issue, his “key representative” in legislative negotiations on the matter, and even the “administration’s negotiator.”

Collins herself saw it that way: when she ran for governor a few years later in 1994, she campaigned on the overhaul, taking credit for having “reformed workers’ compensation” and winning hard-fought “battles” to do so. One Democrat involved in the legislative talks, former state senator Gerard Conley Jr, later recalled her as “a very tough negotiator.”

“She struck me as being extremely bright,” Conley said. “But I also felt she had absolutely no heart. She would get what she knew the governor needed at any cost — even if it included shutting down state government.”

The reforms under Collins came in two waves. The 1987 round took rate-setting out of the hands of the legislature and put it in the hands of a single political appointee, leading to benefits being cut more than 40 percent and premiums being hiked more than 50 percent, with some of the most seriously injured workers bearing the brunt. The 1991 round cut benefits further for some workers and mandated that an independent medical examiner effectively judge in any dispute, streamlining the ability to deny worker claims.

Those who pushed these cuts weren’t wrong that there were real problems facing Maine’s workers’ compensation system. By the late 1980s, the average cost for a permanent injury in the state was $67,861, nearly double that of the second-most expensive state. That and the threat of mass exodus in 1987 by fifteen insurance firms covering 75 percent of the market ostensibly triggered the push to make the overhaul.

Yet for all these very real issues, critics charged that the cuts were driven more by ideology than data. One reason was that besides its most expensive workers’ comp costs, Maine also happened to have the country’s worst workplace safety record: 68 percent above the national average, on the eve of the second set of cuts in 1991. In fact, before the first set four years earlier, state officials, attorneys in workers disability cases, and members of the industry themselves had agreed this was a major reason for the skyrocketing costs.

This fact would be largely ignored in the ensuing debate. Collins simply publicly insisted the real issue was “inflated benefits” while dismissing workplace safety concerns, saying that critics were simply charging “that Maine employers do not care about safety” and that she didn’t “think there is any evidence of that.” Yet after the reforms were a done deal, the governor’s own press secretary would admit that most of the money in the workers’ comp system didn’t actually go to injured workers.

Then there was the fact that, for all of Collins’s claims that cutting workers’ comp would “retain and promote good jobs,” it was far from clear the two things were linked. In the run-up to the 1991 cuts, several experts questioned the claim they would create jobs; one called it “silliness,” while another called workers’ comp a “trivial cost” for businesses in the grand scheme that was only “psychologically” a burden for employers. By the Sun Journal’s calculation, the savings in the proposed cuts were enough to create jobs that would cover only a small fraction of Maine’s unemployed.

Once the second set of cuts were signed into law, the Maine Sunday Telegram would report that “few companies that closed or laid off workers put the blame entirely on workers’ compensation.” In a Maine Chamber of Commerce and Industry survey conducted earlier that year of the seventy-five companies that took either measure, a mere two cited the cost of workers’ comp as the main reason, while only three others called it a contributing factor.

There was also the administration’s ties to the insurance industry. Insurance superintendent Joe Edwards, who controversially approved the carriers’ exit from the Maine market, had previously worked in the insurance industry, and he would draw criticism for using words like “we” and “us” while trying to convince insurance executives to stay in the state. McKernan himself, the governor, had once lobbied for insurance companies. And Collins herself openly appealed to the industry, whose seal of approval for the reforms she sought.

“We’re counting on the business community to mount a lobbying effort to push [McKernan’s cuts] through,” she told the Chamber of Commerce of the Greater Portland Region in October 1987. “It’s absolutely critical that you start today” to reach out to legislators, she urged them.

Sure enough, business wound up spending nearly $50,000 on a lobbying effort for the 1987 reforms, and insurance executives and representatives turned up to the legislature on the day of the vote, reiterating their threats to leave to Democratic leaders. A few years later, insurance agents would receive a letter on behalf of the governor’s campaign calling him “a good friend to the insurance industry” and praising Collins and other appointees for their “knowledge of our industry and fair, balanced approaches to our problems.”

This coziness with the industry helped feed accusations that the carriers’ threats to leave the state was a manufactured crisis, part of an “orchestrated” and “heavy-handed attempt to intimidate the legislature into giving them what they want,” as the Maine AFL-CIO charged. In any case, Collins would use the industry’s threats to build pressure for the cuts, repeatedly pointing to them to demand they be urgently pushed through, warning that Maine workers might imminently be left without coverage.

Despite Collins’s assurances that the solution lay in simply giving the industry whatever it wanted — “to make a market [where] companies want to stay,” she said — the cuts didn’t seem to work. The industry continued to ask and get approval for sizable rate hikes in the years that followed despite the cuts, with the Democratic House Speaker complaining that “the only ones who seem to have profited from the [1987] ‘reforms’ are the insurance companies.”

When 1991 rolled around, Collins was again in a leading role. Heading a task force to investigate whether it took too long for the clock to start ticking on workers’ benefits, she made clear her priorities were to cut costs, decrease litigation, reduce fraud, and get people back to work as quickly as possible.

As nearly forty industry groups put together their own reform wish list, Collins admitted that her own package “parallels some of the themes advanced by” the employer coalition, and that there was “quite a bit of similarity” to what they put forward. The task force would eventually recommend changes like giving employers more time to challenge claims, removing a penalty on employers who get workers at higher risk of reinjury back to work sooner, and having an independent medical examiner rule on workers’ disabilities.

At a March meeting, employers complained to Collins that workers’ comp claims were driven by ambulance-chasing lawyers and complained it created a “subculture” of laziness. She was familiar with their concerns, she replied, and said it was too hard to cut workers off their benefits, which she claimed often went to non-work-related injuries. Elsewhere, she complained that too many claims were now “soft-tissue” injuries — a category that included carpal tunnel syndrome — rather than “the classic kind of industrial accident.”

Collins advised the governor to veto a Democrat-passed package of workers’ comp reforms that would have made benefits more generous. She then embarked on a tour through the state to sell his package of cuts, with the administration’s own analysis found made two-thirds of its savings on the back of injured workers by, among other things, reducing eligibility.

Already controversial, the reforms became the statewide issue in July after McKernan, to push them through over Democratic opposition, decided to link the package to the state budget, causing a more than two-week-long state government shutdown, the first in its 170-year history — a “hostage” situation, as one Democrat put it. At one point, the governor found himself barricaded inside his office as irate state workers stormed the state capitol in protest.

With Democrats holding firm amid the furor over the shutdown, the administration was forced to compromise. The final version of the package was free of the eligibility restrictions and duration limits Collins had fought for but still kept some cuts and maintained the role of independent medical examiners, placing expansive unilateral power into the hands of a single individual to make or break an injured workers’ claim.

Organized labor despaired. Collins told employers it was a “good signal” that should make them “take another look.”

Yet this round of cuts didn’t work either. Meant to reduce the role and cost of lawyers, experts complained the overhaul did the opposite, adding litigation costs and making the system more complicated. The administration itself admitted cuts would only save enough to offset a 14 percent rate increase for employers, and pretty soon Collins was suggesting that more reforms were coming to keep trying to bring down costs. Less than half a year later, nine companies filed again to leave the Maine market and Collins once more was warning of a market collapse. The following January, the business lobby demanded more urgent cuts.

Collins adamantly resisted one long-proposed solution to this: a state-run insurance fund that would inject competition into the industry and wouldn’t up and leave the market. Collins usually threw up objections based on the idea’s supposed impracticality: it would be too time-consuming or too expensive to set up, or that it wouldn’t reduce rates.

But occasionally she made clear that she was against it on ideological grounds. That meant “advocating that the state government get into the workers’ compensation insurance business,” she wrote in August 1990, something she and the rest of the administration wouldn’t abide “because of our philosophical commitment to the private market.”

“It is ironic that at a time when the rest of the world is moving away from state ownership and racing toward private enterprise,” she wrote, proponents of the idea want to “have the state operate an insurance company.”

Collins would not be part of the most far-reaching round of cuts that came in October 1992, having resigned that January to take a regional post in the Small Business Administration. But her efforts set the stage for those reforms, which would echo the more severe cuts her task force had urged.

“This session of the legislature must do something” on workers’ comp, Collins said the day after filing her resignation. “There is a greater realization than ever before that workers’ comp is a great problem. When I came here [to Augusta] five years ago I had to convince people that it was a problem. I don’t have to do that now.”

It took nearly thirty years for the Maine legislature to roll back the workers’ comp cuts that Collins backed and helped set into motion — an effort that, ironically, would be partially led by her current challenger for her Senate seat, Troy Jackson, in 2019. That year, Maine workers testified about the chaos and suffering that they had been plunged into after being injured on the job, thanks in part to a workers’ comp system plainly inadequate for making them whole, especially in the face of significantly higher living costs.

If Collins survives another reelection campaign this November, it will be yet another Harry Houdini–like political escape for a politician adept at putting a moderate face on a record that has been devastating for US workers.

https://jacobin.com/2026/10/naza-film-re.title: Israel Fears NAZA. Why Don’t Our Films Scare Anyone?
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/naza-film-re.text:
It isn’t uncommon for states to retaliate against the filmmakers who insult them. Sergei Parajanov was imprisoned for daring to make poetic cinema in the era of Soviet Realism. Jafar Panahi’s twenty-year ban from filmmaking and six-year prison sentence have become the central theme of the very films the Iranian state seeks to suppress. Even in America, documentarians like Emile de Antonio, Errol Morris, and Frederick Wiseman have faced bans, bomb threats, and personal death threats. Within the long history of the repression of film and filmmakers, it’s hard to think of anything like the fury the Israeli state is raining down on the directors of NAZA, a new documentary tracing the IDF’s brutal campaign in Gaza.

The reaction from the Israeli government has been unambiguously hostile. Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar has threatened to revoke the citizenship of directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. They’re also facing potential criminal prosecution from IDF Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir and threats to their families by members of Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party, who’ve assembled outside Szor’s mother’s house chanting “Death penalty for traitors.” Netanyahu himself, no stranger to violent incitement against political opponents, compared the film to a barrage of ballistic missiles aimed at Israel.

But these attacks have only served to elevate the profile of the film, which has been selling out theaters in New York and fueling the debate about who, if anyone, in Netanyahu’s coalition will end up in the Hague. As horrible as this ordeal must be for the filmmakers and their sources, one can’t help thinking that this reception speaks to the power art and journalism can have on national politics when it strikes the right nerve. American filmmakers should ask themselves why our films have lost this power to threaten the elite.

Israel, to be sure, has its own special relationship to journalism and propaganda, which a film like NAZA was uniquely poised to disrupt. Hasbara, the Hebrew word for “propaganda,” was once an elegantly managed media ecosystem built on the grammatical obfuscations of New York Times and BBC headlines, on the one hand, and the self-serious “shoot and cry” films like Waltz with Bashir (2008) and Lebanon (2009), on the other. In these films, soldiers come close to reckoning with their war guilt, but only as personal trauma devoid of political context. Like most bad apologies, these stories seem like self-justification more and more as they progress: It was my first day on the job as tank gunner; these terrorists keep using civilians as human shields; mistakes were bound to happen. As Prime Minister Golda Meir once said, “We can forgive the Arabs for killing our sons, but we can never forgive them for forcing us to kill their children.”

After a few post–October 7 news cycles, however, the hasbara began to crumble, and Israel launched a new stopgap: a campaign of international intimidation, blatantly corrupt media spin by powerful ideologues like Larry and David Ellison, and an unprecedented massacre of combat zone journalists. For Edward Said’s generation, the task of overcoming Israeli propaganda meant outspending and outmaneuvering an elegantly managed ideological apparatus. For the directors of NAZA, the challenge was simply finding the courage to tell the truth at a time when Western powers had given the green light to any and all forms of repression, reprisal, and bloodshed.

For the time being, American film is still contained by its more or less subtle ideological apparatus, rather than outright skullduggery against filmmakers. Recently, the Warner-Paramount merger put a long list of media properties (CNN, HBO, TBS, BET, et al.) on the same path for political reeducation that CBS suffered under Ellison hatchet woman Bari Weiss. The move is a part of a longer historical assault on America’s ability to understand itself or the rest of the world. Corporate media conglomeration was already a corrosive force in American newsrooms, as were the economic pressures that came with the news avoidance of the Trump years, a result of his “flood the zone” approach to political theater and scandal. And that’s to say nothing of what social media has done to impoverish news outlets.

A great effort is undertaken to keep Americans ignorant of certain truths — particularly when it comes to our history of military interventions. And once the job is done, it’s hard to see one’s own country clearly. Sometimes the only way to recognize our own propaganda is to watch how another country’s falls apart.

One glaring difference between the NAZA filmmakers and their counterparts in American media is that they took their subjects’ moral crisis seriously to begin with. It’s what gives the film its subversive power. When our veterans talk about their feelings of guilt for their participation in the global war on terror, our media treats it as symptoms of a psychological illness, one with a medical solution. A New York Times article from 2024 called “A Secret War, Strange New Wounds” is representative of the genre. The article spends most of its length illustrating the deteriorating lives of veterans suffering from hallucinatory PTSD, on the one hand, and inconclusive science about a new kind of head trauma, on the other. Questions like, What war were these soldiers fighting? In what region of the world were they located? What were they aiming their guns at exactly? are treated as unrelated asides.

The soldiers profiled were a part of the US war on the Islamic State in Syria and Iraq. Because the political cost of boots on the ground was too high, the US elected for a strategy of overwhelming artillery bombardment at a volume and tempo not seen since Vietnam. The result was an unknown number of civilian casualties. The article begins with a haunting encounter between a veteran and the ghost of a little girl, covered in dust, who appears to him repeatedly in his home, following him from room to room, “[staring] at him with a glare as dark and heavy as oil.” The author states that the soldier thought the IS fighters he killed had put a hex on him, even though the figure haunting him wasn’t an enemy combatant.

Yet it takes the author of the Times piece sixty-seven more paragraphs to ask what gunners like these were even aiming at. The answer: nothing in particular. The soldiers, from a top-secret special forces group known as Task Force 9, were firing into Raqqa in a grid pattern, indifferent to who or what they were hitting. Sometimes when they would elect to actually find targets, according to the Times’ own reporting, they would deliberately select “mosques, schools, dams and power plants.” The group, it turns out, had been given “broad authority to use heavy firepower” by President Donald Trump. The article doesn’t spend any time exploring the psychological effect this kind of mass murder might have had on the soldiers or, for that matter, on the lives of the people on the other end of the shelling.

Some Americans might say it’s unfair to compare our veterans to the IDF soldiers profiled in NAZA, but Israel’s conduct against Palestine isn’t that far from the atrocities we’ve visited on neighboring countries during the war on terror. The war in Iraq destabilized one of the most developed states in the region and killed as many as a million people, by some estimates. Throughout the war, the US did everything it could to exacerbate interfaith and tribal conflicts — the very tensions Saddam Hussein, deploying his own bloody methods, had successfully suppressed throughout his rule. This US strategy of tension included hiring notorious war criminal Colonel James Steele as a consultant to train the Shia militias who had infiltrated the interior ministry. Steele was one of the US handlers of the Salvadoran death squads deployed during their civil war, and he shared that experience with the Shia Wolf Brigade, which made a name for itself torturing and murdering Sunni civilians and insurgents alike with power drills.

Our military even shared Israel’s enthusiasm for the outright leveling of cities. During the Second Battle of Fallujah, the US forces damaged or destroyed roughly 70 percent of the city’s buildings. And that’s just what we did in Iraq during the war on terror. One could go on about overt and covert antiterrorism operations reaching across the Middle East, all the way into Africa, and the extraordinary rendition and torture program that spanned the entire globe.

The only person in global politics who seems interested in adjudicating America’s war crimes is Netanyahu himself, who routinely invokes Hiroshima and the Allied carpet-bombing of Japan and Germany whenever he receives calls for restraint from Joe Biden or Trump. As long as America fails to atone for its own historical guilt, nations like Israel will continue to claim our example as a legal precedent.

It’s not just our politicians who have failed in this enormous task. The development of the American mind — our education, our culture, even our medical practices — evinces a trend toward mental and historical oblivion. In her recent book, Traumatized, Catherine Liu traces the history of the PTSD diagnosis as a well-intentioned project by antiwar veterans and psychiatrists to address the unique psychological dysfunction veterans experienced during the Vietnam War.

Where they failed, the NAZA filmmakers succeeded. NAZA addresses war guilt head on in something like a public version of the talking cure, where exploring memories of war and complicity in war crimes is not only therapeutically valuable but politically volatile as well. The doctors who lobbied to include PTSD in the DSM, by contrast, treated guilt itself as a symptom of a mental disease. We often refer to mental disorders like depression and PTSD as “diseases” or “illnesses” even when there is no physiological trace. This use of medical terminology and symbolism was useful at the inception of psychoanalysis to get guilt-ridden Victorians to open up about oedipal fantasies, but as Liu points out, over time this relationship between therapy and the medical establishment resulted in drug companies displacing talk therapy in the search for cures and the development of the DSM from a statistical tool maintained for the US Census Bureau into a therapeutic tool whose use is required by insurance companies. The end result is that when veterans talk to us about their guilt, we talk to them about whether or not their helmets are doing a good job of protecting them from concussions.

American war films have shared this myopic conception of the meaning of war, which is a shame, because many, like The Deer Hunter (1978) and Apocalypse Now (1979), are in fact great works of art made with extraordinary skill and ambition. It’s hard not to feel like some of the effort was wasted, though, when you measure the worth of these films against their own moral aims. Was the point to arrange artistic elements in a pleasing way? Or to stage a drama in a particularly conflict-prone environment? Or was it to change America’s attitude toward these pointless imperial adventures abroad?

If it was the latter, even the best war films fail. François Truffaut famously stated you could never really make an antiwar film, because even the most horrific depiction of war feels exciting and heroic on screen — even some of its darker moments. There are plenty of anecdotal reports of soldiers amping themselves up for battle by watching the “This is my rifle, this is my gun” segment of Stanley Kubrick’s Full Metal Jacket (1987).

The main problem with these films, though, is their narcissism. The filmmakers never make a serious attempt to understand what it’s like to be on the receiving end of American munitions. Pakistani British novelist Kamila Shamsie, in her wonderful essay “The Storytellers of Empire,” shows how rare this gesture is in American letters. She highlights the example of John Hersey’s Hiroshima as the exception that proves the rule. Hersey was the rare American author who actually went to visit the country we bombed before writing about it, and his book is built of six stories that grew out of interviews he did with survivors of the blast. Hiroshima is as concerned about how it would be read in Japan as it would be in America.

The Palestinians, for their part, have not only always made great films but have made ones that make vital political gestures. Their filmmakers often employ styles that are popular in the international art house cinema of their time, sometimes to better effect than those they’re imitating. Leila and the Wolves (1984) is a great film about Palestinian and Lebanese feminism and struggle in the mode of one of those Agnes Varda or Jean-Luc Godard films that wander between documentary and lyrical vignettes. The Time That Remains (2009) uses the loud, ironic design of early-2000s Wes Anderson movies for comedy about an apartment that changes hands between an Arab and Jewish family during the Nakba. Neither film feels derivative of the styles they’re borrowing. The gesture the filmmakers are making is something like butting into a conversation at a party and gently steering the conversation toward what they really want to talk about. This not only has worth as a means of breaking through our heavily propagandized notions; it has a deeper moral purpose of returning cinema to the promise it once held as a means of international conversation, where the meaning of war isn’t personal, psychological guilt but a relationship between two peoples, both of whom deserve justice of one kind or another.

When making a film as a political gesture, timing is also key. The “shoot and cry” films are often made years, sometimes decades, after the conflict has ended, when the dead are buried, the maps redrawn, and the spoils of war long since divided. There’s little the hand-wringing liberals can do to enforce retribution for the crimes of their state at that point. It’s important that NAZA directors Szor and Abraham are making this film now, when there’s still a chance the truth can affect an escalating situation. A thin hope, maybe, but a welcome one in this uniquely hopeless age.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Florida kills 77-year-old man in state’s 18th execution of year
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Vietnam veteran William Reaves executed by lethal injection despite letter from fellow veterans urging halt

Florida carried out its 18th execution of the year on Tuesday under Republican governor Ron DeSantis’s aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term.

William Reaves, 77, was pronounced dead at 6.12pm following a three-drug injection at Florida state prison near Starke. He was convicted of first-degree murder in the 1986 shooting death of Indian River county deputy Richard Raczkowski.

The death chamber curtain went up promptly at the 6pm execution time, and Reaves was already strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm. Asked if he had any last statement, he said: “No, I do not.”

The injection began immediately after that. About 30 seconds later, Reaves took several big breaths and then stopped moving. After a few minutes, the team warden shook Reaves’ shoulders and yelled his name, but there was no response.

A medic was called into the chamber a short time later to check for a heartbeat or any other signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later.

Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over the age of 70 put to death this year, highlighting the nation’s ageing death-row population as Florida continues to far outpace the rest of country in total executions.

Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year and it would tie that mark if another execution is carried out next month as scheduled.

DeSantis, who leaves office in January after two terms, has said his goal is to deliver justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out.

Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986, according to court records. Reaves later acknowledged he had placed the call from a payphone outside the store.

While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The two struggled over the weapon, and Reaves eventually regained control of it. Investigators said the deputy was trying to run away when Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds.

Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. But the Florida supreme court overturned the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted again and sentenced to death in 1992, and subsequent appeals were unsuccessful.

The US supreme court on Tuesday afternoon rejected Reaves’ final appeal without comment.

The Florida supreme court last week also rejected Reaves’ appeals to spare his life.

One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the department of corrections.

The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states such as Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital.

Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the US Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves – an army veteran – as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam war. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter Monday urging him to stop the execution.

A total of 47 people were executed in the US in 2025. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half the 32 total executions in the US so far this year. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.

Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on 5 Novemner. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Ultra-endurance athlete completes 900-mile swim along entire California coast
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Catherine Breed began unprecedented journey at northern end of state, swimming 10 miles a day to reach other end in less than four months

A 33-year-old ultra-endurance athlete has completed an unprecedented swim down the entire coast of California, finishing the 900-mile journey in less than four months.

Catherine Breed will celebrate the end of her swim at San Diego’s Coronado beach on Monday afternoon, 111 days since she began her journey on 1 July at the northern border of California.

“For months, I measured my world in the next few miles,” Breed, a Bay Area native, told the San Francisco Chronicle on Sunday, describing how she had moved through the ocean with “whales beneath me, plastic beside me”.

The record-breaking American open water swimmer previously swam the English Channel in 2018, and completed the North Channel crossing between northern Ireland and Scotland in 2019 – widely considered one of the toughest endurance swims in the world. But those famous 21-mile open ocean crossings were just a quick dip in the pool compared with the 900-mile wild swim along the California coast that Breed and her team began planning three years ago.

“It is like doing a trail 50k or a half Ironman every day for about 110 days,” Breed said in a social media post.

Breed has said she planned the coastal swim to test her own personal endurance, celebrate her love of the California coast, put a spotlight on environmental preservation efforts, and encourage more women and girls to spend time in and on the ocean.

Breed swam the coast in stages, completing about 10 miles per day, accompanied by a shipboard support team who are also officially documenting the endeavor for the World Open Water Swimming Association. Breed slept onboard the ship and made stops along the coast to do events with ocean conservation groups. She also streamed much of her swim on YouTube, including Monday’s “historic finish”.

One of the biggest challenges came at the very end of the swim, Breed said, navigating through the polluted waters by Imperial beach at the US-Mexico border, which she called “some of the dirtiest water in the United States, if not the world”, and that felt like “swimming through sewage”.

“Everyone’s been so fixated on sharks,” Breed said in a video posted on her Instagram Sunday. “We are so scared about these animals that live in the ocean and have no interest in us, and we are more fearful about that than we are about the damage and destruction that we are causing to our own home.”

The swimmer’s journey came during what is expected to be a season of unprecedented Super El Niño weather in the Pacific Ocean, with multiple tropical storms, dangerous waves that battered the California coastline, and a huge surge of warm coastal water called a “Kelvin wave” that moved northward as Breed swam south. Breed told local news outlets that the extreme weather has been the hardest part of the challenge, telling San Diego’s KPBS that because of the Super El Niño, “the current is quite literally going against us the entire way”.

As part of the journey, Breed has reportedly navigated waves as high as 7ft, which she described as feeling like swimming “in a washing machine”.

Breed, a former University of California, Berkeley, long-distance swimmer and member of the US national team, transitioned to open water swimming after graduation as part of San Francisco’s Dolphin Club. She grew up in, on and around the water on California’s coast, telling the local radio station KQED: “At one point in my life, I think I had swum and sailed under the Golden Gate Bridge more times than I had driven over it.”

In 2017, she set the record for the fastest person to swim the length of California’s Lake Tahoe in just under 9 hours. In 2022, at age 29, Breed became the first person to swim from San Francisco’s Golden Gate Bridge to Half Moon Bay, a 25-mile swim. Last year, she completed a 30-mile swim through shark-filled waters from the Farallon Islands to Golden Gate Bridge.

“You cannot bring hubris or expectations into the ocean – whether you’re surfing, spearfishing, sailing or swimming. You can’t,” Breed told KQED earlier this year. “When I get in the ocean, it’s a full surrender. You’re completely present. Your only job is to put one arm in front of the other and be at peace with whatever the ocean gives you that day.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Nigeria confirms Ebola case as outbreak spreads into western Africa
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Case in Africa’s most populous country was detected in a woman who had travelled from Uganda

Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the health ministry said.

The woman began showing symptoms on 7 October and was admitted to a hospital in Abuja four days later, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola. It is unclear when she arrived in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country.

The health minister, Muhammad Pate, said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. “We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had,” he said.

Uganda’s ministry of health said the patient had only transited through Uganda and that she is a Nigerian woman who had been on a business trip to Congo’s eastern region. The Nigerian authorities have not disclosed her nationality.

“Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said in a statement. The ministry insisted Uganda has “no confirmed active Ebola cases”.

Nigeria is the latest country to report an Ebola case as the outbreak spreads across the region. Kenya confirmed its first case earlier this month and has since recorded nine infections. Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases, but it later declared itself free of the virus.

Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control, said on X that “we are facing an extremely serious threat,” with a fatality rate of nearly 50% of cases.

“This Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has already become the most geographically extensive in history, affecting several countries spread across three regions of Africa,” he said.

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control said two weeks ago it was stepping up surveillance following the detection of Ebola in Kenya and strengthening the country’s preparedness for a potential outbreak.

“These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of health care workers,” the agency said.

Nigeria established an Ebola taskforce in June after the outbreak in Congo in mid-May.

The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has infected more than 9,500 people and killed more than 4,600 people.

The latest Ebola outbreak is the fastest-spreading on record and is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, the 11,000 people killed in West Africa’s regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, WHO has said.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Sanae Takaichi took on Japan’s male-dominated politics and won – can she survive a second year in power?
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
The straight-talking PM’s ability to manage Trump and stand up to China have endeared her to the public, but she may need friends closer to home to survive

The visitors squeezed into the kiosk near Japan’s national diet building snap up souvenirs bearing the face of Sanae-chan, the affectionate nickname for the country’s leader: chocolate biscuits, dango sweets, stickers and document files proclaiming that “Japan is back”.

As Sanae Takaichi marks a year since she upended Japan’s male-dominated politics, the country’s first female prime minister has defied predictions that her time in office would be short-lived.

Instead, the straight-talking conservative has rewritten the rulebook on Japanese leadership, led her troubled Liberal Democratic party (LDP) to a resounding election victory, and won support among voters for refusing to back down during a prolonged row with China over Taiwan.

“Takaichi’s direct style has been an asset … particularly in her diplomatic strategy,” says Sheila A Smith, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations in New York.

Recent opinion poll put Takaichi’s approval rating at around 50% – the lowest ⁠level since she ⁠took ​office, but still a robust number for a Japanese leader 12 months into their term, and comfortably clear of the 30% “danger zone” that has signalled the end of previous administrations.

She has won plaudits for her refusal to back down in a diplomatic row with China, while her strong social media presence has helped her connect with younger voters disillusioned with the more analogue political style of her predecessors.

But the 65-year-old protege of the assassinated former prime minister Shinzo Abe marks her anniversary in October at the most precarious point of her premiership. Takaichi is battling the fallout from her first major cabinet scandal, mounting economic pressures and doubts about how she will fund a proposed cut in the consumption tax. She also faces persistent questioning about her work style, including her relationship with party colleagues and the media, and claims that she gets by on minimal sleep.

As the leader of a country with a long security relationship with the US, Takaichi has gone out of her way to endear herself to Donald Trump during their four meetings since she became prime minister. She chose not to respond to his quip about Pearl Harbor when they met in the Oval Office in March, although her body language suggested she was far from impressed.

Awkward moments notwithstanding, she has managed to keep Japan’s relationship with its most important ally on an even keel – even declaring the dawn of a “golden age” between Tokyo and Washington soon after she became prime minister.

At home, however, she faces the strongest political headwinds of her premiership to date.

This month, she initially defended her agricultural minister, Kazuo Yana, who provoked anger for remarks about cutting road funding in municipalities that didn’t support him. Takaichi’s response to pressure for his removal was typically idiosyncratic, describing Yana’s reported comments as “quite honestly, lame,” if true. Pressure built, and on 14 October Yana became the first cabinet minister in her government to resign.

“Takaichi may pay some price for the scandal in forthcoming opinion polls,” says Tobias Harris, founder of the political risk advisory firm Japan Foresight, adding that she had stood by him for almost two weeks while the scandal brewed.

Her current troubles don’t end with Yana. She has been accused of pushing through revisions that practically rule out a change in Japan’s male-only succession law, despite the public’s enthusiasm for a reigning empress, and offered muted backing for Tomoko Akane, the Japanese head of the international criminal court, which has been targeted with sanctions by Trump. She also faces mounting anger in Okinawa following the arrest this month of a US marine suspected of murdering and robbing a local woman.

“She will need to handle slip-ups by cabinet members, hurdles in keeping her coalition partner satisfied and, most importantly, continuing consumer concerns about cost-of-living pressures,” says Smith.

Doubts persist over Takaichi’s plans to ease financial pressures across Japan – a two-year reduction in the consumption tax on food and drink from 8% to 1%, and cash payments to struggling households.

Takaichi insists the measure won’t require more borrowing, but has failed to explain how they will be funded, adding to concerns about Japan’s public debt, already the highest among G7 economies.

Supporters revel in her direct style of communicating, but it has triggered accusations that she is avoiding media scrutiny.

Takaichi rarely grants individual interviews, preferring to explain policies, often in great detail, in posts on X. In her first five months in office, she gave 34 press briefings, fewer than her immediate predecessors Shigeru Ishiba, with 57, and Fumio Kishida, with 90, held over a comparable period. In that time she wrote 370 posts on X, according to the Kyodo news agency.

The tradition of holding background briefings with newspaper and TV executives has fallen by the wayside, says a senior editor at a Japanese weekly magazine who asked not to be named. “She has been aggressive towards the legacy media since day one, something I think she learned from Donald Trump.”

Takaichi’s gamble on the consumption tax, and her belated condemnation of Yana’s alleged comments, point to possible turbulence ahead, according to some observers, leaving her vulnerable to plotting by the same party colleagues who helped put her in the prime minister’s office.

While her predecessors built alliances over dinner at exclusive ryotei restaurants, Takaichi prefers to spend her evenings at home with her husband, Taku Yamamoto, a former lower house lawmaker who suffered a stroke last year. However, she does enjoy a cigarette, perhaps accompanied by a blast of Smoke On the Water by one of her favourite bands, Deep Purple.

She met colleagues over meals only five times in her first six months in office, according to the Mainichi Shimbun newspaper, significantly fewer than her predecessors. Abe, by contrast, hosted 50 gatherings over a similar period, and Fumio Kishida 35, including several during the Covid-19 pandemic. “It’s usual for Japanese prime ministers to hang out with other politicians in the evening and decide on policy,” says the magazine editor.

Takaichi, who vowed to “work, work, work” on behalf of voters, claims she gets only two to four hours of sleep a night, and sometimes summons aides in the early hours of the morning. Security protocols reportedly mean she is forbidden from going shopping, although her husband told a Japanese monthly magazine that he is occasionally permitted to order a pizza, adding that the couple stockpile microwaved ready meals and instant noodles. “In the morning, I have a bath, make breakfast and then wash the dishes, not to mention putting on my makeup,” she told MPs this week. “I feel like I’m spending three or four more hours than male prime ministers doing these things.”

Harris, Abe’s English-language biographer, says there were “notable differences” in style between Japan’s longest-serving prime minister and his protege.

“Takaichi is clearly more isolated, refusing in-person briefings from bureaucrats, having fewer meals with political allies and business representatives, and generally relying on her own judgment and perhaps not hearing as wide a range of views as her predecessors,” he says.

Testy relations with the media will not cause her to lose sleep as long as her message resonates with voters.

Smith says Takaichi’s “willingness to provide clear, no-nonsense responses to difficult policy challenges”, including the need for Japan to raise defence spending and improve its ability to respond to threats from China and North Korea, is likely to keep many voters on side: “I expect her successors will need to adapt and follow her lead,” she adds.

As long as that approach continues to work, even sceptical members of the LDP hierarchy who may wince at her personal style – sharing a laugh with Donald Trump at Joe Biden’s expense or serenading Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni – will continue to back her. What that means for her political longevity is less clear.

“She has a reputation for trusting her own advice and not building up a strong cadre of loyalists … and not playing the LDP’s social game,” says Harris. “That may endear her to voters, but it risks leaving her with few friends if her circumstances take a negative turn.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: After dark, these YouTubers watch over an unlikely charge – a shark stuck in a South Korean canal
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
A group of self-appointed guardians wearing hi-vis and carrying selfie sticks watch over the animal that has been trapped for a month, drawing more than 1.6 million visitors

In South Korea, they call them jagyeongdan, a word that sits somewhere between a vigilante group and a neighbourhood watch.

Each night they don hi-vis vests, pick up their selfie sticks, and gather around the harbour in Busan to keep watch over an unlikely charge: a stranded shark affectionately known as Bukang-i.

A month after the shark became trapped in a city canal, the group of self-appointed guardians are taking turns to protect her, patrolling the waterfront at night for visitors who might disturb the animal.

Most are YouTubers who livestream the waterway, from where the shark has become a national celebrity. They stay up through the night, calling out anyone shining torches or lasers into the water. Some of their videos have been watched hundreds of thousands of times.

“They bring fishing lamps, or the kind of lights people use at a campsite,” says Choi Won-jin, one of the shark’s protectors. He arrives as the lights go out along the canal and waits for the offenders Koreans online call “lantern villains”.

The shark has been marooned in the canal since 18 September. Named after Bukhang, the Korean name for the city’s North Port, and about 3 metres long, the female dusky shark is one of a species classed as endangered worldwide. More than 1.6 million visitors have come to see her, the city says, at a park that used to draw about 2,000 people on a busy Saturday.

Authorities have twice tried to guide her back out to sea and a third attempt is due to take place on Wednesday afternoon.

For now though, the shark remains in the canal, drawing crowds by day and leaving a handful of men to keep watch after dark. They patrol the canal’s park to check everything’s in order, eat snacks as the night goes by, and share their grievances on air about the behaviour they witness.

“We’re ordinary members of the public,” says Choi, who has had a YouTube channel for ten years and covers trending issues in South Korea. “So we have no choice but to put it nicely, and get them to understand as best we can.”

“Don’t, please don’t switch the torch on,” says one of them, a YouTuber who lives nearby and goes by the name Na Tae-soo. Most people comply, he says. “The animal thrashes about at night because of the torches, and it’s dangerous.”

His footage has captured the shark twisting sharply away from a beam of light at 2am and striking the side of the canal. The national institute of fisheries science later confirmed an abrasion on her snout and said a visitor’s torch likely startled the shark into injury.

Korean media report that 105 officials from seven agencies watch over her, with a team on standby to reach the water within three minutes. Choi disputes this, saying that after dark it is almost up to him and the others.

The waterfront is closed to the public from midnight until five in the morning, a restriction the YouTubers say is impossible to enforce across a park that size. One night, livestreaming from the walkway, Choi filmed a man tipping food waste into the water.

Nobody has seen her feed, though experts say that feeding can happen in an instant and sharks her size need not eat often.

Further attempts to free the shark have been paused on the grounds that more force would distress her.

Cooler water might see her move on. Dusky sharks prefer water between 18C and 26C, the fisheries institute says. Experts put 15C as the point below which her physiological functions would start to decline, and about 11C as the point at which survival becomes precarious. Busan city officials expect the canal to reach that temperature after the middle of November.

The fisheries institute recorded 46 large sharks off the east coast in the first half of this year, nearly four times as many as a year earlier, which it attributes to warmer seas and more of the fish sharks feed on.

The affection for Bukang-i has meanwhile become an industry, with a commemorative soju, a baseball mascot in a shark cape and an honorary city ambassadorship, and nearby shops reporting a surge in sales. South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, visited the canal in mid-October.

The shark’s guardians thinks she should be forced out. Choi says the city should protect her where she is until she leaves of her own accord.

Kim Jong-hwan, who runs a small business, keeps watch by day as well and has livestreamed her almost every day.

“I went to pass on information [to my followers], and after that I started observing her”, he says. “Watching her over time, with the water pumps being fired and then the nets, I came to find those things being done to her objectionable. So we ended up cheering her on.”

“If it gets cold, if there’s no food, if the water doesn’t suit her, she’ll leave by herself. I’d like her to just be left alone, to rest there comfortably until then, and go.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: University of Arizona sorority member alleges sexual assault at fraternity house
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Student told the university’s police department that assault by two men occurred in August during a night of drinking

A sorority member at the University of Arizona has alleged she was sexually assaulted by two men at a fraternity house during a night of drinking in late August.

The student told the university’s police department that she consensually kissed one of the men at one point while at the Sigma Phi Epsilon house on 26 August but doesn’t remember agreeing to sex, according to search warrant records posted Monday night by KOLD-TV in Tucson.

The sexual assault allegations surfaced two weeks after the university had suspended activities for its 21 fraternities amid reports of misconduct, including assault, hazing and drug- and alcohol-related behavior. Suspensions on all but five fraternities have since been lifted after they had mandatory meetings with the dean of students.

In speaking with an investigator, the sorority member recalled consuming tequila, including sharing a cup of the beverage with friends; witnessing two men sexually assaulting her, and even feeling one man’s breath on her face; awakening the next morning without pants or underwear on; and noticing a difficulty in swallowing, a possible sign of strangulation, according to the records.

Later that day, she reported the allegations to police and underwent a forensic exam at a hospital.

In a recorded call with the sorority member two days after the encounter, one of the men acknowledged he had sex with her, but said she had agreed to it and denied that another man had had sex with her. He said he had been drunk and “fuzzy” on what happened. He said people took video of the sorority member and him kissing in a bathroom, according to the records.

The Associated Press left email and phone messages with the university Tuesday seeking comment. Its police department said the investigation is ongoing and declined to say whether any arrests had been made. The Pima county attorney’s office said the case hadn’t been referred to it for prosecution.

The university put Sigma Phi Epsilon on probation from July until May of next year after a hazing complaint. Sigma Phi Epsilon isn’t among the five fraternities that are currently listed as suspended.

The national fraternity organization said they ordered members of the Arizona chapter to comply with any investigation.

“The Fraternity has suspended those involved while the investigation proceeds. Any member found responsible will be expelled from Sigma Phi Epsilon, and we will cooperate fully with law enforcement as it seeks accountability under the law,” read a statement from Brian Warren, chief executive officer of Sigma Phi Epsilon.

Retaliation against the alleged victim or any witnesses would also not be tolerated, Warren said.

Other cases of alleged sexual assault at fraternities have drawn recent national attention.

At Cornell University, a former student alleged that multiple Chi Phi fraternity members sexually assaulted her in October 2024. The allegations have sparked campus protests, renewed scrutiny of the Ivy League school’s disciplinary system and a state investigation into the alleged assault. Several of the men have denied that they engaged in any nonconsensual sex or denied they touched the woman at all.

This week, a woman sued Alpha Delta Phi and its Chicago chapter, alleging she was raped in February by a member of the fraternity at the University of Chicago. The woman, identified in the lawsuit as Jane Doe, claimed she was sexually assaulted during a party at an on-campus residence and that she reported the assault to city police the next day.

When asked about the case, Chicago police did not name the fraternity or provide an exact address, but said they were investigating a report of a sexual assault that happened on the same block early on 8 February.

The University of Chicago and Alpha Delta Phi did not respond to emails in time for publication.

Chicago police are also investigating after a woman reported being sexually assaulted during a party at another fraternity earlier this month. The University of Chicago said in a statement last week that a woman reported being sexually assaulted at the Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity house. The fraternity said none of its members took part in the alleged attack.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: A student protest movement has gripped Serbia for two years. This weekend it will try to take power
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Unorthodox campaign is challenging the ruling party’s 12-year reign with a bold democratic experiment

On a cool autumn evening, a team of Serbian student volunteers went canvassing in the housing estates of Krnjača, a Belgrade suburb. They were equipped with lanyards emblazoned with the word “victory”, a stock list of questions and a mobile app that mapped visited homes and the level of support in each.

The volunteers were part of a mass student movement, Student List, that has rocked Serbia with two years of constant protests. On Sunday, the group will represent the most serious challenge Aleksandar Vučić has faced in his 12 increasingly authoritarian years in power, by putting forward their own candidates in parliamentary elections.

They hope to emulate the defeat of Vučić’s ally, Viktor Orbán, in neighbouring Hungary six months ago, in a domino effect that could bring a democratic resurgence to central Europe.

Opinion polls have varied wildly, but many expert observers say a close race is quite possible, with neither side prepared to accept a loss as a legitimate result, raising the risk of post-election unrest and clashes.

In order to win, the students’ list of 250 candidates would have to break the mould of Serbian politics, along with Vučić’s grip on the country. He stepped down as president last month, five months before the end of his second and last term in office under the constitution, but only with the aim of extending his hold on power as prime minister at the head of his Serbian Progressive party (SNS).

In the section of the suburb assigned to them, law student Zak Veličković and campaign photographer Danijela Radojković were welcomed with overwhelming support. Apart from a small handful of polite doorstep rejections, from those claiming they had no interest in politics, people seized the opportunity to air their grievances.

Most promised their vote and a large minority offered help: some taxi drivers with flats in the low-rise apartment blocks said they would help ferry voters to the polling stations.

“Turnout is the key,” one said, adding: “Orbán fell with 80%” – a reference to the Hungarian elections in April.

Veličković began each conversation by asking what was the biggest problem in Serbian society, a query that often raised a laugh and replies such as: “How much time do you have?”

Corruption was the most frequent single complaint. On the corruption index run by Transparency International, Serbia ranks far worse than any of its neighbours, as the most corrupt country in Europe bar the dictatorships in Belarus and Russia.

There are frequent allegations of links between the SNS and organised crime, and the Student List’s slogan confronts that widespread perception head on, posing the question: “Serbia or Mafia?” The government denies all accusations and officially claims to be tackling organised crime.

The key local issues in Krnjača were the poor repair of the road bridge linking the suburb and central Belgrade, and the sewage system, which repeatedly fails in heavy rain, despite a personal promise by Vučić, who residents said had visited a few years earlier, to fix the problem.

The economy has been growing in recent years, but there is a widespread opinion that the fruits are not being fairly distributed. Porsche and Land Rover car showrooms have been established in Krnjača but public spaces look neglected. Some of Belgrade’s trams are more than 50 years old.

It was a major infrastructure failure that sparked the student protests – the collapse of a concrete canopy in Novi Sad railway station on 1 November 2024, killing 16 people. Evidence pointed to botched modifications made during refurbishment work, but so far there has been no official finding on the cause, and no official has been held accountable.

When Belgrade students blocked a road in a vigil for the victims three weeks after the disaster, they were attacked by a SNS mob and the protest movement went nationwide.

The students initially distanced themselves from opposition parties and avoided any kind of hierarchy or conventional leadership structure. That was partly an ideological choice and partly practical. The SNS and state-run media rule in part through smearing opponents and the student’s collective approach offered fewer targets.

Vučić rose to prominence in the 1990s as a radical nationalist, who supported the policies of Serbian expansion and ethnic cleansing led by Slobodan Milošević, who died of a heart attack in detention in The Hague during his trial on charges of genocide and crimes against humanity committed in Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo. He served as Milošević’s information minister throughout the Kosovo conflict. As president, Vučić has not emulated his predecessor’s militarism, but he has maintained his nationalist playbook in domestic politics, dismissing the opposition as stooges of unspecified foreign powers.

So far those well-worn tactics have proved ineffective against the students. A survey published in July by a Serbian pro-democracy group, the Centre for Research, Transparency and Accountability (CRTA) and Stanford University showed significantly more support for the students (45%) than for the SNS (36%), but that was well before Vučić announced his resignation on 27 September and his election machine went into top gear. Other, more recent domestic polls show the SNS in the lead, though the pollsters in question are seen by the opposition as pro-government.

Vučić himself shows signs he is taking the political threat seriously enough to throw himself into the campaign, making 129 live television appearances in August, more than four times the previous month’s total.

“Serbia has been an electoral autocracy and in electoral autocracies only ruling political parties can win,” Raša Nedeljkov, CRTA’s programme director, said. But he added that the status quo was now in jeopardy.

“What we are seeing in the past days, weeks, months, is that strength; the homogeneous government that Vučić used to have is no longer there. He is faced with a completely unorthodox political actor and the toolbox that he has improved over the years since he came to power is no longer effective.”

Unable to crush the students by force, division or denigration, Vučić gambled, announcing his resignation as president on 28 September and calling snap elections, in the apparent hope of catching the students off guard, but they responded by improvising a democratic experiment.

The 250 candidates were mostly nominated by university faculties (there are more than 160 doctorates among them) with a sprinkling of farmers and other professions, and each candidate was subject to approval by plenary sessions of the student protests.

The policy platform has also been decided by plenum, with the result that divisive issues, especially foreign policy, have been played down: the question of future EU membership has been left to a referendum and Kosovo is claimed as an integral part of Serbia.

One of the chosen candidates, Milica Jovanović, an assistant professor at the University of Belgrade, argued the List’s lack of political experience was not necessarily a drawback.

“We are political amateurs, but we are experts,” Jovanović said. “We are people who have led projects, led organisations, led our community, and actually I cannot see that we can do worse than these politicians … The only thing that matters is willingness to improve something, expertise to actually do it and support to do the actual change.”

The Student List is pitted against the political monolith of the SNS, in power for 14 years and with control of the state apparatus. It has accused the foreign ministry of rigging the diaspora vote by keeping polling stations open where support for Vučić is strong, such as the Serbian part of Bosnia, while closing them in parts of North America where the opposition could expect to perform well. The ministry did not respond to a request to comment.
