https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Troy Aikman and Joe Buck: what next for the NFL’s $165m TV power couple as they head for a split?
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
The duo have carved out lucrative and successful careers as TV audiences elsewhere are falling. It seems they won’t be together for much longer

Troy Aikman knew when it was time to go. His aching body made the decision for him when he ended his NFL career in 2001. A quarter of a century later, with one of the top quarterbacks of the 1990s established as half of the pre-eminent broadcasting duo in American sports, his potential exit from the booth is not so clearcut.

Aikman clearly feels his voice remains in fine working order, but his bosses at ESPN may not agree. The color commentator’s Monday Night Football play-by-play partner, Joe Buck, is reported to have agreed a new deal with the network worth $108m over six seasons (his previous deal was for five years at $15m a season), yet Aikman has claimed ESPN does not want to renew his contract.

The longest-running television broadcast partnership in NFL history looks set to end once ESPN broadcasts the Super Bowl in February. It would be Buck and Aikman’s seventh Super Bowl together. After that, Aikman’s existing five-year, $90m deal expires.

The prospective rupture is another tremor shaking the NFL’s media landscape only shortly after another ex-Cowboys quarterback turned high-profile TV personality, Tony Romo, was dropped by CBS. The network formally parted ways with the 46-year-old on 2 October, a month after he pleaded no contest to a civil charge of driving while intoxicated in Wisconsin in July.

Adding to the intrigue, Buck and Aikman argued at SoFi Stadium before the Los Angeles Rams hosted the Buffalo Bills on 12 October after Buck broached the matter of the contract-related tension between them, according to Front Office Sports.

The murky situation is an unwelcome distraction seemingly of its own making for ESPN, which will produce and show a live Super Bowl for the first time next year at SoFi. It wanted hype; now it has hoopla. If Aikman’s version of events is accurate, it’s surprising the company would consider terminating the partnership having earlier this year hailed a “surge” in viewership that “coincides with the Buck-Aikman era”. ESPN representatives did not respond to a request for comment, but the network has previously said it “won’t be addressing talent contract specifics publicly before the Super Bowl”.

Aikman has been less reticent about giving his side of the story. He essentially confirmed the Front Office Sports report in an interview with a Dallas radio station, 96.7 The Ticket: “There’s probably a time and a place for all that to be discussed. I don’t know if now is the time. I don’t know that it’s hard to figure out kind of what’s happened. I’ll broadcast through this season and I’ll be a free agent at the end of the year and kind of see what happens. I’m looking forward to whatever the rest of this year does hold with the Super Bowl and all that and where my next landing spot might be.” He added to Underscore that he expects ESPN to “go in a different direction”. That is a logical assumption: why else enter negotiations with Buck during the season but not his partner?

It could also make sense for Aikman to advertise his imminent availability to alert potential suitors and perhaps galvanize ESPN into making a late offer to keep him away from the competition. But publicly airing his disquiet also seems characteristically on-brand for a man who has built a reputation for candid analysis since swapping the field for the booth.

A Hall of Famer, Aikman retired after guiding Dallas to three Super Bowl titles in 12 seasons. (True fact: the Cowboys used to win things.) He teamed up with Buck at Fox Sports in 2002 and cosplayed as Mr T when the network announced its new “A-Team”. Aikman and Buck loved it when a plan came together for them to jump ship to ESPN in quick succession in 2022, with Buck traded for the rights to a college football game. They have since broken the longevity record held by Pat Summerall and John Madden and brought stability to what was once a problem position for ESPN.

Buck, a 57-year-old NFL and MLB media veteran who is the son of the beloved late St Louis broadcaster Jack Buck, is steady, authoritative but unobtrusive. Aikman, who turns 60 next month, has remained perceptive long after his playing career ended. He has also had many plays in his business portfolio over the years: car dealerships, co-ownership of a Nascar team, a light beer brewery in Dallas and a minority stake in MLB’s San Diego Padres. He’s also been an informal consultant to the Miami Dolphins.

Star broadcasters command similar salaries to elite players and attract similarly feverish examinations of their performances, contract status and potential free-agent destinations. Fox Sports handed Tom Brady a 10-year, $375m contract in 2022 – inflating the market and presumably informing Aikman’s opinion of what his services are now worth – though the fast-evolving broadcasting landscape makes future negotiations hard to predict.

The rise of streaming services has led to more games on more platforms. Unlike when Aikman retired from playing at 34 after concussions and back injuries, he may not be short of suitors. Calling Thursday matchups for Amazon Prime would not carry the same prestige as Mondays on ESPN, though the viewing figures are similar. Amazon may be ready to freshen up its act, given that its lead commentator, Al Michaels, is nearly 82 and the analyst Kirk Herbstreit’s job security is reportedly tenuous. Netflix is streaming five games this season.

Among the legacy giants, CBS promoted former Houston Texans star JJ Watt from its No 2 crew to replace Romo. If it concludes that the solid but relatively inexperienced Watt isn’t ready for primetime, the network may be interested in Aikman as a permanent successor to Romo, who was its lead analyst since 2017.

There’s a lot at stake. Viewing figures for live televised football remain extraordinarily resilient in the era of on-demand streaming and social media. Advertising inventory for the Super Bowl sold out in August, while last season Monday Night Football averaged 15.8 million viewers over 21 games – ESPN’s second-best set of ratings for MNF in the 20-year history of the show at a time when TV audiences in general are plummeting. But anything that damages the product and turns off viewers – a new pairing who don’t have the chemistry and credibility of Buck and Aikman, for example – is a problem, considering the increasingly marginal economics of the media industry.

ESPN completed its acquisition of the NFL Network in January, with the league taking a 10% equity stake in the broadcaster. It pays the NFL $2.7bn a year in rights fees. But estimates suggest that ESPN’s reach via traditional bundled services has roughly halved over the past 15 years from a peak of 100 million households. Over that time, rights fees nearly doubled. And the league wants another huge increase for its next deals.

Half the customers and twice the cost (or thereabouts): it’s not the makings of a viable long-term business in any sector. And other strategies in the cord-cutting era – job cuts, launching on-demand streaming services, embracing betting, more intrusive and pervasive advertising – haven’t come close to replicating the lucrative success of the old-school cable and satellite subscriber model.

The old certainties no longer apply, whether in the boardroom or on the air. One source of intrigue over the next couple of months is whether the teamwork of Buck and Aikman, as professional as they are, is perceptibly affected as the season’s climax and the likely end of their partnership looms. But nothing seemed out of the ordinary on the broadcast Monday when the San Francisco 49ers beat the Washington Commanders.

Buck stressed his friendship with Aikman, and the importance of getting along, in an interview with the Associated Press in 2023. “I think you need to put as much work on the personal relationship as you do the professional. I don’t know that everybody does that,” he said. “I know a lot of stories of broadcast partners that have been together for a nice chunk of time that didn’t really enjoy being with each other. I just can’t imagine being in that situation in this kind of a job when you’re relying on each other in front of millions of people live.”

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: ‘I never saw my son, until they handed him over in a bag’: inside El Salvador’s brutal crime crackdown
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
President Nayib Bukele’s campaign of mass arrest has been marked by allegations of torture and killing. Four years on, 120,000 people are still in prison

At midnight on a Monday in December 2021, dozens of soldiers and police officers stormed into the home of Sandra Carolina Velasco Mena. They were looking for her 22-year-old son, Jefferson Alexánder Hernández Velasco.

“They wanted to arrest young people,” Sandra says. “Two of the policemen said it was because they were short of three people in their quota.”

The arrest came amid an intensifying crackdown on criminal groups in El Salvador, launched by Nayib Bukele, who won the presidency in 2019. For decades, the country of 6 million had been racked by extreme levels of gang violence, with its exceptionally high homicide rate at one point exceeding 100 per 100,000 inhabitants – the highest rate in the world outside a war zone.

Homicide rates in El Savador had been falling, but in March 2022 an alleged truce between the government and gangs appeared to collapse when gangs reportedly killed 87 people in three days. Bukele responded by declaring a nationwide state of emergency.

What followed was an unprecedented campaign of mass incarceration. An estimated 90,000 people were arrested. About 120,000 people remain incarcerated – roughly 2% of the population, one of the highest rates in the world.

The crackdown has swept up tens of thousands of people with no proven links to criminal gangs, human rights groups say. The so-called state of exception allows the government to detain suspects for prolonged periods while curtailing constitutional rights. Thousands have been prosecuted for the vaguely defined offence of “unlawful association” in closed proceedings where evidence is kept under judicial seal and not made public.

Sandra insists her son is innocent and has no gang affiliation. “My son was a family man, very calm, very passive,” she says. “He worked on a farm where they cared for chickens. He loved soccer, and took care of his little brothers. He was a jovial boy.”

A judge ordered Hernández’s release at a hearing more than three years ago, she says, but instead of being freed, he was transferred to Cecot, El Salvador’s notorious maximum-security prison, the centrepiece of Bukele’s war on gangs. Sandra has not seen her son since.

“I don’t know what’s going on. We don’t have any communication with him, nothing. I don’t know anything,” she says.

Beatriz Magaloni, a politics professor at Stanford University and senior fellow at its Freeman Spogli Institute, says El Salvador has become a “carceral state of terror”.

“The atrocities are more than I ever expected,” she says. “The regime can perpetually condemn these people. There is no rule of law, no protection, it is really tragic.”

Bukele’s crackdown has also been marked by allegations of abuses, torture, sexual violence and beatings. At least 513 people have died under state custody during the state of emergency, according to Cristosal, a human rights organisation, while Amnesty International has said most deaths were of people who had not been not convicted of a crime.

Among them was Julio César Santamaría Flores, 32, who worked as a mechanic. His mother, Idalia Flores, 52, says he was arbitrarily detained on suspicion of gang affiliation on 1 December 2022. Idalia says she was initially told her son would be detained for 15 days, before being told his detention would last six months.

“My son was detained under the state of exception, arbitrarily detained, unjustly accused, of gang affiliation,” says Idalia. “I never saw my son again after he was arrested. Until they handed him over to me in a bag.” When she saw her son’s body, she says he had been “practically tortured”.

Behind the prison walls, former detainees describe a system of malnutrition, physical abuse, degrading conditions and torture.

Víctor Barahona, a journalist, was arrested in June 2022 during the wave of detentions, accused of illicit association. Before his arrest, he says, his life had been “joyful”. He spent 11 months and 12 days in custody, much of it in Izalco prison, which he describes as hell.

Barahona says he was also held in Mariona, or La Esperanza, prison where 230 men were crammed into a small cell, enduring degrading conditions. He describes most of his fellow prisoners as “innocent” and “hard-working people”.

“The guards tortured us psychologically and beat us constantly. They treat you like a rat, like garbage,” he says.

Detainees were denied medicine, deprived of sunlight, given just one glass of water a day and punished for worshipping, Barahona says. “When I was released, I had lost 80 pounds. I was malnourished. I had fungal infections. My health was very poor,” he says.

The scale of the crackdown has also raised questions about the incentives driving the arrests. Interviews with El Salvador’s police conducted by Human Rights Watch (HRW) found that officers faced pressure to meet arrest quotas, with those who fell short risking disciplinary action or losing their jobs. HRW says this pressure encouraged officers to accuse people of gang affiliation on the basis of flimsy or fabricated evidence, disproportionately affecting people in poor neighbourhoods who lacked the resources to defend themselves.

Barahona says an intelligence officer acknowledged the scale of the crackdown during his arrest. “Look, Don Víctor, right now they’re arresting everyone,” the officer told him, according to Barahona.

He also believes his work as a journalist made him a target. “I think my work made them uncomfortable. I think that is why they came to me. They did it to silence me, and they did.”

Almost four years into the crackdown, authorities have increasingly resorted to mass trials, trying hundreds of defendants at once by video link.

Defendants are unable to discuss their cases with their lawyers, says Juanita Goebertus, Americas director at HRW, while lawyers are prevented from calling witnesses and witnesses are threatened if they agreed to testify for the defence. “Defence lawyers also operate in a climate of fear, they too are sometimes threatened with being prosecuted or being surveilled,” she says.

“The whole process makes it impossible to separate the innocent from the guilty.”

Idalia Flores says she tried to build a case for her son’s innocence before his death, collecting documents to show that he had a life and livelihood unrelated to the gangs.

“I gathered information as best I could. Documents: proof of enrolment, receipts for [mechanic’s workshop] parts purchases, diplomas for the degrees he earned, the deed to the house where he lived, and letters of recommendation,” she says. “I presented all the evidence to prove my son’s innocence, but they disregarded the case entirely. He was treated like a criminal, despite having a clean record and all his documents in order.”

Yet Bukele’s crackdown has also brought him public support. Homicides have fallen sharply and the country has been transformed into one of the region’s safest. For many Salvadorans, the decline has brought a sense of security after years in which criminal gangs exerted control over neighbourhoods and daily life.

The fall in homicides has not prompted the government to lift emergency powers. The state of exception, initially presented as a temporary 30-day measure, has become a permanent fixture of Bukele’s government.

“This regime of exception is politically very profitable for him, because he can use this against anyone he wants. People are really afraid to express any dissent, any political opposition,” Magaloni says.

In 2024, Bukele acknowledged that 8,000 people who had been detained were innocent and had been released, but rejected estimates by human rights groups that 30,000 had been wrongfully arrested. He has responded to critics by dismissing them as “gang defenders”. The strongman has won the admiration of the Trump administration and conservative leaders around the world.

“I understand that those who commit crimes must pay the price. But not innocent people,” Barahona says. “Justice has been lost in our country.”

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.title: Wonderhaul: has Liam Gallagher really got into metal detecting?
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.text:
The Oasis frontman and famous fibber has claimed on social media that he is a budding detectorist. Some might say it’s a perfect fit, but either way, the gentle pastime is booming in the UK

Liam Gallagher is one of the country’s foremost trendsetters. When Oasis emerged in the 1990s, you couldn’t move for the sight of young men doing their darndest to look like him – wearing parkas and swaggering around as if they had just wolfed down a breakfast that didn’t agree with them.

Which is to say, we should probably expect stocks of metal detectors to run low in the coming days, because Gallagher has apparently outed himself as a keen detectorist. “I’m a big fan of the metal detector phenomenon,” he tweeted on Sunday, adding in a separate message that: “I do it for the buzz n the bing.”

Assuming that Gallagher is telling the truth here – and that’s a big assumption, given his tendency to tweet falsehoods about everything from the existence of a new Oasis album to the possibility that Peppa Pig would soon join them on drums – doesn’t it make perfect sense?

If nothing else, it means that he has finally found an appropriate pastime for his uniform. It’s a little ridiculous for him to wear big coats when he’s singing songs to thousands of people in a stadium, but stick him in a field on a drizzly Thursday afternoon and it suddenly all falls into context. Plus, you know, what is Oasis if not an exercise in getting stuck in the quagmire of the past?

And if it is real, it couldn’t be more timely. Metal detecting, by all accounts, is on the up and up. Not only do 1% of British adults say they have tried metal detecting in the last year, but they are finding things at an extraordinary rate. Last year the government released its reported treasure finds for 2023 and 2024, noting that a provisional 2,883 pieces of reported treasure were found across the UK (though not including Scotland) over those years – the highest figure since records began – with many of the finds being acquired by museums. And the overwhelming majority of these treasures were discovered by metal detecting.

Now, there is no point attributing this popularity solely to Gallagher, because he has only just jumped on to the bandwagon. More likely the rise is down to Detectorists, the bucolic comedy-drama written by Mackenzie Crook, and co-starring Toby Jones, which ran from 2014 until 2022. That show was so gentle, and painted such an idyllic picture of detecting, that membership of the National Council of Metal Detecting has reportedly quadrupled over the last decade.

And, excitingly, there is still plenty out there to be discovered. More than 800 iron age objects were unearthed in North Yorkshire’s Melsonby hoard in 2021. That same year, a medieval gold coin worth almost £650,000 was found in Devon. And two years before that came the Chew valley hoard, where seven Somerset detectorists found 2,584 silver coins that were subsequently valued at £4.3m.

With riches like this still lying beneath our feet, no wonder Gallagher has taken to the pursuit with such aplomb. Especially since, given the perennial palaver over his band’s ticket prices, he seems especially well versed at extracting every last penny from well hidden spots.
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.author: Stuart Heritage

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Gabby Thomas, Melissa Jefferson-Wooden and the doping tensions dividing sprinting
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
As women’s sprinting enters a golden era in the run-up to LA 2028, controversy surrounding a top coach threatens to overshadow the sport’s biggest stars

When Olympic 200m champion Gabby Thomas came second at the recent track and field World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest, she tried her best to be diplomatic: “I am an equal-opportunity doping hater,” she said. “If you are actively doping in sport, I do take issue with that. I’m not saying any names, no names are mentioned. But if you look at yourself and you think that’s what you’re doing, then so be it.”

Thomas then went out of her way to congratulate her compatriot Melissa Jefferson-Wooden, who finished ahead of her that day, aware of the territory into which she was straying.

Last year, Thomas posted on Instagram that “doping coaches should be banned for life from coaching in the sport.” Dennis Mitchell, who is one of the world’s leading sprint coaches, oversees Jefferson-Wooden’s training but had a long history of doping while he was competing. Most notably, he tested positive for testosterone in 1998, claiming the elevated levels were due to having sex four times with his wife the night before. He was cleared by USA Track & Field, but not by the IAAF and was banned for two years. He later testified under oath that his former coach Trevor Graham had injected him with banned human growth hormone. (Graham denied the allegations.)

Thomas and Jefferson-Wooden will probably represent Team USA at next year’s world championships, and then potentially compete to be the homegrown star of the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028. In that scenario, let’s just say that relay practice could be awkward.

Indeed, there is a brewing toxicity in the sprint world that may eventually rival the Ben Johnson-Carl Lewis clash at the 1988 Olympics, with the legally significant caveat that no one involved has failed any drugs tests nor is there any evidence they have taken drugs nor has anyone been officially accused of taking drugs. But the rumors, suspicions and bad blood are simmering just as they were in the two years running up to the Johnson-Lewis clash.

Throw into the mix that Jefferson-Wooden could soon smash the most controversial world record on the track – Florence Griffith Joyner’s 38-year-old 10.49sec 100m mark – and women’s sprinting is likely to be more talked about than at any time since that extraordinary Flo-Jo era.

Jefferson-Wooden is already the fourth-fastest women of all time – she ran the 100m in 10.61sec at the 2025 world championships in Tokyo. Last month in Budapest, she won the 100m at 10.62sec. But the two other athletes in front of her, other than Griffith Joyner, were aided by substantial (yet legitimate) tailwinds. Jefferson-Wooden, meanwhile, ran into a 0.2m/sec headwind in Budapest, meaning she could have come close to breaking Griffith Joyner’s iconic world record with a favorable tailwind. That would be a landmark achievement: there is widespread skepticism that the 1988 Olympic champion was clean. Griffith Joyner, who also still holds the 200m world record, died of epileptic fit at the age of 38. She never failed a drug test but her training partner Darrell Robinson said in a paid interview with German magazine Stern in 1989 that he had sold Griffith Joyner banned human growth hormone. Griffith Joyner vehemently denied the accusation and never failed a drugs test.

It wasn’t just Jefferson-Wooden who ran off with the prize money – she won $300,000 after claiming the 100m-200m double – in Budapest. Kenny Bednarek, another Mitchell-trained athlete, also took home $300,000 after winning the men’s 100m and 200m.

The issue for both of these athletes is not only that their coach, Mitchell, took drugs in his career. He has also been unfortunate in the company he has at times kept as a coach. His greatest success was guiding Justin Gatlin to world championship 100m gold in 2017 but that achievement was tainted by the fact that the Olympic gold medalist had served two previous doping suspensions, one for four years for testing positive for testosterone. Elite sprinting is a tight world of interconnectivity: Gatlin was banned while training under Graham, Mitchell’s own drug cheat coach in his competitive days. When Graham was banned for life as coach, Gatlin switched to train under Mitchell. (Gatlin has denied ever taking PEDs.)

In 2017 Mitchell and athletics agent Robert Wagner were filmed offering to supply testosterone and human growth hormone to a fake actor in an undercover operation conducted by the Daily Telegraph. Mitchell insisted afterwards that none of his athletes had ever taken drugs while Wagner said that they were playing along with the actors, who were pitching a film project. But Gatlin cut ties with Wagner and sacked Mitchell as coach.

More recently, the 2022 world 100m silver medalist Marvin Bracy-Williams tested positive for testosterone shortly after he joined Mitchell’s group and was eventually banned for 45 months. The United States Anti-Doping Agency confirmed at the time that it had been tipped off about Bracy-Williams’s drug taking and sources with knowledge of the case say the inside information came from within the Mitchell training group.

Mitchell’s lawyer, Ryan J Stevens, has told the Guardian that “Coach Mitchell is a different man than he was nearly 30 years ago. He’s committed to clean sport and strict compliance with anti-doping rules. He had absolutely no involvement in Mr Bracy-Williams’ personal choices that resulted in his sanction. Coach Mitchell insists on transparency, accountability, and integrity in every aspect of his coaching.”
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Rob Draper

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Khvicha Kvaratskhelia sustains ACL rupture in most serious of three PSG injuries
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Paris St Germain’s Khvicha Kvaratskhelia ⁠will undergo surgery after rupturing the anterior cruciate ⁠ligament in ⁠his ​right knee in the Champions League win over ⁠Barcelona.

Kvaratskhelia twisted ⁠the knee during PSG’s 4-2 ​victory on ‌Tuesday and was ‌helped off the pitch just ‌before the hour, with the Georgian winger unable to put any weight on his right leg.

Kvaratskhelia landed awkwardly after sprinting back to make a tackle on Xavi Espart and looked in severe pain as he clutched his right knee. He played a leading role in helping PSG to back-to-back Champions League titles and is one of the contenders for the Ballon d’Or, which will be awarded on Monday.

Ousmane Dembélé had earlier been forced off with a thigh injury and the defender Marquinhos was substituted with a similar injury. PSG ⁠said both players would have treatment ​for the next ​few weeks.

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

The PSG coach, Luis Enrique, used Dembélé sparingly in the French league last season and has rested him twice in Ligue 1 this campaign. The France forward, who scored six goals at the World Cup, struggled with injuries last season and had been beset by leg muscle injuries at his previous club, Barcelona.

In the 2024-25 Dembélé played 50 games in a season for the first time in his career and his performances earned him the men’s Ballon d’Or.

Barcelona have made a complaint to Uefa over a “chainsaw massacre” banner displayed on Tuesday. The banner carried the slogan “Massacre, Parisien style” and depicted a masked man in a PSG shirt cutting through a Barcelona crest with a chainsaw, with pyrotechnics giving the effect of sparks flying as the saw made contact.

Sources close to the Catalan club said the content of the banner, and some offensive chants from the stands, were reported to Uefa’s match delegate.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Austin GP is about much more than potential for Antonelli’s first F1 world title
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Young driver’s maiden championship is all but secured but Mercedes upgrades will inform next year’s run to the line

There is nothing quite like a potential title decider to bring the fiercest of spotlights to bear as doubtless Kimi Antonelli will discover when he attempts to seal his first championship at the United States Grand Prix this weekend.

For the young Italian the goal is straightforward and the culmination of a childhood dream. However, for his Mercedes team there will be scrutiny over performance in Austin that has significant implications going into next season.

The 20-year-old Antonelli holds a 102-point lead over his teammate George Russell and will become Formula One’s youngest world champion if he wins, Russell finishes ninth or lower and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton is fifth or lower. It is not an entirely impossible scenario but even if he does not clinch the title in Texas, in all likelihood he will be crowned in Mexico a week later.

Antonelli has been exceptional in only his second season in F1, but also enjoyed what was for the opening half of the season an all but untouchable car. Mercedes can no longer boast that advantage. Max Verstappen has won the past two races as Red Bull’s upgrades finally unlocked the performance they felt was there to be exploited.

Ferrari, too, are now close to Mercedes, capable of beating them and have a raft of aerodynamic upgrades arriving in Austin. McLaren, having dropped back a tad in recent races, have repeatedly proved to have the measure of the championship leaders and have upgrades planned for the coming triple-header in the US, Mexico and Brazil.

Mercedes had not had it all quite their own way then when they brought their second and final improvements to the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. Yet an expected uplift of as much as three-10ths a lap was met with disappointment. The upgrades did not deliver as expected and the car became a handful to drive, gains in lap time unsurprisingly elusive.

The Mercedes is less forgiving, switching between understeer and oversteer in a narrow window, working the tyres harder.

Such was the discrepancy between what occurred on track and what was expected that after Malaysia they reverted to using the old spec on Russell’s car and the new one on Antonelli’s to better assess the issues at the following Singapore GP, after which the Italian felt there had been an improvement.

All of which is part of the development process, especially in a season of new regulations but as the Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff noted, these updates were not only intended to enhance and improve but were of paramount importance because they would inform next season’s car.

“Was it an easy car like the previous one? I don’t think it was. Does it have the performance that we were hoping the upgrade would bring? I don’t think so yet. But it was a step in the right direction,” Wolff said after Singapore. “In Austin, we should see whether we can continue to consolidate that and whether it has more performance, because it’s crucial for the development direction for the next year.”

While Malaysia and Singapore might be considered outliers, Austin is a typical circuit, with medium and fast speed corners on a flowing track where good balance and a quick, well-behaving car is rewarded – the type of track where Mercedes were in control for the much of the season.

That said, some at the team may be forgiven for experiencing a discomforting sense of deja vu. In each of the previous four years, with many upgrades not delivering as expected and in some cases setting the team back.

To be fair, Mercedes are far from such straits now and are still quick. Yet they have nowhere near the level of dominance they enjoyed in the 2014-2020 period when they remained all but untouchable and missteps along the way were almost unheard of.

At the time the opposition closed on them but in most cases that was because Mercedes was already switching resources to the following year, confident they were ahead of the game and in where they needed to go with next year’s model.

As this season draws to a close there is no such clear-cut advantage. The front runners are all still feeling their way toward exploiting the maximum from the new regulations. The direction for 2027 is vital because the field is far more closely matched and developing at a fearsome rate, as Red Bull have demonstrated.

Mercedes’ lead this season is nonetheless formidable and while they cannot seal the constructors’ championship this weekend, Antonelli’s drivers’ title is surely all but done and dusted. Austin, however, might yet suggest whether they can repeat the feat in 2027.
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Giles Richards in Austin

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Football must not be detached from its roots as was the case with Manchester City | Philipp Lahm
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
City behaved much like other top clubs but their rule-breaking deserves to be punished. The Bundesliga, where members have a controlling stake, can show the way forward

Do we have to reassess Manchester City now? In my columns, I have repeatedly engaged with this club and its key figures. Looking back at what I have written over the years, I believe it remains beyond question that the team have achieved greatness. I always loved watching them: they were a true unit on the pitch, a finely tuned orchestra.

I would also write all over again that the conductor, Pep Guardiola, masters his craft like few others. I could recognise his teams even if they were wearing the wrong shirts and the game was broadcast in black and white – by the passes, the distances between the players and the intelligence of their interplay. It is no wonder Guardiola inspires others to become managers; look at Vincent Kompany, Mikel Arteta, Enzo Maresca, and perhaps some time Ilkay Gündogan and Rodri.

As a player and a columnist, I never had an issue with Manchester City. Precisely because, for many years, the club avoided buying the most obvious superstars. Guardiola said it himself: the most valuable of the valuable do not go to a club like City, who aren’t even the biggest football brand in their own home town.

Many became world stars in Manchester. Kevin De Bruyne had been discarded by Chelsea, Rodri’s true class was overlooked in Madrid for a long time, Gündogan’s career was on the brink after injuries, and most recently Gianluigi Donnarumma was no longer wanted in Paris. In Germany, City signed players from Hamburg, Frankfurt and Wolfsburg. Erling Haaland in 2022 was the first player they targeted who was also pursued by Bayern Munich. City did not operate like Paris Saint-Germain did in the era before Luis Enrique.

From the outside, City fundamentally did not do much differently from the other 10 or so top European clubs. But what are achievements on the pitch worth if they are accompanied by rule-breaking? The club has been found guilty of breaching the Premier League’s financial regulations between 2009 and 2018. It allegedly invested almost €1bn more than allowed and declared. The league leaders face potential forced relegation or having titles stripped. City continue to deny wrongdoing and are appealing against the decision.

It is right for the Premier League to crack down on unfair competition. I also appreciate that Germany is holding on to the 50+1 rule, which the federal cartel office recently upheld. It ensures that the majority of voting rights must remain with the parent club – the non-profit section of a professional club. The exceptions that have applied to Leverkusen and Wolfsburg are under review.

The bedrock of our football culture is 50+1. This rule exists only in Germany, yet it speaks to a spirit that fits perfectly with the European sports model: 50+1 maintains a balance; on the one hand it allows for investment, on the other it guarantees participation. It strengthens the rights of members and fans. Perhaps it is because of this rule that the average attendance in Germany is higher than anywhere else in the world.

What is the ultimate purpose of football? It is a business, but its infrastructure is still developed by the general public. That is how I have always understood sport. Even as a professional, it was clear to me that my privileged life was made possible by many people working on a voluntary basis. Through my role as tournament director of the European Championship, these political connections have become even clearer to me.

The stadium and football clubs can remain the final places where people gather and society debates its issues only if the elite and the grassroots stay connected, and the public is involved in the process. Football must not be detached from its roots, as was the case with Manchester City. This becomes possible when rules are enforced by an institution. Ideally, not by a commercial entity but by a non-profit one such as Uefa.

In business, as in politics, I am observing a shift in mindset. Today, it is deemed necessary to invest in non-profit institutions. More and more companies realise that football allows for a genuine exchange with the population – that it provides the perfect vehicle to set up corporate social responsibility projects.

This is what is needed in these politically turbulent times. In our fragmented world, political parties, churches and the media have lost credibility. In sport, however, people still come together. It is a tool to foster social cohesion. Therefore, I consider 50+1 to be a distinct competitive advantage for the Bundesliga.

I also welcome the fact that rules mean something in another case. Uefa is standing firm against Gianni Infantino, who recently wanted to privatise the World Cup and its profits. Along with his friend Donald Trump, he was seen by many as breaking the normal rules when Folarin Balogun’s suspension was lifted. The outcry from the global football community was loud, and it is possible that the Fifa president will fall.

When behaviour like that in Manchester and at Fifa is punished, it is a good thing. Football must prevent questionable ideas from distancing it even further from its grassroots. Only then can it drive engagement in civil society, and only then can it strengthen Europe.

Philipp Lahm’s column was produced in partnership with Oliver Fritsch at the German online magazine Die Zeit.
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Philipp Lahm

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Mikel Arteta has mastered the art of making substitutions at Arsenal
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Arsenal have beaten Nottingham Forest, Sunderland and Leeds this season thanks to goals from players off the bench

They say that once is an accident, twice is a coincidence and three times is a pattern. After Mikel Arteta’s substitutes proved decisive yet again for Arsenal, we can say with certainty that his ability to change games from his bench is a pattern worth noting.

With Arsenal labouring away at Nottingham Forest and the game drifting towards a goalless draw, Noni Madueke – introduced at half-time – won the game for the visitors, shimmying inside and striking a heavily deflected right-footed shot past Matz Sels. It was hardly a glamorous goal but it secured three valuable Premier League points for Arteta’s side.

It continued a recent trend. In each of their past three Premier League victories, Arsenal have won the game thanks to winning goals by substitutes. Bruno Guimarães provided the decisive contributions against Sunderland (2-0) and Leeds (2-1), before Madueke repeated the trick against Forest.

They are the only goals Arsenal’s substitutes have scored in the league this season. Five teams have scored more goals via their replacements, with Ipswich leading the way on five, but all of Arsenal’s substitute goals have been winners.

The record for the most winning goals scored by substitutes for a team in a single Premier League season stands at six. With three in their opening seven games, if Arsenal maintain their current rate, their subs are on track to score more than 16 winning goals. That would obliterate the record. Clearly, that is not going to happen, but it does show how influential Arsenal’s substitutes have been in changing games so far this season.

Funnily enough, that record of six winning goals thanks to substitutes is held by Arsenal themselves. They hit that tally under Arteta in 2024-25. And therein lies the real pattern. This phenomenon is not confined to just this season – it is an area in which Arsenal have excelled since Arteta joined the club. Since his appointment in December 2019, Arsenal have scored more winning goals from substitutes than any other team. Over the course of the past two seasons, Arsenal substitutes have registered more goals and assists combined than any other Premier League side.

We cannot solely attribute this success to Arteta’s in-game management. When you have been given the resources Arteta has to assemble a squad as deep and strong as Arsenal have, it stands to reason that the players you are able to bring off the bench are players who would probably be starters in most other Premier League teams.

Thirteen different Arsenal substitutes have either scored or assisted a goal across this season and last, more than any other side. Having that quality available inevitably increases the likelihood of substitutes making an impact.

Arsenal’s approach to matches is also a contributing factor. They are comfortable controlling games without necessarily blowing teams away on the scoresheet. They are often happy to remain patient and lean on their exceptional defensive strength, safe in the knowledge they will eventually produce decisive moments in the opponents’ final third.

That approach naturally creates situations in which subs can thrive. A substitute introduced with the game level after an hour has a greater opportunity to score the winning goal than one entering a match that has effectively been settled already.

Close victories have been a hallmark of Arsenal under Arteta. Since his appointment, they have won by a one-goal margin 66 times – at least 13 more times than any other manager.

Nevertheless, we still have to give Arteta a lot of credit. Squad depth clearly helps, but there is undoubtedly a skill in knowing when to turn to your bench and who to bring on. You might argue that Manchester City are the only side with a squad that can rival Arsenal’s in terms of depth – yet they do not appear highly on the lists above.

One noteworthy aspect of Arteta’s management is the speed with which he makes substitutions. He has already made four half-time substitutions in the Premier League this season, a tally exceeded only by Brentford (six) and Aston Villa (five). Guimarães came on at half-time to change the game at Sunderland, and Madueke’s introduction against Forest was the latest example of that proactive approach paying off.

Arteta led the league last season for the number of times the first substitute he made in a game came at half-time (11), while on average he made his first sub after 50.2 minutes in games. That made him the second quickest to act, behind only Enzo Maresca at Chelsea (47.9 minutes).

Arteta has also not always had such a strong squad. Arsenal’s current depth is the result of years of meticulous squad-building and coaching, a process in which he has played a central role.

Perhaps the clearest indication of Arteta’s effectiveness in his use of substitutions comes when comparing him with other managers across Premier League history. Among the 81 managers who have taken charge of at least 100 Premier League matches, his substitutes have scored 12.6% of Arsenal’s goals.

That is the seventh-highest proportion in the competition’s history. And, with the possible exception of Unai Emery, the others above Arteta are less comparable in the sense that they have not had the same resources at their disposal.

For Arteta to be as high on the list as he is, despite the overall number of goals his teams have scored, shows there is more to this than simply having talented players to call upon. He has developed a knack for knowing how to change the game with his substitutes. Perhaps that could be the ace up Arsenal’s sleeve when it comes to deciding where the Premier League trophy resides in May.
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Oliver Hopkins

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Can James Carville Please Just Be Quietly Wrong Somewhere Else?
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The omnipresent consultant-cum-tantrum-thrower has long outlived whatever relevance he once had, but cable producers, podcast hosts, and Democratic campaigns haven’t got the memo.

Democratic political consultant James Carville at last year’s New York Times DealBook summit.

Right now there are hundreds of Democratic fundraising e-mails in my inbox, putatively from former Democratic strategist James Carville. If I wanted to avoid them entirely, I could block or unsubscribe from the various campaigns and PACs sponsoring them, but that would not prevent me from having to listen to Carville give terrible advice to Democrats. That’s because he’s also a regular on cable news, heavily quoted in newspaper and magazine articles about election prospects for the party, and an interview subject on seemingly all of America’s political podcasts.

He recently appeared with Bill Kristol on a podcast hosted by The Bulwark and stated that he’d rather Republicans keep the House by a five-member majority after the midterms than have Democrats win, because then “they’re hostage to the DSA.” The Daily Beast, long tethered to a clickbait-through-faux-outrage business model, ran an account of Carville’s comments under the sensationalistic headline “Top Dem Strategist Makes Shock Midterms Wish.” Unfortunately, though, the fact that Carville is bashing progressives and suggesting they’re worse than Republicans is not shocking at all: He’s been doing that for years now, at every opportunity.

This has put me in the uncomfortable position of trusting Carville less than Bill Kristol, one of the architects of the Iraq War and a Republican conservative turned Never Trumper. Unlike Carville, Kristol at least seems to understand what progressives stand for and occasionally concedes that they have good points. “I don’t agree with people saying ICE and CBP need ‘more training,’” Kristol wrote on Bluesky recently. “They’re doing exactly what this administration has trained them to—impose a reign of fear in blue cities. They don’t need more training. They need to be ripped up root and branch.” In the absurdist political world of 2026, in other words, we have Bill Kristol calling for ICE to be abolished, and James Carville rooting for ongoing Republican rule in Congress in lieu of having his political sensibilities unpleasantly challenged.

Carville loathes the left in a knee-jerk way that isn’t backed by any serious thoughtfulness about what progressives want—or even what voters at large want. A majority of Democrats want Medicare for All. Seventy-four percent of Democrats want to tax the rich more. Four in 10 Americans (not just Democrats!) think capitalism isn’t helping them and are open to socialist solutions to some problems. Sixty-four percent of Americans think we should give Israel less military and financial support. These are all things that Carville and his cohort of 1990s-era political power brokers like to characterize as views held by tiny, unrealistic, and leftist minorities.

Carville often distorts the positions of the Democratic Socialists in particular, intentionally reinforcing negative characterizations lofted by fellow pundits at one of his preferred outlets for bloviating, Fox News. In August he criticized a DSA candidate on the basis that he “has the attribute of every DSA member in the country, and that is he has a motor mouth.”

James Carville complaining that someone who is not James Carville has a motor mouth is like Donald Trump complaining that someone who is not Donald Trump has a reputation for bankrupting casinos. But self-awareness is not Carville’s strong suit generally. He also likes to mouth loyalty to the working classes, playing up his “ragin’ Cajun’” persona while being married to a former Republican consultant and from the comfort of one of his multiple multimillion-dollar homes.

Still, Carville’s greatest offense is continuing to live in the reality of Clinton-era politics while spouting advice to those of us who live here in 2026. Some of this might be chalked up to age and complacency. Carville wouldn’t be the first 81-year-old who doesn’t have his finger on the pulse of what anyone under the age of 40 is thinking or doing. He’s also not the first man to enjoy early success and dine out on it for decades—or to assume that the expertise founded on that achievement is stable over time and does not need to be refreshed or reassessed as circumstances change. He is also not the only Democrat to trot out a ’90s-era political playbook posited on the vital role played by s a nebulous center of reasonable moderates in the electorate who switch back and forth between parties. Nor is he the only aging centrist who believes, wrongly, that the far left is as dangerous as the far right.

But he is one of the people who can’t stop talking about it. And for some inexplicable reason, he’s the outraged centrist whom the media can’t stop platforming as an avatar for mainstream Democratic politics—even as he stubbornly refuses to educate himself about who progressives are and what they want, beyond crude ideological caricatures that wouldn’t be out of place in the editorial pages of The Wall Street Journal.

He’s also still leaning on the idea that elections are about one issue: the economy. I watched D.A. Pennebaker’s The War Room three years after it came out, in a political science class taught by a former Republican consultant. I don’t remember any specific lines from it except Carville’s “it’s the economy, stupid” mantra, which, more than anything, defined Carville’s brand as a strategist to the public. Like many early Carville-isms, there was truth to it, but it was also an oversimplification. Voters are always driven by economic concerns, but elections are never about one thing—even Bill Clinton’s victory over George H.W. Bush, in the midst of a deep recession, was driven by increasing disillusionment with the first Iraq War, Clinton’s personal charisma and media savviness, and a host of other things that had little to do with the real economy.

We’re in much the same position now, as voters are angry over the state of the economy, but also register strong sentiments against rampant corruption and threats to democracy. Nevertheless, Carville is relentlessly on his 1992 message, trotting out a variation of “it’s the economy, stupid” on the countless occasions he’s in front of a camera or podcast mic. In a recent Fox News appearance, he brayed that Democrats need to avoid culture-war issues and identity politics and just focus on the economy. “quit f—ing around with all this cultural stuff and start talking about people’s wages…. Start talking about what we can do to protect people who are trying to make it and particularly young people.”

By protecting young people who are trying to make it, he did not mean protecting immigrants as they seek to avoid violence and detention from ICE, young women who need abortions, or young Black men who don’t want to be killed or beaten by the police. Nor was he referring to young trans people who end up murdered because the right paints them as sexual deviants or pedophiles, and people in Carville’s cohort nod solemnly and say maybe they have a point about trans women in sports. He’s talking about wages and the ability of young people to find jobs.

All politics are identity politics on some level, but like many white straight men of a certain age, Carville doesn’t consider “white straight male” an identity. It’s simply the cultural default in his view of America. He assumes the priorities of the liberal or liberal-leaning white straight man are generally good for everybody else.

But in reality, you cannot separate culture from politics, or identity from politics. Politics is about power and its uses—and elections are about who should have it. Voter perception of the economy is heavily driven by vibes in part because the metrics of the real economy—GDP, productivity growth, even inflation—don’t necessarily reflect the situation on the ground for people. Feelings of financial security are often proxies for whether people feel safe and satisfied generally.

In other words, what constitutes a kitchen-table issue—to use the refrain favored by Carville and the centrist Democratic consultant class—depends on whose kitchen table you’re sitting at. If you’re a young woman being forced to carry a baby you don’t want and bankrupted by medical bills for complications or an unexpected C-section, your earnings potential limited because now you’re not going to college and there’s a lower ceiling on your earning potential, that’s an economic issue as well as a bodily autonomy issue.

And you cannot talk persuasively about affordability without talking about class mobility via education. That ideal is under sustained attack from Republicans who oppose DEI on the basis that they do not want women and minorities in power. Meanwhile, our political economy teems with other practical obstacles afflicting the life chances of members of less-resourced communities, from the administrative burdens of receiving public assistance (some of which, it must be said, were created by Bill Clinton’s welfare “reforms”) to the increasing cost of caring for an aging population. The country’s manifold healthcare crisis—a key driver of affordability—has been made far worse by things like caretakers’ being detained and deported and ob-gyns’ withholding care because they fear criminal prosecution for treating complications in pregnancies. It’s affordability, stupid—but not to the exclusion of the things that Carville dismisses as culture war issues. In many cases, it’s an affordability issue because of these things.

Much of Carville’s analysis is facile and blinkered because he does not understand that the electoral environment of 2026 is not the electoral environment of 1992. “It’s negative partisanship, stupid” may not be the pithiest slogan, but it applies much more directly to politics in the Trump era than Carville’s nostrums do. There is no persuading the GOP to make common cause with Democrats—which is why Republican candidates never attempt it or talk about it. But like many self-identified centrist Boomers, Carville spends more energy reaching across the aisle to hypothetical swing voters than he does attending to the real-world plight of core Democratic constituencies.

Progressives—including the DSA members and candidates Carville keeps insulting—overwhelmingly supported Kamala Harris in the last election, far more so than the weaker independent coalitions Carville seems to want to reach with his Fox News appearances. Progressives exhibit the highest levels of political engagement in the Democratic coalition, yet Carville keeps insisting that Democrats win elections in spite of them rather than because of them.

I won’t pretend to know whether he does this because he’s genuinely ignorant of these facts, or because he just sympathizes more with neoliberal interests and thinks that if he paints the left as fringe-y, impractical, or stupid, that voters will internalize that message and pull the core Democratic electorate rightward. If Carville keeps suggesting that any Democrat’s association with Hasan Piker—a streamer he’d never heard of before this election cycle—is a bigger problem for Democrats than the associations of congressional Republicans with assorted white supremacists, technofascist interests, and Donald Trump himself, I’ll assume that Carville actually wants a Democratic Party made up of MAGA collaborationists. Either way, he does Democrats no favors, because that’s not what voters have told us—repeatedly—they want.

When I ponder the stubborn tenacity of Carville’s pundit career, I keep thinking about a recent Wired article titled “Men Can’t Stop Faking How Much They Know About AI.” That headline is not exactly surprising to me, since I’ve had men explain AI incorrectly to me as recently as yesterday. (I’m a former tech equity analyst and cohost a financial news podcast, but I am also a girl, you understand.) But the phony claims to expertise from American men catalogued in the Wired story have strong correlations with Carville-style punditry: One Harvard study cited in the piece found that when quizzed about AI leaders, men were more likely to confidently assert that they knew who specific people were—even when the names presented to them were fictional. They were also less likely to admit that they didn’t know the answer to a question.

Carville fits the same dreary profile: He’s overconfident about what thinks he knows and will not admit to what he doesn’t. Democrats and media organizations do not need to keep giving him a megaphone. There are plenty of smart people in Democratic political circles who have worked on an actual campaign since the turn of the century, who have informed and helpful things to say, and who understand that the Trump-era GOP is not analogous to prior GOP regimes. Nor do they uncritically assume that today’s Democratic constituencies are analogous to the coalition that put Bill Clinton in office.

James Carville has plenty of money, social connections, and leisure pursuits to keep him busy—which is more than most Americans get to enjoy during their retirement years. If he really wants to help Democrats, he might put his energies there—or at the very least, step back, stop talking, and see if he might, at long last, learn how to listen.

Elizabeth Spiers is a digital media strategist and writer living in Brooklyn. She is the former editor in chief of The New York Observer.

It’s a familiar line in the midterms: Anti-trans attacks are a “distraction” from “kitchen-table” issues. That sends a chilling message about whose rights are worth fighting for.

In a world dominated by neoliberal market fundamentalism, “socialism” is what will make a more moderate, regulated form of capitalism work for most people.
