Yet the groups that such policies are supposedly targeting are often exceptionally small: the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association has said that it is aware of only about 10 student athletes who identify as transgender out of more than 200,000 in the state.

A sex-verification requirement adds another barrier for girls to participate in team sports, Loft said, when they are already twice as likely as boys to drop out by age 14.

“I don’t see this as a way to level the playing field for girls, and we’re making a villain out of trans girls who are children,” Loft said.

Let’s Go Washington and I638’s proponents have argued in the voter guide that the sex verification requirement is a standard procedure endorsed by the American Academy of Pediatrics – a claim the medical group has publicly rejected.

Gellner said a genital exam was wholly different from a sports physical, which is used to determine metrics like vision and heart health and, crucially, doesn’t require a student to remove her clothing. She added that any policy that puts girls through intrusive medical procedures “opens up a can of worms” given the horrific crimes of Larry Nassar, an ex-USA Gymnastics doctor who was convicted in 2023 of sexually abusing girls for decades.

“While I believe that a vast majority of people who enter the medical profession do it for the right reason, writing legislation that opens the door to predators is just not responsible,” Gellner said.

Libby Watson, campaign manager for No Hate in Washington State, said organizers have spent the past year and a half building a broad coalition against two ballot measures they consider detrimental to LGBTQ+ rights: the one that targets trans sports athletes, and another that would expand parents’ rights to access public school records.

The No Hate campaign has amassed nearly 600 endorsers, including prominent Democratic politicians like the US senator Patty Murray and groups such as Planned Parenthood and the Washington State Nurses Association. The group is now ramping up its door-knocking, phone-banking and canvassing efforts, powered by more than 6,300 volunteers, Watson said.

Public awareness about the anti-trans sports measure had increased dramatically over the past couple of months, Watson said, as the No Hate campaign held up to four phone-banking sessions a week. Organizers also found that messaging around the unjustness of the policy – the fact that only girls would be affected – and the invasiveness of the genital exams resonated most with voters, she said.

“We have people power,” Watson said. “We have many people who haven’t been involved before but care enough about beating these initiatives so that Washington remains a safe state for queer young people.”

John Gallagher, a Seattle-based high school teacher and former cross-country coach, said the measure put coaches in an especially tough position because their priority is to support all athletes, no matter their gender identity.

“To me, this particular policy is incredibly exclusionary,” Gallagher said. “It’s a lot of effort to exclude a very small population of kids who are just trying to be themselves.”

Despite being heavily out-funded by Let’s Go Washington, Watson said she was optimistic that the No Hate coalition is building up more than enough momentum to mobilize voters and defeat the two measures at the polls.

“These are culture-war wedge issues to divide and conquer us,” she said. “The cost of housing, gas prices – these are the real issues people are facing and want to see addressed.”

Advocates say the state’s school-records proposal also could disproportionately hurt LGBTQ+ youth. The measure would prevent school counselors from providing a safe space for students to disclose bullying, substance use or struggles with their physical or mental health. As LGBTQ+ youth are more likely to experience homelessness, domestic violence and suicidal ideation, Jaime Fineman-McKinney, a school counselor in Tacoma, said many may not feel safe at home and need protection from their parents.

“If they’re coming to me as a trusted person and I have to then out them, I just put them in a very unsafe situation,” she said.

Loft, the Spokane-based family doctor, said it did not surprise her that medical professionals have come out in droves to fight the two ballot proposals.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/2.title: ‘They try to break us’: Pro-Palestine activists in Czech custody
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/2.author: Isabella Fattore
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/2.text:
Prague, Czech Republic – Youssef Moursi, a 25-year-old Egyptian university student and activist in Prague, has spent the last six months in pre-trial detention, accused of an arson attack in March against a Czech weapons factory with alleged ties to Israel.

Moursi is one of 11 people being charged with “terrorism” for the attack and could face up to 20 years in prison if convicted.

The case has echoes of legal battles in the United Kingdom, where Palestine Action activists have been sentenced under terrorism laws, and Germany, where five people accused of targeting a site linked to Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest weapons maker, are on trial.

Moursi, a humanities student at Charles University, said in a statement to Al Jazeera that “a group of armed and masked policemen smashed down [my] front door”, two days after the alleged attack, in which he denies any involvement.

He spent the first three months of his detention in solitary confinement, according to his lawyer. Today, he is allowed one hour outside his cell and 20 minutes on the phone a day, with visits from friends and family every two weeks.

“[There] is the psychological front being waged against us, where [the police] deliberately try to break us by putting some of us in solitary confinement for months, denying us visits, blocking correspondence, or spreading fear,” Moursi said. “Putting people in custody and prolonging it time and time again without direct evidence, mainly based on a mix of inclinations, activism, racism, and an attempted blurring of freedom of speech, is unacceptable.”

Moursi and his lawyer, Pavel Cizinsky, believe he has been targeted because of his involvement in pro-Palestine activism in Prague.

Cizinsky said part of the evidence police have against Moursi is that on the day after the fire, he posted advice for pro-Palestinian activists on social media, should they be approached by officers. Cizinsky called this “ridiculous.”

“If you put into Google what to do when interviewed by the police, the first advice is wait for your lawyer. But if you say it as a pro-Palestinian activist, if you write it to your friends, then it’s reason against you that you are guilty,” Cizinsky said.

At the beginning of the investigation, Cizinsky said he faced pressure from the authorities not to take the case. As a result, he was not present during the initial interrogation and house raid on Moursi’s flat.

“It is clear that there is extraordinary attention to this investigation by the police, and really great resources dedicated to this case,” Cizinsky said. “But the fact that he is already five months in prison is surely a breach of law.”

Under Czech law, individuals held in pre-trial detention who have not been convicted must have their detention reviewed by a court every three months. Moursi’s detention has so far been reviewed twice, with the court deciding each time that he must stay in prison.

His detention will be reviewed again in early December, and the trial is expected to start within a year.

The fire broke out in the early hours of March 20 at LPP Holding, a Czech weapons factory in Pardubice, about 120km (75 miles) east of Prague.

No one was injured but police said the building was destroyed, with damage estimates reaching hundreds of millions of crowns, or at least four million euros.

A previously unknown pro-Palestinian group called The Earthquake Faction claimed responsibility and posted videos of the fire, saying it targeted LPP Holding for its cooperation with Elbit Systems, an Israeli weapons company.

In 2023, LPP Holding and Elbit Systems announced a partnership to build drones in the Czech Republic. But on the day of the fire, an LPP Holding spokesperson told Czech media the collaboration never happened.

In the weeks following the attack, police launched a manhunt and arrested several foreign nationals including Ukrainian, Czech, Slovak, Polish and American citizens. Of the 10 other individuals accused, three are under house arrest in Poland and seven remain behind bars in the Czech Republic.

Over the past two years, Elbit Systems has become a primary target for pro-Palestine activists across Europe.

In June, a UK court convicted four imprisoned Palestine Action members of criminal damage with a “terrorist connection” after a raid on an Elbit Systems factory in Filton, near Bristol. In September last year, police in Poland arrested protesters at an arms fair for throwing red liquid over an Elbit Systems stand. This week, an elderly man in Germany was arrested after protesting against the Israeli weapons giant.

In Prague, the atmosphere for pro-Palestinian activists has grown increasingly tense.

A collective called Prague 4 Palestine Youth stopped organising demonstrations and charity events after police investigations into dozens of its members in the months following the arson attack.

Rue, a 25-year-old Czech activist who requested anonymity, said that friends of those detained in the arson case and fellow activists are being subjected to interrogations, house raids, and indefinite confiscations of their devices as the investigation continues.

Nine days after the fire, Rue said, “[The police] interrogated us, and then they took us back to [our] apartment where they did a search of the house. They kept us awake for more than 24 hours. I was having panic attacks for a week straight after it happened.”

After the interrogation and house search, Rue was told they were being treated as a witness to the arson attack. The police confiscated their phone and computer, which have not been returned.

Rue believes they were investigated because of their friendship with suspects in the arson case. They have visited two in prison; one is in solitary confinement for 23 hours a day, Rue said.

“When it comes to the end of the visit, the tears come,” Rue added. “You’re free to go anywhere and do anything, and they go back to being in those four walls.”

The individuals detained in the Czech Republic could remain in prison for up to four years without being convicted, according to their lawyers.

Police confirmed they have arrested and charged suspects of several different nationalities and remanded them in custody.

“Given the gravity of the case and the ongoing investigation into terrorism-related offences, the supervising public prosecutor’s office has assumed exclusive authority to release information,” the police said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/2.title: Iran’s enriched uranium re-emerges as point of contention in US talks
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/2.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/2.text:
The renewed diplomatic push to end the United States-Israel war on Iran is facing headwinds as Tehran’s nuclear programme, which the two countries invoked to launch the war in February, has once again emerged as one of the biggest stumbling blocks in reaching a ceasefire.

Nearly eight months into the war, which has caused a global energy crisis, a deal to ensure a permanent ceasefire remains elusive. Moreover, the war has since spilled into a regional conflict, with Yemen emerging as its latest theatre.

The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz – a global oil chokepoint – was the focus of the June Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed between the US and Iran.

The MoU had also stated that Iran “shall not procure or develop nuclear weapons”, but a comprehensive deal, including the nuclear issue, could not be thrashed out within the stipulated 60-day period. Analysts said that differing interpretations of the agreement clauses caused the MoU to fall apart.

Now the nuclear issue has once again emerged as the central point of contention, with Tehran insisting that uranium enrichment is a right guaranteed under the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT).

US President Donald Trump, on the other hand, has called for “zero uranium enrichment”. His ally, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, on Sunday reiterated his pledge to topple the Iranian government, which he said is key to preventing it from developing nuclear weapons.

Earlier this week, US Vice President JD Vance appeared to offer concessions on the nuclear doctrine to reach a deal.

While Qatar and Pakistan are engaged in mediation efforts, how will they get the sides to agree on the nuclear enrichment issue?

Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir, who is also a key negotiator in the conflict, is currently in Tehran, where he met Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei on Tuesday.

In the meeting, Rezaei said “even a particle of enriched uranium will not exit Iran at all,” according to comments carried by Iran’s semi-official Fars news agency, describing the material as a major national asset that would remain in the country for domestic use.

His response came amid media reports that the US wants Iran to transfer part of its enriched uranium out of the country. Trump has previously called for the removal of the enriched uranium stockpile from Iran.

Rezaei also said negotiations with the US would not begin until Washington fulfils trust-building measures, including meeting the latest conditions Iran has set.

Iran wants the US to lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waive sanctions, and release frozen Iranian assets as part of its latest terms to end the war. In return, Iran has promised to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Another Iranian lawmaker, Alaeddin Boroujerdi, also a member of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, reiterated that Iran is not seeking the production of nuclear weapons.

“Iran’s enrichment activities are unrelated to the US, and Washington should focus on fulfilling its own obligations regarding nuclear arms reduction,” he said.

Addressing a Republican Party campaign rally earlier this week, Trump claimed that the US bombing had destroyed Iran’s nuclear facilities and that he would not allow Tehran to rebuild them.

“They cannot have a nuclear weapon,” Trump told his supporters at a rally at Northern Kentucky University.

Vice President Vance said earlier this week that the US has “in some ways decisively won” the war on Iran and has destroyed the country’s nuclear programme.

He told a town hall hosted by CBS News that the US was now focused on ensuring that Iran makes a “long-term” and “verifiable commitment” not to rebuild its nuclear programme.

“Not over the administration of Donald Trump … but five years from now, could the Iranians rebuild that nuclear arsenal? Could they try to rebuild that enrichment capacity?” he asked.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said this week that a decision to end the war finally rests with Trump. “The US will not support any deal that creates a pathway for Iran to have a nuclear weapon. As long as President Trump is in office, they will not have a nuclear weapon,” he reiterated.

Last month, Vance told the Reuters news agency in an interview that Tehran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the war.

“If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60 percent enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don’t build highly enriched fuel. That’s a very basic threshold issue,” Vance said.

“I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity,” he added.

The MoU signed on June 17 left the future of Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile to further negotiations, but identified downblending under international supervision of the International Atomic Energy Agency as the minimum approach to resolving the issue.

Downblending involves mixing highly enriched uranium with lower-enriched material, making it less suitable for rapid conversion into weapons-grade material.

The MoU left room for Iran to reduce the material’s enrichment domestically rather than surrender it. However, it did not specify the quantity to be downblended, a target enrichment level or a detailed implementation timetable.

“The two parties also agreed to discuss the issue of enrichment and other mutually agreed matters related to the Islamic Republic of Iran’s nuclear needs, based on a satisfactory framework being agreed upon in the final deal,” the MoU clause reads.

That final deal, of course, could not be reached as the MoU expired in mid-August.

The Trump administration invoked the imminent threat of Iran acquiring nuclear weapons to launch the war on February 28, 2026. On the first day of the war, US-Israel strikes killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who had banned the development of nuclear weapons in a fatwa, or religious edict.

President Trump has often argued that Iran would use the nuclear weapon “within moments after getting it”, and then “the Middle East would be gone, Israel would be gone, and then hit Europe probably next.”

The US president has spoken out against Iran’s nuclear programme numerous times in the past.

As the war progressed over months, the US focus shifted gradually towards reopening the Strait of Hormuz as a base condition of the ongoing fighting.

Speaking in Alaska last week, Trump again falsely claimed that he had to start his war on Iran because, “[Iran was] two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon.”

In April, Trump had warned that “the enriched material, sometimes referred to as ‘Nuclear Dust,’ will be unearthed by the United States … and DESTROYED.” Later in the month, he told reporters on board Air Force One that the US would “go in with Iran, and we will take it together, and we will bring it back. 100 percent of it back to the United States.”

Mostafa Najafi, a foreign policy analyst based in Iran, noted that “despite [the US’s] insistence on nuclear negotiations and obtaining tangible concessions in this area, [Washington is] unwilling to offer significant concessions such as lifting sanctions.”

The US wants “to secure major concessions solely in exchange for lifting the blockade and releasing some of Iran’s assets”, he wrote in a post on X. “From Iran’s perspective, lifting the blockade and releasing assets is no longer a noteworthy concession for Tehran!”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Thousands of California public employees set to strike over contract
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
SEIU Local 1000, representing nurses and teachers, pushing for higher wages, telework and affordable healthcare

Thousands of California state workers were set to strike on Wednesday, rallying outside government buildings in several cities, as tensions boiled over lapsed contract negotiations with Governor Gavin Newsom’s administration.

SEIU Local 1000, a union that represents roughly 100,000 public employees, including nurses and teachers, has been pushing for higher wages, flexible telework and affordable healthcare.

The union has been at an impasse with the state since its contract expired on 30 June.

SEIU Local 1000’s negotiators say state officials rejected their key proposals: a 20% salary increase over three years, higher state healthcare contributions and flexible telework – Newsom has required state workers to be in office four days a week.

Union representatives also argued in a complaint filed with California’s public employment relations board that the state engaged in bad faith bargaining, by allegedly waiting until 30 June to respond to some of the proposals and saying there was “no money” for additional compensation.

The state has not commented publicly on the status of the contract negotiations, citing confidentiality.

A spokesperson for Newsom’s office did not immediately comment on the work stoppage.

California’s department of human resources (CalHR) had reportedly attempted to block the strike, arguing the union did not have plans to exempt essential workers and thus was compromising public health and safety. The labor board determined a list of about 5,000 workers deemed essential, according to the union, who will report to work during the strike.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: NYC built a monument to Khalil Gibran and Little Syria. Why was there global uproar?
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: Saam Niami
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
Lebanese officials were furious, claiming the city erased Gibran’s identity. Yet there was a time when Arab immigrants in the US thought ‘we were all Syrians’

This is Muslim New York: artists, thinkers and politicos on defining a new era for the city

On the morning of 30 April, in the shadow of the financial district’s skyscrapers, a gold cloth slid off a bright yellow sculpture of painted stainless steel, 7ft (2 metres) tall, that spells an Arabic word: “al Qalam”, the pen.

The monument, Al Qalam: Poets in the Park, stands in Elizabeth H Berger Plaza and honors the writers of the vanished neighborhood that New Yorkers once called Little Syria: an Arabic-speaking immigrant community that ran along Washington Street, blocks from where the World Trade Center would later rise. The monument was the first commemorative artwork unveiled under Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Little Syria produced one of the most famous poets ever to live in New York: Kahlil Gibran, author of The Prophet, a book of poetic prose that has never gone out of print. The monument honors the Pen League, the circle of writers Gibran led in Little Syria in the early 20th century.

Its designer, the French Moroccan artist Sara Ouhaddou, wept as she addressed the crowd. Discovering the story of this community, she said, had made her “truly aware of my position in the world as the child of immigration”.

“Thousands of people are going to see Arabic every day of their lives, and it’s in perpetuity. It’s for ever,” the historian Dr Linda Jacobs, who led the Washington Street Historical Society through the project’s final years, told me.

In the weeks that followed, the piece settled into the anonymity that is the fate of most public art, with tourists pausing to gawk on their way to the Statue of Liberty. That would have been the end of the story, until the government of Lebanon found out about the small parks department sign beside the artwork.

Lebanese diplomats, politicians and cultural leaders were incensed at what they read on the sign. Henri Zoghaib, director of the Philip A Salem academy for Lebanese heritage at the Lebanese American University, called the monument “wrong in time”. The Gibran National Committee, which runs the poet’s museum in Bsharri, Lebanon, his birthplace, issued a formal objection. Two Lebanese ministries complained through diplomatic channels, and in May, Lebanon’s foreign minister, Youssef Rajji, announced that he had directed his ambassador in Washington and his consul general in New York to contact “the relevant authorities, with the aim of correcting the text”.

What was the problem? As Beirut saw it, Gibran and most of his fellow honorees should not have been labeled Syrian. They were born in Mount Lebanon. To call them Syrian – as the sign did in six places – was to erase their Lebanese identity.

This might seem like a petty fight over a sign, but the circumstances are not abstract. Lebanon has been battered in recent years – economically collapsed, politically paralyzed, under Israeli bombardment and its south occupied. Two weeks before the unveiling, an Israeli airstrike razed the shrine of Shamoun al-Safa at Shamaa in Tyre, a holy site. A nation in that condition holds hardest to the things that prove it exists, and no one is more indispensable to Lebanon’s cultural identity than Gibran. Why else, under bombardment and occupation, would a foreign ministry spend its diplomatic capital on a park sign an ocean away?

The problem for the dignitaries demanding the change is that Gibran never thought of himself as Lebanese. Though he was born in Mount Lebanon, he has always called himself Syrian.

This could not be more explicit. In January 1929, for example, 200 guests in evening dress filled a ballroom at the Hotel McAlpin in New York to honor Gibran’s 25 years of work. The community’s English-language magazine, The Syrian World, ran the story under the headline: “Syrians Show Pride in Writer Who Has Brought Honor to Race”.

The paperwork tells the same story. When he first landed at Ellis Island in 1895, traveling under his mother’s name, he was recorded as “Jubran Rhamé”, nationality: Syrian. In 1902 he returned as “Gibran K Gibran”, Syrian again in 1910 as “Kahlel Gebian”, nationality: “Turkey, Syrian”. Never once Lebanese, because Lebanon, as a state, did not yet exist.

From 1861, Mount Lebanon was an autonomous Ottoman district with its own Christian governor. It was a province of an empire, not a nation, and it lost even that autonomy in 1915. Beirut, Tripoli, Sidon and Tyre were never a part of it: they belonged to the Ottoman province of Syria, and from 1888 to a Beirut province carved from it.

Lebanon was assembled only on 1 September 1920, decades after Gibran’s generation had relocated in Manhattan.

Historian Hani Bawardi – who has spent decades interviewing the children of the first wave of Arab immigrants to America and served on the committee for the Pen League monument – said that he heard “over and over and over” from the sons and daughters of the very first immigrants whose histories he archived: we were all Syrians. Though today they would be considered Lebanese, Syrian, Jordanian, Israeli or Palestinian, then they were all children of Bilad al-Sham, greater Syria.

Many of the writers in this monument spent their lives dedicated to unifying this community. They did so through creating a newspaper and literature publishing universe, on a few streets of downtown Manhattan.

Roughly 95,000 Arabic-speaking immigrants came to the United States between 1880 and 1924, and New York was their “Mother Colony”. The neighborhood that would become Little Syria grew at Manhattan’s south-western corner, along Washington Street. Its arrivals were escaping conscription, sectarian pressure and economic ruin after the collapse of Mount Lebanon’s silk industry. They were overwhelmingly Christian: Maronites, Melkites and Orthodox.

They took what work they could. Men and women alike peddled goods through the city and beyond, and Washington Street workshops later turned out most of the cotton kimonos American women wore in the early 20th century. Jacobs’ own grandmother rolled cigarettes, taking one of the only jobs available to women.

And as the community stayed, grew and became more affluent, one of its first acts was to write home. In April 1892 the brothers Najib and Ibrahim Arbeely founded Kawkab America, the first Arabic newspaper in the United States. Over the following decades the working-class colony became a temple of the written word, its presses sending dozens of newspapers across the diaspora to Egypt, Brazil, and back to the Levant.

“I still have the stamps that my grandfather used to send his newspapers out,” said Bob Madey, one of the monument’s earliest advocates. His grandfather was Elia Abu Madi, featured in the monument, who founded the journal As-Samir and is one of the most beloved poets in the modern Arabic canon.

This literature of emigration was called the Mahjar, and New York was its western epicenter; it was one of the earliest literary movements from any willing immigrants to the United States from non-European countries.

Karen Zraick, a New York Times reporter and great-granddaughter of Little Syria writer and publisher Antoine Zraick, wrote to me that writers like her ancestor discussed “western colonialism, nationalism and the re-emergence of a shared Arab identity after centuries of Ottoman subjugation”. Antoine Zraick edited a vehemently anti-Ottoman satirical magazine, Jurāb al-Kurdī, from New York. On a visit home to Mount Lebanon in 1915, he and his brother were arrested by Ottoman officials and executed for what they had published.

Many of these diasporic New York newspapers and journals of literature dreamed of what the future held for greater Syria. The historian Stacy Fahrenthold has described the Mahjar press as “a place of semiotic contest”, where activists became “Syrian” or “Lebanese” by fighting in print for the right to speak for the community. During the first world war, Gibran and Rihani helped lead New York’s Committee for the Liberation of Syria and Lebanon. On the other side stood Lebanese nationalists such as Naoum Mokarzel, publisher of the longest-running Arabic-language daily, Al-Hoda, who championed a French-protected Lebanon. “He was an agent for the French,” said Bawardi.

Yet even those born in what is now Lebanon would describe themselves as Syrian. In 1926, six years after Greater Lebanon was proclaimed, Naoum’s brother, Salloum, founded an English-language magazine for the American-born generation called the Syrian World. In its first issue, Gibran published Message to Young Americans of Syrian Origin. To be a good American of Syrian origin, Gibran wrote, is to say: “I am the descendant of a people that builded Damascus, and Biblus, and Tyre and Sidon, and Antioch, and now I am here to build with you, and with a will.”

Little Syria, meanwhile, was disappearing. The 1924 Immigration Act capped each nationality’s annual arrivals at 2% of its foreign-born population in the 1890 census, and Syria’s quota was set at 100 people per year. A migration that had carried 95,000 people to America all but stopped, and the gates would not reopen until 1965.

The colony was thinning. As soon as families could afford to, they moved to Brooklyn, first along Atlantic Avenue and later to Bay Ridge. “There’s this idea that Robert Moses came in and put in the tunnel and just expelled everybody,” said Jacobs about the city’s master builder and his Brooklyn-Battery tunnel. “That’s not totally the case.” The historical society holds the tunnel’s eviction notices; she counted perhaps 10 Syrian names on them. They had gone already.

As the place emptied, the name changed. Paula Hajar, now the historical society’s interim president, watched it happen in her own Boston childhood. In 1958, Syria merged with Nasser’s Egypt to form the United Arab Republic, and in American eyes turned radical, Soviet-adjacent and suspect. “In the early 60s Lebanon was seen as a beautiful little country, a vacation destination, capitalist and pro-west,” Hajar said. “There was a pall over Syria and a bright light over Lebanon.” It was safer to switch. “When I was quite small, I was Syrian,” she said, “but by middle school, in the early 60s, I was identifying as Lebanese.”

Only three buildings of the old Little Syria survive on lower Washington Street, among them St George’s Syrian Catholic church, landmarked in 2009 as what the city’s preservation commission calls the most vivid reminder “of the time when Washington Street was the Main Street of Syrian America”.

With the homes paved over and the name fading, the history faded too. “No one – any of the Lebanese people I’ve ever met, or Syrians – has known about the Manhattan colony,” Even her grandmother, who lived at 2 Washington Street from 1897, “never, ever mentioned Manhattan”. And she understood why. “It was embarrassing, or not good memories. They were poor. They lived in these tenements, seven, eight people to a room. I think none of them wanted to remember that.”

A century after Arabs first made their home on Washington Street, catastrophe arrived. On 11 September 2001, the twin towers fell blocks from where the colony’s tenements had stood, and in the “war on terror” that followed, the US began treating their descendants as suspects. The NYPD spent years surveilling the city’s Muslim communities, including the mosque of Asad Dandia, now the Brooklyn borough historian. In 2013, Dandia and others sued the department, alleging unconstitutional religious profiling – the city settled.

And still, the community came back. More than 300,000 New York state residents now claim Arab ancestry. The city has a mayor who told supporters on election night, “As we say on Steinway, ana minkum, wa ilaykum” (“I am from you, and with you”), and who is married to Syrian American artist Rama Duwaji.

In August a New York magazine cover story declared the city “Habibi City”, heralding a Swana (south-west Asian and north Africa) renaissance. A century after Little Syria’s editors argued Ottoman politics in Arabic publications, reading series filled Brooklyn back yards; the Yemeni cafes of Atlantic Avenue and Steinway Street play the role Little Syria’s coffeehouses once did. Last winter the New York Public Library gave this history its first exhibition: Niyū Yūrk: Middle Eastern and North African Lives in the City, curated by Hiba Abid, the library’s curator of Middle Eastern and Islamic studies.

“There’s a sense of community that comes with a lot of the cultures involved in this renaissance,” said Madey. “I think it’s transformative, breaking down barriers between ethnic and nationalist sentiments … It’s a long time coming.”

The renaissance has arrived as the federal government ends the protected status Syrians have held in the US since 2012 and detains green-card holders for their politics. “The Syrian community was in New York City 60 years before Donald Trump’s mother became a naturalized American citizen,” said Dandia. “And the Trump administration is now revoking the status of a community that has been here for two generations before he was born.”

No one embodies this whiplash of identity like Mahmoud Khalil, the Columbia protest leader whose detention made him, for a season, the US’s most famous green-card holder. Khalil was born to Palestinian parents in a refugee camp in Syria, and holds Algerian citizenship through his mother’s ancestry. He calls himself Palestinian, and almost everyone, friend and enemy alike, identifies him as so. His son, born in New York while his father sat in a Louisiana detention center, is by the plain arithmetic of birthplace a young American of Syrian origin: the literal addressee of Gibran’s letter.

If Khalil’s chosen identity is honored even by the government persecuting him, why should Gibran’s identity be overruled by the two modern states that claim him? This monument, which cost $1.6m – $1.4m of it from the arts non-profit the Mellon Foundation – was supposed to honor him and to make Little Syria something to be proud of. So how did they settle the dispute over whether it was Syrian at all?

When the monument went up in late April, its sign, drafted by Jacobs and edited by Parks, described “immigrants from Greater Syria, which encompassed modern-day Lebanon, Syria, and historic Palestine”, in a neighborhood “known as ‘the Syrian quarter’ or ‘Little Syria’”, home to “about 1,200 Syrians”. Within weeks, Lebanon’s foreign minister announced on X that his ministry’s efforts had gotten the sign taken down, and that its replacement would reaffirm the writers’ Lebanese identity. By July, a new sign took its place.

Set the two side by side and the edit is surgical: “1,200 Syrians” became “1,200 immigrants”. “A Syrian school” became “a school”. The excerpts in the mosaics, once “the works of Syrian writers”, are now the works of “those writers”. The poets, once “respected members of the community”, now merely “performed”. The word “Syrian” has been removed six times; apart from the neighborhood’s own name, it no longer appears.

Jonathan Kuhn, the parks department’s director of arts and antiquities, saw the change as routine. “They’re not permanent signs, they’re temporary signs, and they can be modified over time,” he said. Others among the monument’s original stewards were outraged. In July, Madey and the historian Todd Fine, a co-founder of the historical society, took their case to the community board. “This is not the way we normally do public history,” Fine said. Yet he sympathized with the Lebanese outcry. “The fact that a government, in the middle of a war in their country, took the time to intervene on this … shows that it’s worthy of serious thought.” But he believed the revisions went too far.

For Madey, whose grandfather’s verse is on the benches, the new sign “is an erasure of the writers and what they wrote about”, of “how they stood on the colonialist project, and how they saw themselves”. Yet Gibran’s call is still being heard. It was heard by Bob Madey, turning up at the community board to fight for his grandfather’s legacy. It was heard by Paula Hajar, who was Syrian as a small girl and Lebanese by middle school without moving an inch. It was heard by Linda Jacobs, who saw this monument through its completion, wrote its first sign and accepted its second.

Jacobs, for her part, would rather the fight not eclipse the achievement. “The history of the first Arabic-speaking community in the United States is finally being recognized and memorialized, in large part because of the beautiful monument in Elizabeth Berger Park,” she wrote in an email in October. “We as Arabs should be so proud of that accomplishment.”

https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/oc.title: What is Black journalism for?
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/oc.author: Nesrine Malik
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/oc.text:
In honour of Claudia Jones’ memory, I reflect on how diasporic reporting provides community and avoids being defined by the western white experience

This week, I had the great honour of delivering the Claudia Jones memorial lecture, hosted by the UK National Union of Journalists. It is partly inspired by the Long Wave and the extraordinary response it continues to receive from readers. As the newsletter turns two, I reflect, in the abridged version of the lecture below, on the importance of making space in an embattled political climate.

It feels like a particularly difficult time to say anything with much certainty. We stand today in the shadow of the Black Lives Matter Movement – as well as the wreckage brought about by neoliberalism, the rise of the far right, and ongoing culture wars. In the last decade, several moments have swelled with possibility and then melted away – not quite into nothing, but certainly, less than we would like. Where do we go from here?

It feels to me, as someone who began writing as a columnist and journalist proper less than a decade ago, that I broadly could always tell what my marching orders were – who the antagonist was. In Britain, a Conservative government enacted large-scale cuts to public services, and the police and Security Service institutionalised Islamophobic and anti-Black policies such as the Prevent duty and stop and search. It was a hostile environment that meted out treatment so cruel that I am still haunted by some of the stories I heard from victims I met while reporting on it. And it was a broader political culture that refused to acknowledge that institutional racism existed. Things were said to us, and about us, while we lived an entirely different reality. The sense was of a particular sort of psychological agony, one which powered much of my writing.

I remember when the lies began, after what appeared to be giant breakthroughs in 2020. There were always lies but these had a different quality – a coordinated feel. The Daily Mail would print something, and then Tory ministers would run with it, conveying outrage and dismay at the special treatment Black people were supposedly demanding and receiving. Then, the airwaves and social media would hum with discourse and debate for days in the aftermath. One particular episode comes to mind: when the BBC shortened its Last Night of the Proms broadcast due to Covid-related precautions, and the rightwing media claimed Land of Hope and Glory was cancelled because of the BLM movement. Even then-prime minister Boris Johnson joined the condemnation.

After the death of George Floyd, similar stories followed. Trying to correct and counter media coverage, rightwing myths, and mainstream discourse about race became like playing whack-a-mole. The right and those influenced by them worked together to produce a blanketting account of Blackness. If you challenged or complained, you were labelled as entitled, and addicted to a victimhood that the government had disproved once and for all in the form of an official report. Even if you said or did nothing, stories would be made up about you for sport.

The progressives were the most infuriating of all. Posting black squares and taking the knee when the cost was low and reward was high, but then retreating to the pompous and disingenuous argument of “going high” in the face of Black vilification because culture wars aren’t “salient” to voters. They were pretty salient to Black people. I experienced this time as one of almost physical savaging.

In hindsight, I see we were rapidly boxed in, with no room for manoeuvre. I felt a sinking realisation in my work: every objection I wrote or spoke was happily gobbled up by the very ecosystem it fought. Journalism regarding Black concerns and public figures became a matter not of reporting and opinion, but instant recruitment into a war. Our opponents were a disparate bunch, but were the product of a majority white establishment that just did not want to listen to the experiences of Black people, to the facts about disproportionate policing and racial profiling, and vastly unequal maternal health, unemployment, education and income. It felt like a trap. In responding to this climate, our orientation was not towards each other, even though it felt like we were defending each other. We needed to turn away from white-facing discourse and into Black-facing and intra-communal discourse. A step back became necessary. What was journalism for?

In 2024, we began publishing the Long Wave. I have learned a lot in the past two years, but the main lesson is just how much more distinctive the Black experience is, even more than I thought or intuited, because no other people were enslaved, traded and removed from their lands in such numbers and over such a long time. The Black diaspora is among the largest and most sprawling of them all, connected by similar histories that often shock myself and the team with the specificity of practices, ways of living and challenges on entirely different continents. Whether it was in common linguistic heritage, musical influences, resistance politics, and in one particularly bewildering report, shared mystical pre-Abrahamic practices.

Diaspora is not a people scattered from a homeland, but a homeland that has travelled with the people and remains, in different forms, still within them. It makes space for a multifaceted form of Blackness, which can incorporate co-existing identities. For me, these identities have included being Sudanese, from a certain tribe, and Muslim. Following that, I have found other ways of self-defining – African, pan-African, and Black. I have found that Black can mean belonging to part of something bigger. Acknowledging this follows the legacy of Claudia Jones herself, who inspired this speech. Jones’s journalistic endeavours at the West Indian Gazette supported anti-racism in the UK, but also fostered dialogue between West Indians and international freedom movements. And in establishing the precursor to Notting Hill Carnival, she also galvanised a form of Black culture that insists on its endurance on its own terms.

In these forms of thinking, writing, organising and community-building, we might find that space for manoeuvre. That breathing space as a Black British journalist, and a Black Briton who gives a damn. That space to be Black and care and write about racism – because it is simply a fact of one’s life. That space to do so without being limited by it and defined by it. And that space to be confident and ambitious and global with our own stories, without having to worry about how this looks to “them”. This feels all the more pressing to me as a Black journalist who is also Muslim and Arab. None of this will change the media or the environment we live in, but it will help us navigate it without being subsumed by it.

This is the process of identifying with a diaspora, and actively seeking ways in which we can re-connect with it. It is also a process of divesting from the particular, and embracing something more whole. To think in different strategies and approaches to surfacing Black life beyond its treatment by white majorities and hegemonic histories. To understand that wherever we feel kettled in, suffocated and disempowered, so much exists beyond the reach of the online troll or rightwing columnist. There is history, literature, political activism, carnivals, music, travel and, wherever we stand – community and gathering in the spirit of what Claudia Jones created. There are also vast opportunities for journalism that reports the diaspora not simply as an addendum to a western white experience. What is journalism for? For me, it is to exist on your own terms.

Send us your name, location, your chosen edition, and 3-5 sentences explaining why. Last week, Long Wave editor Micha Frazer-Carroll shared her experience of attending a Jamaican Patois class, and the barriers to Caribbean diasporans learning Creole languages. Here’s what readers thought:

double quotation markLiving in Scotland, I rarely speak patios, but I enjoy hearing it and sharing a few words. Its etymology is what fascinates me. I cried when I learned that nyam, our word for eat, comes from the Fulani word, nyami, meaning to eat. Also unu is plural for “you” in Yoruba. I cried because it brought home all those lost voices, words from home, and people displaced against their will.

double quotation markI grew up also surrounded by Indo-Guyanese English Patois. My grandmother’s Patois included many Bihari, Sanskrit, West African and Indigenous Arawak terms. I remember speaking on my first day of kindergarten and my teacher being quite confused. My grandmother died a few years ago and when she was admitted to hospital the staff did not know what language she spoke. Her doctor very rudely joked: “we thought she was from another planet and that she was speaking some Martian language.” I feel that she could’ve lived many more years had there not been a perceived language barrier during her care.

double quotation markI’m a Jamaican living in Canada, but I go to Jamaica every year. In Canada, the Jamaican language is much more recognised, taught at the university, translated into the New Testament and celebrated thanks to the work of many people. I write poetry in Jamaican (the term that marks it as a language as opposed to a dialect). I think we have come some way away from the stigma. You should hear my Canadian born 10-year-old grandson speak it as his mother practices with him and teaches him the grammar!

double quotation markI am pleased to know someone is teaching Jamaican Patwa, but I did not agree with parts of this newsletter’s description. I doubt that anyone would overstand kin for “skin” or kalp for “skyalp” (the usual pronunciation). For me, when I returned from England speaking “the Queen’s English” I learned Patois by being in and around Patois speakers. It blended into my language and musical rhythm until it is completely a part of how I now speak. However, may the students press on. Learning more languages is always good for everyone.

double quotation markAs someone born and raised in Jamaica, I’ve never even thought about how Jamaicans born and raised abroad may feel about speaking Patois. This newsletter was enlightening and opened my eyes to how they suffer a pain that I cannot understand, and instead of teasing them about how they sound when they try to speak like a native Jamaican, I need to give them grace and help them with their Patois. I’ll make sure to tell my friends as well.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: Why has a crumbling bottle plant been rebuilt in Paris? The stunning show suggesting the future is Ghana-shaped
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Eddy Frankel
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
Fondation Cartier, ParisIbrahim Mahama put an entire factory in this exhibition exploring Ghana before and after it was ripped to shreds by colonialism. And it’s just one dazzling installation in a show full of hope

Ibrahim Mahama has dug through the ruins of post-colonial Ghana, sorted through the ashes of its ancient history, picked through the industrial detritus, the corporate waste, the piles of rubbish, and found something pretty unique: hope.

Sit on one of the Asante stools in his circular Parliament of Ghosts and you can almost feel a new future being worked out right in front of you. It’s the first installation in this huge exhibition at the Fondation Cartier in Paris, and it sums Mahama up pretty neatly. He’s looking at the collapse of the Ghanaian government in 1966, the way the hope of the post-colonial project was crushed in a military coup, and he’s looking at ancient Ghanaian history, at the empires that fell centuries ago and the way colonialism tore them to shreds. But he’s not lamenting any of them. He’s not mourning. Instead, he’s reclaiming them, asking how things can be rebuilt, how we can move forwards by learning from the past.

And he does it over and over. In 2024 he bought an old bottle factory – a symbol of industry and its collapse. He’s rebuilt it here, in the centre of Paris. Its steel roof beams, rusted and crumbling, reach up to the ceiling, its walls are lined with thousands of green bottles in Coca-Cola, Schweppes, Kool and Club Minerals crates. It’s a whole history of manufacturing, of commerce in West Africa post-independence. Not left to rot, but rebuilt and reconfigured into something new.

Nearby, he’s taken some of those bottles and piled them around a collection of local pottery. The industrial meets the artisanal, two lost arts creating a new one.

But this huge show isn’t really about Mahama, it’s about the people around him. Most of the work here is by nine other artists and collectives. Mahama runs three art centres near Tamale in Ghana, giving time, space and opportunities to local artists. Their work is given priority here, alongside art by his mentors and collaborators. He’s taken this massive exhibition opportunity and used it as a chance to celebrate his community. It’s almost as if he’s trying to make the rest of us feel bad.

Way up on the top floor, a long scroll of jute and bark by Dorothy Akpene Amenuke undulates across the floor. If it looks like Mahama’s work, it should: she was his art teacher back in 2013. Knowledge, and the past, gets reconfigured and reshaped once again.

Nearby, the wall of a farmhouse has been built by artist and architect Courage Dzidula Kpodo out of red earth clay, a material lost as modernism brought in concrete. Now, historic methods become a kind of resistance, a symbol of tradition’s ability to endure.

Those core ideas get repeated through pretty much every presentation here. Influential 97-year-old photographer James Barnor captures the communities around Mahama in large format, grainy Polaroids. Gideon Appah’s hazy, dream-like paintings imagine fictional Ghanaian youths staring out to sea, congregating on beaches in utopian, idealised visions of the country’s past. Some of the works are absolutely stunning, like Peter Doig and Noah Davis transported to Accra.

The best work, appropriately enough, isn’t by one artist but a collective. On the top floor, a bunch of lumpy, surreal sculptures of birds, bodies and men wrestling bulls is by the Congolese Plantation Workers Art League (CATPC). Each one is made of chocolate, sculpted in the DRC but poured into moulds in Amsterdam. Everything they make from selling the art goes towards buying back land confiscated in the early 20th century by the Lever Brothers, who we now know as Unilever. The work is a whole conversation about global trade taking place in sculptural form, an act of resistance and reclamation through chocolate.

This exhibition is essentially an ambitious, ultra-idealistic group show of West African art. It is art exhibition as political utopianism. Which is great, even if not everything in it is good. And the real draw is Mahama, with his archival approach to monumental installation art, and it’s a shame to not get a load more of it.

Mahama has sacrificed himself for the greater good, basically. But this collaborative approach is the point: he’s saying collective action, community, togetherness, that’s how we’ll build a future. It might sound a bit cloying and earnest, but then you see the results, you see the art and the ideas, you see the community and the hope and the idealism and you eventually say: “Get me a one-way ticket to Accra. I’m in.”

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Cristiano Ronaldo asked for punishment ‘without mitigation’, then fought to cut it
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Miguel Dantas

Cristiano Ronaldo successfully fought to reduce his punishment for walking out on a Portugal training camp, after publicly saying his sanction should be imposed “without mitigating circumstances”.

Ronaldo said in a lengthy statement on social media after he left the camp in Denmark last month that he should be punished as the Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) saw fit and that his role as captain constituted “an aggravating factor”.

However, during the disciplinary council’s inquiry the 41-year-old put forward several arguments for cutting his punishment, including his clean disciplinary record in recent seasons and his services to football.

Ronaldo received a 30-day suspension and €255 (£215) fine, and the document accompanying the ruling reveals he presented three arguments in mitigation: his disciplinary record this season and in the previous three seasons, his services to football including recognition for sporting merit, and his contribution to establishing the facts of the case.

To support these arguments, Ronaldo listed the club titles he has won and his achievements with the national team: the 2016 European Championship and two Nations League titles. His individual awards were also highlighted, including the fact that the Al-Nassr forward has won the Ballon d’Or five times. Beyond his achievements on the pitch, he mentioned the honours he had received from senior state officials.

The decision-makers accepted Ronaldo’s arguments concerning his achievements and services to the country, using them to halve his suspension and fine. The punishment was then halved again because Ronaldo had accepted responsibility for his actions.

Ronaldo’s suspension will be served in a period during which there are no international matches. It is unclear whether he intends to return to the national team – or whether the coach, Jorge Jesus, will select him again.

The account of events provides a clearer picture of the circumstances surrounding Ronaldo’s departure from the training camp. After head coach Jesus held a press conference in which he reiterated that he was in charge of the team and that no player would influence his selection decisions, Ronaldo requested a vehicle from the FPF and set off for Copenhagen airport.

During the journey, he called the Portuguese federation’s president, Pedro Proença, and told him he was “not in the right frame of mind” to remain with the team.

“The defendant [Ronaldo] did not inform or provide prior justification to the federation or the men’s national team officials regarding his intention to leave the stadium and the training camp,” the ruling states. It says that between 30 September and 4 October, Ronaldo missed more than 30 team activities, including travel, training sessions and meals.

The federation says that Ronaldo’s promise on social media, after leaving the training camp, to tell his fans “the whole truth” brought further negative attention to the incident: “Given his prominence as a public figure on a global scale, the defendant could not have been unaware that his conduct, in the circumstances in which it occurred, would be subject to intense media scrutiny, as indeed it was.”

Ronaldo was therefore “expected to exercise particular caution in choosing the timing and manner in which he expressed his dissatisfaction with the manager’s decisions and conduct”. Instead, the player “further fuelled speculation and public curiosity by posting on Instagram on the very day he left Copenhagen, announcing that, ‘in due course’, he would tell ‘all Portuguese people the truth about the reasons that led to his departure from the men’s senior national team’,” the inquiry concluded.

Portugal are scheduled to play Denmark again in their next game on 14 November in Braga.
