This is to say: the United Nations already existed on the streets of Gotham — and in that and other ways, New York was a model for, metonym of, and capital of the emerging postwar order.

Mike’s last story is the madcap tale of the real estate deal that brought the United Nations to town in 1946. This evokes nothing so much as Washington Irving’s original Gotham — a city of ridiculous “bulbous-bottomed burghers” spreading “forth over the land until they covered the actual site of this venerable city.”

In literal landownership and in spirit, Wallace’s last tale about the Astors and the slaughterhouses and the land that became the United Nations harkens all the way back to old John Jacob Astor himself: “If I could live all over again, I would buy every square inch of Manhattan.”

There’s an important question here about the “capital of the world” argument that Mike leaves to us. What about New York as the center of the postwar world was historical necessity amid the longue durée?

What about the big architectonics — class struggle in uno plures; what Samuel Stein has called New York’s “real estate state;” the city’s place in the military-industrial complex; Wall Street; the diasporic links New York already had to the rest of the world — made the contingent possible, sealed the deal? How then can we account for the very contingent, uncertain, touch-and-go way it came about?

There’s something to be said here on New York and the “real estate state” — its longue durée in Gotham. All I know is, as O. Henry once said, “It’ll be a great place if they ever finish it.”

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Ex-tennis pro Megan Rose appointed to lead 2031 men’s Rugby World Cup in US
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Martin Pengelly in Washington DC
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
World Rugby has appointed Megan Rose, an American tennis pro turned United States Tennis Association (USTA) executive, as managing director of the 2031 men’s Rugby World Cup, a key appointment as the governing body prepares to host what is by some measures the third-biggest global sporting event on American soil for the first time.

Rose said: “Rugby World Cup is one of the iconic events in global sport, defined by unforgettable moments on the pitch and the passion of fans around the world. To be entrusted with bringing Men’s Rugby World Cup to the United States for the first time is an extraordinary honour, and I’m thrilled to join this team.”

As a tennis player, Rose was a five-time collegiate All American out of the University of Miami, and a national indoor champion. After competing on the WTA Tour, she coached Princeton to an Ivy League women’s tennis championship then worked for the WTA and the USTA, becoming managing director of major events and team leader for USA Olympic Tennis.

Measures vary but on a world scale, the Rugby World Cup is generally placed third in size and prestige behind the Fifa World Cup and the Olympic Games. Australia will host the next two Rugby World Cups, men in 2027 and women in 2029. The US will host the 2031 men’s tournament and the women’s World Cup in 2033.

Rose’s appointment comes a little more than a month since more than 68,000 fans traveled to Baltimore, Maryland, to see South Africa’s men beat New Zealand in the fourth Test of the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series, an attendance record for rugby union on US soil. Smaller-scale internationals will be played this weekend in Nashville, Tennessee, where the US Eagles women will face Italy before the Eagles men take on an Australia XV. The following weekend in New Jersey, the Eagles women will play England, the world champions, while the men face the Australians again.

Rose said the 2031 World Cup was “a once-in-a-generation opportunity to bring millions more Americans into the game and create a lasting impact for rugby in this country. I look forward to working closely with USA Rugby, and the clubs, players, supporters, and stakeholders who have built rugby across the United States, alongside the global rugby community, to deliver an incredible Rugby World Cup and build something that lasts well beyond 2031.”

The World Rugby chief executive, Alan Gilpin, said: “Megan is an outstanding leader with a proven track record of delivering world-class sporting events and driving innovation. She joins us at a pivotal moment as our US project enters its next phase – an appointment that reflects the scale of our ambition. Her experience, vision and deep understanding of the US sports landscape make her ideally placed to deliver a defining chapter for rugby in the United States and around the world.”

The US currently supports a men’s pro competition, Major League Rugby, and a women’s semi-pro league, Women’s Elite Rugby. MLR has survived since 2018 but is now down to just five teams after a series of failures, with a possible sixth entrant for 2027 mooted but not confirmed. WER has just five teams too. The US college game has deeper roots and greater strength than is generally known around the rugby world but is politically split and subject to steep challenges in funding and facilities. The US Eagles men failed to qualify for the 2023 World Cup in France but will compete in Australia next year. In England last year, the Eagles women fielded breakout social media star Ilona Maher but failed to get out of their pool.

Such hard realities have fueled skepticism around the global game about whether a US World Cup can be successful, at least in terms of engaging the American public and boosting the American game. In Baltimore, around the Springboks-All Blacks fixture, executives from World Rugby and the competing unions expressed confidence that it can.

Announcing the appointment of Rose, World Rugby said: “With more premium match content being played in the US than ever before, 25 highly engaged cities involved in the applicant process and stakeholder engagement building and fan and media interest continuing to grow, the US is poised to provide an unprecedented stage for Rugby World Cups that will redefine the sport’s future and support the ambitions of its global growth strategy.”

https://www.propublica.org/article/color.title: Colorado Marijuana Regulators Failed to Protect Consumers From Potential Contamination, Audit Finds
https://www.propublica.org/article/color.author: Christopher Osher
https://www.propublica.org/article/color.text:
The agency charged with regulating Colorado’s first-in-the-nation legal recreational marijuana market potentially put consumers at risk of using contaminated products, a new state audit found.

The report pointed to inconsistent oversight by the Marijuana Enforcement Division and loose state rules around testing marijuana products or contaminants. As a result, it found, nearly 75% of marijuana processed for eventual sale from 2023 through 2025 evaded testing for pesticides.

The audit, released Monday, identified a host of issues, including regulators’ failure to meet regular inspection schedules or to conduct sufficient random checks at dispensaries for contaminated products. It also found that delayed agency warnings to the public allowed potentially contaminated products to remain on shelves for months, sometimes years.

The audit’s conclusions echo several findings of an investigation this year by The Denver Gazette and ProPublica into the Marijuana Enforcement Division’s lapses in policing contaminants entering the legal marketplace.

In one case highlighted by the newsrooms, it took 15 months for a manufacturer to discontinue production of a marijuana sleep aid pill despite consumers warning regulators that the product was harming their livers. The pills had herbal extracts that researchers say can cause liver damage.

Auditors said they did not identify evidence of “widespread health and safety issues” but did find that deficient regulations still left consumers vulnerable.

The audit found that unsafe products had remained on the market for as long as three years before the Marijuana Enforcement Division issued a public warning. The auditor’s review of the agency’s health and safety advisories found that, on average, from 2023 through 2025, contaminated products that were the subject of an advisory remained on shelves for more than seven months. That’s the same number of months the news organizations found contaminated products stayed on shelves before warnings were issued.

The audit also found that it took the agency three and a half months, on average, in 2025 to issue an advisory once it launched an investigation into potential contamination. Even after investigators determined an advisory was needed, it still took the agency a month on average to issue one.

“These issues limit MED’s ability to meet its core objective to identify product safety risks and to help ensure that licensed marijuana businesses meet product safety requirements,” the audit stated. “As a result, there is an increased risk that marijuana products sold in Colorado may have contaminants or that the potency listed on the labels is inaccurate.”

We reported that a top Marijuana Enforcement Division official acknowledged in a meeting with industry representatives that the amount of chemically converted hemp being sold as marijuana is greater than the agency has publicly disclosed.

State regulators announced a plan to crack down on companies that illegally sell cheaper and potentially hazardous hemp products as marijuana, citing potential tax avoidance and “serious risks to public safety.”

Colorado regulators discussed a proposal to do away with the current testing system that allows marijuana manufacturers to choose their own samples. Instead, independent labs or contractors would collect the samples.

The Denver Gazette and ProPublica reported that intoxicating hemp has seeped into Colorado’s marijuana market because the state had failed to adopt safety measures. Tests found signs of hemp in vapes sold at marijuana dispensaries.

After hemp companies figured out how to convert CBD into the high-inducing compound THC, Colorado became one of the first states to ban chemically converted hemp products, first with regulatory advisories and then with legislation.

President Donald Trump signed the Farm Bill, which legalizes hemp. Congress’ intent was to help farmers along with people who believe hemp’s high levels of the nonintoxicating compound CBD can help with seizures, pain and sleep.

Colorado became the first state to allow retail sales of marijuana for recreational use.

Colorado allows marijuana businesses to test far less frequently than required by state guidelines if they can show consistent compliance with testing rules. The reduced testing program results “in a significant portion of the marijuana product being sold in Colorado not undergoing testing to ensure it is safe,” the audit stated. Manufacturers also can rely on other testing exemptions, such as for certain marijuana-derived skin and body products, but there is “limited MED oversight” of how manufacturers determine they qualify for an exemption.

Auditors reported that a survey of MED investigators found that more than half said there are or may be widespread marijuana product safety issues in Colorado’s regulated market.

In a statement released Monday night, the Marijuana Enforcement Division emphasized that state auditors found no evidence “to support claims of widespread health and safety issues” with marijuana products for sale in Colorado, but the agency agreed the audit identified areas for improvement. It said that among other things, it would be assessing exemptions to tests currently allowed under state laws and regulations.

The state auditor’s review “allows us to take a critical look at how we can continue to carry out our work, consistent with our commitment to integrity, safety, and continuous operational improvement,” Dominique Mendiola, senior director of the MED, said in a statement.

The auditor’s report highlighted a criticism her agency has repeatedly sidestepped: the absence of independent collection of samples for safety testing. The Denver Gazette and ProPublica found that more than half of states with regulated marijuana markets rely on private labs or an independent third party to collect samples. Colorado marijuana businesses are free to collect their own samples submitted for testing.

The enforcement division’s own investigators told auditors that, as a result, Colorado relies largely on an honor code to ensure the safety of marijuana sold in the state’s dispensaries.

Auditors said that allowing businesses to select their own samples “increases the risk that businesses do not pick samples that are representative of the overall quality of their marijuana product.”

MED regulators at the start of the year said they planned to pursue an overhaul that would have required private lab personnel to collect samples, but they abandoned that effort after manufacturers said it would increase their costs. On Monday, Kyle Lambert, the enforcement division’s deputy senior director, told legislators that the agency opted against an overhaul this year, chiefly because he said it would be a geographic challenge to do away with self-sampling for rural businesses.

“It was decided now wasn’t the right time to propose that as a policy change,” Lambert said, adding that the agency still might revisit the issue.

State Sen. Byron Pelton, a Republican from Sterling, pushed back, saying it was a loophole he thinks the agency should consider closing.

“If I’m a shady character, I know which products I’m going to go sampling and which ones I’m not,” he said. “That’s a pretty gray area to me.”

The audit also questioned the agency’s reliance on businesses voluntarily recalling contaminated marijuana products, saying that “some of these recalls did not succeed at stopping the businesses from selling potentially unsafe product.”

Just last month, The Denver Gazette and ProPublica reported that a Colorado manufacturer voluntarily flagged 49 of its popular marijuana vapes for recall, nearly six weeks after a third-party lab notified the company and regulators that it detected methylene chloride, a chemical the Environmental Protection Agency has sought to ban for most uses because it can cause cancer. The MED issued a health and safety advisory a day after the publications first reported the manufacturer had warned dispensaries to stop selling the vapes, which consumers had been purchasing for over a year.

Your support today will directly fund investigations that shine a light on urgent issues: corporations prioritizing profits over public safety, health insurers denying coverage to patients, unintended consequences of new laws and more.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Supreme court blocks Trump’s bid to restrict gender care for trans prisoners
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Marina Dunbar
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Decision stands in contrast to recent trans rights actions from court that often sides with Trump administration

The US supreme court went against Donald Trump’s administration on Wednesday, refusing to allow the immediate enforcement of sweeping restrictions on gender-affirming care for transgender individuals held in prisons and federal facilities.

The decision marks an unusual victory for transgender rights before the nation’s highest court, which has largely sided with the administration and other opponents of transgender rights in several major cases.

In its latest action, the supreme court turned away an emergency appeal from the justice department seeking to overturn a federal judge’s order that prevents the Federal Bureau of Prisons from putting the controversial restrictions into effect while a lawsuit challenging them moves forward.

Two conservative members of the court, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, publicly opposed the decision.

At the center of the legal battle is a policy introduced earlier this year that would sharply limit medical care and other accommodations available to transgender people in federal custody.

Under the measure, medical and surgical treatments related to gender transition would be prohibited. The restrictions would also extend to “social accommodations”, including access to clothing and hair-removal devices intended to help prisoners present themselves in a way that matches their gender identity. Psychiatric care would remain available under the policy.

The restrictions prompted three transgender people incarcerated at federal correctional facilities in New Jersey, Florida and Minnesota to bring a class-action lawsuit challenging the government’s actions.

The proposed changes represent a big departure from longstanding federal prison practices. According to the plaintiffs, the federal prison system has provided hormone treatment to prisoners experiencing gender dysphoria since at least 1992.

The dispute comes amid Trump’s broader campaign to roll back transgender rights since beginning his second presidential term.

On his first day back in the White House, Trump signed an executive order declaring that the federal government would recognize only two genders, male and female, while portraying transgender identity as false.

The order directed multiple federal agencies to revise their practices, including requirements ensuring that “males are not detained in women’s prisons” and ending government funding for medical procedures provided “for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex”.

In defending the prison restrictions in court, government lawyers have characterized gender-transition medical treatment as “unproven sex-rejecting interventions”.

But the plaintiffs challenging the policy have warned that allowing the restrictions to take effect could have devastating consequences. In their legal filing, the plaintiffs argued that a decision favoring the administration would result in “immediate and catastrophic” harm.

They pointed to serious mental health concerns, warning: “Patients who are denied hormone therapy can suffer from increased depression, anxiety, suicidal ideation and self-harm.”

Wednesday’s decision stands in contrast to several recent supreme court actions involving transgender rights. The court, which holds a 6-3 conservative majority, has issued multiple decisions since last year that have favored restrictions affecting transgender Americans.

Among those decisions, the justices supported state laws preventing transgender athletes from competing on female sports teams at public schools, including colleges and universities.

The court also permitted the Trump administration to enforce its ban on transgender people in the military. In another decision, the justices allowed the administration to prevent passport applicants from selecting gender designations reflecting their gender identities.

The legal fight carries potential consequences for thousands of people within the federal correctional system. More than 2,000 transgender prisoners were housed in federal prisons and halfway houses in 2025, according to reporting from NPR.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Controversial US-backed vaccine trial in African newborns halted
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Melody Schreiber
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Hepatitis B study in Guinea-Bissau that was to be funded by CDC and that drew global backlash ‘will not move forward’

The US-backed hepatitis B vaccine trial in African newborns that drew global backlash was halted, the lead researcher said on Wednesday.

It was “now clear” that the study “will not move forward in Guinea-Bissau”, Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, a Danish researcher, wrote on LinkedIn, adding, “we were not given the necessary governmental approval.”

The minister of health in Guinea-Bissau, Quinhin Nantote, previously denied that the project would move forward. “This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese last week.

The study was to be funded with $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with another $1.6m from private partners like the Bill Ackman-backed Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.

“The solution is clear here: take the money and vaccinate as many kids as you can,” said Paul Offit, a vaccines expert at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, who sharply criticized the proposed study as unethical.

The government of Guinea-Bissau now has control over the researchers’ vaccines, which they apprehended when they searched the offices of the Bandim Health Project on Monday.

It was vital to support Guinea-Bissau in rolling the immunizations out to all newborns as soon as possible, Offit said. Guinea-Bissau currently plans to offer the universal birth dose in 2028.

The Danish researchers, led by Schaltz-Buchholzer, Christine Stabell Benn and Peter Aaby, hypothesized giving live vaccines, like the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), may have an overall mortality benefit beyond simply preventing illnesses like tuberculosis – but giving another vaccine like hepatitis B alongside it could dampen that effect.

Such a hypothesis was “fanciful” because the hepatitis B vaccine is a single protein among billions encountered by the immune system each day, Offit said.

“There’s no evidence for that, and it doesn’t make biological sense,” he continued. He also added that there was a very clear benefit to giving the vaccine to babies as soon as possible, because of high rates of hepatitis B in the country and the possibility of lifelong illness and death from infection.

The Danish researchers did not respond by press time to questions about the study or to this criticism. The CDC did not respond by press time to questions about whether the funding, which was appropriated through its global health work, would now be used to roll out the vaccine to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO).

“WHO recommends that all infants receive a first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth – preferably within 24 hours – followed by at least two additional doses,” said Tarik Jašarević, a WHO spokesperson. “WHO remains committed to working with national authorities, researchers, and partners to ensure that all newborns – in Guinea‑Bissau and worldwide – receive timely, evidence‑based protection against hepatitis B.”

Those who declined participation in the study would not have received the vaccines – making true informed consent impossible, experts say.

“Imagine you’re a mother. You want to do the best for your child,” said Henrik Støvring, a Danish researcher who has co-published research raising questions about previous research from the Bandim project.

“If they decide to participate in the trial, they have a 50% chance of getting the vaccine for their children. But if they stay out, they have a 0% chance of getting the vaccine. So how can you say that’s a non-coercive informed consent?” Støvring asked.

The proposed trial led to distrust among Bissau-Guineans, who wondered if the vaccine – which has a decades-long record of being safe and effective – was being tested on Africans because it was dangerous, Schaltz-Buchholzer said in his post.

It “should be clear” that both birth vaccination schedules – with or without hepatitis B – are not “dangerous to anyone”, he wrote. There is a clear benefit to giving hepatitis B vaccines at birth, and not doing so can lead to lifelong danger, experts say.

Conducting a study like this “makes the case that there’s something that’s worthy of study, for which they have no evidence”, Offit said.

“We have millions and millions, arguably hundreds of millions, of children in this world who have gotten that vaccine as a birth dose or haven’t. If there was any evidence that this was problematic, you would know this by now,” Offit added. “We eliminated hepatitis B in the United States in children virtually within years of starting that program, so the benefits are clear.”

Schaltz-Buchholzer also cast doubt on the effectiveness and safety of the hepatitis B vaccine at birth, noting that he believes the study was canceled because it challenges “prevailing medical assumptions, such as that HBV0 does not have non-specific effects”. The study, in addition to looking at mortality, would have also examined side-effects such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. Dozens of studies have shown no link between vaccination and autism.

“All newborns should be given a birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine,” Offit said. “Guinea-Bissau is a country that suffers a high incidence of chronic hepatitis B. That country, more than any other country, arguably, needs to launch this program.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump’s approval rating drops to 36% two weeks before midterms, poll finds
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ariana Baio
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Voters disapprove of Trump’s handling of economy and cost of living, says poll in new low recorded by NY Times/Siena

Donald Trump’s approval rating sank to 36% just two weeks before the midterm elections, the lowest recorded in a poll by the New York Times/Siena College, with most respondents expressing frustration over his handling of the US economy, cost of living and Iran war.

In an October survey of approximately 3,494 likely voters, 59% said they disapproved of Trump’s handling of his job, and 52% said they planned to vote for the Democratic candidate in the upcoming election.

Much of the disapproval toward the US president was associated with frustrations over Trump’s handling of economic and cost-of-living-related issues. On gas prices, 73% of registered voters said they disapproved; on the cost of living, 69% said they disapproved, and on the economy, 64% said they disapproved.

Approximately 65% said they disapproved of Trump’s handling of the Iran war, which has dragged on for nearly eight months and pushed gas and oil prices up.

The new polling numbers paint a gloomy picture for Trump and Republicans, who have embarked on an uphill battle to defeat Democrats in the upcoming midterms to maintain their majority control in Congress.

Trump, whose name recognition has largely helped Republican candidates in past elections, has been on the road campaigning for Maga-aligned candidates. However, some candidates have sought to distance themselves from the president, who has become increasingly unpopular over his economic policies.

In 2024, Trump promised to lower everyday costs for Americans, keep inflation low and to keep the US from starting more wars abroad.

But as of 21 October, gas prices were more than $4.25 a gallon, inflation increased to 3.7% last month and the president’s war with Iran remained steady.

Between September and October, the US president’s approval rating decreased by two percentage points in the New York Times/Siena College polls.

Democratic candidates, meanwhile, have seized on the cost-of-living issues to appeal to independents and undecided voters, promising to rein in the president’s policies that have pushed costs up, such as tariffs.

While polling from the New York Times/Siena College indicates Democrats have the upper hand headed into next month’s election, the party is still fighting against a massive financial war chest in competitive races in Texas, Ohio, New York, Alaska and Iowa.

https://jacobin.com/2026/10/egypt-middle.title: Medieval Egypt Was No Stranger to Class War
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/egypt-middle.author: Nicholas Liu
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/egypt-middle.text:
On Roda Island in the Nile stands a stone column nineteen cubits (thirty-four feet) tall and nearly 1,200 years old. It is called the Nilometer. Before the construction of the Aswan Dam, an official would measure how high the river rose and from that reading determine the fate of the country’s annual harvest. By the eleventh century and continuing until the Ottoman Turkish conquest of 1517, the rulers of Egypt had made a tradition of exorbitant pageantry whenever the waterline reached sixteen cubits: the harvest would be reaped, the cosmic and communal order confirmed, the people fed and placated, and the land tax collected.

But not all Nilometer news was good news. If, by around the end of August, the water still had not reached sixteen cubits, the festivities and the land tax would be canceled, and the people would know that hard times lay ahead. Conversely, a continued rise to eighteen or nineteen cubits would mean the Nile was flooding and could take thousands of homes and people with it.

Some believed that such disasters were cosmic warnings against society’s sins, and that the ruling class — military cliques, government officials, and private landowners — was to blame for those sins. But God’s punishment did not fall only on the guilty. “Fear a trial which will not strike those who have wronged among you exclusively,” reads a verse in Al-Anfal, the eighth chapter of the Qur’an. Tyranny and corruption (fasad) were seen as a rot that spread through the entire communal order, as with the People of Lot before their destruction. Divine wrath was an elemental force, not a paper writ delivered to particular individuals. Popular protest was different, as the ruling classes were sometimes reminded. It could be just as sudden, furious, and overwhelming, but it was precise in its targets, and its moral and religious justification was plain to all.

The wealthiest members of society often profited most during these periods of heightened suffering. Merchants and nobles would hoard grain even in good times to anticipate a future shortage, but most forms of state discipline targeted only bakers and millers of the lower middle class, or what medievalists often call the “conjunctural poor” — those who fluctuated between subsistence and poverty as economic conditions shifted. Al-Musabbihi, a chronicler and official under the Fatimid dynasty (969–1171), lived through the famine of 1024–25 and wrote of grain shipments diverted to the palace, the sight of bodies buried without ritual washing or shrouds, and starving people reduced to eating grass.

The threat of popular violence put the palace on edge. On January 16, 1025, the caliph, making a procession through Cairo, was confronted by shouting: “Hunger, oh Commander of the Faithful, hunger! Neither your father nor your grandfather did such a thing to us.” Hunger spread from the civilian population to the black infantry of the caliph’s army, a corps composed of Sudanese slave soldiers. Soon both were rummaging for grain wherever they could find it, including in government warehouses opened by sympathetic or terrified officials.

That famine set a pattern that would hold for more than five hundred years. When the river failed, the people who controlled the grain found ways to profit, and the people who went hungry found ways to make them pay, or at least fear.

The Fatimid regime was dismantled in 1171 by the Kurdish warlord Saladin, whose Ayyubid dynasty was in turn overthrown in 1250 by its own Mamluks — Turkic and Circassian slave soldiers who subsequently established a military-patronage state that controlled Egypt, Palestine, and Syria until 1517. Despite the perennial hum of coups and infighting around the sultan’s throne, 250 years of relative administrative continuity lent the regime enough time and resources to build towering institutions of religious welfare and political legitimacy, patronize a literary renaissance, and organize Egypt as the focal point of Mediterranean and Indian Ocean commerce.

Nevertheless, the limited safety net and trade money were parts of a system far more extractive than the Fatimid state had ever been. Mamluk captains, trying to control a potentially restive population and needing money to keep buying new Mamluks from the slave markets of Crimea, parceled out iqta (revenue assignments) among themselves and hoarded supplies to an unprecedented degree. The traditional lines between military and civilian roles blurred as some captains in turn leased their iqtas to non-Mamluk administrators, while they themselves lobbied the sultan for lucrative administrative positions, like that of muhtasib, the office responsible for policing the markets. Compounding disasters then made a bad situation far worse: the black death of the mid-fourteenth century wiped out the rural workforce, dikes and canals silted up (which meant the Nile had to rise higher for a sufficient harvest), and the effects of the Little Ice Age made the river itself far more erratic.

Matters came to a head in 1403 during the rule of the teenage Sultan Faraj ibn Barquq, when the Nile once again failed to rise just after the Turco-Mongol warlord Timur had ravaged Mamluk Syria and another wave of the black death approached. Mamluk amirs, or commanders, responded by fighting each other and squeezing their tenants even harder to keep their own ledgers balanced. Faraj and his government, unable to materially solve any problems or admit to their own failures, resorted to massive public prayers for rain and crackdowns on supposed expressions of moral decay like alcohol, prostitution, and religious minorities who flouted sumptuary laws. Adam Sabra writes in Poverty and Charity in Medieval Islam: Mamluk Egypt, 1250–1517 that during the 1403–4 crisis, chroniclers made no mention of any state-sanctioned relief efforts, though individual sultans and amirs were typically more generous with their alms whenever they themselves fell sick, hoping God would reward their charity with a cure.

The sense of insecurity and trauma brought by calamity and misrule may have encouraged Mamluk-era historians to increasingly supplement their record of events with commentary on the conditions of the wider city and common people. Al-Maqrizi (1364–1442), the most prolific among them, opined that the Nile disasters were not merely acts of God or unlucky natural patterns but a product of three human causes: a corrupt government lubricated with bribery, extreme rent-seeking and hoarding behavior by the moneyed and landowning classes, and the reckless policy of flooding the market with low-value, inflationary copper coins.

“Whoever reflects on this occurrence from its beginning to its end and knows its origin and development realizes that what has befallen the population is caused solely by the malfeasance of the leaders and rulers and their negligence with regard to the public interest,” he wrote in his treatise Helping the Community by Examining the Causes of Its Distress (Ighathat al-ummah bi-kashf al-ghummah). “Indeed, wherever the causes are known, it is easy for the knowledgeable person to remedy all conditions, whether significant or insignificant. I seek God’s help in facing both difficult and easy matters; indeed ‘He tells the truth and He shows the way.’”

The people in the streets had reached the same conclusion on their own. And when the powerful pushed too far, they pushed back.

Al-Maqrizi’s chronicles record the constant protests that emerged in reaction to state depredation. Throughout the Middle Ages and even more frequently during the Mamluk period, ordinary people channeled their frustration through tax evasion, smuggling, blocking the sultan’s or governor’s processions, collective petitioning (shouted or in writing), and, in extreme cases, violence.

Those activities often came hand in hand, with petition typically following demonstration. Protest had no realistic chance of overturning state power (nor was that its purpose) but could apply sufficient pressure on authorities hoping to maintain their government positions and protect their property from physical damage. In pursuit of material reward and social correction, crowds applied violence systematically, indicating that they had a clear sense of a moral economy and the wrongness of transgressing it.

One favored tradition of anti-profiteering protesters was finding the local muhtasib they deemed responsible and stoning him. The Mamluk-era historian Ibn Taghribirdi recorded how in 1435, a crowd in Cairo sent the muhtasib fleeing into the Citadel for protection. Another example of this occurred in 1487, when, amid rising grain prices, the muhtasib of Damascus was found to be mixing his government duties with his private involvement in the grain trade. Shams al-Din ibn Tulun recorded that an organized crowd found him patrolling the market and proceeded to unload its displeasure on him. These two officials may have suffered a nasty shock and some injuries, but they were fortunate compared to the governor and deputy governor of Damietta in 1417, who, as al-Maqrizi records, were “arrested” by the crowd, humiliated, and then struck dead.

The elite response to such protests was varied. Amina Elbendary writes in Crowds and Sultans: Urban Protest in Late Medieval Egypt and Syria of the fluidity of such crowds and indeed of social categories in general. The protesters, consisting not just of the “structural/permanent poor” but also artisans, shopkeepers, and lower-level clerics, often sought out members of the clerical establishment (ulama), or even a muhtasib they considered to be morally upright, to intercede with the government on their behalf. In the case of the 1417 incident at Damietta, the crowd brought some of their local religious judges to register a case against the same governor they were about to lynch.

These actions sometimes elicited refusal or even more punitive taxes. Other times, the protest and subsequent petition secured localized, temporary alleviation rather than structural reforms. But the broader tradition of protesting economic predation was understood by both rulers and the people as a constant threat or leverage that punished anyone who overstepped the line.

Muslims are instructed by the Qur’an and hadith to enjoin good and forbid wrong — a commandment that extends beyond personal survival and piety to the proactive pursuit of social justice. Innocent victims of misfortune could be seen as casualties of elite misconduct or, if they bore their suffering patiently, even as martyrs. But a society that accepted unjust rulers and did not rise up against them was itself complicit. Both sides, then, took their case to God. In a crisis, the ruling class organized mass public prayers for rain. Protesters often shouted “God is great” before a demonstration, and chroniclers described such moments by writing that “prayers against the sultan [or governor] increased.”

The Mamluk regime did not survive the collapse of its trade revenue, driven by Portuguese naval ambitions, and the Ottoman advance into the Levant and Egypt. Qansuh al-Ghuri, the penultimate Mamluk sultan, regarded by chroniclers as the most avaricious among the rulers of that period, supposedly died of a stress- and battle-induced stroke on the plains of Marj Dabiq in front of his Qur’an readers.

A change in regime, however, did not keep people off the streets whenever greed or misrule threatened their livelihoods. In 1591, not long after the Cairenes “prayed against” him, Awis Pasha, the city’s governor, died of a stroke.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/2.title: Macron makes surprise Saudi visit as France secures extra diesel supplies
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/2.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/2.text:
French President Emmanuel Macron visited Riyadh on a surprise “solidarity” visit, making him the first Western leader to touch down in Saudi Arabia since the Houthis intensified their attacks this month.

The unannounced trip comes as Saudi Arabia agreed to supply extra diesel to France “for as many months as necessary”, the Elysee Palace told the AFP news agency on Wednesday.

The visit aims to “demonstrate France’s solidarity with the kingdom in the face of the attacks carried out by the Houthis against its territory, and to continue efforts undertaken on securing and diversifying hydrocarbon supplies”, the French presidency said earlier.

The diplomatic push follows days of rioting in France, fuelled by the cost of living, especially as the US-Iran war and Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz have kept energy prices high.

Faced with criticism of his Gulf tour at home, Macron told reporters he was just “doing his job” in a bid to “ease tensions” over petrol prices, one of the causes of social unrest in France.

“There must be no sign of febrility,” he said. “I am fulfilling my role. I am at my post.”

Macron met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in the Saudi capital, and the two agreed to consult on expanding security cooperation and on infrastructure projects to bypass the blockaded strait, the palace said.

The deal follows pledges secured earlier in Macron’s Gulf tour. The presidency said on Tuesday that the United Arab Emirates had committed to about 100,000 tonnes a month, with a further 100,000 tonnes monthly to be secured in Bahrain.

Together with Saudi deliveries, France now has commitments for 295,000 tonnes a month, just more than 10 percent of its consumption, it said.

Meanwhile, France is also sending military assets to Saudi Arabia, under an earlier agreement, to help protect the Red Sea port of Yanbu, which has come under attack from the Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God).

The United Kingdom also announced on Tuesday that it would deploy fighter jets to help shield the kingdom. Both countries say their support is purely defensive.

Analysts say the moves protect Saudi oil exports that matter to Europe’s energy markets and bolster the Gulf alliance as the US shows reluctance to offer direct military help. They also carry risks, analysts say, potentially drawing the two European states into the protracted Saudi-Houthi conflict.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Heidi Levine recounts how Palestinian youths helped save her in settler attack
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Julian Borger in Petah Tikva
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
US photojournalist describes ‘protective shield’, vows to return to work in West Bank and criticises Netanyahu comments on incident

The Washington Post photojournalist who was attacked and seriously injured by Israeli settlers on the West Bank on Friday has described how she was saved with the help of local Palestinians.

Heidi Levine sustained four fractured vertebrae, two broken ribs and four puncture wounds when she was knocked to the ground and repeatedly beaten by a crowd of masked settlers while she and other journalists were covering the olive harvest in the Palestinian village of Abu Falah, north of Ramallah.

It is unclear whether the puncture wounds were caused by knives or other weapons. Levine said a witness to her attack had seen nails sticking out of some of the wooden clubs wielded by her attackers.

Levine, 64, has covered multiple wars and had just returned from an assignment in Ukraine before Friday’s attack. She said she would most likely have been killed had she not been wearing protective body armour and a helmet.

“I probably would have been dead, because for sure it doesn’t take much to kill a person with blows to the head,” she said shortly before being discharged from hospital on Wednesday in the Israeli city of Petah Tikva.

Levine pointed out that Palestinians did not have such protection and more than 20 had been killed in settler attacks so far this year, in the course of an escalating campaign of aggression – described as terrorism by Israeli security leaders – across the West Bank aimed at driving Palestinians from their land.

“Every single journalist who looked at [the attack on me] are thinking they and I have gone to so many funerals of Palestinians killed by settlers,” Levine said.

She said the olive harvesting at Abu Falah had begun peacefully but at some point a group of young masked settlers appeared on a nearby hilltop watching the group of Palestinian villagers, journalists and human rights activists accompanying them. Levine said the attack began only after the Israeli army arrived on the scene.

“Then all hell broke loose. Some of the farmers started to gather their tarps and bags of olives that they had picked,” she said. “Then all of a sudden I hear a machine gun, and then saw teargas in the distance. I started to run … It was just like a lot of commotion and then all of a sudden I see a dozen of them and they started charging at me.

“I managed to keep my face to the ground, and I don’t know if I took that position to protect myself with my face down or it was their initial blow. Otherwise my whole face would have been broken and I could have suffered brain damage or lost an eye.

“They started kicking me and beating me with sticks. I can’t even count how many times, probably more than a hundred times. I actually tried playing dead so that they would stop. But it didn’t work.”

Witnesses said the beating only ceased when young Palestinian men used slingshots to aim stones at settlers forcing them back, allowing another American journalist, Jasper Nathaniel, to reach Levine and, with other reporters, help her to safety.

“The shabab [Palestinian youth] put themselves in front and were trying to keep them [the settlers] away, keep a protective shield, which was amazing. It was like a biblical battle,” Levine said.

After the attack, Nathaniel wrote: “Had the shabab not stepped up to protect her, she might well be dead. It is no exaggeration to say that young Palestinians armed only with stones risked their lives to save Heidi Levine’s.”

He said the army pursued the young Palestinians in the wake of the incident, rather than the settlers. Palestinians risk being shot by settlers or the soldiers if they try to resist attacks, and can face long periods in detention without charge.

Levine, who has lived in Israel for four decades, said she would go back to reporting on the West Bank as soon as she recovered. “My work is important,” she said. “They have bruised me, broken some bones, but they haven’t cracked my spirit.”

Since the attack, she has received letters from Israelis expressing regret, and an apologetic phone call from the president, Isaac Herzog.

“He was a teddy bear on the phone,” she said. “He kept saying I just want to give you a big hug and these are not representative of who this country is, they’re a dark stain, and he called them thugs.”

The office of the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, however, put out a statement on X seeking to cast doubt on witness and video accounts of what he called an “alleged attack”.

Levine was particularly angered by Netanyahu’s claim that some video footage “appears to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual”.

“That’s such bullshit. They helped me up because they couldn’t get my things off of me. That’s why,” Levine said. “They robbed me of everything I have – a pouch with my documents, my American passport, credit card, camera disk and a small camera bag with two other lenses. Everything is gone … That’s why [they stood me up], and then they threw me back down and continued to kick and hit me.”

The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, called the attack a “despicable act of terror” and demanded prosecutions. Israeli police arrested 10 suspects after the Abu Salah incident and another attack on Saturday aimed at European diplomats near the West Bank village of Taybeh. Several of them were subsequently released. Prosecutions of settlers, who have allies in the army, police and Netanyahu’s cabinet, are very rare.

Asked if she expected her attackers would be brought to justice, Levine said her level of confidence was “two out of 10”.

“I am not very hopeful,” she said. “Of course, if the government made the decision to do something and crack down on this and get people arrested, they would do it. But it’s not just arresting these teenage thugs. It’s going after their leaders, the rabbis, and how they’re organised.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Chemical tank explosion in Toledo, Ohio, prompts mass evacuation
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Auzzy Byrdsell
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Officials say the explosion released an airborne irritant that can cause burning of the eyes, nose, mouth and skin

Officials are investigating a tank explosion in Toledo, Ohio, that released a chemical into the air, causing a mass evacuation in the area.

One person, a first responder, was injured and taken to the hospital, but officials believe the injuries are non-life-threatening. They are also unsure about the cause of the explosion.

An employee at the company, MC Tank Terminal – which specializes in transporting bulk liquid chemicals and provides tank container transportation, storage and maintenance – called on first responders late Tuesday night to address the explosion.

Wade Kapszukiewicz, Toledo’s mayor, announced in a news conference on Wednesday that residents within a 1-mile radius of the explosion needed to evacuate and those within 3 miles were being asked to shelter in place with their windows sealed. He said executives from MC Tank Terminal were en route to Toledo to assess the situation.

“We understand the seriousness of what has happened here,” Kapszukiewicz said. “That’s why we took the actions that we did. That’s why we’re going to continue to monitor and communicate with the public throughout the day.”

The chemical released was glycidyl methacrylate, an industrial coating product used in plastics, rubbers and resins. Local officials say the airborne irritant can cause burning of the eyes, nose, mouth and skin; they have suggested Toledo residents who experience serious symptoms like difficulty breathing, nausea and vomiting, dizziness or confusion, go to the emergency room or call 911.

When the chemical was released in the explosion, it became a gas, but when it settles back into the tank, it will turn again into a liquid, Kapszukiewicz said at Wednesday’s conference.

“The hope is that at that point, the risk of explosion will have expired, and that efforts can be made to contain and eliminate the hazard,” he said.

Local news outlets in Toledo have reported a visible, dense fog over the town and a lurking plastic-like odor.

The city, which has a population of roughly 265,000 people, per the US Census Bureau, had already issued an evacuation order on Tuesday night for about 300 people who live within a half mile of the explosion. That was later expanded to a full mile, evacuating about 1,000 people.

City officials said Wednesday that as far as they knew, all residents had been evacuated. Kapszukiewicz said officials were unsure how long the evacuation and shelter orders would last.

Residents were being asked to communicate with local businesses and schools within the evacuation zone to see what their plans were during the evacuation. Some schools were closed Wednesday and others delayed their opening, according to NBC News.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US busts Massachusetts marriage fraud ring: ‘American dream is not for sale’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Reuters
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Accused allegedly arranged hundreds of sham marriages for immigrants to obtain green cards

Federal prosecutors on Wednesday charged six people with participating in a long-running scheme to reportedly arrange hundreds ⁠of sham marriages in Massachusetts in order to help immigrants unlawfully obtain green cards and potential US citizenship.

US attorney Leah Foley during a press ⁠conference in Boston said ⁠the scheme’s alleged ​mastermind, Jennifer Gonzalez, helped organize sham marriages for over a decade in Massachusetts, a Democratic-led state the defendant described as a “sanctuary” jurisdiction where “you get ⁠a lot of help as an immigrant”.

It marked the latest such case by the US Department of Justice as part of Donald Trump’s immigration ⁠crackdown. In August, it brought one of the largest such cases when in New York it ​charged 11 people over a scheme prosecutors said ‌facilitated about 1,000 sham ‌marriages.

Gonzalez, 43, told a cooperating witness posing as a client that her group helped obtain hundreds ‌of permanent resident cards, or green cards, for undocumented noncitizens living in Massachusetts, charging between $38,000 and $40,000 for marriages to US citizens, according to a criminal complaint.

Authorities said the operation ran for about 12 years and averaged about 18 to 20 fraudulent marriages annually, generating more than $6m in profits.

Gonzalez, a US-born citizen, told the witness her goal was “for you to get the American dream”, but ‌that her business had become more difficult after Trump returned to office in 2025, the complaint said.

Foley, whom the Trump administration appointed as the state’s top federal prosecutor, ​called it a sophisticated scheme that Gonzalez was “operating with impunity under the last administration”.

“My hope is that today the charged defendants and others like them realize that the American dream is not for sale,” Foley said. “It is earned. And when you try to pilfer it for profit, we will hold you ⁠accountable.”

Gonzalez is charged with harboring immigrants living illegally in the US and ​marriage fraud. Her lawyer did not ​immediately respond to a request ​for comment.

Other defendants include people accused of aiding Gonzalez’s scheme or entering into ​sham marriages with immigrants.

Foley ‌said Gonzalez entered ​such a marriage ​herself and obtained Snap food benefits from Massachusetts without listing any income from her scheme, which she used to buy property in the Dominican Republic.

Foley said the investigation was ongoing and could result in future charges against anyone found to have obtained legal status through the scheme.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on the Republicans’ midterms struggle: Trump has circuses, but voters also want bread | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Guardian Staff
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
As prices keep rising, more of the president’s supporters are asking what happened to the economic good times he promised

It is no great revelation that Donald Trump is enriching himself as president. He raked in $2.2bn in 2025, with his position and his personal interests frequently overlapping. Yet this week’s poll finding that 34% of Republicans (and 66% of all American voters) think that he is using his position to make himself rich merits attention. Separately, voters in a Fox News poll last week put government corruption at the top of their list of concerns – just ahead of inflation and high prices.

Mr Trump pledged that people would be better off if they voted for him. The billionaires are; not the rest. He promised to lower the costs of groceries (they have risen again) and to cut the price of gasoline to below $2 a gallon. It’s more than double that, thanks to his reckless and illegal war on Iran. Tariffs have bumped up the cost of living too. Incumbents will always struggle when the economy does. But the gulf between his own prosperity and the daily life of his base now looks less like an inspiration and more like an insult. Cash offers seem unlikely to help much.

The president’s popularity rating sank to a record low of 36% in a poll on Wednesday. Mr Trump, of course, is not on the ballot. But he is touring red states as he seeks to shore up the vote in places where the idea of a Democratic victory looked laughable two years ago. Democrats are rightly cautious about their midterms prospects, having been burned too many times. But less than a fortnight from 3 November, with many votes already cast, polls suggest that they will take the House and could well claim the Senate too.

The party is still unpopular, though impressive candidates are performing far better than anyone expected in surprising places – notably Texas and Kansas. But they are now more trusted on economic issues. Independents are turning away from Mr Trump and his party, and many Republicans seem unenthused, for multiple reasons. The “Maga-sympathetic” pollster Rich Baris argues that “Donald Trump did this to himself”. His base believed Mr Trump was their champion. Now they suspect that he is “just another politician”.

There is merited concern about how the president has already used his power to tilt the midterms, and more about what he may do if his party fares as badly as forecast. Republicans still hope to reclaim ground through traditional if unsavoury means, massively outspending Democrats.

Yet while some polls are tightening, culture war attacks and salacious lies about opponents such as James Talarico in Texas do not seem, at least so far, to be as powerful as Republicans hoped. That’s not just because Democratic candidates are repositioning themselves. The toxic messaging of the presidential race – that Kamala Harris “is for they/them, President Trump is for you” – doesn’t land if voters believe that he’s actually for himself and his friends.

Republicans now point to France’s unrest and claim that a Democrat-dominated Congress would bring chaos and destruction to America. Their fearmongering has often motivated core voters. But while Democrats stick to the economic attack, Republicans are trying to change the subject instead of offering answers. Mr Trump’s bread-and-circuses politics is floundering, cage fights on the South Lawn of the White House notwithstanding, as voters ask what happened to the bread.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: ‘You are a humanitarian also, sir’: the US feeds Putin with lies as Ukraine’s children take cover and die | Andrew Roth
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Andrew Roth in Kharkiv
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Steve Witkoff’s flattery of the Russian leader could be just the start of a mendacious stratagem from a US president who says Moscow ‘has been fine on Ukraine’

They say the first casualty of war is truth. For the Trump administration, the road to peace with Russia now encompasses some extraordinary lies.

Steve Witkoff delivered one as he sat down with Vladimir Putin in his native St Petersburg on Wednesday, aiming to close the deal on Russia’s land grab in Ukraine with the White House’s strategy of maximum pressure on Kyiv and saccharine flattery of the Kremlin.

“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” said Witkoff, a real-estate mogul who, thanks to being Trump’s friend, is now the US’s senior envoy and diplomat to end the largest European conflict since the second world war. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that. I commend you.”

In Putin’s 26 years in power, it is a rare moment when he has been granted that specific honour. Skim through Russia’s past wartime exploits, the bombing campaigns in Chechnya and Georgia and Syria, to the thousands of Russian citizens jailed for dissent, to the violent deaths of prominent opposition journalists and politicians in barely disguised assassinations and poisonings – and it will be difficult to identify Putin’s credentials as a humanitarian.

And that is before looking to Ukraine, where Russia chose to launch a full-scale invasion that has now claimed hundreds of thousands of lives. The Guardian recently obtained a Russian strategy document showing the Kremlin’s potential to black out Ukrainian cities this winter, cutting off up to 90% of electricity to cities such as Kyiv and Odesa and Kharkiv – where millions of people live – to intentionally create a humanitarian catastrophe. And judging by the nightly barrages levelled at power plants for cities across Ukraine, the Kremlin has decided to move forward with that strategy until Kyiv surrenders.

As Witkoff met Putin on Wednesday, schoolchildren in Kharkiv hustled down a reinforced stairway, sirens announcing the arrival of Shahed drones overhead. This is no ordinary bomb shelter; it is one of 10 underground schools Kharkiv has constructed because of Russia’s regular bombing of the brotherly city less than 20 miles from the border.

Parents had welcomed the schools because they were safe, said teachers, and this was the one way that young people could have an uninterrupted school day during a war that could last years more – and reignite even if a shaky peace deal is reached.

“We all believed in Trump. We all really had hopes for America and for Trump to stop this monster Putin,” said Olena Svytlychna, the head of the education department of the Novobavarskyi region in Kharkiv, sitting in the school’s cafe on Wednesday.

As Witkoff spoke, the families of six people killed in a drone strike in a park near Kharkiv this week were still holding funerals. The youngest victim of the strike was a one-year-old girl, Anhelina, who was killed as she was sitting strapped into her stroller in a playground. Her mother, Inna Mariukhna, a local schoolteacher, was also killed in the strike. The final death toll was four adults and two children, Anhelina and an 11-year-old girl.

Those lives have barely earned a mention from the White House as it pushes for Ukraine to capitulate as quickly as it can this week – and crucially before the 3 November midterm elections when voters will deliver a referendum on Trump’s leadership for the last two years.

Shortly after the bombing, Trump told reporters on the White House lawn that Russia “has been fine on Ukraine”. After taking criticism for that remark, he mentioned the attacks in passing just to downplay the shelling of civilians: there were “some people in a town that got hit or whatever, but mostly young soldiers” died, he said from the Oval Office on Tuesday.

For the White House, those words cost little. Witkoff’s goal was to bring home a US citizen, a 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan, who had been detained in Russia. But if Witkoff wants to buy a peace deal by 3 November through flattering Putin, then this will only be the White House’s opening salvo in its war on truth.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Europe’s far right seizes on protest violence to push authoritarian anti-immigration agenda
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Jon Henley and Guardian correspondents
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Nationalist leaders are framing unrest as consequence of failed liberal governance and open borders

Europe’s far-right leaders have jumped on the violence that rocked numerous cities last weekend, framing it as the inevitable consequence of failed liberal governance and open-border policies and insisting only they can restore law and order.

Months away from key elections in Spain, France and Italy, authoritarian nationalists are eager to weaponise the wave of street unrest, originating in peaceful protests over the cost of living and deteriorating public services but hijacked by violent rioters.

Those in opposition have not held back. In France, where cities such as Paris, Marseille and Lyon faced widespread rioting and looting, the far-right National Rally (RN) has denounced centrist incompetence and promised a crackdown.

The party’s president, Jordan Bardella, said the government was “impotent”. The RN leader, Marine Le Pen, said on Wednesday the state was “collapsing” and had “lost control of everything” amid “migratory, budgetary and security chaos”.

Ahead in presidential polls and seeking voters beyond her base, Le Pen has resisted explicitly racialising the unrest, but has framed it more broadly as a result of state and policy failures leading to “anarchic immigration” and “a total loss of authority”.

In Germany – where there were no major protests – the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has stoked fears rioting could spill over the border. Its co-leader Alice Weidel said France’s “violent excesses” were a “warning for Germany”.

Weidel also linked the unrest to immigration, posting: “The dangerous mix of mass migration and leftwing extremism threatens to lead to civil war-like conditions here too … There will only be a turnaround on migration with the AfD!”

In Portugal, populists have used peaceful protests to blame immigration for the country’s housing crisis, which André Ventura of the far-right Chega party said was chiefly a consequence of an “uncontrolled influx of people from abroad”.

In Spain, where the housing crisis has led to huge protests and a Madrid encampment, and prompted the socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, to call a snap election next month, the far-right Vox party has sought to demonise the protesters. “They’re not defending the right to housing, or asking for work, they’re serving Pedro Sánchez,” the party’s leader, Santiago Abascal, said. “They’re Sánchez’s militias.”

Vox has also attempted to link the housing issue to migration. In a message posted on social media last month, the party falsely suggested that the 87-year-old woman whose eviction sparked the mammoth protests would have had a home had she been an immigrant from north Africa.

In Belgium, where cost of living protests also escalated into street clashes in Brussels and Liège, the far-right Flemish nationalists of Vlaams Belang framed the rioting as a failure of integration and open borders, characterising it as “imported violence”.

Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, has adopted another strategy – as head of a far-right government she has headed for four years, she cannot simply blame failures of the state. Instead, she has expanded her law-and-order agenda, and framed rioters as extremists.

“Demonstrating is a right, but setting our cities ablaze is not,” Meloni said after rioting in Milan and Bologna. “Hooligans have exploited the protests to sow chaos, attack those responsible for ensuring security, and hold entire cities hostage.”

Meloni has previously enacted sweeping security measures aimed at hindering public dissent, including jail terms for blocking roads, tough sentences for resisting police officers, and pre-detention for demonstrators thought likely to cause trouble.

This week she passed emergency decrees creating an offence of violent participation in ⁠a demonstration, imposing tougher penalties on ⁠rioters and organisers of violent groups, and penalising parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting.

But she too has highlighted immigration as a factor, noting that “nearly half of those stopped or arrested” after the Milan riots were “of immigrant background, including individuals born abroad and second-generation children of immigrant families”.

Beyond Europe’s orthodox far-right parties, anti-immigration polemicists have gone further, interpreting the violence not as state and policy failures but as evidence of a looming civilisational war fuelled by multiculturalism and non-EU immigration.

Éric Zemmour, the founder of France’s Reconquête! (Reconquest) party, demanded an immigration halt and the deportation of “foreign delinquents”, declaring: “These are not riots, but the warning shots in an ethnic war. Either we establish absolute order or we yield.”

The far-right narrative has been reinforced by similar comments from the US, where both the president and vice-president have sought to turn the unrest in France in particular into a cautionary tale for voters before midterm elections.

Donald Trump described France as a once-great nation that had been “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists”, adding on social media that immigration “has shattered that once great country”.

JD Vance echoed the same view, saying: “Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion.” In doing so, they “ignored fundamental questions about assimilation and compatibility”, he said.

Deborah Cole in Berlin, Angela Giuffrida in Rome and Sam Jones in Madrid contributed reporting

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Epstein’s attorney and accountant accused of ‘facilitating and concealing’ his crimes in lawsuit
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Anna Betts
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
New Mexico lawsuit claims ‘in exchange for furthering Epstein’s criminal project, his associates received generous salaries’

The attorney general of New Mexico on Wednesday filed a civil lawsuit against Jeffrey Epstein’s longtime attorney, Darren Indyke, and Epstein’s longtime accountant, Richard Kahn, accusing them of having “facilitated and concealed” Epstein’s crimes, and is seeking to stop them from being paid by Epstein’s estate while the litigation plays out.

The lawsuit, filed in the US district court for the district of New Mexico, names Kahn and Indyke as defendants both in their individual capacity, and in their capacity as co-executors of Epstein’s estate. The complaint also names the Epstein’s estate, and the 1953 Trust, which holds the estate’s assets.

“Epstein, with the help of his associates, trafficked, isolated, and abused survivors at alluring locations” including at Epstein’s ranch in Stanley, New Mexico, known as Zorro Ranch, the complaint claims. It goes on to allege that “in exchange for furthering Epstein’s criminal project and remaining silent about it, his associates received generous salaries, access to elite social circles, and lavish gifts, including being named beneficiaries of his multimillion-dollar estate”.

Lawyers for Kahn and Indyke did not immediately respond to a comment request from the Guardian on the new lawsuit. Previously, Kahn and Indyke have said that they had no knowledge of Epstein’s crimes during their employment.

Among the demands the lawsuit seeks is a court order preventing Indyke and Kahn from receiving estate payments while the case proceeds.

The complaint alleges that both men profited personally from their relationships with Epstein. It alleges that from 2011 to 2019, Indyke received more than $16m from Epstein and related entities and that Kahn received more than $10m.

In a statement on Wednesday, Raúl Torrez, New Mexico’s attorney general, said that Epstein “did not operate alone, and his death does not end the pursuit of accountability for the people who helped make his crimes possible”.

“The allegations in this lawsuit describe a network of people and financial arrangements that helped sustain and conceal the abuse of vulnerable girls and young women, including here in New Mexico,” he said. “Those who allegedly enabled this exploitation should not be allowed to profit from it while survivors continue to live with its consequences.”

In the complaint, Torrez wrote that “through this action, the State seeks to hold these individuals accountable to the fullest extent possible and to ensure that Epstein’s assets are distributed to the survivors of his horrific crimes”.

Several survivors of Epstein’s abuse signed a letter on Wednesday in support of Torrez’s lawsuit “because it can expose what roles Indyke and Kahn played in Epstein’s operation, examine how they handled survivors’ claims, and prevent Epstein’s trusted loyalists from being rewarded for their roles in Epstein’s organization”.

“Survivors deserve accountability and answers under oath. Epstein’s chosen confidants should not get the last word – or the money,” they added.

At a news conference on Wednesday about the new filing, Epstein survivor Anouska De Georgiou thanked Torrez for “standing with survivors”.

“We have carried this burden for long enough,” she said. “It is time for those responsible to answer for their part in it.”

The announcement on Wednesday comes amid a separate ongoing dispute between New Mexico officials and the Department of Justice over files Torrez is seeking as part of the state’s investigation into Epstein’s possible crimes in the state, including at his ranch outside Santa Fe, where multiple survivors have said they were abused.

Torrez sued the DoJ in August, accusing the department and Todd Blanche, the attorney general, of “stonewalling” the state’s investigation, which was reopened in February. Torrez asked the court for access to unredacted Epstein-related files held by the DoJ, and said in its filing his prosecutors had requested access to the records but had “faced sustained resistance” from the department.

The case is ongoing and the DoJ recently filed a motion to dismiss, arguing that “decisions about law-enforcement information sharing are committed to the agency’s discretion” and that turning over unredacted files would violate victims’ privacy.

Epstein’s Zorro Ranch came under renewed scrutiny after the DoJ’s release of roughly 3m files related to Epstein late last year and early this year. The Guardian reported in early February that the newly disclosed Epstein files contained thousands of references to Zorro Ranch, and numerous photos of men and young girls at the property, and that several survivors of Epstein’s abuse had also previously given testimony about abuse they say they were subjected to there.

The Guardian investigation also revealed that, unlike Epstein’s other properties in Palm Beach, in New York and on his private Caribbean island, federal authorities had apparently never searched the New Mexico ranch.

Epstein, who died in a Manhattan jail in 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex-trafficking charges, bought the property in New Mexico 1993. It was later sold by his estate in 2023.

In late February, Torrez announced that New Mexico would reopen its investigation into Epstein’s activities at the ranch, after the state’s initial investigation was put on hold in 2019 at the request of federal prosecutors in New York, who were pursuing the investigation into Epstein’s sex-trafficking operation that led to his arrest. In March, New Mexico authorities launched a search of the ranch.

Torrez has said that he wants to establish what took place at Zorro Ranch. New Mexico lawmakers also established a “truth commission” to examine activities at the ranch.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Meta ordered to pay $25bn to New Mexico in Cambridge Analytica data-privacy case
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Reuters
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Jury had found Meta misled consumers after Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign obtained user data without consent

A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms to pay $25bn on ⁠Wednesday after a jury found the company had misled consumers in a case arising from allegations that a political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign obtained data from millions of Facebook users ⁠without their consent.

“Facebook’s wrongdoing – ⁠over the course of ​years and systematically broadcast to the public – goes to the heart of Facebook’s core business practices,” Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order following the verdict.

Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219bn was warranted, based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25bn.

A spokesperson for Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The state’s attorney general had sued Meta in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica, ⁠a British political consulting firm, had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app.

The state accused Meta ​of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had ‌access to their data, how the ‌company handles hate speech and misinformation posted on the platform, and other internal policies. The company knew that third parties had broad access to ‌users’ personal data, and it tolerated hate speech or other harmful content when it benefited the company’s bottom line, the state said.

Jurors on 25 September found that 26 of 29 statements made by the company and its leadership on those issues were misleading. They said the company had committed more than 43m violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws, based on the number of Facebook users or New Mexico residents who were the audience for each misleading statement.

State law allows a penalty of up to $5,000 per ‌violation, and directs that all of the money go to New Mexico’s school system, New Mexico’s attorney general, Raúl Torrez, told reporters after the verdict. At a hearing on 1 October, Randi McGinn, a lawyer for New Mexico, had ​asked Mathew to award the state between $35bn and $40bn, saying that would be supported by the US constitution’s protections on due process and the jury’s verdict.

“This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money, and the value of its stock price,” McGinn said.

In court filings, Meta urged Mathew to cap the penalties at $3.45bn, saying a higher penalty ran the risk of scaring businesses out of the ⁠state. The evidence showed that Meta does not sell user data and New Mexico did not prove ​that any consumer had actually been misled, the ​company said in court filings.

The ​verdict was the second in six months by a Santa Fe jury in a lawsuit brought by the ​state of New Mexico against ‌Meta Platforms.

In the first trial, ​which ended in March, a ​Santa Fe jury found Meta misled users about young users’ safety on its Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp platforms and ordered the company to pay $375m in civil penalties. After a second phase of that trial, a judge directed the company to pay $567m into a New Mexico fund for teen mental health and ordered Meta to implement measures to protect teen Facebook and Instagram users in New Mexico.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/liv.title: Bayern Munich v Arsenal: Champions League – live
https://www.theguardian.com/football/liv.author: Scott Murray
https://www.theguardian.com/football/liv.text:
⚽️ Champions League updates from 8pm BST ⚽️ Clockwatch | Live scores | Table | Mail Scott

Vincent Kompany and Mikel Arteta worked with each other at Manchester City. When the former emerges from the tunnel, the pair embrace warmly and have a quick catch-up. And then Arsenal get the game started.

The teams are out! Bayern are in one of their all-red phases, while Arsenal are harking back to the early 90s with a blue version of the famous bruised banana. Vincent Kompany is in the house, by the way, having recovered from a virus that threatened to keep him in bed. And so is Germany boss Jurgen Klopp, in the stands flashing that smile and throwing his arm around the shoulder of another erstwhile Liverpool manager, Rafael Benitez. Everyone having a good time, it seems, and looking forward to this big showdown, including Arsenal fan Charles Antaki … well, kind of: “Pretty dismal, the fare served up in the game against Forest. But! Pundits have assured us that because Bayern are going to be on the attack, Arsenal will be free to entertain us with a dazzling display of skill, ambition, irresistible cheeks and above all, goals. Not much to say about that except We Shall See.” We’ll be off in a minute or two.

Mikel Arteta speaks to TNT Sports. “We’re gonna have to play, I expect, three or four different games at different stages … we need everybody ready because we need to change and adapt to that … freshness … very excited … we have talked about our enthusiasm for playing on these big stages … that’s where you want to get tested … play with a lot of courage … a lot of aggression … be decisive … we have prepared for what we have to do.”
