There are plenty of other Champions League matches about to kick off tonight. Sarah Rendell has you covered in the latest edition of your super soaraway Clocko. Get on it!

Shoogly Peg news. Michael Carrick’s coat is hanging on one. The first big result of the evening is in, and Simon Burnton has all the details.

Look at that bench; Arsenal’s squad goes deep. Which doesn’t necessarily explain the headline below … but it can’t not help. The good people o’ Opta explain all.

Bayern are without Joshua Kimmich following a death in his immediate family. Harry Kane leads the line, while former Liverpool winger Luis Diaz is on the bench. Michael Olise is suspended following his two-yellows-in-two-minutes fiasco during the 3-3 draw at Viking.

Arsenal make two changes to their starting XI following the staunch 1-0 win at Nottingham Forest. Noni Madueke and Jurriën Timber replace Eberechi Eze and Ben White, who drop to the bench.

Bayern Munich: Neuer, Laimer, Upamecano, Kim, Stanisic, Pavlovic, Bischof, Gnabry, Saibari, Davies, Kane. Subs: Ulreich, Urbig, Tah, Brown, Diaz, Ito, Boey, Ndiaye, Karl, Binder.

Arsenal: Raya, Timber, Konsa, Gabriel, Calafiori, Odegaard, Rice, Guimaraes, Saka, Havertz, Madueke. Subs: Arrizabalaga, Meslier, Mosquera, White, Eze, Gyokeres, Merino, Zubimendi, Lewis-Skelly, Dowman.

Arsenal’s last three visits to Munich have ended badly. In reverse order: 0-1 (2024), 1-5 (2017), 1-5 (2015). All three worthy of a large bräukeller-infused GULP. On the other hand, Arsenal won the last meeting between these two sides, 3-1 last November at the Emirates, and they go into this match having won 10 of their 11 games in all competitions so far this season. Bayern by contrast aren’t at their usual steamrolling best: OK, they’ve just mullered RB Leipzig 6-1, but before that they dropped Bundesliga points at Augsburg (2-2) and should really have been beaten by Viking in a 3-3 draw last week. So both teams have positives to draw on and negatives to try their best to ignore. Kick-off is at 8pm BST. It’s on!

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Titans reportedly released Jordan Elliott after he fetched gun following scuffle in practice
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Reuters
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Tennessee Titans coach Robert Saleh confirmed Wednesday that defensive tackle Jordan Elliott was released after pulling a gun in the parking lot of the team facility but said it was a “terrible lapse in judgment that I recognize as a call for help more than a criminal act”.

The Titans had announced Tuesday that Elliott was released, but said only that it came after his involvement in an unspecified incident at the team’s facility five days earlier.

A person briefed on the incident told the Associated Press on Wednesday that Elliott had a gun in his car and went to the parking lot to retrieve it after a dispute with another player. The person spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity because the incident is being reviewed.

Speaking to reporters, Saleh defended Jordan’s character. “Unfortunately, rules are rules with regard to guns on property, and sometimes it’s far greater than the kneejerk reaction of kicking somebody when they’re down,” the coach said.

“He’s a good man. Made a terrible, had a terrible lapse in judgment that I recognize as a call for help more than a criminal act,” Saleh added. “He’s never committed a crime in his entire life and he pulled a gun, in the parking lot.”

Right tackle JC Latham, who was involved in the altercation with Elliott on the practice field, called the episode an unfortunate situation.

“I don’t really have too much to say about it,” Latham said Wednesday. “There ain’t never been no bad blood between us two. We were here on the summer getting treatment. Before that, we hung out whenever we were in the same city together. We actually had never had an argument leading up to it.”

Elliott appeared in five games this season with one start and had 11 tackles. He followed Saleh to Nashville after a two-year stint with the San Francisco 49ers, where he played in 31 games with 29 starts.

The 6ft 4in defensive tackle was selected by the Cleveland Browns in the third round of the 2020 draft. He spent his first four seasons in Cleveland before signing a two-year, $7m deal with San Francisco.

Tennessee added him as a free agent in the offseason on a two-year, $8m deal.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: Clayface review – flesh-stretching DC body horror is very gory but not very good
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Benjamin Lee
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
Liverpool makes for an unconvincing Gotham City in this effectively gross but otherwise middling attempt to milk money from a lesser-known Batman villain

A sense of desperation is understandably in the air over at DC, the company, like Marvel, slowly realising that the mass superhero fever has finally broken. There’s still interest there, of course (this summer’s Spider-Man is now the biggest film of all time in the US after all), but it’s no longer good enough to leave a high-speed conveyor belt unmanned, purpose and quality control be damned. 2019 saw a staggering 10 superhero films released in cinemas, and the inevitable exhaustion that followed, also fueled by Covid, led to a gradual winding down, monster hits turning into minor ones and sure bets often becoming expensive flops.

As Peter Parker winged his way to box office records this summer, DC’s Supergirl bombed so hard that experts believe it might have cost Warners upwards of $200m in losses. It was just the latest disappointment for the brand after Black Adam, Joker: Folie à Deux, Blue Beetle and The Flash all underperformed while even last year’s much-heralded Superman reboot only grossed a solid $618m, a far cry from the $1bn heyday of the genre (things got so bad that even a fully filmed Batgirl adventure was deleted for the tax break). Notably, the last DC film to swoop past that magic figure was Joker in 2019, a darker, lower-budget attempt to spotlight a villain rather than a hero, a big swing with relatively low stakes. Todd Phillips’s film might be best known by some for being brave enough to ask the question, “What if Taxi Driver sucked?” but for all of its many issues, it brought buzz and prestige and, shockingly, Oscars, to an easily ridiculed universe. It was also, crucially, something rare in that world: a close-to-good idea.

The evolution of Clayface, another R-rated villain origin story with a markedly lower budget than the DC norm, was not in direct response to Joker (it is allegedly the first in a new “Gods and Monsters” strand) but its path is one that head James Gunn would clearly like to emulate, albeit financially rather than awards-wise. One of many thoughts I had during Clayface, other than what I should have for dinner and how long I might be able to make a small popcorn last, was just how striking Phillips’s film stands in comparison. It remains shallow and smug and cursed with a grating lead performance, but it was visually punchy and, like the very best comic book adaptations, genuinely transporting, rich on dank atmosphere and thoughtfully curated production design. It was an undeniable moment.

Clayface is overwhelmingly not a moment. Admittedly its targets are way lower (Mike Flanagan’s original script, allegedly more texturally complex, was entirely rewritten) but even as a similarly new way in, as a relatively standalone horror movie for those who wouldn’t now rush toward a superhero caper, it’s a clumsily missed opportunity and another reminder that those at DC don’t seem to know what they’re doing and why they’re doing it.

Rather than feeling like a lower-budget DC movie (it was made for around $40m), it looks closer to a network TV series, more Fox than HBO Max, more Gotham than Lanterns. With the standard there now so high (The Penguin looked every bit a blockbuster movie), the distractingly tinny aesthetic and lack of confident directorial style is disappointing both as a horror (especially at a time of micro-budgeted films such as Obsession and Backrooms looking so very distinctive) and as a tale that takes place in the DC universe. Liverpool was used as a stand-in here and if, like me, you found Manchester to be an unconvincing New York in Brand New Day, you won’t realise how good we had it …

Gotham is where working-class boy done good Matt (Welsh actor Tom Rhys Harries, fine enough) is from and a place that he was desperate to leave. He’s a rising movie star, riding high after his first Oscar nomination (“Nominees don’t wait in line!”) and on a trip back to his home town, he makes the mistake of sleeping with the girlfriend of a violent gangster, introduced by Goldfrapp’s Ooh La La, one of the film’s many dated attempts at cool. As a result, he has his money-making face sliced up by goons and his career soon crumbles, back to a bedsit with all his money wasted on useless surgeries orchestrated by his viperous lawyer.

Matt is desperate for revenge and resurrection, and after stumbling upon a doctor working on experimental skin surgery (Naomi Ackie, trying her hardest), he thinks he’s found his chance. But before you can say Substance (the elixir is at least red here over Brat green), things go horribly wrong …

What the film does do is successfully gross us out, as Matt’s skin starts to morph in tune with his emotional state, which might be enough for some, and in the screening I attended, mostly filled with rowdy non-journalists, there was a vocal response to the goriest and gloopiest moments. The trailer scene, of Matt trying to cut through flesh growing over his eyes while on a bumpy flight, is brilliantly awful to watch, and it’s in these more intimate, uneasy moments where director James Watkins shows off his dusty genre mettle. His best films have been his earlier, smaller attempts – 2002’s genuinely creepy and forward-thinking reality TV horror My Little Eye and 2008’s brutal hoodie thriller Eden Lake – but he’s less assured when the canvas is expanded.

Clayface is as poorly lit and junkily made as the very blandest of streaming movies and never once do we feel transported to Gotham with a cast of exclusively non-American actors trying to out-accent each other (Eddie Marsan, as ever, loses that game). It doesn’t help that what could have been interesting at one point (perhaps when Flanagan was the sole author) with briefly pointed at issues of AI, unreality and method acting, has been sanded down to a kill-by-numbers revenge thriller led by a character who feels like an off-brand swirl of Venom, Hulk, Joker and Mystique. His abilities, and the rules of how they work, are so poorly defined, that he just becomes a screenwriting device, able to do whatever is needed in the moment.

Any tragedy that could and should have come from the character and his journey – boy from the wrong side of the tracks to privileged Oscar nominee to flesh-stretching, face-changing supervillain (!) – is excised for an easier video game trajectory, from one familiar level to the next (despite those involved comparing this to The Fly, this is very much not that). Clayface might be the start of a “bold” new era for DC’s superhero output but for anyone outside of a boardroom, it’s a face we have seen many times before.

Clayface is out in Australian cinemas on 22 October and in US and UK cinemas on 23 October

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Como demolish dismal Manchester United to pile more pressure on Carrick
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Jamie Jackson at the Giuseppe Sinigaglia Stadium
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
In sight of the Alps, a boat ride from George Clooney’s villa, Manchester United will hope, in what has been a terrible start to the season, that things do not get any worse.

They can’t – for the team’s prospects, and Michael Carrick’s job security, because witnessed here by Lake Como was a humiliation of the three-times European champions by Cesc Fàbregas’s competition debutants, as United suffered their worst defeat in continental football since 1994.

By 57 minutes this was over, as Como were 3-0 ahead, and Nico Paz had destroyed Carrick’s men with a scintillating display featuring two goals and the assist for Tasos Douvikas’s strike.

When Como attacked and defended it was as a unit supremely drilled by Fàbregas. Carrick, on this and the evidence of only two wins all term, is a coach struggling at elite level.

Como’s supremacy in the most famous victory of their 119 years came despite 62 total Champions League appearances v United’s 242. Or, more simply, the Italians’ men against United’s boys.

At a sold-out Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia (capacity 13,602), the visitors went down to a club whose tagline is “the most beautiful football in the most beautiful location”. For United, though, this was an ugly night in Lombardy.

Disaster hit two minutes in. Carrick’s men snoozed, allowing a Paz curler from the right to beat Senne Lammens, and the local faithful partied.

This was a whole 60 seconds longer than Atlético Madrid were kept out in last week’s 2-0 defeat, as United became the first English team to concede inside two minutes in consecutive major European matches.

The opener came moments after Diogo Dalot spurned a simple opening to dizzy the hosts: Matheus Cunha flipped the ball to his right-back, Dalot’s touch was awful, yet after possession was retained, he ballooned wide.

This was United’s current form crystallised at each end of the pitch: a basic lack of quality. When Paz left Noussair Mazraoui gasping, as the No 10 careered along Como’s right, another example was on show. Cunha, running back, could not stop Paz and if his cross had found a colleague, and not Mason Mount, Lammens might have been beaten again.

Mount lined up alongside Andrey Santos in a midfield that had Cunha, Youri Tielemans and Bryan Mbeumo ahead, with Bruno Fernandes again a false-ish 9.

Como hogged the ball throughout so any United foray needed to threaten Jean Butez’s goal: Mbeumo’s corner from the right patently did not when failing to clear a first defender.

Como had United’s number, penetrating at will, and when the ball was moved into the area and Martin Baturina went to grass, a penalty was claimed. Sven Jablonski, the referee, turned this down.

After a near 24-hour deluge the rain did finally stop but Como’s blue wave, when attacking or closing down, continued relentlessly. United’s press was piecemeal, maybe involving one or two, but was never a group act, unlike Fabregas’s players who hunted the ball in packs.

One more scare in a half studded with these came when Douvikas went clear, then down under Lammens’ attentions, but he was flagged offside. United were impotent and at the interval, Carrick had to earn his corn. In missing nine players due to injury, suspension or illness, there was some mitigation.

Mathijs de Ligt, partnering Harry Maguire in central defence, being thrown straight in for a first appearance in 325 days after a serious back injury illustrated Carrick’s straitened resources. This, too, was shown by Tynan Thompson and Jack Fletcher being on the bench, after each played for United Under-19s in the afternoon’s 2-1 Youth Cup defeat to Como.

Carrick’s move was to take off Cunha and Santos for Carlos Baleba and Amad Diallo in a reshuffle that took Tielemans into central midfield, Fernandes to No 10, and Mbeumo leading the line.

The net result: Como’s second. Once more, it was too simple. Paz enjoyed a universe of time to thread in Douvikas, and he ran on and powered past Lammens.

This was a mere four minutes into the second half and thoughts turned to the clock ticking on Carrick’s tenure, before Como netted twice more.

First came Paz’s second, this time the Argentinian skating along the right and beating Lammens for 3-0. Then, on 76 minutes, Como waltzed through for a fourth time.

Up rose Jacobo Ramón to head home Kaiki Bruno’s cross from the left and United’s disintegration was complete, many of their travelling fans already heading for the exit and local hostelries to try and drink away the pain of what they had witnessed. Josh Zirkzee’s stoppage-time goal was not even a consolation.

By the end Carrick was as broken as his team. Next up for United is Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday. Even if Carrick survives until then, who knows how much longer he will remain after this.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: ‘He was a great kid’: Chiefs mourn death of former player Allen Bailey at age of 37
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Guardian sport
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Patrick Mahomes and Andy Reid have spoken of their sadness after former Kansas City Chief Allen Bailey died at the age of 37.

The defensive end was found dead at his home in Florida on Tuesday by his wife. He is believed to have died from natural causes.

“It’s terrible, especially with all the good he [did],” Chiefs head coach Reid said. “He’s got a family and that’s a sad deal. I know his father passed away young, too. It makes you sick when it happens to somebody that young … He was one of my favorite players, a great kid. I’m just sorry to see that happened to him.”

Mahomes spent two seasons with Bailey after the quarterback was drafted by the Chiefs in 2017.

“I tell this story every year: He was the first person I saw when I stepped into the locker room after the draft,” Mahomes said. “I see Allen Bailey and I’m like, ‘This isn’t [college] anymore.’ It was surreal to see him.

“Obviously, it’s terrible to hear the news. A great teammate – he’s one of those glue guys on the team. He makes plays. He’s not necessarily a superstar, but the guy that kind of makes everything go. We’re praying for his family. [As] teammates, we’ve talked and we know that we’re going to do whatever we can to support those guys.”

Bailey grew up on Sapelo Island, a barrier island off Georgia only accessible by boat and with a population of fewer than 70 people. “I’m from a place a little out of the normal,” Bailey told Distraction magazine in 2018. “It’s relatively quiet; no stop signs, no traffic lights. It’s mostly dirt roads.”

From there he played college football for Miami before becoming a third-round draft pick for the Chiefs in 2011. He played for the team for eight seasons before spending the final two years of his career with the Atlanta Falcons.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Declan Rice strikes late for Arsenal to deny Bayern Munich in blockbuster
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: David Hytner at the Allianz Arena
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
It is as if Harry Kane cannot get enough of tormenting Arsenal. The Bayern Munich striker has plenty of form from his Tottenham days. He remains the top scorer in north London derby history with 14 goals. He made an impact yet again here and yet it was not a night when he had the final word. That honour fell to Declan Rice, the Arsenal midfielder storming into the Bayern area in the 82nd minute to guide home a low finish that Kane would have been proud to call his own.

Arsenal were hunting their latest statement result. Only once had they ever won away against Bayern – the 2-0 in the Champions League last 16 second leg in 2013, although it did not prevent an away goals exit. Mikel Arteta was an Arsenal player that night. When Eberechi Eze, who came on for the injured Bukayo Saka in the 10th minute, gave them the lead midway through the first half, their hopes surged.

Enter Kane. He wore his playmaker’s hat; some of his passing was sumptuous and it was his assist for Alphonso Davies that helped Bayern to draw level. He wore his finisher’s one, too, scoring from the penalty spot to put his team in charge. It meant he had scored in 10 consecutive Champions League games; one short of Cristiano Ronaldo’s record. There is a reason why Kane is the favourite to win the Ballon d’Or on Monday. He now has 16 goals against Arsenal; he has only scored more against one club – Leicester, against whom he has 20.

Rice loosened Bayern’s grip. It was a lovely goal from him and Arsenal even hinted at a late winner, Jurriën Timber drawing a tip over from Manuel Neuer in stoppage time. That would have been too much because Bayern shaded an absorbing tie in terms of clear chances created. But Arsenal made their point. They were value for it.

Arsenal knew they were inside a fortress. Bayern had not previously lost a Champions League group or league phase match at their own stadium since the 3-2 reverse against Manchester City in December 2013, 40 games ago. The following 39 featured 37 wins and two draws. Arteta’s players were not intimidated. They bristled with assurance at the outset and Rice rewarded their never-say-die spirit. Bayern had wanted revenge for their 3-1 defeat at the Emirates Stadium in the league stage last season. They did not get it.

Arteta’s idea was to go pretty much as strong as possible with his lineup. He made just two changes, Timber for Ben White and Noni Madueke for Eze, albeit the latter was not on the bench for long. Saka had tussled with Davies and it looked innocuous. The alarm bells rang when Saka grabbed his thigh and went to ground, waving his hand in the air.

Was it possible for the Arsenal support to think that Bayern had been stripped of their fear factor in the line behind Kane? Michael Olise was suspended, Jamal Musiala was injured and Luis Díaz was a substitute. He came on in the 68th minute only to be forced off before the end. Bayern were without the midfielder Joshua Kimmich for personal reasons.

Arteta moved Madueke over to his more natural position on the right wing when he introduced Eze on the left and Bayern will still be wondering how the latter was afforded so much space up the inside channel on that flank to put Arsenal in front.

It was a fabulous ball from Martin Ødegaard, who was in the mood, full of sharp turns and urgency, and Eze had the time to let it bounce before shooting first time into the far corner. An offside flag killed the Arsenal celebrations and there was one of those weird waits before the video assistant referee ruled that Eze was in fact onside.

Kane was booed by the Arsenal fans. Of course he was. He dropped deep to link the play and there was a moment in the 17th minute when he started a move with a pass from inside his own penalty area. There was a glorious ping over Gabriel Magalhães, who was the last Arsenal defender, for Ismael Saibari on 23 minutes, although his teammate could not control, and Kane’s fingerprints were all over the equaliser. He was on halfway when he sculpted the low through ball for Davies which took Timber out of the equation. The Bayern winger’s finish was clinical.

Bayern had other chances in the first half, none better than the one for Serge Gnabry, the former Arsenal winger, in the 21st minute. It was Kane who began the attack, taking a quick goal kick – yes, really – and Gnabry was the man over on the right when the Bayern forwards worked it that way. Gnabry’s shot was too close to David Raya. Kane also saw Ezri Konsa produce a fine block to keep him out.

It is never anything other than a pleasure to be at the Allianz for a showpiece match. All the staples were present and correct. The en masse scarf waving. The slightly slapstick oompah band notes. The fans at either end of the ground calling to each other. The non-stop drumbeat and songs from the Südkurve, who also bounced as one at times.

The pre-game surprise had been the sight of Vincent Kompany in the Bayern dugout; the manager made a Lazarus-like rise from his sickbed and the action after the restart kept the blood pumping. Arsenal thought they had gone back ahead when Bruno Guimarães rose to meet Rice’s corner only for Neuer to produce an extraordinary save.

The goalkeeper touched the ball up and on to the crossbar and away. Shades of Gordon Banks against Pelé. It was Raya’s turn next; his save to keep out Dayot Upamecano’s close-range header from Gnabry’s cross was of the highest order.

It was interesting to watch Kane after the penalty was awarded for handball against Timber. Bayern had worked the ball back to their No 9 and, when he shot, Timber’s arm was outstretched. Kane went through his mental processes. He could see that Raya did not retreat to his line for what felt like an age. Kane delayed even longer. He was in total control. He stuttered before banging the ball hard into the right-hand corner.

Bayern were close to putting the game to bed. Konrad Laimer dragged narrowly past the far post when well-placed but it was Arsenal who produced the sucker punch. Eze was dangerous throughout. And when the opportunity knocked for Rice after a pass from the substitute Viktor Gyökeres, he made no mistake.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Pope will not need further cancer treatment, doctors say
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Nadeem Badshah
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Medics indicate pontiff’s tumour had not spread, but doubts remain about planned trip to South America next month

Pope Leo will not need any further ⁠treatment after undergoing lung cancer surgery last week, his doctors said, indicating ⁠that his tumour had ⁠not ​spread.

The ⁠71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his ​right lung removed on 13 October and was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most ‌common form of lung cancer.

Final histological examinations and molecular biology analyses of the tissue removed confirmed the diagnosis, with the disease remaining localised, the doctors said in a statement released by the Vatican.

“A subsequent ‌oncological evaluation has confirmed that no further therapy is required,” the pope’s lead surgeon, ​Stefano Margaritora, and his personal physician, Luigi Carbone, said.

However, it was still unclear whether the pope would ⁠proceed with a planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, scheduled for 6-17 November.

Leo was discharged from hospital on Saturday and is gradually resuming his normal duties. On Wednesday, he returned to ⁠St Peter’s Square for his weekly audience with ​pilgrims.

The pope had been working from hospital, including making a phone call last Friday to Vladimir Putin, during which he urged the Russian president to call a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.

Last Sunday, the pontiff told a crowd gathered in St Peter’s Square that he would “gradually resume” his activities.

He also thanked those who had prayed for him, saying that he appreciated the support while adding that the experience had made him feel especially close “to all those who are going through illness or a state of infirmity”.

Margaritora said ​last week there ​were “no clinical reasons” preventing the pope from travelling ​to South ‌America, but ​the Vatican’s ​secretary of state indicated that the pontiff may need to adjust the pace of his schedule to aid his recovery.

Before the cancer diagnosis, Leo, who enjoys playing sports including tennis, was generally believed to be in good health. He often makes use of the papal retreat in Castel Gandolfo, close to Rome.

In May last year, Leo became the first US-born leader of the Roman Catholic church.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Some US diplomats told to leave Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Jonathan Yerushalmy and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Reports emerge of similar withdrawals in UAE, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain amid concerns about a return to conflict with Iran after US midterm elections

The US state department has ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia, as the gulf kingdom faces a barrage of near-daily attacks, with at least three people killed at an airport and oilfield on Wednesday evening.

Attacks on “civilian airports and other critical infrastructure” by the Iranian-supported Houthis in Yemen were highlighted as the reason for the drawdown. State department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said: “The safety and security of department personnel and their families remain our highest priority.”

The state department said the order covered its embassy in Riyadh and its satellite consulates. The embassy had been badly damaged at the start of the US war on Iran and had been operating with only a skeleton staff for months, although in recent weeks some diplomats had returned.

The announcement comes as some media – including NBC and AFP – reported that families of US embassy personnel were also being withdrawn from the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain, while the New York Times said the Trump administration was developing plans to restart the war on Iran.

However in his statement on Wednesday, Pigott described the reports of further withdrawals as “inaccurate” and stressed that the state department order was for the departure of staff and their families from Saudi Arabia only.

Saudi Arabia has faced a succession of deadly attacks from the Houthis over recent weeks, including a strike on Riyadh’s international airport that was the kingdom’s deadliest in years, as the war with the group escalates.

On Wednesday evening the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority announced that one Saudi resident was killed in attacks on King Fahad international airport in Dammam, on the Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar.

Eight people were injured and the airport also suffered some material damage, according to officials. Global flight-tracking service Flightradar24 said flights had been diverted away from the airport.

Separately, falling debris from the successful interception of a drone targeting an oil facility in the country’s south-east also killed two people and injured a further two, the Saudi energy ministry said.

Neither attack was immediately claimed by the Houthis, but airports and oil facilities have been a major target of the militant group in their recent wave of missile and projectile strikes on Saudi Arabia.

The US previously ordered non-essential staff to leave the Gulf ahead of the start of its war against Iran in late February. NBC reported that the US military has been quietly scaling back its presence at bases across the Middle East in recent days, however a spokesperson from US central command told the US outlet that service members are regularly moved to “optimize mission readiness”.

The withdrawal of staff from the region comes amid reports that Trump has been presented with plans for restarting strikes on Iran, after the midterm elections.

The New York Times reported that the US and Israel developed plans for a “short but intensive operation”, after defense secretary Peter Hegseth travelled to Israel earlier this week for meetings with prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Last week ⁠Trump said the US was looking to knock out Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a site linked to the country’s ⁠nuclear program, however the president has publicly said that he does not intend to restart the war before the 3 November elections.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Ilhan Omar says US agents seized 17 items in raid designed to ‘freak’ her out
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Democrat, in first interview since pre-dawn raid, denies immigration fraud and says ‘I have a legal right to be a member of Congress’

The Minnesota congresswoman Ilhan Omar denied allegations of immigration fraud in a Wednesday appearance on MS Now, her first interview since federal agents raided her residence last week.

Those in Donald Trump’s orbit – cabinet officials and rightwing influencers alike – have promoted baseless theories about the Democratic congresswoman, accusing Omar of being in a sham marriage with her brother and fudging details of her immigration paperwork.

The brother rumors circulated on a Somali blog, Omar told MS Now host Chris Hayes, before it gained traction with rightwing conspiracy theorists in Minneapolis.

“They kept alluding to the fact that something was going to happen to me,” Omar told Hayes. “They had to do something, I believe, to say, ‘Hey, look we raided her house.”

The 12 October raid marked an escalation of a years-long feud between Omar and Trump.

The president has repeatedly denigrated Omar’s character, faith and Somali heritage, most recently on Tuesday, when he called her a “sick, very dishonest person who hates our country” while answering reporters’ questions at the White House.

Trump had been asked if Omar could face deportation over alleged misstatements in her immigration paperwork, to which he replied: “Well, she could be. She could also go to jail.”

In the MS Now interview, Omar also shared further details about how the raid was conducted.

About 10 to 15 Homeland Security Investigations agents pounded on her door at 6am, then executed a search warrant, she said. According to Omar, after scouring her residence room by room for nearly five hours, the agents took 17 items, including several phones.

“You don’t show up to somebody’s house that early in the morning unless you’re trying to freak them out,” Omar said.

“Obviously, they’d like to see me locked up, deported and all of those things. But I think the bigger satisfaction for them would be for me to be like, ‘I’m tired of all of you and I’m going to leave,’” she said. “I have a legal right to be a member of Congress.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘Man, I loved that’: Trump cheers South Carolina rally attender who hit protester
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
President was reportedly heckled at least nine times during campaign event for Darline Graham

Multiple protesters were removed from Donald Trump’s rally at South Carolina’s Clemson University on Wednesday, including one who was apparently punched by a rally attender – to the US president’s delight.

“That was great, man. Wow. Man, I loved that. I watched that,” Trump said. “That was incredible. Wow. That was unbelievable. Is everybody OK?

“Who’s the guy that threw that punch?” he continued. “You know, you reminded me of Evander, the real deal, Holyfield,” referring to the former heavyweight champion, who was also in attendance at the rally.

“You gotta give them credit. It takes courage to do that at a Trump rally,” he said. “He got whacked.”

According to a pool report, the president was interrupted at least nine times by hecklers. The crowd chanted “USA” as security guards escorted the ​protesters out of the arena.

One protester who was removed by security was followed by a rally attendee, who appeared to slap the demonstrator on the head.

Trump was in South Carolina to support Darline Graham, the sister of late senator Lindsey Graham who died suddenly in July from a heart condition. Graham, elected to her brother’s seat in a special election, is facing Democratic challenger Annie Andrews in her bid for a full six-year term.

Protests have frequently erupted at Trump rallies in recent weeks, as the president has ramped up his campaign stops in the final weeks before the 3 November midterm elections. The president often brushes off the demonstrations as being carried out by “paid protesters”.

Trump’s 32-day campaign blitz has largely taken him to Republican-leaning areas that he won comfortably in previous elections, underscoring the challenges facing Republicans as they try to retain control of the US Senate and the House of Representatives.

The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll, published on Monday, found that 31% of Americans approve of Trump’s performance in office, a record low for the president.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Angel Reese stars again as Atlanta Dream thrash Valkyries to seize WNBA finals lead
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Angel Reese had 21 points and 12 rebounds to help the Atlanta Dream beat the Golden State Valkyries 97-71 on Wednesday night and take a 2-1 lead in the WNBA finals.

Rhyne Howard added 16 points and Naz Hillmon had 15 for the Dream, who host Game 4 on Saturday.

It was the second straight strong game for Reese, who had 30 points and 16 rebounds in Game 2, which the Dream also won for their first victory in the finals. She now has a double-double in each game of the finals.

“It feels good when you’re in the finals. It’s a long season and you play against everybody and go through and push through, but when you can do it at the highest level, this is what you live for, this is what the offseason is for,” Reese said. “I put the work in for this moment and I’m just happy I could lead the team to a win. We’re feeling good going into Saturday.”

In the US, the series will air on NBC, USA Network and CNBC, with all games streaming on Peacock. In the UK, it will be carried by Sky Sports. In Australia, fans can watch through WNBA League Pass, with selected coverage also available through ESPN.

With the game tied at 49 in the third quarter, Atlanta scored eight straight, including four by Reese. Golden State got within 59-55 on Tiffany Hayes’ layup, but could get no closer as Atlanta closed the quarter by scoring 12 of the final 14 points.

Atlanta have dominated the third quarter so far in the series, outscoring Golden State 63-35 across the three games.

With Atlanta up 17 in the fourth quarter, Jordin Canada overthrew Reese on the break, but she saved the ball by throwing it over her head underneath the basket to Howard, who was fouled.

Golden State could never recover. Gabby Williams scored 15 points and Hayes added 14 for the Valkyries.

This game was originally scheduled to be played on Thursday at the Gateway Center Arena, where the Dream play most of their home games. The league was able to work with the Atlanta Hawks and State Farm Arena to play the next two games of the championship series there so that they could have a much bigger crowd. Gateway seats only 3,500. State Farm Arena can seat more than 17,000 fans.

“Protect home court,” Howard said of the team’s focus. “Giving our fans a show. We fought for this arena so we had to protect it. It’s big. We went and stole one but we can’t let them come in and do the same thing.”

Wednesday night’s game was sold out, as is Game 4 on Saturday, which will also be played at State Farm Arena. The crowd included several music stars, including Ludacris. Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom said he was going to be at the game. The Atlanta Dream and State Farm Arena offered him a private suite for his protection. He refused to sit in it and was removed from the game.

The game got off to a slow start as Atlanta led 9-1 after the first five minutes. Golden State missed their first eight shots before Aminata Gueye scored the first basket for the Valkyries with 4:39 left. They got within 13-10 before Naz Hillmon hit consecutive three-pointers and then Reese hit one. The Dream led 23-15 after the opening quarter.

The hot three-point shooting continued in the second quarter as Atlanta built their lead to 37-26 midway through the period. Golden State were able to hang around and trailed only 46-40 at the break as the teams combined to shoot 15-for-31 (48%) from behind the arc. That was more made three-pointers in the first 20 minutes than in either Game 1 or Game 2.

Reese had 15 points and WNBA sixth woman of the year Janelle Salaun had 11 for the Valkyries.

Games 1 and 2 had huge ratings, with the opener on NBC averaging 2.1 million viewers, the most ever to watch the first game of the finals. Game 2, which was broadcast on USA Network, averaged 1.33 million viewers.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Anthony Edwards scores 45 as Timberwolves spoil Giannis Antetokounmpo’s Heat debut
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Anthony Edwards scored 45 points as he and the Minnesota Timberwolves spoiled Giannis Antetokounmpo’s debut with the Miami Heat in an emphatic 131-106 season-opening win on Wednesday night.

Edwards became just the third player in NBA history to record multiple 40-point games in season openers, joining Wilt Chamberlain and Michael Jordan.

Antetokounmpo scored 35 points and grabbed six rebounds after joining Miami in an offseason trade with the Milwaukee Bucks.

Edwards checked out with 3:51 remaining and Minnesota leading by 28. He shot 16-for-29 from the floor, including 9-for-17 from three-point range, and added 10 rebounds.

His 45 points were the most by a Minnesota player in a season opener and marked his 125th career game with at least 30 points.

LaMelo Ball, making his Timberwolves debut, hit five three-pointers and finished with 21 points and six assists. Jaden McDaniels scored 17 points, and Rudy Gobert grabbed 15 rebounds for Minnesota.

Antetokounmpo checked out with seven minutes remaining after hearing MVP chants from the home crowd early in the game. He shot 13-for-19 from the floor but also airballed a free throw and was assessed a flagrant foul after elbowing Terrence Shannon Jr in the head on a drive.

Antetokounmpo was Miami’s most productive scorer. Bam Adebayo had 15 points, Andrew Wiggins and Davion Mitchell added 11 apiece, and Mitchell also dished out 10 assists. Klay Thompson scored 10 points in his Miami debut.

Edwards and Antetokounmpo each scored 21 points in the first half, but Minnesota carried a 10-point lead into the break.

The Timberwolves opened 11-for-14 from the floor and led 27-19 after eight minutes. Miami pushed back in the second quarter and briefly took a 50-49 lead on a three-pointer by Bobby Portis Jr.

Minnesota controlled the final five minutes of the half. Shannon hit a pair of corner three-pointers, Edwards recorded a steal and an easy dunk, and Ball scored on a drive and added two free throws to make it 69-59.

The momentum carried over into the third quarter. Edwards and Ball each hit a three-pointer in the opening two and a half minutes. Edwards added another as Minnesota extended their lead to 78-61, and the Timberwolves remained in control the rest of the way.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: History comes home as St Louis City top Columbus Crew to win US Open Cup
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Jeff Rueter
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
For much of the 20th century, winning the US Open Cup required a team to beat someone from St Louis. The Gateway City was home to many of the nation’s best teams during some ramshackle eras of soccer in the United States, with six different clubs combining for 10 trophy lifts. The most recent came in 1988, when St Louis Busch Seniors beat San Francisco-based Greek-American AC in the last throes of a tournament history dominated by amateur and semi-pro teams. MLS has won every Open Cup but one since starting play in 1996, and St Louis didn’t have an MLS club until 2023.

From the beginning, club figures spoke of aims to restore the city to soccer prominence. Well, mission accomplished. St Louis City are US Open Cup champions, outlasting the Columbus Crew 5-4 on penalties away from home to end the city’s 38-year wait for a major US soccer title and earn a place in the field for the 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup.

Daniel Edelman scored the decisive penalty, with backup goalkeeper Ben Lundt making a save on Columbus’ first attempt, himself having entered the match in the second half.

Fittingly given their home city’s rich soccer history, City’s first trophy is also the nation’s oldest. Wednesday marked the 109th final in the history of the Open Cup, which was first held in 1913–14 and has run continuously save for a two-year hiatus during the Covid-19 pandemic.

However, St Louis did so with MLS’s youngest manager – Yoann Damet, the 36-year-old Frenchman who was previously Wilfried Nancy’s top assistant in Columbus but was passed over for the top job after Nancy left. St Louis will be thankful that he was.

Often two of the nation’s most aesthetically pleasing teams, Columbus and St Louis opened the final by minimizing risk. For the opening half-hour, St Louis carried a 60% share of possession but failed to muster a single shot. The hosts were a bit more incisive whenever they found the ball, working to advance upfield and trying to fashion chances for Brais Méndez, but failed to threaten Roman Bürki’s net.

Referee Guido Gonzales Jr promptly blew his half-time whistle after the 45th minute. No need for stoppage time after that half, and few could argue.

Both teams returned with intentions to sustain the caginess after the break. Columbus continued to dramatically tilt the field, taking 11 touches in St Louis’ box after half-time before the visitors managed a single one. Still, Bürki kept their sole on-target effort from rippling the net. The visitors responded by upping their fouling volume to further impede the Crew’s efforts.

The 69th minute provided an inflection point as Columbus again entered the St Louis box, where Santi Rodríguez took a clattering from behind by Carlo Holse but saw the referee play the advantage. Méndez picked up the loose ball, strafed across the top of the box to his left, and played a through-ball to former Morocco international Anass Zaroury, whose shot was blocked by a fearless Bürki who took contact to his head from the wing-back’s knee, staying down as the play fizzled.

As the former Switzerland international received medical treatment, the VAR had ample time to review and, ultimately, clear the potential penalty on Holse’s initial tackle. Ultimately, a six-minute examination led to Bürki exiting the match on a stretcher, leaving to a stadium-wide applause. Later, the CBS Sports broadcast relayed that Bürki was “OK” shortly after his departure, though he was taken to the hospital for an evaluation. In stepped Lundt, a backup since coming to MLS in 2019 – but one who had played shootout hero before for St Louis, winning their quarter-final shootout against Houston.

Another injury, seemingly a leg muscle issue to promising Columbus midfielder Taha Habroune, brought Eric Bailly off the bench with captain Sean Zawadzki pushing into midfield to accommodate. The fourth official showed 11 minutes of stoppage time, perhaps cashing some rollover minutes from the first half on top of the lengthy delay as Bürki was examined. The Nordecke increased the volume of their support, but the game’s established physicality hardly waned for their efforts. St Louis seemed to fashion a clear look inside the box in the 10th minute of stoppage time, but US international Damion Downs took too heavy a touch to fashion a shot.

A minute later, the whistle blew. Despite Columbus outshooting St Louis 16-3, both teams finished the 90 minutes without a goal to their name or a trophy to their claim. Another 30 minutes of brawling followed.

Neither team ceded an inch in the opening minutes of extra time, exchanging hard challenges and failing to maximize their ensuing set pieces.

After Timo Baumgartl started the sequence with a make, Columbus’ Santi Rodriguez sent his attempt to Lundt’s left only to be stifled by a strong left hand. The teams each converted their next three attempts, although Lundt nearly ended the sequence with a finger to Andrés Herrera’s effort in the fourth round. Edelman stepped up and made no mistake with his trophy-winner.

The MLS schedule-makers did the finalists no favors as both teams played on the road this weekend, although St Louis enjoyed an extra day of rest. St Louis also entered the final at a known disadvantage, playing without striker Rafael Navarro. A front-runner for the year-end MLS Best XI, Navarro played for the Colorado Rapids through the quarter-final stage, cap-tying him for the remainder of the tournament.

While Columbus was recently a contender on all fronts under Nancy, his departure at the end of 2025 forced the Crew into a stylistic reset. Rather than hire his top assistant, Damet, Columbus looked beyond the league and hired Henrik Rydström, a self-proclaimed acolyte of “relationism”. The Swede never adapted to MLS, quickly leading Columbus toward the bottom of the East before being shown the door in May after just 17 matches.

His replacement, Laurent Courtois, was another Nancy disciple. Meanwhile, Damet is a frontrunner for coach of the year, is in line for a top-three finish in the Western Conference – and, now, is the Open Cup champion.

In an era where fiction fixates on multiverses, Columbus will no doubt wonder what could have been had they opted for continuity and retained Damet. Their loss is St Louis’ gain, as the Western Conference club will hope this is the first of multiple trophies to be won under MLS’s youngest manager.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: ‘I’d consider replacing one of my children’: Taika Waititi on robot kids, his cheese-o-meter and Klara and the Sun
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Xan Brooks
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
The director has turned Kazuo Ishiguro’s acclaimed novel about an ailing adolescent and her glitchy robot friend into a thought-provoking film. What do the pair think this story says about tech, love and grief?

In the wings of the London film festival, a group of young influencers are discussing their personal highlights. Klara and the Sun, says one, and her colleagues agree. It’s not just that the film is still so fresh in their memory, or that they have gathered today to meet its creators and stars. Klara is funny and moving; it’s their festival favourite so far. I relay this exchange to Taika Waititi, the film’s director, who is sipping bottled water in a room down the hall. His gaze widens. He almost chokes. “Thank God!” he exclaims with just a bit too much heat.

Everybody has a perfect film, just as everybody has a perfect friend, and they vary because everybody is different. In the film, sick 14-year-old Josie loves her discontinued robot doll Klara, whereas most kids her age opt for brighter, shinier models. And the young influencers love Klara and the Sun – Waititi’s adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s acclaimed novel – while most older critics vehemently, violently disagree. All of which shows that there’s no accounting for taste, that people are confounding, and that our hearts and our brains are not always in sync. That keeps life interesting. It’s partly what the film is about. “The emotions that we give very simple labels to are really complex,” says Ishiguro, who is seated alongside the director. “The thing we call love, for example, is incredibly noisy and multifaceted. Nobody knows what the hell love is.”

For what it’s worth, I loved Ishiguro’s distinctively spare and poignant source novel and am less convinced by Waititi’s screen version, which is certainly noisy. Jenna Ortega stars as Klara, the perky solar-powered AI who plays soulmate to adolescent Josie (Mia Tharia), at a remote country house. She’s a warm splash of sunshine in an otherwise frosty environment, a fish out of water in a tragicomic sci-fi caper. But there is a glitch in the matrix; the component parts don’t align. Waititi adds sugar and caffeine, pratfalls and one-liners. Klara misreads social cues and steers the family car off the road. She fears she’ll be shipped back to the factory and melted down for scrap.

Perhaps the perfect friend is independent, self-directed. Ishiguro has seen several of his Nobel prize-winning books – The Remains of the Day, Never Let Me Go, A Pale View of Hills – adapted for the screen. He feels that the best films break away and that the worst are too faithful. “Sometimes it’s not just loyalty but laziness,” he says. “You can’t just have the text there in front of you. You need to use your imagination to move it on. A film needs to step forward, out of my book on a journey to being something bigger.”

Waititi agrees. “Why would you do a cover of a song with exactly the same instrumentation? You make the film because you love the book. But you at least want to bring some original ideas to the table.”

The book and the film are so different, it follows that their creators would be too. Ishiguro is sober, soft-spoken and writes delicate dramas about the deep mystery of life. Waititi is voluble, peacockish and makes uproarious films such as Jojo Rabbit, What We Do in the Shadows and Hunt for the Wilderpeople. He tends to view the world through a comic lens. “Yeah, that’s my instinct. I can’t make a Schindler’s List, that’s not in my wheelhouse. I want to push everything towards comedy and then reel it back.”

It’s a defence mechanism, he admits, part of his cultural DNA. “I’m from New Zealand,” he says. “In New Zealand, my friends and I always had a very sensitive cheese-o-meter. We thought the Americans loved cheese and saw sentimentality as a good thing. But of course that’s also me being scared of it. Now I think there’s a way of being more emotional and dramatic. Hopefully that’s a sign of me maturing.”

Waititi’s work, though, has always carried a pleasing eddy of sadness. His 2010 feature Boy was a comedy about child abuse, while What We Do in the Shadows reframed the vampire as a lost, lonesome immigrant. Klara and the Sun is a love story but it’s also about isolation: the gap between people; the limits of understanding. “Oh, I’m definitely interested in loneliness,” he says.

Ishiguro chips in. “Yeah, I think you’re right, there’s a crossover between our preoccupations,” he says. “But this isn’t just everyday loneliness, it’s something more fundamental. It’s about the human experience. There is part of each of us that remains alone. There is stuff that we all have to face alone. Not least death.”

That’s the other big looming topic of Waititi’s film: death. Klara works as an “artificial friend” while other robots serve as “bereavement dolls”, filling in for lost spouses, siblings and children. That’s a sound business model, the director insists. “As a father with two kids, I always fear I’ll lose one. The younger me would have thought, ‘Oh, you can’t replace someone special.’ But the older I get, and the more in love with my kids I get, I think, ‘Oh, eventually I’d believe it was them.’ The human brain is easily adaptable. A therapist will tell you that you can programme anyone to fall in love. Tell someone you love them 50 times a day and in a few months your brain will give up and believe it. So I’d definitely consider replacing one of my children.” He laughs. “They don’t even have to be dead. I’d just like a version that’s nice to me and doesn’t ask for money.”

Ishiguro once joked that he essentially writes the same story in a variety of guises. He is drawn to flawed eyewitnesses and a partial view of events; groping narrators who try to make sense of their places in the world. The Remains of the Day’s rigid butler doesn’t know he’s in love, nor that the stately home where he works contains Nazis. Never Let Me Go’s hothoused schoolgirl finds out she is held captive and being used in terrible ways. Ishiguro’s books are unique but each connects to the world, and sometimes in ways he could not have foreseen. Klara and the Sun, for instance, was recently cited as a potential handbook for the development of generative AI. Tom Lue, VP of global affairs at Google Deepmind, suggested it be used as an “ethical touchstone”, the centrepiece of a “human-centred” approach to the future of frontier AI.

So the book has been co-opted. It has taken on another fresh life of its own. Waititi turns to the author. “It’s all your fault,” he says. “That’s incredible,” says Ishiguro. It’s the first he’s heard of it. “I know a lot of people within the AI industry are worried about its impact on society. It’s got to the point where they feel the need for a handbrake. So they are surprisingly keen to talk to creative people and road-test various ideas and scenarios.” He frowns. “But here I do become protective of both the book and the film. Because our story really isn’t about all that. If someone is trying to figure out the ethics of AI and where we should all be going, I’m not sure they’d be well-guided by this story. There are other, better places to go.”

Klara has been built with a sweet, simple purpose: to provide friendship and support. But the human world is hazardous, unstable, which means she has to update her files and adapt her approach. Waititi’s film veers and darkens, riffing off its downbeat source novel, finally closing in towards death. “There’s another version of this story where Klara would turn into a murder-bot,” he points out.

Robot dolls fill a need, plug a gap and ideally make life better. But artificial friends, by their nature, are replaceable too. In the press room next door, the influencers are still comparing notes, killing time between interviews. Klara and the Sun is receding; the conversation has already moved on. One says: “You have to see La Bola Negra. It’s my film of the year.”

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: 18 again: I returned to my life in 1983 – to reckless adventures, in a world soaked in alcohol
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Rick Williams
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Sundays were deadly, the generation gap between parents and their kids was enormous, and a pint cost 50p. The frisson of casual violence was everywhere. When I left school and set off to travel, I had no sense at all of where I was going or what I would find

I am wandering down a steep and unfamiliar street in Saint Peter Port, Guernsey, a force seven gale blowing in my face, when I look up to cross the road and see a back garden running up the hillside opposite. It ends in a granite rock face about 30ft high, and in that moment, I have a vivid flashback to being sat on top of it, watching a group of people in the garden below. I can’t conjure their faces, but the memory is all too real: the sun on my face, a woman calling up: “Don’t break your neck!” I can tell she’s not worried and neither am I. Nobody is. It’s a party and we’re young and we’re drunk and we’re carefree, without a worry in the world. Or at least, that’s how I remember it.

I continue down the street, spooked by the power of the recollection, how it has ambushed me. I stand outside the house. I could swear I’ve never seen it before. Did I come to the party over the cliff? Should I knock on the door? Hi, this is going to sound weird but I was in your back garden about 42 years ago and I haven’t a clue why but I’ve just remembered it like it was yesterday …

There are no lights on, no car outside. I carry on down to the coast, where huge waves crash against the sea wall.

“A single person’s memory, uncorroborated and unsubstantiated by other evidence, is a feeble guide to the past,” the novelist, Julian Barnes, wrote in the Guardian last year. I am in Guernsey because it’s where I lived when I turned 18, even though I spent most of that year working and travelling abroad. I’m trying to recapture what my life was like then and it’s a good place to start. In Back to the Future, Michael J Fox’s Marty McFly gets in a DeLorean time machine. I have flown in an ATR 72-600 turboprop, and it is only my second time on the island in 35 years.

On 26 May 1983, a 7.8 magnitude earthquake in the Sea of Japan triggered a tsunami that devastated Honshu. Across the Pacific, the US conducted a nuclear test in Nevada, while Candy Girl by New Edition topped the UK charts. Manchester United beat Brighton & Hove Albion 4-0 in the replay of the FA Cup final (a painful fact to write as a Liverpool fan and now Brighton resident) and Star Wars: Episode VI – Return of the Jedi was bossing it at the box office. It was also my 18th birthday. Two weeks later, on 9 June, the Tories had a landslide general election victory that cemented Thatcherism for the next decade, a far more unpleasant detail to recall than the football result.

I don’t remember any of that – a quick internet search has filled me in. But it can’t tell me what I did that day. A Thursday in the middle of my A-levels, I would have probably been revising in my bedroom (although I remember spending more time doing keepy-uppies in the garden, struggling to focus), eager for the exams to be over, to leave school and home and go travelling. Top of the Pops was on that evening but it was no longer the weekly ritual of my earlier teens. Apparently the Police performed Every Breath You Take, today the most-streamed track of the 80s. I didn’t like it back then. The month before, Bowie’s Let’s Dance had been No 1 for three weeks. I loved Bowie and bought the album, but was disappointed: it was too polished, too commercial, a new direction for him I disapproved of, all tan and white teeth, a sign of much of the 80s to come.

When I was 11, my family moved from Wirral (or the metropolitan county of Merseyside, which it became part of in 1974) to Guernsey. My dad worked for the Midland Bank on Dale Street in Liverpool and was being transferred. Five days before I was due to start secondary school in Birkenhead, we drove south and caught a ferry. I’d never been on one before, never been abroad (neither had my parents). I told my mates I was going to live on the equivalent of a Caribbean island. It was the heatwave of 1976; the sun had clearly gone to my head. That first winter in Guernsey it seemed to rain incessantly and as a family we struggled to adapt to a very different way of life in a rented bungalow. My sister, Sue, who was two years older than me, never adjusted. When she was 16, three years after our move, she went back to Birkenhead to finish her education, living with the family of a friend of hers, only returning to the island for holidays. Which meant that from the age of 14, I was essentially an only child.

I had a troubled relationship with my parents, as did my sister; it was a big reason she left. The generation gap was huge. My parents had no experience of being a teenager. Born in the 1930s, they grew up in north Wales before youth culture. My father had a motorbike, but he wasn’t a biker. He couldn’t understand why I had to question and challenge everything. Because I did. I struggled with authority and I saw him as compliant. We were chalk and cheese. Even my being left-handed, which he jokingly called “cack-handed” when I laid the table with the fork on the right, was further evidence of our difference. A friend said once: “Everything we did was a way of saying to them: ‘I don’t want to be like you.’” Their politics, their clothes, their music, the TV they watched and the jobs they did (my mother was a housewife) were anathema. Such rejection must have been difficult, but perhaps not that unusual. Late 70s punk shocked not only my parents’ generation but its own. Rebellion was in the air. Another friend, who had a similarly difficult relationship with his conservative father around the same time, puts it: “He didn’t have the tools to deal with me.”

There was also the growing disparity in our educations. My parents left school at 16 but their ambition was for me to go to university (about 7% of 18-year-olds in the UK went to university in 1983, compared with 40.6% in 2025, despite there being grants and not crippling loans). English was my favourite subject (I was a big reader) and two books I studied for A-level helped broaden my horizons: As I Lay Dying by William Faulkner introduced me to stream of consciousness and more experimental writing, while Strait is the Gate by Andre Gide for my French A-level got me reading Sartre, Cocteau, Camus and Kafka – and opened the door to a morally ambiguous and transgressive world that I embraced for its essential absurdity. This was perhaps not the education my parents had in mind.

Before going to Guernsey, I arrange to meet my old friends Paul, Jay and Steve, who still live there. In the pub, as we chat about the past, I am initially struck – and a little alarmed – by how much more they remember than I do: people, pubs and clubs, parties and incidents. I tell myself it’s because they still live there, the constant reminders, but I also wonder if it is more about what we choose to remember.

Over dinner, we talk about how we understood the world in 1983 and what shaped us, with no internet and only four TV channels. Apart from our peers, we agree that NME and other magazines such as the Face were hugely influential, along with the John Peel show and Radio Caroline. I first started reading NME when I was 14 from cover to cover (the classified ads were as fascinating as the editorial). A review or interview might mention an older band or influence, and at the record shop (No.19 in Saint Peter Port, today a White Stuff), you’d search through the racks for them. Did the Teardrop Explodes and Echo and the Bunnymen trigger an interest in the Doors and 60s psychedelia, acid and Carlos Castaneda, the beats and counter culture?

You often had to take a punt on a record, parting with your hard-earned cash (I had a job as a milkman on a Sunday and in the holidays throughout my school years). Did I buy Thermonuclear Sweat by Defunkt in 1983, a band I’d never heard of, because I picked it up in No.19, drawn to the title, and saw a Joseph Bowie in the lineup and I was a Bowie fan? Its punk-jazz threw me, but I grew to love it, learned that Joseph was the brother of Lester Bowie, co-founder of The Art Ensemble of Chicago, my hardcore introduction to jazz. In that random way, one thing could lead to another, so slow compared with today, when we have a world of knowledge at our fingertips.

The early 80s were tribal: punk, mod, skin, rude boy, new romantic, indie: you dressed like the bands you listened to (on Saturday afternoons, we would go to jumble sales and find clothes to customise). The music you bought spoke volumes. Talking to my own three children, Connor, 27, Ella, 23 and Jake, 21, I get the impression that they didn’t listen to music with the same prejudices when they were 18. Fleetwood Mac, Genesis, Led Zeppelin and all those 70s “rock dinosaurs” would never have darkened my turntable (or increasingly, my cassette player; although I still have a lot of my records, not a single cassette has survived, all those cherished mixtapes, often painstakingly recorded off the radio, gone).

I remember being interested in the news, what was happening in the world (it was easy to feel cut off on an island). I read the Guernsey Evening Press (I liked the crime pages) and the Times, which my parents got, every day. They listened to BBC Radio 2 at breakfast, Terry Wogan to start the day, and watched The Nine O’Clock News in the evening. The news events that I remember were acid rain destroying the forests of northern Europe, high unemployment of 11.5% in the UK (though in Guernsey the rate was negligible), the Soviet Union invasion of Afghanistan and the tensions of the cold war growing with Reagan in the White House. There had been the Falklands war in 1982, a 74-day conflict that saved Thatcher’s premiership but seemed a world away. (The landlady of Taylor’s Long Bar in Saint Peter Port didn’t like serving groups of young men, but made an exception for servicemen. My friends and I happily told her we were back from the Falklands and she served us underage.)

The biggest threat was nuclear Armageddon. In September 1983, only the quick thinking of a Soviet officer averted catastrophe, when he interpreted a reported US nuclear strike as a false alarm and didn’t push the button – the closest the world has come to nuclear war since the Cuban missile crisis.

We all knew the name of Greenham Common, but I didn’t fully understand what was happening there. We would laugh about the advice of hiding under a table, in the case of a nuclear attack. Yeah, right.

Alcohol played a massive part in my life when I was 18, as it had done throughout my teens. It was easy to get served underage, so turning 18 wasn’t a landmark moment in terms of legally buying a drink (no one carried ID). Alcohol and tobacco were cheap on Guernsey: we all drank and smoked. You could go out with a fiver and have a night of it at about 50p a pint, the same for a packet of cigarettes. (It’s no longer cheap there, more or less the same as the UK.) During my visit, I pop into a pub at lunchtime that we used to frequent. It has seen better days. There is one customer, a woman at the bar having a large glass of wine. While I am chatting to the barperson about why I am on the island, the woman turns and says: “Love, all you’ve got to write about Guernsey is: 70,000 alcoholics clinging to a rock in the middle of the sea.”

There is certainly a wild and reckless alcoholic haze to a lot of my memories. A time and a pub would be agreed and the night would go on from there. Afterwards, we might go to a club or a house party, invited or not. We were all sexually active, quite promiscuous. Aids was still a few years off from being widely reported and we took few if any precautions. We drank and drove, motorbikes when we were younger (my friend Paul was a mod and we went round on his Lambretta), cars once we were 17. Guernsey didn’t have breathalysers at the time. If you were pulled over, you had to walk toe to heel for about 10ft, bend down and pick up a coin, and toe to heel back. If you didn’t lose your balance, you were fit to drive. I got away with it several times.

Apart from the record shop, the bookshop was another important place of discovery. It was there that I bought Jean Genet’s Miracle of the Rose when I was 17 and got chatting to the owner about literature. He invited me to his house for a cup of tea and showed me around the place. The last room was the cellar, which turned out to be a sex dungeon: handcuffs on the wall, whips and masks. He casually explained that he threw parties down there and if I ever fancied coming to one … I declined as casually as I could. Maybe we’d talked about De Sade earlier in the bookshop. The next time I saw him we chatted as if it had never happened. He must have trusted me not to tell anyone, which I didn’t (it would have been scandalous in such a conservative place). But it seemed like confirmation of the edgy and exciting world that books could lead to.

It’s hard to say if our lives were better or worse than they are for 18-year-olds today. We experienced boredom more – Sundays were deadly, everything closed. Sexism and racism and homophobia were commonplace, as was casual violence; parents physically disciplined their kids and corporal punishment wasn’t banned in state schools until 1986, so it’s perhaps no surprise that, with a few drinks, punches got thrown. Football hooliganism was rampant, making headlines. On a night out, there was a mild expectation of trouble.

We would occasionally go to London to see bands (in my early teens, bands came to Guernsey – Elvis Costello, the Jam, Depeche Mode, Adam and the Ants – but then stopped. I’m not sure why, but logistics, costs and the island not having a big enough venue were all probably part of it). There was a world out there – and I was desperate to explore it.

Three months after my 18th birthday, my friend Joel and I set off travelling. I had saved £400 from working all summer in a greenhouse that was pioneering the cultivation of kiwifruit on Guernsey, to replace the dying tomato industry (it never took off). Our vague plan was to work our way across Europe, maybe end up on a kibbutz (which still had a reputation as socialist paradises), then travel further. A gap year before university. In the bookshop I had chanced upon Work Your Way Around the World, which was in its first edition; we’d never heard of Lonely Planet and were perhaps as informed by the spirit of On the Road and Genet. Our only map was of all of Europe, taking in the top of north Africa and some of the Middle East. It was somewhat lacking in detail. No one else we knew was going travelling or had been. Looking back, Joel and I agree that naivety was as much our guide.

After grape picking in the Champagne region, we hitchhiked to the south of France. Often, no one would pick us up (including Björn Borg, who drove past us twice in his black Porsche near Monaco) and we would walk for miles, sleeping rough. On the French riviera, we bought a cheap summer tent and crossed northern Italy, sleeping in railway stations. In Venice, a guy tried to rob us in the middle of the night. When I woke, he threatened me and carried on going through my bag so I pulled out my knife to scare him off. I’d had it since I was 14, when I saw it glinting at the bottom of the marina in Saint Peter Port and dived down to retrieve it, a British second world war Fairbairn Sykes stiletto fighting knife; no plaything. He looked at it and laughed, whipped out a switchblade and waved it in my face, to show I didn’t stand a chance, before strolling off. I vowed to never pull a knife on anyone again. But what amazes me now is that I carried that knife through dozens of border checks and on numerous flights, and it was never an issue.

We continued through Yugoslavia and into Greece, where Work Your Way Around the World said there was orange picking on the Peloponnese. We met a few other northern Europeans, older than us, also looking for work. They told us the harvest was late. We wandered around Greece for weeks, ending up in the small town of Gargalianoi, where we stayed for three months, helping with the olive harvest, working in construction and an olive oil factory. Most of the time we slept in woods on the edge of town, our own little squatter camp that the locals turned a blind eye to, once a week going to the fleapit hotel in town, for a cold shower and the comfort of a bed. We were the only foreigners, apart from a couple of French guys, Gilles and Eric. They were recovering heroin addicts (Gilles had done nine months in Paris’s notorious La Santé prison for possession) and were planning to stay out of France for seven years to avoid military service, that length of absence granting exemption. We became friends and also increasingly aware that being British, we were the envy of European youth for not having national service: a Greek friend we were working with, Tomas, was about to start his two-year military conscription, a bleak posting on the troubled Turkish border.

That eight-month journey sometimes feels like a fever dream. It defines being 18 for me: freedom and adventure, living on your wits, never knowing what the next day might bring. From Greece we went to Egypt and across north Africa, back up through Spain and France and home. There were tough times, but no question of turning back. People on the whole were kind – we were kids and they wanted to help us. Our map was so basic, we had little idea where we were going, following the setting sun. For a time, we used a copy of David Copperfield we picked up in a hotel in Cairo as toilet paper, each reading the same 20 or so pages a day and then tearing them out.

There were two threatening periods: in Tunis, we became the target of unwanted sexual attention, followed night and day, men waiting outside our hotel room, every invitation for coffee turning into aggressive attempts at seduction; and in Tétouan in Morocco, we were hounded by dealers for days, sold hash and then told we would be shopped to the police unless we bought more. They were still threatening us as we left on the bus.

“The stories we tell most often about our lives are likely to be the least reliable, because we will have subtly amended them in every retelling down the years,” Barnes wrote in the same article. “It’s salutary to discover, from time to time, how other people’s memories are often quite different from our own – not just of events, but of what we ourselves were like back then.” Joel had forgotten the use of Dickens as toilet paper; I’d forgotten the level of hassle in Tétouan. Maybe I was too stoned. The truth is there, somewhere, among the stories.

In 2019, when my mother went into a home, I was clearing my parents’ house with my sister when I came across a folder of old documents and papers of mine that they’d kept. Looking through them for this article, I found five letters I wrote during my time away – I’d forgotten they existed, this was the first time I’d read them since I wrote them 42 years ago. Would they corroborate what I was really like as an 18-year-old? The fact that I sent only five letters and made no phone calls in eight months shocks me now as a parent (my sister says she asked my mum if she worried about me when I was away and she said she did, but that she felt there would have been disapproval, possibly from my father and no doubt from me, if she had expressed it).

To be honest, I’m surprised I wrote any letters at all, from how I remember our relationship. Instead, I find myself joking to them about being hungry, about roughing it, my hair getting longer, losing weight. There are things I had forgotten – our plan to go to a kibbutz in Israel thwarted by “war and conflict”; another plan to take a two-week boat trip from Athens to Alexandria (why would it take so long?!); our intention to cross the middle of the Sahara, only to find out in Egypt it would take three months to get a visa to enter Sudan and continue into Chad. I can see I am trying to shock them at times, but not too much. I tell them about Gilles and Eric and getting drunk on New Year’s Eve with them, Gilles throwing up in our hotel room, but I don’t mention their heroin addiction or the pills we took that had me hallucinating large insects crawling over my body, something that I thankfully found hilarious rather than terrifying. I say how beautiful Venice is, being kicked awake by Italian cops at dawn, but I don’t mention the incident with the knife. I complain about being sexually harassed in Tunis, but brush it off.

What surprises me most though is a warmth I hadn’t allowed for. Maybe distance did. Letters tell their own stories.

Most of us look back at our 18-year-old selves and do a little editing. As F Scott Fitzgerald wrote: “At 18, our convictions are hills from which we look; at forty-five they are caves in which we hide.” What were my convictions? Is the unheralded memory of being sat on that rock face – acting fearless, reckless, carefree, about to leap into the unknown – as accurate a picture as any? I spent most of my 20s after university travelling, living abroad. I still love to travel, even if kids and a career and the realities of adult life have restricted the opportunities. I still love the feeling of the bag on my back containing all I need. My kids love to travel too; I like to think my wife and I have given them that sense of adventure. We plan to go travelling for a year when we stop working. I like to think that 18-year-old is still with me.

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: Tied up and tortured: Israel using US-made electroshock weapons on Palestinian detainees
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.author: Mustafa Abdel Raouf
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
Investigation suggests American company Axon still supplies Israel with Taser weapons despite evidence they have been used to torture prisoners

The soldiers drag the man into a section of the prison known as Hell’s Wing, a metaphor for its notoriety for acts of brutality. Shoving him violently into a corner, they take a step back before one of them draws his weapon and fires two rubber bullets at his body. The man, a double amputee, collapses to the floor.
