He stayed when Ole Gunnar Solskjær replaced the Portuguese and was credited with having a strong tactical influence as United secured second place. It is often a strength to have a link to a club but considering the struggles Solskjær and Carrick have endured, an external candidate seems more appropriate. He departed to become a head coach at Ipswich and his work there meant he was linked with a return to United to replace Erik ten Hag. McKenna resigned in June after securing promotion to the Premier League for a second time to take time away from the day-to-day grind of managemen. Would he want to end his sabbatical by jumping into a precarious situation after five or so months?

The English option and a manager with plenty of Premier League experience who took Newcastle to the Champions League. Arguably this makes him the safest pair of hands. A hard worker, Howe was often first in and last out at the Newcastle training ground as he pored over every detail. A lover of wingers and 4-3-3, he would be reliant on a central striker such as Benjamin Sesko to step up. He likes to work closely with his nephew Andy, who held senior roles at Bournemouth and Newcastle, which would create an interesting dynamic if he wanted similar at United. Howe, like others in contention, would not cost anything in compensation – and every penny counts at Old Trafford.

The 33-year-old has a growing reputation, with his Brighton team third after scoring 23 goals in seven games. This could explain why he is not particularly keen on leaving at the moment. His team are outperforming United with a squad that looks stronger. The size of United is alluring for many coaches but moving mid-season to a struggling club is not always advantageous because it means stepping into a firefight.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Teacher wounded in Oregon school shooting played dead after she was shot
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Dani Anguiano
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Becky Drury says she was hit by gunfire before she could intervene in attack that killed four, including three children

A teacher wounded in last week’s shooting at a Bend, Oregon, elementary school shared her account of the incident, and how she was shot before she could intervene and “[pretended] to be dead”.

Becky Drury was seriously wounded at Silver Rail elementary when Griffin J John II, a 16-year-old former student at the school armed with a shotgun, broke in and headed toward a special education classroom. He shot six people, killing Megan Lambert, a 25-year-old teacher, and three children, including five-year-old Rhoam Summer.

Drury and Saylor Graham, a seven-year-old student, were also shot. Another teacher threw her phone at John and tackled him before a parent fatally shot the teen gunman.

“Here is what I remember: Once I realized something was happening outside, I ran to see what was going on. I then saw the shooter and immediately ran back into the classroom. I turned to shut the door behind me, but the shooter was already there. Before I could do anything more, he shot me at close range and I fell to the ground,” Drury said.

Her left hand was almost completely severed, and her other arm was also badly injured, Drury said.

“I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else. So, I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again,” she said. “I know there has been contradictory reporting about my actions that day, but the truth is I was shot before I had any chance to act.”

Drury’s account contradicted some reporting that she had thrown herself on top of a student in an effort to protect her, and the 54-year-old said she wanted to ensure “the events of that day and my actions in particular are reported accurately”.

She described the violence as “unimaginable” and said “my heart is broken for everyone affected by this tragedy.”

Public schools in the central Oregon city began reopening this week. Dozens of officers have welcomed students as they return to their classes.

The shooting remains under investigation. The Bend police department said this week that the shotgun used in the incident was purchased legally.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Aipac halts candidate endorsements amid US backlash against Israel
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Alice Speri
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
‘Political candidates’ once reflexive support for Israel has increasingly become a liability

When the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the most prominent pro-Israel lobby group in the US, announced on Wednesday that it would stop endorsing candidates or make direct contributions to them, its many critics were quick to hail the development as Aipac’s admission of how toxic its brand had become.

The announcement marked a significant reversal that underscored just how profoundly US public opinion of Israel has shifted over the latest war in Gaza, and how political candidates’ once reflexive support for Israel has increasingly become a liability.

But Aipac, which only launched its political action committee and started endorsing candidates three cycles ago, is hardly getting out of US elections. It pledged to maintain the work of its deep-pocketed Super Pac, United Democracy Project, and to continue to funnel millions of dollars to prop up pro-Israel candidates through individual donors and Aipac members. The shift in strategy was a sign it was adapting to a changing political landscape, not that it was giving up its efforts to shape it.

“Historically, AIPAC sustained an aura of invincibility that ensured it won most battles by walkover – if you are perceived as invincible, the other side doesn’t even bother to fight you,” the political analyst Trita Parsi wrote. “Rather than invincibility, AIPAC’s name now carries such toxicity that the group doesn’t want its own name on its political donations.”

Aipac did not respond to a request for comment. On Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Aipac, which normally backs Democrats, was planning to give as much as $9m to a Pac supporting Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers over Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. The group had already spent $32m seeking to defeat El-Sayed, an outspoken critic of Israel, in the primaries.

But the announcement that it would stop directly backing candidates going forward was seen as tacit recognition that Aipac’s open support risked hurting pro-Israel candidates more than it helped them.

“Through this shift, AIPAC openly admitted that their brand has become toxic in the political world,” Beth Miller, political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action, one of Aipac’s most vocal critics, said. “Fewer and fewer candidates are willing to be publicly affiliated with this extremist, warmongering group. This is a clear signal: being pro-genocide is bad politics and bad policy.”

In a letter from Aipac to members first reported on by Jewish Insider, the group’s leadership seemed to acknowledge that its once formidable power in US elections had suffered as more candidates openly distanced themselves from Israel and from the group itself. In the letter, they noted that the 2026 election was “one of the most challenging environments in recent memory” for the group and predicted that the “challenges we are confronting will continue to grow in the years ahead.”

“To win the fight for the future of the country and the U.S.-Israel alliance, we must build a more strategic, consequential, and nimble political operation,” they wrote. “The only tactic we’re married to is the most effective one.”

While Aipac boasted that it helped 290 candidates this election cycle, leading to the defeat of 29 candidates it described as “anti-Israel”, the group has also suffered major blows – including in Michigan and New Jersey. More than a dozen candidates who took Aipac contributions in the past have since publicly distanced themselves from the group, and New York congressman Pat Ryan announced last week that he would return nearly $250,000 from the group, the latest of several elected officials to return Aipac funds or say they would turn it down.

Dion Nissenbaum, a journalist whose documentary on Aipac was published this week, featuring interviews with former Aipac insiders, told the Guardian that the announcement appeared to be the “first real admission from Aipac that their campaign strategy has backfired”.

Still, he warned, “if Aipac’s super PAC – the main source of its campaign donations – is going to keep operating, it may be an attempt to reinvent itself without ceding the battlefield.”

Tuesday’s announcement would change little in practice, those who have monitored Aipac’s political funding say. An Aipac spokesperson told Jewish Insider that Aipac members had contributed over $90m to candidates this election cycle – far more than the $3m in donations the group contributed directly through its Pac.

“This is not new,” Hady Amr, a former secretary for Israeli and Palestinian affairs with the US state department, noted. “This is Aipac going back to their tried and true approach.”

Groups like TrackAipac and initiatives like the Reject Aipac campaign, that have in recent years played a growing role in calling out candidates over their ties to the group, are already attuned to the varied avenues through which the pro-Israel lobby funnelled contributions to candidates, some more visible than others.

“[Aipac] has already been experimenting with ways to make their support more untraceable,” said Hamid Bendaas of the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, one of the groups behind the Reject Aipac campaign. By dropping endorsements and direct contributions, Aipac was giving up one tool available to lobby organizations to signal to politically-aligned donors who may not be active members which candidates to back. Aipac had calculated that approach was more risky than worth it, he added, but it had plenty of other tools available.

“It’s akin to an animal that chews its leg off to get out of a bear trap. It’s a last resort choice to survive and stay relevant, which they will on both counts,” Bendaas added. “Aipac is going to continue influencing elections. If you’re someone who wants Aipac out of politics entirely, this is not that.

“We know they’re going to continue driving tens of millions of dollars into our elections to support Israel’s atrocities,” echoed Miller of JVP. “And we will continue to fight to fully get them, and their dirty money, out of our politics and out of Congress.”

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: James Bond finalists to screen-test for role for this week – reports
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Adrian Horton
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
Actors in the mix to play 007 in Denis Villeneuve’s installment include Callum Turner and Jack Lowden

The search for the next James Bond may finally be nearing its end: according to reports, a very select group of actors will screen-test to become the next British agent 007 this weekend.

According to the Hollywood Reporter and Variety, citing several sources, a group of very select actors reportedly including Callum Turner and Slow Horses’ Jack Lowden, will appear in front of cameras as the secret agent this weekend in London.

The tests supposedly include three elements: stunts, camera presence and dialogue. Reports vary that between three and five actors are finalists for the role, which was vacated by Daniel Craig after 2021’s No Time to Die. Despite speculation to the contrary, Sinners’ Jack O’Connell and Wuthering Heights star Jacob Elordi are not testing, according to the Hollywood Reporter.

Dune film-maker Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next installment of the Bond franchise for Amazon MGM studios, which bought the series rights as part of an $8.45bn (£6.9bn) deal in 2022. Peaky Blinders scribe Steven Knight will pen the script.

The company, which paid more than $1bn last year to wrest “creative control” from the Broccoli family, has neither confirmed nor denied the reports, and referred the Hollywood Reporter to its earlier statement: “The search for the next James Bond is under way. While we don’t plan to comment on specific details during the casting process, we’re excited to share more news with 007 fans as soon as the time is right.”

In April of this year, Amazon film executives urged fans to exercise patience in waiting for the casting announcement, citing an abundance of caution in making the closely watched decision. “I know you’re all wondering when we’re going to announce who’s playing James Bond,” said Courtenay Valenti, the company’s head of film. “Don’t get too excited. Please know that we’re taking the time to do this with care and deep respect. It is the dream of a lifetime for all of us to bring audiences this next chapter, and it’s a responsibility we don’t take lightly.”

Villeneuve, a “diehard Bond fan”, has said the opportunity to add to the beloved franchise is what drew him away from the Dune franchise that has consumed the better part of a decade of his life.

“I said, ‘Maybe it’s a good idea to go back to this project, not out of nostalgia, not because I miss it, but the opposite – I’m tired of it,’” he told Empire of Dune: Messiah, which will premiere this December. “I want to make sure that I will be severe with the material. That I will not be complacent,” he said. “I thought, ‘When it’s done, I need a very powerful rocket to pull me away from Arrakis.’ When I was asked to do the next Bond, I said: ‘OK, this is what I need.’”

It’s been more than 20 years since the last full screen test for Bond; future Superman Henry Cavill was reported to be a finalist, but the role eventually went to Craig, who first appeared in 2006’s Casino Royale.

Speculation over the new Bond has intensified in the months since Villeneuve was revealed as director in 2025. The film is still reportedly positioned for a 2028 release.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Bournemouth enjoy night to remember as 10-man Milan fail to weather storm
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Nick Ames at the Vitality Stadium
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
This was a momentous night in Bournemouth’s history, although the truth is they would have been given a far sterner examination by Coventry or Hull. You can only beat what lies in front of you and Marco Rose’s players never relinquished control against a rotten impersonation of a Milan side. The visitors resembled holograms even before Mike Maignan, their goalkeeper, rendered their task impossible with a deserved sending-off in the first half.

By then Justin Kluivert had given Bournemouth the lead with a penalty and it was another spot-kick from Marcus Tavernier, given after Maignan’s rush of blood, that underlined their overwhelming superiority. Amine Adli applied the garnish with a late free-kick and it meant an abject return to British shores for Ruben Amorim, who would have been excused seeing this particular week as the opportunity to make a point. On this evidence Manchester United, to whom Bournemouth travel on Sunday, share more than a few similarities with the modern version of Milan.

At kick-off the local and broader contexts were impossible to ignore. Bournemouth could hardly have imagined, making their great escape from the fourth-tier trapdoor in 2009, that their modest home would host such a luminous name in a competitive fixture. On the weekend they beat Grimsby, the Rossoneri were overcoming Palermo thanks to goals from Kaká and Filippo Inzaghi. However hard you squinted, seeing the seven-time European champions’ colours on display here felt a trick of the light.

“How did we end up here?” asked the public address announcer, a question repeated on a banner hoisted by the north stand. It was worth posing with a bigger picture in mind too. After all, what has happened in football’s ecosystem to ensure the Premier League’s 15th-placed team, for all their merits, could justifiably be named pre-match favourites against one of the most decorated institutions in Serie A?

Sheets of swirling, driving rain were packaged in the south coast welcome for Amorim. He braved the elements without recourse to hat or hood; England had, perhaps, left him more bedraggled in the past. But within eight minutes he suffered a further dampener when, after a rapid Bournemouth start, Kluivert converted from the spot.

The scorer had been involved in a close call directly beforehand, failing to apply contact after fine work from Evanilson and seeing Ben Gannon-Doak’s strike deflected wide as the ball ran on. Milan did not clear their lines from the resulting corner and were punished when VAR found Koni De Winter had deflected Evanilson’s header wide with his arm. There could be no complaints for Amorim.

Bournemouth, whose colours were derived from those of Milan in 1970, continued to force the pace. Yunus Musah was dispossessed and Ryan Christie forced Maignan into a save. When one of Milan’s three Englishmen, Omari Hutchinson, tried to profit from a loose Gannon-Doak pass he could only run into António Silva.

Unlike most of his teammates, Hutchinson at least looked capable of matching Bournemouth’s intensity. Overall Milan could not cope and before the half-hour they self-destructed dramatically. It was a moment of supreme idiocy from Maignan, who had just clawed James Hill’s deflected strike wide but elected to shove Tyler Adams in the face as the subsequent corner was sent in. The penalty award was clear and so was the red card shown to Maignan.

Hutchinson was sacrificed for the replacement keeper Lorenzo Torriani, who was quickly beaten. This time Tavernier, unfazed by a lengthy wait, did the honours in style. An easing-off of the downpour before half-time was scant comfort for Amorim.

Adrien Rabiot was introduced at the break for Milan, whose best hope now was that Bournemouth fancied keeping something in reserve. Their right wing-back, Diego Moreira, bustled forward in a rare suggestion of appetite but it was Gannon-Doak, on the other side of the pitch, who threatened more consistently with a series of darts to the byline.

The wind had swelled to the extent that an Ardon Jashari free-kick, aimed from just inside Bournemouth’s half, blew back towards him before reaching the box. Bournemouth had no need for such help from the elements. They were hardly assisted in their quest for a third by the referee, Vasilis Fotias, who pulled play back to book a lumbering Fikayo Tomori for a foul when the substitute Lewis Cook was clean through.

Christie sliced wide before Adli, a substitute, curled in delightfully from 22 yards. Bournemouth’s faithful could sing in the rain to their heart’s content.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: New York city council votes to ban horse-drawn carriage rides
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Marina Dunbar
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
City’s council passed Romanch’s Law, named after teen who died when he was ejected from carriage earlier this year

The New York city council has voted to ban horse-drawn carriage rides in the city by 2028 in a decision that has widespread implications for hundreds of jobs.

The council voted on Thursday on Romanch’s Law, legislation named in memory of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, who died this summer after he was ejected from a runaway horse-drawn carriage in Central Park.

Under the measure, carriage operations will cease completely in June 2028. The legislation also called for a plan to help affected employees and business owners transition out of the industry in 2027.

Earlier on Thursday, the city council’s committee on health voted six-three in favor of the ban, clearing the way for the full council vote later in the day.

The final vote came just hours after workers and members of the Transport Workers Union (TWU) Local 100, which represents horse carriage drivers, gathered outside city hall in a last-minute push to stop the legislation.

Protesters called on lawmakers to either vote against the proposal or postpone the decision to allow further negotiations. They rallied and held signs decrying the vote, including one person who raised up an actual bag of horse poop in protest.

At the center of their objections is the uncertainty surrounding what happens to workers once the industry shuts down. Carriage operators maintain that their livelihoods are being taken away without a clearly established path forward.

John Samuelsen, president of TWU, told Spectrum NY it is “utterly false” that the bill includes real plans for retraining the workers. “There’s nothing concrete at all,” he said. “The language says consideration will be given. The language should not say that.”

The measure could also put dozens of carriage medallions in jeopardy, including those belonging to immigrant-run family enterprises that have been passed down through generations.

Industry advocates argue that the carriage trade has significant financial importance, saying operators conduct more than 100,000 rides each year and contribute to the city’s tourism sector.

Some carriage drivers expressed disappointment that Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, who has championed himself as a voice for the working class and unions, would take a stand in favor of the ban.

One longtime driver, Conner McHugh, told Gothamist that the mayor “gets up on his podium and announces that he’s just shutting us all down, putting us out of business, doesn’t even talk to us”, adding, “I think this guy is as phoney as a $3 bill.”

McHugh, a second-generation driver, had previously told the Guardian that he feels there is an ongoing effort to drive people like him off land and buildings in Manhattan that coincides with the rezoning of the area where horse stables are located.

“Intimidation has taken various forms,” he said, including “reporting us to ICE and the IRS, keyboard warriors trashing us on social media, animals rights volunteers who have come to Central Park to harass our drivers and create an unsafe situation”.

But advocates pushing for the ban have repeatedly raised concerns over the years about the dangers associated with the rides and the risks to passengers and pedestrians, with those dangers gaining national attention after Mahajan’s death.

The treatment of the carriage horses has also been controversial. Animal welfare campaigners have questioned conditions in the industry, pointing to several horse deaths since 2020, including incidents in which animals collapsed while pulling carriages.

Before the decision, Donald Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform he is “so sad to see the beloved Central Park Horse-drawn Carriage Industry ending after over a Century, based largely on one tragic accident.

“When there is a car accident in the area, of which there are many, they don’t stop cars from entering the Park,” he wrote. “So why would they stop the Carriages? It was a Great Tradition. Another piece of History that’s gone. It will be missed!”

In a separate post, he added: “The Horse-drawn Carriage in New York City is a quintessential New York experience. So sad that, for political reasons, we will see it go!”

The Transport Workers Union had already informed city officials that it plans to pursue legal action in federal court if the legislation passed. Union officials maintain that the measure would unlawfully deprive carriage owners of their operating licenses, valuable medallions and businesses built over many years.

Thursday’s vote follows an agreement reached earlier this month between mayor Mamdani and the head of the city council to eliminate horse-drawn carriage rides across New York City.

Mamdani previously made clear that the administration intended to move ahead with ending the practice while addressing the consequences for those involved. “The horse carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City. Our administration will make sure workers and owners are protected and the horses are safe,” Mamdani wrote on X.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Elon Musk reportedly invests $1bn in David Ellison’s Skydance
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Maya Yang
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Musk’s investment into the new media empire comes after Paramount’s $111bn merger with Warner Bros Discovery

Elon Musk has reportedly invested approximately $1bn in Skydance, the new media empire led by David Ellison.

The deal comes alongside fresh equity infusions from existing investors, including board member Laurene Powell Jobs, Steve Jobs’s widow. Semafor first reported the news.

The investment follows Paramount’s recent $111bn merger with Warner Bros Discovery, a huge acquisition that brought the media companies together under the Skydance name. At the head of the new media empire is David Ellison, the son of billionaire Oracle co-founder and Donald Trump ally Larry Ellison.

The cash infusion solidifies an alliance between two of Trump’s richest monetary backers. In September, Semafor reported that Paramount executives had considered Musk as an equity investor, citing his close ties to Larry Ellison, who invested $1bn in Musk’s acquisition of X in 2022 and also $45m in support of Trump’s re-election bid in 2024. Musk spent more than $290m on Trump’s re-election bid and has spent more than $350m backing Republicans in the current US midterm elections.

After the merger, Skydance co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz, who previously led Mattel, informed employees that the integration would involve layoffs, stating: “Integrating two companies will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce.”

The company’s leadership – which now oversees Paramount and Warner Bros’s movie studios, HBO Max, CBS News and CNN – has set a target of more than $6bn in cost savings over the next three years, a goal that Los Angeles county officials estimate could lead to the loss of 4,500 film and television jobs in Los Angeles alone.

Prior to the merger, a coalition of 12 states, including California and New York, sued Paramount, arguing that the deal would “extinguish” competition and result in “higher prices, lower quality and less content for film and television”.

In September, a settlement agreement required Skydance to release at least 30 films and more than 180 television shows annually, while ensuring that CBS and CNN maintain editorial independence.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Dollar General agrees to nearly $1.9m settlement for overcharging New York customers
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Michael Hudson
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Government inspections showed overcharges as high as 39% on some items. The discount store giant was the subject of a 2025 investigation by the Guardian

Dollar General, the nation’s largest dollar-store chain, has agreed to a $1.875m deal to settle allegations that it “repeatedly and persistently” overcharged customers across New York state.

The New York attorney general’s office found that Dollar General often charged customers higher prices at checkout than the prices it promised on shelf labels, signs, advertising circulars and its mobile app. The state agency said one check of 114 items across multiple stores revealed overcharges on individual items as high as 26%, 38% and 39%.

Under the settlement, Dollar General will donate $1.875m in food and personal items to a regional food bank in upstate New York. The agreement also requires that the company put in place comprehensive price-accuracy safeguards at its more than 600 stores statewide.

“When New Yorkers see a sale price advertised on the shelf, they should be able to trust that they’ll be charged that same price at the register,” the New York attorney general, Letitia James, said.

The pricing issues at the company – which promotes itself as “a lifeline for affordable, everyday essentials” – are not limited to the state of New York.

A Guardian investigation published in December reported that the chain frequently overcharged customers across the nation for such items as Flintstones vitamins, Peter Pan peanut butter and Prego pasta sauce. Dollar General stores flunked more than 4,300 government price-accuracy inspections in 23 states between 2022 and 2025, the Guardian found.

An inspection at a Dollar General in Port Henry, New York, for example, flagged overcharges on 78% of the items checked.

Under the terms of the New York settlement, the company will be required to embrace a long list of policies and procedures – including scheduling staff to ensure shelf tags are updated for pricing accuracy and hiring independent auditors to conduct secret shopper tests.

The company will also be required to reformat its receipts. State investigators found Dollar General’s receipts included “various confusing formats” that made it difficult for consumers to figure out what they were really paying.

In a statement in response to questions from the Guardian, it said: “Dollar General is committed to providing customers with accurate on-shelf prices on items purchased in our stores, and we are disappointed any time we fail to deliver on this commitment. When a pricing discrepancy is identified, our store teams are instructed, expected and empowered to correct the matter on the spot for our customers.”

It added that “we have in place a number of measures designed to promote pricing accuracy, and we continuously evaluate and evolve these measures”.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Sharp drops for AI stocks overwhelm markets worldwide as oil prices jump
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Datacenter and chip costs fueled sharp decrease in AI sector although non-AI stocks still had a strong showing

The latest shudder for stocks in the AI industry pulled markets lower worldwide on Thursday, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May on worries about the war with Iran.

The S&P 500 fell 1.2% for its worst day since July, while the Nasdaq composite tumbled 2.6%. The weakness for tech stocks was so overwhelming that it masked strength for the rest of the US market, in which the majority of stocks actually rose. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 11 points, or less than 0.1%.

AI-related stocks have been swinging on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to build datacenters and buy more AI chips. Concerns also remain that their prices shot too high following a years-long frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth.

Lam Research, whose equipment and services help make semiconductors, reported gains in profit and revenue for the summer that were slightly stronger than analysts expected, for example. Usually, that helps boost a stock’s price, but Lam Research’s tumbled 11.8%.

Other big tech stocks likewise fell following quarterly reports that included at least some encouraging nuggets.

Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 7% after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, shedding tens of billions in market value, though its profit fell short. The company behind Facebook and Instagram also said it was creating a new class of stock to raise money to pay for AI investments and other expenses.

Tesla fell 3.1% after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast.

The global tide against AI stocks knocked Nvidia down 4.4%. Because the chip giant is the largest company on Wall Street by total value, movements for its stock carry more weight on the S&P 500 than any other, and it was the single strongest force pulling the index lower.

CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 10.1%.

The weakness for AI and other tech stocks began in Asia, where indexes are full of players in the industry. South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 3.5%, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 3% and Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 2.7%.

The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil leaped 4% to $113.17 after touching its highest level in five months. It’s shot up from less than $97 at the start of the month on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal.

In Europe, France’s CAC 40 stock index fell to one of the continent’s sharpest losses with a drop of 1.4%. It has fewer tech stocks than Asian or US indexes, but it was hurt by another jump in yields for French government bonds.

Yields have been generally climbing there because of worries about the government’s big debt load and strained budget. Violent protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt.

Worries about big government debt are weighing on almost every developed economy in the world, including the United States. Such concerns, along with high inflation, signals of a still-strong US economy and other factors, have pushed yields in the US bond market recently to their highest levels in decades.

But US yields nevertheless fell sharply on Thursday in a signal that investors were buying US government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled.

The yield on the 10-year treasury tumbled to 4.97% from 5.13% late on Wednesday and from more than 5.30% earlier this month. That’s a major move for the bond market.

Thursday’s drop in yields came even as another report suggested the US economy may be doing better than economists expected. It said fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could signal that layoffs remain low across the country.

That solid economy has helped US companies broadly to make bigger profits, which is what propelled the US stock market to a record high earlier this month despite the many worries tugging at it. Two out of every three stocks within the S&P 500 rose on Thursday, only to get drowned out by the drops for more influential tech stocks.

Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin and CSX were among the latest companies to join the list of those topping profit expectations for the summer, and gains for their stocks helped limit the market’s losses on Thursday.

CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said Procter & Gamble expected “geopolitical and economic challenges” to continue, but it stood by its forecasts for growth in revenue, profit and other measures for the full year. The stock price for the company behind the Crest, Olay and Oral-B brands rose 5.6%.

All told, the S&P 500 fell 93.74 points, to 7,663.43. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 11.89, to 52,867.98, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 694.00, to 26,008.86.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: A financially comfortable friend has set up a GoFundMe for vet bills. Is this socially acceptable? | Leading questions
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Eleanor Gordon-Smith
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Your friends may have had good intentions when making this request, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. But that needn’t dictate how you feel about it

A friend, who I believe is financially comfortable, set up a GoFundMe page to pay for vet bills for their sick dog while on holiday overseas.

The family appears to be financially comfortable; both adults have good jobs, own two cars, have all the latest gadgets like expensive bikes and sporting equipment, take an annual holiday overseas and domestic holidays throughout the year, and live in a big house in a well-to-do area.

Eleanor says: I’ll never forget someone posting their household expenses as proof it’s hard to get by on two six-figure incomes. By the time they’d paid for holidays, two cars, private school fees, insurance, extracurriculars, the mortgage and savings, there was nothing left!

They really did think this was proof they weren’t well-off. I suppose in some sense they’re right. Once you use your money to secure your financial future and have a high quality of life, you don’t have a Scrooge McDuck pile left over.

Point of story: moving up the wealth hierarchy moves your sense of what’s normal. Comparison looks up, not down, so people lose track of how many people they’re above. What they first experienced as an advantage slowly starts to seem like background. It’s possible your friends feel and are genuinely burdened – “we can’t cover this!” – in a situation other people would covet. And importantly, we don’t know their finances. They may not be liquid, precisely because of the holidays and the house and the equipment.

But in the ethics of asking for and giving money, it’s important that money isn’t just money. It has social meaning. Money talks, in the sense that it says things.

What it says isn’t always exhausted by how much people have. It may be important for the less well-off child to take their parents to dinner because that says “thank you”. Or for colleagues or dates to split the bill, because that means neither owes a debt of gratitude. Or to help pay for your child’s wedding even though they could afford it themselves, because that feels significant as a parent.

Where we go wrong is when our interpretations of what money says differ. Somebody thinks they’re being generous; others experience their largesse as domineering. Somebody – like a newlywed drafting the gift registry or, possibly, your friend – thinks they’re making it possible for people to give them money without any expectation of receiving it. Others experience that same action as tone-deaf and entitled.

They might feel as if it says one thing: “Something unexpected happened, we’d be touched if anyone wanted to contribute.” You might feel as if it says another: “We expect you to cover our bills.” One is an appeal to friendship, the other is an appeal to need.

In fairness, a GoFundMe isn’t means-tested. They can ask, and other people can say no. In their social circle, they may be the least well-off, which would change the dynamics of making this ask.

They’re the authority on what they meant when they uploaded this, but they don’t get to be the authority on what everybody else hears. Meaning isn’t determined solely by our intentions. Their motivations might have been totally benign at the same time as their impact was gauche.

Asking for money introduces a question that nobody had beforehand; why should I help pay for this? They may think that’s a mean-spirited question, if they intended this as an appeal to friendship. But it’s a question they’ve invited people to ask, and you’re allowed to decide your own answer.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Guardian sport
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Max Dowman may get a chance, Spurs need to find balance at Stamford Bridge and Axel Disasi must make amends

After seven games, Nottingham Forest’s record is eerily similar to last season: five points, five goals scored. A year ago Forest’s eighth game was a 3-0 home loss to Chelsea that marked the end for Ange Postecoglou, the second of four managers to occupy the dugout last term. There is no suggestion that Oliver Glasner is under similar scrutiny yet, but the Austrian needs to find solutions for the league’s lowest scorers. Morgan Gibbs-White is available after missing the narrow defeat by Arsenal, while Liam Delap may benefit from a return to familiar surroundings – 12 of his 14 career Premier League goals were scored for Ipswich, six of them at Portman Road. “What we need to improve is getting [Delap] into more positions where he can score,” Glasner said before Friday evening’s game. “He’s one of our best finishers.” Gary O’Neil also lacks a standout scorer, but he is squeezing goals out of his side. Eight different Ipswich players have scored in seven games; only Brighton and Brentford can better that total this season. Niall McVeigh

It was five months ago but it feels a lot longer. When these two sides met in May to finish the season, the contest doubled as Pep Guardiola’s leaving party after 10 years in the job and twice as many trophies, an era now laden with asterisks. It must be surreal for Aston Villa supporters, too. Their 2-1 victory at the Etihad Stadium, inspired by two goals from Ollie Watkins to complete a league double over City, came only four days after their Europa League triumph in Istanbul, where Youri Tielemans, Morgan Rogers and Emi Buendía were the scorers. Buendía is the only one left in claret and blue as Unai Emery builds a new side, one that has picked up in form after a single point from their first four league games. City, meanwhile, are thriving on the pitch: victory would make them just the third side to win their first eight games of a Premier League season. Taha Hashim

Max Dowman became the youngest goalscorer in Premier League history with his dazzling solo strike against Everton at the Emirates in March. But the supremely talented 16-year-old has found opportunities limited this season. Dowman has played only nine minutes in the Premier League despite scoring twice against Ipswich in the Carabao Cup last month as Arsenal have tried to protect their rising star. Yet the suspected quad muscle injury suffered by Bukayo Saka in Wednesday’s 2-2 Champions League draw at Bayern Munich means Mikel Arteta is short of attacking options. With David Moyes’s side back in north London, it could be the perfect chance for Dowman to step up in his favoured position on the right flank. Ed Aarons

Coventry and Fulham have only met twice in the English top flight – back in 1967-68, when the promoted Sky Blues took a single point from two meetings, but stayed up by a point while Fulham went down. It is too early to call Saturday’s game a six-pointer in the relegation battle, but the two teams sit either side of the dreaded dotted line after shaky starts. Coventry have shown glimpses of their Championship swagger, particularly in the 4-1 rout of Newcastle, but Frank Lampard wants his players to start thinking like a Premier League team. “I can’t keep applauding the players, believing they deserve to be here,” the Coventry manager said. “Now we have to get over that. We can’t be too soft.” Sunderland, Crystal Palace and Ipswich all visit the CBS Arena in the coming weeks, so there is an opportunity to consolidate. Fulham were linked with Lampard in the summer, and questions remain over whether Álvaro Arbeloa is pragmatic or flexible enough to succeed. Will these sides meet in the Premier League again next season? The jury is out. NM

Tottenham’s recent record against Chelsea is miserable. They are on a six-match losing streak against their London rivals and have collected a paltry two points at Stamford Bridge since last winning there in April 2018. Tottenham finally have a league win – they beat Coventry 3-1 on Monday – but remain unconvincing. Roberto De Zerbi used a 3-4-2-1 system against Coventry. He had problems in midfield but now has to work out whether to change a winning team. Does he stick with James Maddison after the No 10’s excellent goal against his boyhood club? Spurs still looked short of energy at times. There is an argument to bring back Conor Gallagher’s dynamism, but would that hurt the side’s quality on the ball? Mateus Fernandes is another option but is yet to establish himself since joining from West Ham. Spurs’ approach remains hard to decipher. De Zerbi likes possession, but Chelsea want teams to open up as the Blues have searing pace on the break. Given their history in this fixture it seems Spurs should focus on tightening up. Equally they can’t be passive and need a threat on the break. De Zerbi will be searching for the right balance. Jacob Steinberg

Talk of Brighton achieving Champions League qualification for the first time will gain more credence, even at this early stage, should Fabian Hürzeler’s confident side extend their winning streak to seven matches in all competitions. There have been five clean sheets and 22 goals scored in their six-game winning run and the Premier League’s highest scorers will take encouragement from Liverpool’s defensive problems in the comeback against Villarreal, which were not limited to Virgil van Dijk’s early lapses. Andoni Iraola is yet to savour a first home league win as Liverpool head coach – Anfield has seen only four home wins in 13 league games this year – and he will be wary of Brighton’s various threats. But with Rio Ngumoha electric in the Champions League win, Florian Wirtz improving and Alexander Isak increasingly decisive, the ingredients are in place for another enthralling spectacle. Andy Hunter

Who can or will lift Manchester United after the latest dismal/embarrassing week? Bruno Fernandes’s abdication of captaincy duties – accusing his manager of being tactically inept – showed what a rabble the team has become under Michael Carrick; and beyond the double footballer of the year, is there another star act who can win a game? Bournemouth will hope to take advantage, register only a second league win of the season, and deepen the misery for their hosts and fans. If his side goes down to the Cherries, Carrick will surely follow: the latest victim of the United circus. Jamie Jackson

It’s been six months since Crystal Palace recorded a clean sheet in the Premier League at Selhurst Park and the pressure will be on Pierre Sage against Newcastle on Sunday. Palace have conceded eight goals in four home league games this season, although they welcome back Axel Disasi from suspension after his reckless red card against Ipswich. The French defender was brought in on loan from Chelsea to add experience but cost Palace in the defeat by the newly-promoted side and had to watch from the sidelines as the Eagles were humiliated against Brighton last weekend. Disasi owes Sage a favour and he will be desperate to make up for his poor start to life in south London. EA

Something unusual will happen at the MKM Stadium on Sunday; either Hull City or Brentford will register more than 50% possession. In seven league games, Brentford only had more of the ball in their 1-1 draw at Leeds. The hosts, meanwhile, are comfortably the most possession-averse team in the top flight so far this season, at an average of just over 30%. Both teams have been effective on the break and successful at set-pieces, with three goals apiece from dead balls. This may prove to be a match for the purists, where one clinical moment makes the difference. The Bees head coach, Keith Andrews, will hope it comes from Igor Thiago, yet to recapture the prolific form of last season. “Thiago at the moment is a very marked man, but we’ve got goalscorers throughout the team,” Andrews said of the Brazilian forward, who has scored one goal in seven this season. “Thiago being Thiago wants to score more goals, and he’s certainly not far away.” NM

Nordi Mukiele ranks among Sunderland’s best players and most influential dressing-room figures. Tellingly the former Paris Saint-Germain defender has been scathing about his team’s dismal start to the Premier League campaign and expects a reaction when Leeds visit Wearside on Sunday. “Leeds will be the right moment to show everyone we are not dead,” says Mukiele, well aware that Régis Le Bris’s side start this weekend on the bottom of the table. “We have not been good enough. Right now it’s not us; we are not Sunderland. I believe we can go back to the top. I believe in this team and this staff. We have quality.” Sunderland must use their three league fixtures before the international break – Leeds, Coventry away and Chelsea at home – to remind everyone why they finished seventh last season. Louise Taylor

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Department of Justice opens criminal investigation into Corey Lewandowski
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Reuters
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Ex-Trump adviser and former top aide for homeland security alleged to have profited off government role

Corey Lewandowski, a former political adviser to Donald Trump and ⁠top aide at the Department ⁠of Homeland Security, ​is under criminal investigation over allegations he profited off his role in the US government, three US officials and a fourth person familiar with the matter told Reuters ⁠on Thursday.

The investigation began with a criminal referral to the justice department from the internal watchdog at DHS, according to the four people. The DHS inspector general’s office has been investigating ⁠Lewandowski’s involvement in the handling of certain government contracts, according to one of the people, a DHS official.

A lawyer ​for Lewandowski, Adam Trigg, did not immediately respond to ‌a request for comment. The ‌investigation was first reported in the Wall Street Journal, which quoted Lewandowski’s lawyer as saying that his client denies ‌all allegations of wrongdoing.

The DoJ has not yet issued subpoenas or other legal demands in the criminal investigation, according to one of the people. All four of the people spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The justice department under Trump has investigated several prominent critics of the president, including the former FBI director James Comey and the New York attorney general Letitia James, but investigations of people close to Trump have been rare. The department has also moved ‌to dismiss several existing cases involving Trump allies, including supporters charged in connection with the 6 January 2021 attack on the US Capitol.

Asked about media reports on the investigation, Trump told reporters ​that he did not know the specifics of the investigation, but said: “I want my people to be honest.”

“And if they’re not honest, I’ll have my DoJ go and do whatever they have to do,” Trump added.

Lewandowski served as a top aide to the former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem during her tenure leading DHS. Trump fired Noem in March after ⁠months of controversy, including the fatal shootings of two US citizens by federal officers ​in Minneapolis and lawmakers’ questions over a $220m advertising contract promoting Noem that was ​awarded without a standard bidding process.

Lewandowski had signed some DHS contracts despite having questionable legal authority ​as a special government ‌employee, according to the ​DHS official. Certain grants ​and contracts, including those involving the Federal Emergency Management Agency, were put on hold at Lewandowski’s direction, according to two of the people, both of whom are DHS officials.

Lewandowski previously served as a campaign manager during Trump’s first presidential run in 2016 and advised his 2024 campaign.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: ‘The Bird Reich’: Atlanta Falcons roasted over throwback logo with Nazi resemblance
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Guardian sport and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Social media erupted in jokes and memes on Thursday after the Atlanta Falcons unveiled a logo that instantly drew comparisons with the imagery of Nazi Germany.

The logo – posted by the Falcons on the NFL team’s social media channels – shows the team’s old falcon symbol from the 1960s and 1970s, emblazoned on a background of red, white and black stripes.

The “throwback” design is being used in the run-up to Atlanta’s game against the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday.

But the design prompted an avalanche of comments from social media users who said it resembled iconography of Adolf Hitler’s Nazi Party.

The Falcons’ post revealing the design on X had attracted some 26m views since being published early Thursday.

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Comments beneath the post lampooned the logo mercilessly over its perceived Nazi resemblance.

“I must say, I was not expecting to wake up this morning to see that the Atlanta Falcons are preparing to invade Poland,” one user wrote.

Another referenced the Falcons’ notorious 2017 Super Bowl collapse against the New England Patriots.

Others found ways to combine football terminology with second world war references. “Falcons leading the league in blitzkrieg,” one user joked.

One commenter dubbed the team the “28-3rd Reich”, combining the Nazi reference with Atlanta’s infamous Super Bowl meltdown.

“Now they just need to hire Frank Reich and it’ll be complete,” another wrote, referring to the former NFL head coach.

Another user commented that after this weekend’s home game against San Francisco, the Falcons had “road games in Dunkirk, Normandy, and Stalingrad”.

Others suggested the Falcons might need to change the NFL’s “End Racism” end-zone slogan to “Start Racism”, while one commenter offered a new billing for Sunday’s matchup: “49ers vs 39ers.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Flu cases rise on west coast earlier than usual as US health experts encourage vaccine
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
California flu test rate at 9.65%, higher than normal 1% rate for early October, amid mutation of H1N1 influenza A strain

Flu cases on the west coast are on the rise months earlier than normal, prompting US health experts to stress the importance of the annual vaccine.

Flu activity typically ramps up in December, hitting its peak in February. But this season has kicked into action earlier this year, with higher positive cases than normal recorded.

Several experts have credited the early seasonal start to a new mutation of the influenza A strain H1N1, which was behind the 2009 swine flu pandemic.

This strain has accounted for 242 of 300 influenza viruses reported by public health laboratories to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to date (CDC).

In California, during the past two flu seasons, influenza test positivity hovered slightly above 1% in early October. As of 10 October, that rate is 9.65%, according to data from the state’s department of health.

As of 11 October, Utah has recorded 242 influenza A cases, up from 10 cases this time last year, according to Germ Watch, an Intermountain Health database.

Influenza vaccines can reduce severe illness and hospitalization, according to the American Medical Association, which recommends flu shots for all people 6 months and older.

The 2026-27 flu vaccines, approved by the FDA in August, ​target H1N1, H3N2 – the dominant strain last flu season – and one influenza B virus.

Scott Hensley, a microbiologist at the University of Pennsylvania, said two of the three components of this year’s vaccine appear to be very well matched to circulating flu strains.

However, the H1N1 mutation might affect antibodies in younger people, and with flu season picking up steam, “it is probably a good idea to get vaccinated early”, Hensley said via ​email.

Promotion of flu shots has been reduced under US health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, a longtime anti-vaccine activist who has engineered an overhaul of long-standing childhood vaccine schedules.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Trump, Musk, Zelenskyy: who is blaming who in the Ukraine-Starlink row?
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Jonathan Yerushalmy
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
A war of words has erupted over who is responsible for the restrictions on Starshield access in Ukraine

A war of words has erupted between the Trump administration, officials in Kyiv and Elon Musk over who is to blame for limiting Ukraine’s access to Space X’s military-grade version of Starlink.

The restrictions to Starshield have rendered many of the drones used by Kyiv to strike behind the frontlines inoperable and hampered air defence systems that stop Russian attacks, according to Ukrainian officials.

Donald Trump said on Thursday that the service was running again at full speed, but a European official speaking to the Associated Press denied the service was fully functioning.

Amid the diplomatic handwringing, civilian casualties in Ukraine have surged, and the question over who is ultimately responsible for limiting Kyiv’s access has remained unanswered.

The restrictions came as relations between the US and Ukraine hit their lowest point since Russia’s full-scale invasion nearly five years ago.

Donald Trump has accused Ukraine of driving up diesel costs for Americans through its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Analysis by the BBC found that the US-Israel war on Iran and resulting restrictions on oil exports from the Gulf have likely had a greater impact on global diesel supplies.

Trump initially denied any responsibility for the changes to Starshield, telling reporters last Friday: “I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” referring to Musk, SpaceX’s CEO.

Trump’s cabinet backed him up, with secretary of state Marco Rubio saying on Wednesday: “What I can tell you with certainty is the president of the United States nor anyone in our system ever requested that any changes to that system be made.”

Rubio, however, also made a comment that threw suspicion on to Musk, the world’s richest man.

double quotation markThe president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk. That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that the US president had asked Musk to restore the service, with Trump later telling reporters the system was “back”.

He refused to comment on whether he had spoken to Musk, but appeared to suggest the ultimate power to limit the service rested with the SpaceX CEO. “I guess the bottom line, he put it back,” Trump said, referring to Musk.

However, John Cornyn, a Republican who is in his final weeks as the US senator for Texas, told US media that he didn’t believe Musk would have acted “without at least the acquiescence of the White House”.

Musk has supported Trump’s calls for Volodymyr Zelenskyy to be replaced and has been highly critical of the Ukrainian president. However, he was quick to blame the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration, writing on X last week that the systems were “owned and controlled by the US government”.

double quotation markAny limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.

Musk – one of the Republican party’s biggest donors and a Trump ally – continued to deny responsibility for the changes. However, on Tuesday the Wall Street Journal reported that Musk made the order to slow down Starshield, with the paper’s sources in disagreement over whether this was made in concert with Trump.

Vice-president JD Vance backed Musk on Thursday, saying the billionaire “doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the United States government effectively directing him on what to do”.

double quotation markSo I don’t think this is about Elon. I think it’s fundamentally what is America’s policy in Ukraine and Russia going to be.

The Ukrainian president initially blamed the restrictions on “SpaceX and the United States”, saying on Wednesday last week that the move would “bring a lot of human losses … of course, people will die”.

Shortly after the systems failed, Zelenskyy said there were no similar restrictions on Starshield terminals in European Union countries and that they applied only to Ukraine. “In other words, this is a planned operation.”

Zelenskyy said at the weekend that Musk’s SpaceX was ultimately responsible for suddenly limiting the speed at which Starshield worked in Ukraine. “It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed ... And technically, SpaceX did it.”

Despite Trump’s insistence on Thursday that the service had resumed, a senior European official told the Associated Press that nothing had changed in the operation of Starshield.

Prior to Trump’s comments, Zelenskyy ⁠said full Starshield speed had still not ⁠been restored ⁠for Ukraine, ​adding that he hoped for talks ⁠with Rubio in the ⁠coming days.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Lewis Hamilton aims to extend career till early 2030s so he can race in African Grand Prix
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Giles Richards in Austin
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Lewis Hamilton has said he hopes to remain racing in Formula One until he can take part in the African Grand Prix which is set to take place in Rwanda in the 2030s. The seven-time world champion believes it is right that F1 is to hold a race there despite criticism of the country’s human rights record.

Last week F1 confirmed Rwanda was to host the African Grand Prix having concluded a 10-year agreement for the meeting on a purpose-built circuit, with the first race set for the early 2030s. It is lined up to be held on a circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital, Kigali, which has yet to be constructed and marks a return to the African continent for the first time since it last held a race at Kyalami, South Africa in 1993.

Hamilton has been championing a race in Africa for some time. The 41-year-old is understood to be currently contracted with Ferrari until the end of the 2027 season, and speaking before this weekend’s US Grand Prix he said he would like to continue racing for at least another four years in order to make it to the meeting in Rwanda.

“I’m now forced to have to stay a lot longer because we have a race in Africa and that’s been my dream to be able to race in Africa,” he said. “So, I have to keep fighting to try and stay fit if I can. If I can still punch out good results over the next year, we’ll keep it going.”

Hamilton would be at least in his mid-40s if he was to continue until 2030. F1’s current oldest driver is 45-year-old Fernando Alonso.

F1’s deal with Rwanda is for a 10-year period but because of the country’s human rights record the award of the race has been criticised as an act of sportswashing.

Britain’s 18-year-old Freddie Slater will make his Formula 1 free practice debut for ⁠Audi at next week’s Mexico City Grand Prix.

Audi entered Formula 1 this year ⁠after taking over ⁠the ​Sauber team, and Slater was the first driver signed to the team’s new driver academy.

Slater ⁠finished second in the Formula 3 standings to Ugo Ugochukwu in his debut season while ⁠racing for Trident Motorsport. He is slated to move ​to Formula 2 with Invicta ‌next year.

"Getting behind the wheel of an F1 car at a grand prix weekend is a big moment for me and something I’ve been dreaming of since I was a kid," Slater said. “I’ve learned a ‌lot this year, and these Free practice outings with Audi F1 Team will be another opportunity ​to keep gaining on-track experience."

Slater is also slated to drive in the first practice session at next month’s Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

"We have seen Freddie making great progress ⁠throughout recent years, both on and off the track; ​it is ​the right time for ​Freddie to step up," Audi racing director and ​academy director ‌Allan McNish, a former F1 driver himself, said.

"These ​appearances ​in Mexico and Brazil will give him valuable experience of a Formula 1 race weekend, and another chance to continue his development." Reuters

“A 10-year grand prix ‘presented by Visit Rwanda’ is a sportswashing prize for the Rwandan authorities,” said Felix Jakens, Amnesty UK’s head of campaigns. “Rwanda is buying into the world’s biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from ⁠its appalling human rights record. Formula One says sport can be ‘a positive force for good’. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with. Rwanda’s authorities are prolific in arbitrary detention, torture and the repression of free speech.”

Hamilton nonetheless felt the meeting would serve as a force for good in Africa and that there also should be more education about the continent.

“I’m really, really hopeful for that grand prix,” he said. “Of course, I don’t get to choose where we go, and naturally there’s problems all over the world today, so I’ve seen many of the stories but I think we really have to approach it with humility.

“There’s a lot that we don’t know. I mean, growing up in England, they never ever taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum. A lot of the problems they have there are still results of colonialism, and the West intervening.

“I really hope, and I still have hopes, that Africa unites. I know there’s many people that don’t want that to happen, because they would be so powerful if they did, but I’m still hopeful that at some stage they will.”

The new race is being backed by the government of Rwanda and the Rwanda Development Board, who intend to develop the venue as a destination not only for motorsport but for promoting economic growth. The country has recently invested heavily in hosting sporting events, including cycling’s road world championships, cricket’s Women’s Challenge Trophy, the 2023 Fifa congress and the Basketball Africa League.

Hamilton felt that at least the race would present an opportunity for people to take a greater interest in Africa.

“Going doesn’t mean that you neglect the things that are happening there,” he said. “Hopefully many people start to educate themselves a little bit more of what is happening there, what has happened there for hundreds of years and I hope that does spark the conversation. Then I guess I’ll finish it off with, I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping that at some stage we get to.”

Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli goes into this weekend’s US Grand Prix in a position to clinch his first F1 title. The 20-year-old holds a 102-point lead over his teammate George Russell and will become Formula One’s youngest world champion if he wins, Russell finishes ninth or lower and Hamilton is fifth or lower.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Emery and Nagelsmann are top targets if Manchester United sack Carrick
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Jamie Jackson
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Unai Emery and Julian Nagelsmann have emerged as leading targets to replace Michael Carrick as Manchester United’s head coach should the board decide on a change after the club’s poorest start to the season since 1986.

Carrick is expected to remain in place for Sunday’s visit of Bournemouth – he is due to hold his pre-game media conference on Friday – but the 45-year-old’s job is in the balance after two wins from 11 games this season.

Wednesday’s 4-1 humiliation at Como in the Champions League has focused attention at United on a potential candidate to succeed Carrick should he be removed. Emery and Nagelsmann have admirers at board level.

Emery is contracted to Aston Villa until 2029, and Nagelsmann is unemployed after leaving his position as Germany’s manager in the wake of the team’s last-32 World Cup exit in the summer.

Emery has impressed since taking over Villa in 2022, last season winning the Europa League, the club’s first major trophy since 1996, and finishing fourth, one place behind United.

But Emery earns between £10m and £12m a year, so the compensation package United would have to pay Villa may be a stumbling block. He has also won trophies with Sevilla, Paris Saint-Germain and Villarreal and had a less successful spell with Arsenal.

Nagelsmann has managed Hoffenheim, RB Leipzig and Bayern Munich, with whom he won the Bundesliga in 2022 before being sacked in March 2023. He is highly regarded by United’s head of recruitment, Christopher Vivell.

The 39-year-old Nagelsmann guided Germany to the Euro 2024 quarter-finals, where they were knocked out by the eventual winners, Spain. It is understood Nagelsmann would be interested in an approach from United.

Other potential candidates who may be considered include Antonio Conte, Eddie Howe and Kieran McKenna. They are out of work after leaving jobs with Napoli, Newcastle and Ipswich respectively. It is understood Fabian Hürzeler is not open to leaving Brighton at this stage.

Bruno Fernandes’s house was the target of a break-in while United’s captain was away with the team at the Como defeat. His family were not at home, it is understood, and the intruders were inside for less than five minutes before the police arrived.

The club is supporting Fernandes and his family and have asked for privacy regarding what it said was a difficult time.

Meanwhile, the 32-year-old midfielder is not expected to face any disciplinary action for his criticism of Carrick on Wednesday. Fernandes questioned the head coach’s tactics following the Como defeat.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Caleb Williams outduels friend and rival Drake Maye as Bears beat Patriots
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Caleb Williams threw for 308 yards and two touchdowns, and the Chicago Bears cooled off Drake Maye and the New England Patriots with a 30-24 win on Thursday night.

Williams was 22 of 33 passing in his second game back after being sidelined by a hamstring injury. He became the first Bears quarterback to throw for more than 300 yards in consecutive games since Mitch Trubisky had a three-game run in 2018.

“It’s amazing [having Williams on the field]. His leadership, his competitiveness, everyone around here feels it. He gets us going,” said Bears running back D’Andre Swift after the game.

Williams outdueled Maye in their second meeting since the longtime friends were part of the 2024 NFL draft. Williams went No 1 to Chicago, and Maye was selected by New England at No 3.

Luther Burden had four catches for 130 yards for Chicago (5-2), and Colston Loveland had a 12-yard touchdown reception. Cairo Santos kicked a 58-yard field goal with 1:34 left, a career long and matching the franchise record, after he missed a 53-yard attempt earlier in the final quarter. That made it 30-21 but Maye then drove New England into range for Andy Borregales’s 47-yarder with 37 seconds to go. However, Chicago recovered the ensuing onside kick and ran down the clock.

Maye was 24 for 31 for 321 yards and two touchdowns. He also threw a costly interception in the end zone in the first half.

New England (4-3) had won three consecutive games behind Maye, who threw 10 TD passes and one interception during the win streak. Rhamondre Stevenson had five catches for 93 yards and a touchdown for the Patriots. Eli Raridon had a 30-yard TD catch in the third quarter.

It was Chicago’s first home game since Mike Ditka died on 9 October. The Bears saluted the Hall of Fame tight end and longtime coach with a pregame moment of silence, and they also handed out fake mustaches to the crowd of 60,520 at Soldier Field. Ditka’s No 89 jersey dotted the stands, and fans also donned Bears sweaters in a callback to the gear he wore on the sideline as a coach.

The Bears jumped out to a 10-0 lead in the first quarter thanks to a ‌Santos 43-yard field goal and Swift’s four-yard touchdown run.

New England responded when Maye scored on a seven-yard run early in the ​second quarter, but Santos made a 31-yard field goal to give Chicago a 13-7 lead.

The teams traded touchdowns in the final 14 seconds of the half. After Williams connected with Burden for a 24-yard TD pass, ⁠New England scored on a 48-yard pass from Maye to Stevenson ​with no time remaining ​on the clock. Stevenson caught the ​pass on the Chicago 47 and eluded several defenders ​on his way to ‌the end zone. ​Borregales made the ​extra point, which pulled the Patriots closer at 20-14. Chicago extended the margin to 27-14 when Loveland capped the second half’s opening drive with a 12-yard TD catch, but New England answered with a 30-yard scoring pass from Maye to Raridon on the ensuing drive.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: ‘I struggle to see myself as someone special’ Sandra Hüller on being the star of four - or, possibly, five - of the year’s biggest films
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Danny Leigh
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
New film Fatherland took Sandra Hüller back to a divided Germany. She talks about damaged dreams, Hollywood feelgood and - just maybe - appearing in the new Marvel movie

Sandra Hüller is crying, and it feels very strange. A wildly gifted actor, she can convey every human emotion there is. On screen, though, she is most often asked to embody deep self-possession. Even doing karaoke, Hüller is in control. And in real life, life is good. Her 2026 will end with four high-profile movies this year alone. Two (Fatherland and Rose) are black-and-white arthouse films that centre on her brilliance, and though one of the others (Digger) is already a Hollywood cautionary tale, a second (Project Hail Mary) was a giant $684m hit. (There may also be a fifth movie, bigger still. We will come back to that.)

And yet, dressed in film star black, she is in tears. “This is really hard for me,” she says.

We are talking about Fatherland. Directed by acclaimed Polish film-maker Paweł Pawlikowski, Hüller plays the German polymath Erika Mann, who in the film drives her novelist father Thomas Mann through newly divided postwar Germany. The Nazi past shadows everything – but the movie is also tied up with the birth of East Germany, where Hüller grew up. (She still lives in what was once the GDR.) I tell her I’ve never before seen a film that acknowledged the utopian dreams of that place and time, however damaged they became. Yes, she replies: German directors don’t know how to approach it.

And then her voice cracks, and she cries. We reflexively apologise to each other. “I’m just grateful Pawel gave space to this political idea that didn’t survive in Germany, but is one maybe people can still think about. The socialist idea.”

Hüller wipes her eyes. Finally, she laughs. “You’re going to say I cried, aren’t you? I can see the headline.”

And yet she has always been open about the nuance to the East Germany she remembers from childhood – a place defined by more than the Stasi men of cold war thrillers. “What fascinates me is that in East and West were two systems that for a certain time could have learned from each other.” She apologises again; I’m not sure why. “It is this situation we live in now. I feel like I’m on thin ice.”

Inevitably, we come to the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD). The subject is doubly unavoidable in light of Fatherland. The Manns originally fled the country in 1933 and they would end up in the US. “It’s no secret there are similarities now,” Hüller says. “Fascism doesn’t arrive overnight. It gets here slowly, in little doses.” Her tone turns businesslike. “The question is what we do about it.”

We all contain multitudes, but Hüller more than most. At home in Leipzig, she is a co-founder of the experimental Farn Kollektiv theatre group; a politically engaged woman of 48, she is the single mother to a teenage daughter. She is also deadpan funny. An account of her excellent safety record as a driver is a comic treasure. “That should be your headline. ‘Sandra Hüller – a clean licence.’”

She is also a movie actor with snowballing momentum. In 2024, she astonished twice over as the wife of the commandant of Auschwitz in The Zone of Interest and a woman suspected of murdering her husband in Anatomy of a Fall. The latter saw her Oscar-nominated. Now, after Project Hail Mary, Digger and Fatherland, there will also be Rose, a stark 17th century fable in which she plays a war veteran – who is, in fact, a woman passing as a man. Oscar talk is simmering once more. America is freshly excited.

“OK, so what is happening is that I made very different movies at different times, but they’re all coming out together. It’s nothing I control.” What is good, she says, is that, with her as the common thread, Hollywood marketing budgets end up spotlighting the likes of Fatherland too. “On the other hand, I struggle with seeing myself as someone special. I still consider myself part of a group. That is actually the highest praise I can give myself.”

Curiously, a collective spirit might also apply to the fifth film Hüller is strongly rumoured to be in this year: Marvel relaunch Avengers: Doomsday. Whatever else Marvel movies represent, they have a reputation for an oddly egalitarian vibe on set. I wonder aloud if that’s true. “Me too!” She gives an impish tilt of the head. Ah. For the record, then, Hüller still may or may not be part of the new Avengers.

But in theory, a Marvel film might feel unexpectedly non-hierarchical? “I heard that as well! Which would show having a lot of money available doesn’t have to mean abusing your power. And that would be a great thing. In theory.”

If the thought of Hüller doing Marvel takes getting used to, it makes more sense after Project Hail Mary. In a deft piece of Hollywood feelgood, she proved the perfect foil for Ryan Gosling’s reluctant spaceman as stone-faced mission controller Eva Stratt. The air of ultra-competence was very Sandra Hüller for Beginners. The film even harked back to her 2016 breakthrough in skewed German comedy Toni Erdmann. Hüller has a glorious singing voice. Then, she karaoked Whitney Houston’s Greatest Love of All. Now, it was Harry Styles’ Sign of the Times.

“But I think Eva Stratt made some people uncomfortable. It can feel unusual to be governed by a woman.”

Still, making Project Hail Mary was another pleasant surprise – her first Hollywood set where the directors – Phil Lord and Christopher Miller – actually lightened the mood. “They made sure we could actually play. Have fun.” She did, though, find it strange being wrangled by runners on the kind of blockbuster where producers want to know where a star is at all times. (Unlike almost every actor on her level, Hüller doesn’t even have an assistant.) “But you can always hide in the bathroom.”

Would she spend more time in the US than necessary? “Not right now. No. It’s a workplace.” Anyway, she says, she likes where she lives. “It’s simple. America is just very far away.” And she smiles.

She believes audiences embraced Project Hail Mary because the film-makers sought to unite them, inside a cinema at least. “And entertain them without the usual things – death and weapons. So you have a story about a human with a task that lets them be bigger than themselves. That inspired people.”

But what about their response to Digger? Directed by Alejandro González Iñárritu, with Tom Cruise as a cartoonish oil tycoon, the movie got poor reviews, then did cataclysmically at the box office. Can we talk about it? “Sure!” she says brightly. “I mean, we expected a strong reaction. It’s a polarising movie. And a political movie, which we weren’t able to say in interviews. For whatever reason.” A beat. “But personally – I was surprised by the harshness of the rejection. People really hated it!”
