There was a point in the 2010s when she considered giving up acting completely. “I hadn’t worked in over a year and I had just got a litany of nos,” she remembers. “And now it’s getting harder and harder for not-rich people to be an actor.” McSweeney had received grants from the EU and a scholarship to study drama at the Central School of Speech and Drama – and that kind of funding literally doesn’t exist any more. “I get really panicky thinking about the other Siobháns who don’t get what they’re meant to do,” she says, and her face is unusually serious for a moment – but then she looks at me and her eyes begin to twinkle. “I mean it should be better, it should be a bit more useful than being a clown – but, you know, it’s what I’m meant to do.”

Part of the struggle when she was being rejected at auditions was the lack of decent roles available for women. In previous interviews, McSweeney has said that casting directors explicitly told her that even though she was the funniest person in the audition room, they were going to give the part to a “prettier, younger, less funny” woman. “I graduated into a world where I really hoped somebody had a girlfriend because there was no way on earth a programme was going to centre on a woman,” she says to me now. But she wouldn’t even be in the running for the girlfriend part because “they wanted somebody who was more ‘girlfriend material’, ie, more acceptable – so, bland and pretty”.

McSweeney says she would never be considered for the main character, “always the satellite”. She rolls her eyes. “And now I’m the mother.”

McSweeney tells me that she is deliberately taking on more presenting work because properly meaty, complex acting roles for women on TV are still so rare. As well as The Traitors Ireland, McSweeney hosts The Great Pottery Throw Down. She landed the job after an appearance on a Great British Bake Off festive special in which she had a meltdown over making a trifle and ended up sitting on a bench with Sandi Toksvig, drinking champagne (“They went, that’s who we want”).

McSweeney is also an acclaimed theatre actor. She played opposite her Derry Girls co-star Nicola Coughlan last year in The Playboy of the Western World at the National Theatre, and says that being onstage is what she has always enjoyed the most (she remembers being a child and “seeing red curtains on the telly and having a funny feeling in my belly”). But presenting is “work I find interesting – and it also pays more than the theatre”, she says, with characteristic honesty.

Presenting jobs pay better than TV shows do, too – even the most successful ones. McSweeney has said publicly “I think I got 40 quid” in residuals when Derry Girls sold to Netflix. The programme has been viewed for a total of 17.3m hours on the platform. Can that figure possibly be true? McSweeney nods enthusiastically. “When Netflix bought it we got fuck all!”

When she was 27, McSweeney lost her mother, who never saw her daughter succeed as an actor. In her Bafta acceptance speech, which has been viewed 467,000 times on YouTube, McSweeney told a story about how, as her mother lay dying, she pleaded with her to retrain as a teacher. “If she could see me now, winning a Bafta for playing a teacher,” she said, wearing a red vinyl dress and laughing, lifting her bare arm above her head to punch the air with her award: “Joke’s on you, Mam!”

Would her mother feel pride, if she could see her daughter now? Or relief? “Er, relief,” says McSweeney, quick as a flash. Then she pauses for a second. “And I think she would like … I have a lot of opinions and she would like the way I speak about certain opinions.” In the same Bafta speech, McSweeney thanked the people of Derry, calling out the “ignorance and stupidity” of their political leadership, and she is a vocal critic of both English and Irish policy. Last year she was among those who campaigned successfully for the thousands of UK-based survivors of the work camps for “fallen women” that were in operation until the 90s in Ireland – known as the Magdalene laundries – to be given compensation without losing their rights to benefits.

Would her mother have been proud of her feminism? “I think she would have been as close to proud as I would allow her to be,” says McSweeney, almost shyly. “And my dad, too … He was a natural feminist rather than a learned one – couldn’t think of anything I couldn’t do because of my gender, that would make no sense to him.”

Her father died in 2018. McSweeney moved back into the family home to live with him during his final illness. She drew on those experiences to make Spud in 2024, a beautiful, surprisingly funny short film about a middle-aged woman caring for her dying father (McSweeney summarises the plot, with fabulous bluntness, as being about “an unfuckable woman who is rural and who cleans her daddy in a bath”).

In one particularly tender scene, the father and the daughter, who is played by McSweeney herself, sit eating rice pudding together in front of the telly. Was that drawn from life? Was food a comfort for them both during that time? “The really sad thing about illness is that it often takes your appetite away,” she says. “I found it with my mum, too: her appetite went towards the end.” She tells me a story about sneaking a carbonara into the hospital to give to her mother, and the sadness of her not being able to eat it. “She was so beautiful and everybody’s mam is beautiful, but she ended up with a flat belly – and I was, like, what use is a flat belly? I want a lovely big belly.”

Right at the end of Spud, McSweeney’s character finds out her father has died, and the camera closes in on her face. There is pain there but there is also something else: she is smiling slightly. It’s a great moment because it is so unexpected – and so honest. You can see in the daughter’s expression that, on some level, her father’s death has come as a relief. “I remember when my dad died, I was sort of manic for about six months because I suddenly was free, and I was grieving, but I was also free,” McSweeney says. In the immediate aftermath of her father’s death, McSweeney was bursting with ideas for new projects. “With no parents, you don’t feel like you’re letting the entire family down if you say or do something.”

Between 2018 and 2021, McSweeney went through a period that she has described – in a moment of understatement worthy of Sister Michael herself – as containing lots of “life stuff”. Her aunt, who had been a kind of surrogate mother to her, died the year after she lost her father. In 2019, her London flat burned down because of a faulty plug adaptor. Then, in 2021, in the middle of filming a Kathy Burke-directed crime drama, Holding, she broke her leg so badly that at one point the doctors thought they would have to amputate it.

How did she cope? “We place romantic and biological relationships at the heart of our sort of experience,” says McSweeney, but it was her friends who got her through it. She tells me that when she was struggling the most, she became furious with one of her friends and accused him of talking about her behind her back with the rest of the group. “I was, like, ‘Are you all talking about me?’” She puts her hands on her hips here and mimes outrage, and then she switches characters so she can play her friend’s role: “And he was, like, ‘Yeah! We’re meant to do that! We care about you! We’re making sure you’re OK, we’re asking each other, how do you think she’s doing?’”

McSweeney talks about this being a moment of realisation. She saw that friendship has an elasticity and a resilience that no romantic relationship can ever really have. “You have a fight with your boyfriend and that could destroy the relationship, right?” she says. “You have a fight with your friend, you go into your respective corners, you sulk. You call other friends. You bitch about each other. Then you go back, you have a coffee, you get drunk!”

McSweeney’s friends are annoyed with her at the moment, because she is getting her kitchen redone in her new flat, and she is refusing to install a dishwasher – as a way of preventing them from popping in for meals. “I don’t want you coming over and eating my food,” she says. She has described herself as a “sociable misanthrope” in previous interviews. As much as she loves her friends, she is not that fond of cooking and cleaning for them. I tell her I like going to other people’s homes and letting them cook for me, and then leaving without doing any washing up at all. “I bet you do!” she says. “It’s horrible for the other person – get out of my house!”

So who does she cook for? “Myself!” she says, looking me right in the eye – and for the first time there is a kind of challenge in her voice. She doesn’t like to talk about any romantic partners.

She lives alone in a flat she recently bought in London. What does she cook for herself? “It’s so boring, but I’ve been working so hard for the last five years that all my food is comfort food and I try to make it as healthy as possible,” she says. She makes a lot of bone broth and a lot of ramen. “Also, I like white bread toasted till it’s nearly black, with Kerrygold butter” – but the butter has to be sliced extremely thickly, she specifies. It has to be “sliced like cheese”.

We’re nearly out of time – and Dair y Milk. McSweeney has been hospitably breaking off slabs of chocolate and handing them to me every few minutes for the last half hour, so I can keep making Guinness-crisp soup in my mouth. I’ve got time for just one final question, so I ask McSweeney what she is looking forward to. “I’ve got my first day off for 26 days tomorrow,” she says, “but I’ve got nothing in the fridge.” She plans to go to a bakery round the corner and buy some freshly made soda bread. Ironically, after all that teenage rebellion, she likes it now. Would her mother be pleased to look down on her doing that? “Yes,” she says. “And I’m going to buy it with the money I earned being a clown.”

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: The sexual assault scandal rocked gymnastics – but has pace of change in the sport been too slow?
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Suzanne Wrack in Rotterdam
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Former USA team doctor Larry Nassar’s 2018 conviction sparked a global reckoning in gymnastics, yet gymnasts say they are still being let down

It has been 10 years since the Indianapolis Star published allegations of sexual abuse by Larry Nassar, the former team doctor for USA Gymnastics, setting off a chain of events that would lead to a reckoning for the sport. Hundreds of women came forward with their own allegations against Nassar, who also worked at Michigan State University, leading to his conviction and jailing.

The exposure of his crimes sparked a wider investigation into how gymnastics had allowed predators to abuse young athletes around the world. While Nassar was the worst recorded case, it emerged many other countries had questions to answer about the failure to protect victims from not only sexual but physical and emotional abuse. But a decade later, on a large houseboat moored in Rotterdam three tram stops away from the Ahoy Arena, where the World Gymnastics Championships are taking place this week, survivors and advocates raised fears about the slow pace of change.

The impact of the Nassar case was seismic, not least because of the decision of Judge Rosemarie Aquilina, on agreeing to Nassar’s plea deal, to allow his victims to have their say in her courtroom. People tuned into Aquilina’s courtroom from all over the world to watch as 169 people took to the stand across seven days, delivering blistering, emotionally charged and brave testimonies of Nassar’s abuse and the impact of that abuse. Aquilina sentenced him to up to 175 years in jail with other convictions, federal and state, making a total of 300 years to life.

“I know, dealing with so many victims, that when they speak publicly you see them shed their pain and get taller. You see them have a relief, an automatic release,” says Aquilina, perched on a seat in the helm of the boat. “The most interesting thing was that at first I had a list of maybe a dozen names who wanted to speak, then it was 20, then it was 30, and then it got up to 80, 100, etc.

“What happened was that one girl empowered the next, who empowered the next. It was the beginning of their healing because they felt finally heard and believed, in a safe space, and they got to tell him to his face, eyeball to eyeball: ‘You hurt me. I am not a number, I am a name, how dare you?’”

“Nassar constantly wanted control. He wanted to continue to control me, to control the girls, and to say: ‘Look what I’ve done. I took the plea for you’. That was constant … Did he deserve my respect? No. Did he give me respect? No. Did he give any of the victims respect? No. He never owned it. That infuriated me. It should infuriate everyone.”

Among the victims motivated to speak after hearing others’ statements was the Olympic gold medallist Aly Raisman, who was excoriating in blaming USA Gymnastics for enabling Nassar. She was joined by fellow gold medallist Jordyn Wieber, Olympic bronze medallist Jamie Dantzscher and former US national champion Mattie Larson. The mother of the athlete who first complained about Nassar, Maggie Nichols, read out a powerful statement on her behalf. Simone Biles, the most famous gymnast of her generation, revealed she was a victim on social media and later testified publicly in front of the US Senate Judiciary Committee.

Two years after Nassar’s sentencing, a documentary film named after Nichols, called Athlete A, was released, shining a spotlight on the traditional coaching system of compliance, fear and silence and how it allowed Nassar to operate. The documentary opened the global floodgates.

Kim Shore, who was a gymnast in Canada in the 1980s and “experienced all forms of abuse, but also all forms of joy”, was then on the board of directors of Gymnastics Canada, the national governing body, after stepping into governance when her own experiences and direct intervention had failed to prevent the cycle of mistreatment repeating with a family member.

“I absolutely love the sport. I love how it feels in my body. I love so many aspects of it. And yet I spent most of my time surviving it,” she says.

Shore, who is an independent safe sport advocate, says of the impact of the Nassar case: “I was floored, understanding: ‘OK, I wasn’t a bad kid, I wasn’t a bad gymnast, this is why I was treated that way, it’s endemic.’”

Yet the reaction from the organisation was “absolutely lacking”, says Shore. “I remember I sat and watched those girls tell their story in the courtroom and I just bawled. I encouraged the board members that I was associated with to watch it as well.” She does not believe any of them did.

Eloise Jotischky, 23, who at the end of last year won the first civil case against British Gymnastics for the abuses she suffered in the sport, says the impact of the film was being able “to articulate what you’ve been through and find the terms to understand and talk about your experience”.

“It’s very hard to explain it to people who are not within that culture, that sport,” she says. “The only way I can really describe it is that it’s sort of like a cult in a lot of ways. It’s a very closed system, you’re very isolated, in a lot of cases you’re pulled out of school, you’re removed from your friends, you’re travelling to competitions all the time and you’re deprived of a normal social life. I’d say it’s very similar to a coercively controlling relationship in a domestic setting, there’s a lot of parallels there, but you’re a child, so there’s the duty of care issue as well.”

Jotischky stopped training at 14. “By the end, it wasn’t joyous. I think I hated it. You just blame yourself and you think that you’re the problem, until Athlete A comes out. That was about sexual abuse, but the underlying themes of Athlete A are about the physical and emotional abuse, the non-contact physical abuse, which made it get to that point. That’s what all resonated.”

At the same time, the life of former British gymnast and athlete Claire Heafford was in transition. She was splitting from her husband, leaving her dream job and taking up wrestling. “Those major changes were partly taking place because I hadn’t yet realised I’d been so badly abused and that I had some psychiatric issues,” she says.

“I got into professional wrestling when I saw it and felt very drawn to it. I didn’t really understand why, but it’s a performance art that is largely about the performance of masculinity and the violence is clear and obvious. I was really attracted to that being the inverse of my own experiences. I couldn’t understand that at the time. I was like: ‘I’ve gone mad, I’m 36, I’m learning to be a Mexican wrestler. I’m splitting up with my husband. What the fuck’s gone wrong in my life?’

The documentary made Heafford want to act; she decided to set up Gymnasts for Change, an alliance to bring about safer sport. As the head of Gymnasts for Change International, she brought together the advocates and survivors in Rotterdam.

“Athlete A was seismic. It came out just as Me Too had started,” she says. “On the one hand, Athlete A showed how awful the sexual abuse was and on the other it demonstrated to everybody in the world that gymnastics was a coercively controlling environment built on control and power. It showed that was just what the sport was, that everybody in it had experienced it and that they almost believed that it was necessary.”

The Nassar case triggered a series of reports and new measures in the US including the FBI acknowledging its handling of the case was “inexcusable” and Congress establishing the US Center for SafeSport. That organisation has since faced heavy criticism. USAG went through four presidents in less than two years, said it would adopt 70 of the recommendations in an independent report into preventing sexual abuse and set up an Athlete Bill of Rights. USAG now says athlete safety has been its “top priority since establishing a new board of directors and leadership team in 2018-2019”. It emphasises that “a culture of safety is something that has to be worked on every day, at every level”, requiring all adult USAG members to be trained in safeguarding. Eight members of the board are former elite athletes and one seat is dedicated to that of a survivor.

The case also inspired athletes around the world to speak up about their own experiences of abuse, including in Australia, Brazil and Britain. In Britain, an independent review led by Anne Whyte QC found that physical and emotional abuse were systemic, leading British Gymnastics to launch a 40-point plan aimed at changing the sport. That included a zero tolerance approach to abuse and a gymnast-coach led environment where “both feel empowered to create safe, positive and fair experiences at every level”.

Such an environment is something Aimee Boorman, who is Simone Biles’ former coach, has spent her career advocating for. Boorman channelled her anger at her own experience of negative coaching as a child gymnast into her coaching philosophy. “I knew that I never wanted to make another child feel the way that I felt as a child. So, that was the basis of everything,” she says. “So many times I was told that I wouldn’t be successful because I was too nice. I was like: ‘Well, then I guess I’m not going to be successful by your metrics, your standard, your qualifier for success’. For me, success is having happy, healthy athletes who want to put their children in gymnastics because they have such a good experience.

“Then, I went from being too nice to just being lucky that I had Simone, she’s successful and I’m successful because I was lucky that I had her. No, the reality is that Simone never would have gotten to where Simone is without the training she had from me and the other coaches that she had growing up. So, I’ve just had to hold on to my core beliefs.”

Across Europe, too, gymnasts have spoken out to force change. Former Dutch gymnast Petra Witjes and Germany’s Adina Hausch document falling out of love with the sport because of their experiences.

“At the elite club in the city I moved to it wasn’t fun anymore,” says Witjes, whose book, Silenced for Gold, is a memoir about the systemic abuses within sport and her battle to expose it. “My dad taught me to let my voice be heard but in the gym it was the opposite.”

Witjes was terrified of speaking to her parents, she was taught not to trust them. “I didn’t feel safe at first, because my coach always said that parents don’t understand elite gymnastics,” she says. “They push your parents away from you. We were in total isolation.”

Hausch says an injury that forced her from the sport was a relief. “I was on beam and I slipped with one leg and fell with the other on to the beam and then crashed down,” she says. “The leg was pushed sideways so much that it broke. From the age of 13 I don’t think there was a week without training through pain. When I left after the injury, the worst injury I’ve ever had, I was really happy that I didn’t have to go to the gym anymore.”

In Rotterdam, survivors vary in age from their 50s to their teens; it is hard not to view the issues as systemic and global. And ongoing. Charlotte Jacobs, who is only 18, quit the sport after suffering emotional abuse when training in the UK.

“It got to a point where I was like: ‘I can’t do it anymore’,” she says. “My experience was strange because it wasn’t physical, it wasn’t sexual, but it was emotional. You were ridiculed all the time, constantly. You weren’t allowed to cry, you weren’t allowed to talk, you weren’t allowed to sit down, if you were caught leaning on anything you’d have to run, you needed permission to go to the toilet, you needed permission to drink, and it’s that sort of really controlling, consistent and dismissive behaviour so that no one really felt safe that was prevalent.”

Shore, who is a member of G4C Canada, argues that if a big list of cultural reforms comes from the top, that is then normalised within the national federations and then the clubs “all the way down to grassroots, then I think we would see faster reform and less resistance”.

“The more I learn that the stories are consistent internationally the more it says something about the need for World Gymnastics to take a leadership role,” she says “The treatment across the world is pervasive and coaches are moving from space to space, country to country, more frequently now or they’re not even staying in this sport, they’re moving into other sports, especially if they’ve come into trouble.”

World Gymnastics has moved to address the cross-border issue within the sport at least, publishing a new safeguarding policy last week which notes that the Gymnastics Ethics Foundation, which it launched in 2019 and has handled nearly 500 reports, has the power to extend sanctions imposed by member federations providing they are compatible with the rules of the governing body and general principles of law.

Among the efforts of World Gymnastics to address safeguarding concerns was the launch of the 10 Golden Rules of Gymnastics in 2021, the establishment of a safeguarding commission in 2022 and, this year, the launch of a safeguarding newsletter and the appointment of a full-time Safeguarding Manager.

Shore believes the pace of governing bodies fully engaging with the change needed has been slow, however, “because to admit that there is harm going on in the sport puts organisations into a liability risk. Also, they have been able to deflect responsibility for so long. They don’t know how to solve it and they are getting pressure from all sides. By putting their head in the sand for literally 50 years we’ve now got to a crisis.”

A statement from World Gymnastics said: “Creating a safe environment for current and future generations of gymnasts is a responsibility that World Gymnastics takes extremely seriously and shares with all stakeholders across the sport. The priority for World Gymnastics is not only to strengthen safeguarding rules and policies, but to ensure that they lead to meaningful changes in everyday practice.”

Heafford alleges that British Gymnastics isn’t entering into meaningful engagement and collaboration with Gymnasts for Change and other survivors in the sport and says that she finds that “extremely frustrating”. She is also hugely critical of the processes gymnasts have to go through in raising a complaint against a coach or gym and what resolution looks like, saying: “In six years, we haven’t had one outcome that we can stand by and say that was a good outcome.”

British Gymnastics, however, insists it has engaged with the organisation regularly which has “helped shape its approach”, including a meeting with G4CI and others in Rotterdam as well as introducting a new complaints and disciplinary process “to improve transparency and fairness” .

Minky Worden, of Human Rights Watch, fears the situation could worsen. “Sport is getting younger. There’s a youth Olympics about to launch in Senegal. There’s going to be thousands of athletes, every one of them 18 or younger. They’re all children and they’re at a very elite level,” she says. “These children are being monetised and they are not protected because we know the systems are not in place to protect them.”

Hausch wants to see “measurable boundaries, for example increasing the competition age to 18,” she says. “I would root for Germany not to join youth international competitions. Having a 13-year-old do youth European championships is the same as doing it as an adult, it’s the same amount of work you have to put in, the same amount of pressure, it’s not a softer version, it’s the full version, and it doesn’t make sense.”

All agree there needs to be more done to help athletes advocate for themselves and others. Jacobs says: “There needs to be a sort of package of what to look out for. I think there needs to be more training for coaches in terms of mental wellbeing, disability, neurodiversity, all that, alongside what are and are not best practices.

“We need more regulation,” she adds of the British landscape. “Look at the new guidance that’s come out about keeping children safe in education. That’s all been updated. Where’s the guidance for anything sports-wise, extracurriculars, whether it’s swimming, gymnastics, dancing, anything like that?”

British Gymnastics says that it “recognises there is always more to do” but that prevention is “at the heart of our work. We have overhauled learning and development … and set clearer policies and guidance to drive meaningful change.” It says a coach developer network, regional teams and safeguarding and welfare officers in every club support communities.

Jotischky, who is now studying law off the back of her experience, says there are changes needed there too. “The legislative gap that exists is astonishing. You have the 2015 Serious Crime Act section 76, which talks about coercive control, but it’s limited to domestic and familial relationships. Then you have the 2021 Domestic Abuse Act which lists personally connected individuals as only being family members. In a coach-to-athlete relationship where you spend 30 hours a week in the gym with your coach, and some gymnasts even go and live with their coach because they’ve formed such a close relationship, of course coercive control and emotional abuse can happen but it’s not recognised within the law. So, we have very little legislative ground to deal with the most serious cases in particular.”

Listening to this group of women in Rotterdam, what becomes clearer is that while federations, to differing degrees, make changes in the name of athlete safety, survivors are still being failed. Meanwhile, these survivors and knowledgeable advocates remain isolated from the very structures that should be embracing them and channelling their knowledge and understanding of their experiences into the changes necessary to ensure the future health of the sport.

Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Blind date: ‘We overstayed our welcome – the waiters were shaking the cutlery drawer really loudly’
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Guardian Staff
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
What did you talk about? The sports we do. Books. Family. Friends. Our jobs. Travelling and travelling mishaps. Vermin infestations. Stocks and shares. ISAs.

Most awkward moment? We both arrived at the restaurant on time but there was a big queue which resulted in me sitting at the table alone for about 10 minutes – I got a bit nervous.

Best thing about Pardis? He is very sincere. He asked lots of questions, seemed interested in what I was saying and was a great listener. I also loved how laid-back he was – he went with the flow when I proposed the tasting menu.

Would you introduce Pardis to your friends? Of course – he’s interesting and really good company.

Blind date is Saturday’s dating column: every week, two strangers are paired up for dinner and drinks, and then spill the beans to us, answering a set of questions. This runs, with a photograph we take of each dater before the date, in Saturday magazine (in the UK) and online at theguardian.com every Saturday. It’s been running since 2009 – you can read all about how we put it together here.What questions will I be asked?We ask about age, location, occupation, hobbies, interests and the type of person you are looking to meet. If you do not think these questions cover everything you would like to know, tell us what’s on your mind.

Can I choose who I match with?No, it’s a blind date! But we do ask you a bit about your interests, preferences, etc – the more you tell us, the better the match is likely to be.

Can I pick the photograph?No, but don't worry: we'll choose the nicest ones.

How should I answer?Honestly but respectfully. Be mindful of how it will read to your date, and that Blind date reaches a large audience, in print and online.

Will I see the other person’s answers?No. We may edit yours and theirs for a range of reasons, including length, and we may ask you for more details.

Can I do it in my home town?Only if it’s in the UK. Many of our applicants live in London, but we would love to hear from people living elsewhere.

What do you think Pardis made of you? A ray of sunshine, akin to what everyone else thinks of me!

Did you go on somewhere? No, but we did overstay our welcome at the restaurant, to the point where the waiters were shaking the cutlery drawer really loudly.

If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be? I would have loved it to be in Paris. Pardis in Paris!

Would you meet again? Pardis is a lovely guy but I think we’re better suited as friends.

What were you hoping for? The scene in About Time where the protagonist meets Rachel McAdams in that dark dining restaurant. (I appreciate that isn’t quite the same concept as a blind date.)

First impressions? I was a few places behind her in the queue to get in the restaurant. I could only see the back of her head but thought: nice hair, good fashion sense.

What did you talk about? There was a healthy amount of chat on the life cycle of a fly and the declining quality of mousetraps. We’ve both had minor pest issues recently – a perk of living in London.

Most awkward moment? Probably mistaking her Irish accent for a Scottish one. Not my finest hour.

Best thing about Alexandrea? Very down to earth, clearly adventurous and a great dinner party guest.

Would you introduce Alexandrea to your friends? I wouldn’t put the poor girl through the trauma of meeting my rabble …

What do you think she made of you? I think she enjoyed my chat. Either that or she’s great at acting entertained (or I’m completely oblivious).

Did you go on somewhere? No, I was on early morning uncle duty the next day, so had to call it a night.

If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be? I’d brush up on my accent recognition beforehand.

Marks out of 10? 8 (for a friendship connection, otherwise it would have been higher).

Alexandrea and Pardis ate at Mildreds, London W1. Fancy a blind date? Email blind.date@theguardian.com

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: As Trump’s time runs out, this could be his most dangerous legacy: a world divided into three | Steve Bloomfield
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Steve Bloomfield
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
We’ve heard much about the end of the west. At the proposed summit between Trump, Putin and Xi, those fears could crystallise

In the final two years of a US presidency, when Congress has been lost, approval ratings have sunk like a stone and their party has started to think about who’s coming next, the person occupying the Oval Office can feel their power draining away. Domestic legislation, particularly in an era where bipartisan cooperation is almost nonexistent, grinds to a halt. But as the days tick by until the end, and as presidents begin to think about their legacy, there is one part of the job where they still have power: the rest of the world.

In the final weeks of his presidency in 1992 George HW Bush sent 28,000 American troops to Somalia to help end a famine. For Bill Clinton, it was a quixotic attempt to bring peace to the Middle East by ending the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Barack Obama restored diplomatic ties with Cuba, making a historic visit to Havana, as well as a final, successful push on the Iran nuclear deal.

In 10 days, Donald Trump will enter his own twilight zone. He is almost certain to lose control of the House and it’s not impossible he will face a Democratic Senate too. Any hopes of passing domestic policy – not that he’s bothered with that much during his first two years – will disappear. Instead, he will face a series of investigations that could lead, once again, to impeachment.

On the world stage, however, it will be a different story. And unlike Bush senior, Clinton and Obama, his ambitions won’t be peaceful. The first two years of his second term have been catastrophic; the final two could be even worse.

Once the midterms are over, the US is understood to be planning to restart its unwinnable war with Iran, already carrying out exercises with the Israeli military and withdrawing diplomats from the region. Trump’s sellout of Ukraine is well under way. In the past week he has argued that “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine”, while his envoy Steve Witkoff met with Vladimir Putin in Moscow, praising him in a televised meeting as a “humanitarian…and I salute that, I commend you and I thank you again.”

On top of a reckless war in the Middle East and appeasement in Europe, the shadow of a new world order is emerging, which Trump will relentlessly pursue in his final years. Putin has proposed a summit between himself, Trump and China’s Xi Jinping, to be held in China next month.

Such an unprecedented meeting, were it to take place, would have potentially devastating consequences for the rest of us. The three leaders have ambitions to transform the way the world is governed, essentially dividing it into spheres of influence. One summit wouldn’t turn an idea into reality, but it would send us down a very dangerous path. In Europe, it would have an impact beyond Ukraine if the US refused to help protect nations threatened by Russia. In east Asia, the withdrawal of the American security blanket would cause enormous problems for Taiwan, South Korea and Japan, as well as Australia.

We’ve talked a lot about the end of the west over the past two years – this feels like a moment when many of those fears will crystalise.

The Trump administration’s ambition to divide the world into spheres and side with dictators over democrats has long been evident. Last year’s National Security Strategy was deeply critical of the US’s traditional allies in Europe and east Asia. But it was what it didn’t say that was most shocking. Both Russia and China avoided direct criticism. In six paragraphs describing the threat to Taiwan, China was not mentioned once. Elsewhere in the document, China was actually praised as “rich and powerful … us[ing] its wealth and power to its considerable advantage.” The section on Russia’s war in Ukraine failed to mention how it started and did not suggest that Putin should be defeated; instead it focused on how the US could help Europe and Russia mend their relationship. The 33-page document discussed the importance of the US controlling the western hemisphere, but made clear that so long as the US still had economic dominance, it cared little whether other parts of the world are protected. “The affairs of other countries,” it stated, “are our concern only if their activities directly threaten our interests.” For too long, it argued, America’s allies had “suck[ed] us into conflicts and controversies central to their interests but peripheral or irrelevant to our own”.

For Putin, this is a success almost three decades in the making. He has long viewed American support for democracy in eastern Europe and central Asia as “interference” in Russia’s backyard. Now he has a US president who agrees. Trump has also placed Putin on a far higher pedestal than Russia’s economy and its technological prowess deserves.

Xi, too, has welcomed the US’s rhetorical retreat from east Asia, particularly if it allows China greater maritime control in the East China Sea and South China Sea. World opinion on China has dramatically improved as that of the US has slid. As Chrystia Freeland, a former Canadian foreign minister, put it this week, “there has not been a president who has been more beneficial for China than Donald Trump”.

At stake is not merely territorial control. All three governments see the possibility of increasing economic ties. For the US and China, the bigger issues are future control of economic supply chains and technology platforms, while Russia’s fossil fuel resources are also a factor. All three are key players in the next space race, both in terms of commercial and military control. If these three nations begin to work together, at the expense of Europe and the rest of the world, it will fundamentally change the nature of geopolitics. A decade ago, talk of a multipolar world was based around the idea of the US, China and the European Union as the three most powerful blocs. Somehow, Brussels has been replaced by Moscow.

Until now, the rest of the west has – on the whole – tried to muddle through. Nato still exists on paper, G7 and G20 summits may be chaotic but they still take place. Optimists in the Foreign Office point out that Trump turned up to the UN general assembly and his administration is still deeply involved in the UN’s day to day activities.

Mark Carney spoke of a “rupture” and warned the old post-cold war world was not coming back, but despite warm words from Emmanuel Macron, and renewed discussion about how Europe can protect itself without the US, there is still a sense that everyone is waiting for Trump’s time in office to end. A Great Powers summit makes this harder to ignore.

While US presidents seek foreign policy success in their final months, history suggests they rarely find it. Clinton’s Camp David talks collapsed after Ehud Barak and Yasser Arafat were unable to reach an agreement. Bush would argue that his initial intervention in Somalia eased a famine, but it ended in humiliation. A botched raid on a warlord led to the deaths of 18 US soldiers and several hundred Somalis. Obama’s diplomacy in Cuba and Iran succeeded, but were both promptly ripped up by Donald Trump.

Trump will get his photoshoot – and maybe that’s all he wants – but there is no guarantee that this unsavoury troika becomes a permanent geopolitical fixture. Trump’s foreign policy has divided his Maga movement and has shocked traditional conservatives. The Wall Street Journal editorial board described the proposed summit as “arguably the worst idea of the second Trump term”. A President Vance or Rubio might be less willing to throw in their lot with dictators; a President Ossoff or Ocasio-Cortez certainly won’t.

But just because Trump won’t win, doesn’t mean that the US won’t lose. He will be arriving in Shenzhen at the weakest moment in his presidency. An 80-year-old lame duck leader fated to limp towards the finish line unable to pass any legislation and threatened by two chaotic years of investigations into his alleged corruption. Opposite him will be two authoritarian leaders in their early 70s who believe the only thing preventing them from ruling their nations for another two decades is death. Indeed, given their “hot mic” discussions about longevity drugs last year, perhaps they both believe they can rule for even longer.

If it goes ahead, this summit will bring Putin back in from the cold and reiterate Xi’s position as a global leader who cannot be ignored. The image of the three leaders will come to define this era when the rules-based international order was torn apart and a new, uncertain period began to form.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: ‘It’s part of our history’: can the menú del día survive Spain’s changing eating habits?
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Sam Jones in Madrid
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Established under the Franco dictatorship, the lunchtime ritual is in decline but all is not lost

A little before lunchtime each working day across Spain, evidence of one of the lingering, if less notorious, legacies of the Franco dictatorship is carefully traced in chalk, marker pen and printer ink.

Beckoning to hungry workers from blackboards, whiteboards and pieces of paper hastily taped to windows, the competitively priced menú del día, or daily set-price lunch, has been part of everyday Spanish life for more than half a century. But while 4m menús are still served each weekday, Spain is slowly losing its appetite for the familiar ritual.

Back in 2009, the country’s best-known chef, Ferran Adrià, went so far as to pronounce it dead – a victim of changing eating habits, economic downturns and bistro-style restaurants trying to charge €20-€30 (£17-£25) for what should be a simple starter, a hearty main and a choice of pudding or coffee … with bread and a drink thrown in.

Seventeen years later, however, the diagnosis seem a little premature. A new book by the Spanish food journalist Lakshmi Aguirre charts the history and evolution of the menú and argues that while the tradition is indeed in hot water, it hasn’t quite had its chips.

Her book – Menú del Día: Everyday Scenes of a First Course, a Second Course and Pudding – begins with the unpalatable fact that it all began with a tourist menu dreamed up in the mid-1960s up by the Spanish dictator Francisco Franco’s information and tourism minister, Manuel Fraga.

The regime was keen in the aftermath of the “years of hunger” that followed the Spanish civil war to show foreign visitors that food was plentiful, good and affordable. So it was that establishments serving food should offer “a starter of soup, a main course chosen from at least three options and based on egg, fish or meat and accompanied by a side dish, and a pudding based on fruit, something sweet, or cheese”.

The price was set at between 50 and 250 pesetas and, to stop unscrupulous restaurant owners watering down the drinks, the law stipulated that the accompanying quarter-litre of vino had to be “reds and whites from Spain that are pure, clean, pleasant on the palate and with an alcohol content of not less than 12%”.

In the early 1970s, the menú del día was rebaptised to make it look less like an attempt to woo – and sometimes gouge – tourists, but also to give ordinary Spaniards the idea that they, too, could indulge.

It is now so ubiquitous that many in Spain have no idea of its genesis. “When I was working on the book and people asked me about the menú del día, I’d mention Manuel Fraga and lots of them would throw their hands up in shock,” Aguirre said. “Some people know, but the vast majority don’t. It says a lot about us Spaniards; we forget very quickly.”

Researching the book, which includes personal reminiscences and a hefty selection of recipes, led Aguirre to consider the place of the menú in the popular consciousness.

“It’s part of our history, yet it’s changed over the years, reflecting the evolution of Spanish society,” she said. “It originated from something as terrible as a dictatorship, and today it has become a deeply ingrained custom. We feel a sense of nostalgia as we realise it’s fading away.”

The threats to the set lunch, whose average price today is €14.70, are many. Increasingly time-poor, many Spaniards now opt for a quick lunch, eating food from home at work or popping to a supermarket for a ready meal to microwave in a soulless canteen. Rising energy and food prices are making it harder for small, family-run restaurants to offer a rotating daily selection of starters and mains.

All of which explains the rise of the “dish of the day”, which offers restaurants a cheaper alternative to the traditional choice of three or four mains, and the increasing diversity of some menús, which now feature Latin American staples as a reflection of Spain’s changing demographics.

“The menú del día purists reject such options, but it has always been a reflection of the society that consumes it – and that’s exactly how it should be,” Aguirre said. “Spain today isn’t the same as it was in the 1980s, it is far more diverse and pluralistic, and as a result diners have changed as well. The menú del día exists for those who need it, for people who may come from many different backgrounds.”

Aguirre’s menú of choice would be a simple but well-cooked vegetable stew followed by hake in green sauce or baby squid in ink, and then leche frita (fried custard) or rice pudding.

But, as she points out in her book, the surroundings are almost as important as the cooking. Her benchmarks for a good menú del día spot include simple dishes, a regularly changing menu, chips that aren’t frozen, a chorus of regulars and “a chalkboard free of any trace of words such as avocado, burrata, tartare, truffle or sourdough bread”.

That chalkboard should, by preference, be written “by someone who’s never heard of lettering”, and bonus points are awarded if the child of the owners is doing their homework on a table down the end.

As it hobbles slowly towards what may be its demise, the menú del día has become something that transcends a filling and reasonably priced midday meal.

“What’s being lost is a meeting point,” Aguirre said. “A centre of community gravity where families with limited financial means can afford to eat out, and where those who live alone can find some company during a meal, which remains a deeply social activity.

“It’s a place where joys, sorrows and problems can be shared, or where you can simply enjoy a bit of breathing space, as well as a place for those who live far away or who don’t have the time to go home for lunch.”

The true privilege of the menú, she added, lay “not just in being able to pay for a meal, but also in having the time to enjoy it”.

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: A Course Called Ireland: Bill Murray clearly hated making his new golfing show – but it’s extremely fun to binge
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Rhik Samadder
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
In his rogue new travelogue, the Hollywood star tees off, has drunken pub singalongs – but mostly just proves how tired he is of fame

I’m suspicious of travelogues, which often feature celebrities in contrived situations, serving up a sentimental postcard of a place that is tantamount to a lie. I also hate how famous people are inexorably drawn to golf: a boring game historically predicated on a rancid mix of social exclusivity and extensive land ownership. So it was perverse of me to watch a show in which author Tom Coyne drives around Ireland playing various courses with his friend, actor Bill Murray. It’s the perfect intersection of none of my interests.

I was, however, hooked by a strange promise in A Course Called Ireland’s introductory sequence. “This is not a show about golf,” it says. “It’s not even a show about Bill Murray.” This was immediately followed by a scene in which an Irish woman standing by the roadside misidentified the actor as Bill Cosby. OK, I thought. What are they teeing up here?

There’s a hole in at least one of those promises. A Course Called Ireland (Sunday 25 October, 9.30pm, BBC Two) is intended to be a jocular road trip, in which the two friends meet colourful characters and reflect on their own Irish heritage, between spectacular rounds on the rugged links. It’s based on a journey Coyne documented in his book of the same name, in which he played every course in the country. Which again, sounds like a marriage in crisis to me – but the book is very popular.

What we get is a fascinating, existential snapshot of fame. A camera crew trailing a Hollywood legend around a series of Irish villages is, unavoidably, the story. Murray can’t stop for a wee without being mobbed. The director wants as much Murray on screen as possible. The 76-year-old Ghostbuster wants to give the spotlight to anyone else who’ll take it. The wheels quickly start to come off. He rips up the itinerary, digs in his heels, grouches. He cringes at the artifice of making TV, such as pretending to meet people for the first time. He’s been famous for 50 years – and it shows.

He also embodies the paradox of the reluctant celebrity, which is that most of them can’t stop doing things that perpetuate their myth. They hate the fame, they need the fame. The oddball actor is known for giving regular people “a Bill Murray story”, crashing graduation ceremonies or stepping behind the bar to pull pints. We see that here, as he hoists a groomsman on his shoulders, or gently pushes an ice-cream in a woman’s face. As he jokes, “If I wasn’t famous, I’d probably have a few more cuts and bruises to the face.”

In one sequence, Murray refuses to attend a pub as scripted, and disappears to a nearby evening of folk music instead. Later, once filming has been aborted, he returns to the pub to lead the room in a drunken singalong. It’s exactly what the producers would have wanted; for Murray, such larks only have meaning if they aren’t being manufactured for the cameras. There is something heroic in his stubbornness. (Of course, someone films the whole thing on their mobile phone.)

The show bends many of the format rules, by necessity or design. The BTS feeling of a crew working around a recalcitrant star is juicy. Each episode also boasts a voiceover from a supporting character – the proprietor of a tweed shop, a junior runner, Ireland’s former minister of the arts. The best is Margaret, an elderly woman outside a sweet shop who tells Murray he was the best thing in “Gorseboosters”. “Bill is 98% Irish if you look at his DNA, which I haven’t, but it says so here in the script,” she lilts. These unexpected and charming turns ground a show that otherwise feels like Lost in La Mancha set in Ballybunion.

If the show fails by its own marker, it succeeds at being funny, peculiar and melancholy: a much higher bar. It’s as unconventional and highly watchable as its impish star, the one it pretends not to be hopelessly in thrall to. What’s more, I finally understand why celebrities love golf so much. They want to be as far away from other people as possible.

Lunch with my agent is going nowhere, so I decide to share my latest motoring anecdote

I’m having lunch with my agent – an infrequent occurrence, because neither of us ever has any good news for the other. This lunch is no different.

“Sorry to make you come all this way,” she says, “but I had to be near the office today.” She hints at some complex contractual negotiations involving an author for whom, I suspect, she always has good news.

People sometimes ask why I bought an electric car. What did I want from it? To save money? To help the environment? To guard myself against future fuel shortages, or toxic emissions, or both?

The truth is: I wanted a medal. I wanted people to see the little green rectangle on my number plate and think: there goes a great guy, doing his best; let’s slow down and give him plenty of room to pull into our lane.

This does not happen. The official honours bestowed on electric car owners are actually pretty paltry: a discount on the London congestion charge and a slightly abbreviated MOT test. And you get no credit for being the green part of a traffic jam.

A few days earlier my wife and I had been invited to have lunch with the older one and his girlfriend, on the other side of town. In the morning, my wife declares that she will drive.

Traffic is light on the way, and we arrive ahead of schedule. There is, however, absolutely nowhere to park. Every available space is occupied.

On a second trawl through the neighbourhood a sudden gap appears ahead of us. “What about there?” my wife says, slowing down. I look up at the sign as we pass.

“But wait,” I say. “It’s actually a charging point. You have to be actively charging the car while you’re in it.”

“Fine, we’ll do that then,” she says. “It can’t be more expensive than parking.”

“I think that if I were a parking warden, I would love to give this car a ticket.”

“Oh, for fuck’s sake,” my wife says, choosing, on this occasion, to shoot the messenger.

We make two more wide circles of the area, varying the route slightly each time until we are a little lost.

Behind us a man in a car beeps, his impatience unmodulated by the green band on our number plate. My wife pulls over to let him pass. I have to open my door to examine the plug situation more closely.

“Yeah, but our socket’s on the other side,” I say. “It won’t reach unless we’re facing the other way.”

“And also,” I say, craning my neck, “this particular charging point seems to be part of a local scheme. Like, you need a special parking permit from the borough to even use it.”

I stand up and shut the door. My wife reverses down the road, leaving me on the pavement. So, I think. This is how it ends.

But it turns out my wife has noticed that the man who beeped at us had just vacated a parking space half a dozen car lengths back.

“So,” I say. “If you get the right tariff and you only charge at night, it is a lot cheaper. But don’t expect special treatment. There’s no medal.”

A brief silence follows – neither of us willing, for the moment, to be the first bearer of bad news.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: He wants to clean up the city and banish high prices. But who is ‘London’s Batman’?
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Sammy Gecsoyler
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
The caped crusader is paying for hospital parking fines, giving out fuel to drivers – and sponsoring the return of cut-priced Freddo bars

In the harsh light of day, a caped crusader storms the streets of London to tackle a crime that has long blighted the capital: littering.

“When I said I wanted to save London, I meant it. I will not stop until every single bit of trash is off the streets,” he says in a viral video, narrated in his trademark deep, husky and (suspiciously) American voice, joined by a gang of hooded helpers clearing rubbish-strewn streets in Tower Hamlets.

This was Batman’s first good deed for the capital and, in the month since relocating from Gotham, he has carried out many more: paying parking fines for those visiting loved ones in hospital, giving out “free fuel” to motorists and bringing back £1 chicken and chips to those who once savoured this cheap and filling after-school meal.

But who is he really and what does he stand for? In a recent interview with a BBC reporter, who was only given a time and location before the masked figure emerged in an alleyway, he summed up his mission: “People are struggling and I want to help them.”

As for his identity, Niko Omilana – YouTuber, prankster and fifth-placed London 2021 mayoral candidate, who has pulled off similar stunts – is the most obvious guess, though he has denied it.

When asked by BBC London if he was the city’s masked mystery saviour, Omilana sent the team a voice note saying: “BBC, just to tell you, I’m not Batman.”

Count Binface, who has faced off against some of the nation’s most high-profile politicians in elections across the country, is another name in the mix, though he denied the rumours.

He told the Guardian: “I can see why a human might think that ‘London’s Batman’ is me, but it is actually a bit armour-ist of you. We’re not all the same.

“I’m happy to make the clarification and I would like to take the opportunity to wish London’s Batman well, including with his inevitable battle on the planet Copyright.”

Omilana remains the most likely suspect. His 2021 mayoral manifesto pledges included turning off all power in London once a year to “call it Londoff”, forcing then-prime minister Boris Johnson to “shush” and reducing the price of a Freddo chocolate bar to 5p.

Curiously, in one of his most viral stunts, London’s Batman set up a stall in Oxford Street where a Freddo could be exchanged for a tiny, silver 5p coin. (The frog-shaped chocolate bar was never officially sold for this sum, with 2p in the 1970s and 10p in the 1990s and early 2000s being the lowest retail prices documented.)

Ace Clvrk was in the area buying a guitar when he came across the stall. “I was lucky that day I had exactly 5p. It felt like fate,” said the 32-year-old musician.

He was approached on the street by some “hooded, masked youths” who “seemed really friendly”. They stopped him and asked: “Do you want to buy a Freddo?”

Clvrk was guided to a stall where he saw the caped crusader in the flesh. He told Clvrk he was “trying to bring attention to lowering the cost of Freddos”.

Like Gotham’s caped crusader, his London doppelganger appears to have significant resources behind him. His social media videos are slickly produced and the tasks he has carried out are hardly cheap.

For the “free fuel” stunt, one resident, speaking to the Times, estimated he gave away more than £3,500 to motorists throughout the day. The Guardian contacted several organisations that had benefited from London’s Batman’s good deeds who declined to speak citing confidentiality reasons.

Clvrk said it looked like a well-run stunt. “Everyone that I spoke to was really friendly and the actual content came out looking great too. I don’t remember actually seeing the camera,” he said.

In the video touting his bargain frog-shaped chocolates, London’s Batman featured a clip of Andy Burnham holding a Freddo while declaring it the “most talked about cost of living symbol in the UK” before going on to say he “might not be able to do anything to reduce the price of these”.

The caped crusader’s Freddo policy could suggest he’s vying for real power. “I’d vote for him, 100%,” said Clvrk. “5p Freddo, £1 chicken and chips and paying for fuel. What’s not to love?”

There could be some weight to this, especially if two-time political candidate Omilana, who also ran against Rishi Sunak in his Richmond and Northallerton seat in 2024, is behind the mask.

The message appears to be resonating. On TikTok, he has already amassed 315,000 followers in just over four weeks.

“I think everything he’s doing is amazing,” said Clvrk. “Politics and prime ministers are removed from the everyday Londoner and British person on the streets who used to be able to get a Freddo for 10p or cheap chicken and chips.

“With rising prices, it’s shining a light on things that seem small to those that are removed from it, but not for the everyday person.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Blaze engulfs Hitler’s ‘Eagle’s Nest’ mountain retreat in Bavaria
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Agence France-Presse
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
About 200 firefighters deployed to tackle the blaze at former Nazi retreat in a remote part of southern Germany

German police said Saturday they had detained a suspect after a fire at Adolf Hitler’s former mountain retreat, known as the Eagle’s Nest, in the state of Bavaria.

About 200 firefighters were deployed to tackle the blaze at the Nazi dictator’s remote and difficult-to-access Kehlsteinhaus residence, on the peak of Obersalzberg in southern Germany.

Firefighters saw flames rising high into the air as they approached the scene, only to find the building “completely ablaze”, police said.

“A suspicious person was taken into temporary custody,” they said in a later statement, adding that nobody was injured in the blaze.

Police spokesperson Lisa Maier said firefighters struggled to tackle the fire due to its location at an altitude of 1,834 metres (6,000 feet).

The building was only accessible with “heavy breathing apparatus”, she said.

Authorities were alerted to the fire on Friday evening, when a smoke detector triggered a fire alarm at about 9.50pm (1950 GMT), police said.

No potential reason for the fire was given, but the German media reported that the investigators suspected it was the result of arson.

As snow fell on the Alpine peak, the Eagle’s Nest was still engulfed in flames in the early hours of Saturday, a weather camera showed.

Officers blocked access to the road leading to the retreat, according to an AFP photographer.

Maier said police were still investigating but will hold a news conference later on Saturday.

German tabloid Bild reported that the authorities had arrested a motorcyclist they came across on their way to the scene.

Built between 1937 and 1938, the Eagle’s Nest forms part of the toxic legacy of Hitler’s Third Reich, which was responsible for the deaths of millions of Jews as well as Roma, LGBTQ people and Communists in the Holocaust.

It was designed to serve as a monument to Hitler’s rule, although the dictator rarely visited the complex.

It survived the second world war undamaged, and since 1952 has hosted an exhibition recounting the house’s Nazi history and a restaurant.

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: The Guide #266: The knives are out at Netflix – maybe now it will make something worth watching
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.author: Gwilym Mumford
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
In this week’s newsletter: Stalling subscriber numbers have led to a corporate bloodbath, but the streaming giant has an inherent quality problem that will be a lot harder to fix

In all the fevered hype around a certain three-hour, form-breaking documentary portrait of a disgraced tech CEO, another big Hollywood story this week has been relatively sidelined: the drama at Netflix, where sluggish subscriber numbers and a general lack of Wall Street enthusiasm has led to a remarkable spree of sackings. A thousand employees, or 6% of its entire workforce, have been laid off – including some very big names. Among a clutch of other execs, chief content officer Bela Bajaria – the figure most synonymous with Netflix’s tone and ethos over the past decade – has been fired. The company’s head of film, Dan Lin, has gone too. That shade of red on the streamer’s logo has never looked more bloody. You Can See Everything getting very messy indeed.

We’ve been here before, of course. Netflix – giant, controversial, inescapable – is the sort of company people love to make grand speculations about. Pencils were sharpened in 2022 when Netflix lost subscribers for the first time and saw its share price plummet as a result, before the company enjoyed a notable resurgence. Just as the obituaries written for the streamer were premature then, writing it off now would be foolish too.

But a cull of this magnitude is still telling, indicating that Netflix itself thinks something has gone badly awry – particularly in terms of the actual stuff it’s been pumping out. Bajaria was the exec who famously likened the streamer’s programming to a “gourmet cheeseburger”; a premium product that was also highly snackable. Her exit suggests that recipe isn’t as appealing to viewers as it once was.

It’s a question that gets asked more often than the streamer would like: when was the last time you watched a truly great new show on Netflix? Adolescence tends to be a popular answer, but that series (a limited run of only four episodes, let’s remember) was released 18 months ago. This year the cupboard has been extraordinarily bare. You might make a case for How to Get to Heaven from Belfast, or East of Eden at a push, but neither feel unmissably brilliant. And the streamer’s record with returning series is strikingly shaky, with precipitous audience drop-offs for shows’ second seasons.

Netflix’s quality issue is baked into its very model. The limitations of the company’s all-at-once, binge-friendly release strategy have been obvious for some time, resulting in shows that burn brightly but briefly for a week or two, before disappearing from the cultural conversation. But just as damaging, I’d argue, is a complete disinterest in cultivating shows with the potential for real staying power. Shows are often cancelled right as they are finding their voice, and flashy limited series with big names are prioritised over ones that could run and run. (Name-led series tend to take longer to return too, due to their stars’ many other commitments.) With the exception of cosy heartlands romantic drama Virgin River and Black Mirror (a bit of an outlier given it is an anthology series and debuted on another platform, Channel 4), no current Netflix drama has been airing for more than four seasons.

Netflix isn’t alone in its aversion to lasting, sprawling TV: in this era, post-the golden age of The Sopranos, Breaking Bad and the like, shows have tended to get shorter both in season and episode counts, with bigger gaps between seasons. TV as a whole feels less ambitious and substantial – not to mention reliably delivered – than it once did. But it is Netflix, as the chief disruptor of the old TV model, that bears the most responsibility for this shift – and that is perhaps most vulnerable as a result. It has become, for many, a platform that is clicked on to out of habit, rather than rushed to in fevered anticipation of the latest episode of a great show.

Perhaps that will change in the wake of all the corporate bloodletting; the new chief content officer, British industry veteran Peter Rice, has been talked up for his excellent taste, having overseen a dynamite run of films (28 Days Later, Sideways, Juno) when he was head of the Fox Searchlight studio. Or perhaps it doesn’t really matter either way: habit is a strong drug, and Netflix equals TV for many people. Indeed, its primary rival, in its own estimation, is not the BBC or Disney+ or the like, but YouTube, which is why it has been trying to hoover up many of the same things that are popular on that platform: influencer videos, podcasts, live sport.

Netflix has long dreamed of being the “everything store”, a place that has all the content you could ever need – which is a fine ambition. I just wish there was something good to watch on it once in a while.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: ‘We can’t let the far right take power again’: Lula voters in final push before Brazil runoff
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Tiago Rogero in Belo Horizonte
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
In bellwether Minais Gerais, with polls about even, president’s supporters are striving to win over those who abstained or voted for Flavio Bolsonaro

Naiara Boroni, Nikolas Domingues and Jodersson Diego live in the same city and do not know one another, but said they had done the same thing in recent days: persuaded at least one person who had not voted for the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the first round to choose him in this Sunday’s runoff.

In Boroni’s case, it was her grandmother who had not turned out; in Domingues’s, a cousin who had chosen a candidate who finished fourth. But Diego achieved what to many sounds almost impossible in such a polarised country: he said he had persuaded a woman who voted for the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro to switch sides.

“She’s a student of mine and didn’t vote for Lula because of her evangelical church. I didn’t argue; I tried to explain that he wasn’t everything they said he was, and she said she had changed her mind,” said Diego, 33, a dance teacher from Belo Horizonte, the capital of the state of Minas Gerais.

Winning over voters who abstained or cast null votes, and flipping as many others as possible, is at the heart of Lula’s strategy as he tries to do what no presidential candidate has ever managed in Brazil: overturn a first-round defeat like the one he suffered to Bolsonaro on 5 October.

Lula received 3.8 million fewer votes than in 2022, when he ran against the senator’s father, then president Jair Bolsonaro – who would go on to lose the runoff and try to stage a coup, which failed after the heads of two of the three armed forces refused to join him.

Serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest, he chose his eldest son to stand in his place. Flávio Bolsonaro has said that, if elected, he will pardon his father and receive the presidential sash from him.

The senator won 5 million more votes than his father and saw his party sweep elections for congress, state governments and state legislatures, which made him the clear favourite for many analysts.

In the three weeks of campaigning since then, however, polls have shown the gap steadily narrowing, and the two are now about even, with Bolsonaro still slightly ahead, but only by fractions of a percentage point.

“The scenario is one of a very tight tie, but with Lula’s campaign performing markedly better in the runoff,” said political scientist Manoel Leonardo Santos, a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais.

The incumbent’s hopes rest on the narrowest-ever gap between first and second place, at less than 2% of the vote, while abstention reached a record 21%, which tends to hurt Lula more because it is more common among groups that favour him, such as lower-income and less-educated voters and older people.

Of the 10 cities with the highest abstention rates, eight are in Minas Gerais, the country’s second-largest electorate after São Paulo and a historical bellwether in presidential elections. No candidate has ever won nationally without carrying the state, where Lula now finished almost five percentage points behind Bolsonaro.

“If Lula’s voters turn out, he can win, but there is absolutely no guarantee that he will manage to make that happen,” said political scientist Helcimara de Souza Telles, also a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais.

Last Tuesday, at an event with local politicians that included an appearance by the senator via video call on a big screen, as well as a 23ft inflatable figure of his father, Minas Gerais governor-elect Cleitinho Azevedo urged the dozens of people present “not to think that we have already won the election and keep asking for votes”.

Pharmacist Magda Aparecida Araújo, 44, lives in the working-class neighbourhood next to the exhibition centre and was sitting in the back row. “I’m not going to belittle Lula’s governments, because I went to university thanks to a scholarship, but I now vote for Bolsonaro because he defends the family and I support traditional values,” said Araújo.

Given its electoral importance, both Lula and Bolsonaro chose the state capital for some of their final rallies: the senator’s was scheduled for this morning, while the incumbent held his last Wednesday.

“I’m here because we can’t let the far right take power again and destroy all of our rights,” said student Ester Nascimento, 17, who was with friends her own age, a symbol of what many see as perhaps the main catalyst behind Lula’s hopes of a comeback: young people who organically took to the streets in large protests all across Brazil.

Following advice from young, digitally native politicians, Lula’s team overhauled his online communications, and the 81-year-old incumbent, who does not even own a mobile phone, began recording selfie videos. Millions of his supporters joined a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army”, where congressman André Janones sent dozens of daily instructions on how to make pro-Lula content go viral, and for the first time, the president’s digital reach overtook Bolsonaro’s.

Lula also approved a “package of benefits” at the limits of what electoral law allows, including increasing and bringing forward payments from the main cash-transfer programme for poor families, while also securing a major political victory by getting congress to approve a shorter working week that could affect 30 million workers.

Even so, many analysts see much of the narrowing gap in the polls as driven more by Bolsonaro losing support, with his rejection rate having risen while Lula’s has fallen slightly.

Experts say some of Bolsonaro’s recent moves may have alienated the indecisive voters, including what was seen as an aggressive performance in the first presidential debate and a controversial speech in which he said he would use the new highly conservative congress to “change the constitution and re-democratise this country”.

That was the first warning sign that led administrative assistant Douglas Pereira Melo, 25, who voted for far-right influencer Renan Santos three weeks ago, to now choose Lula.

“It’s very dangerous for him to say that he’ll change the constitution. His father tried to stage a coup, and I’m afraid he’ll follow in his footsteps,” said Melo, adding that “the Bolsonaro scandals” had also weighed on his decision.

The senator is under investigation in two federal police inquiries, one into what happened to the £20m he was caught on tape asking a disgraced banker accused of corruption to provide for a biopic about his father, and another into alleged money laundering and a possible business partnership with a close friend, the betting-sector businessman and lawyer Willer Tomaz.

The senator is also embroiled in a dispute with the footballer Richarlison, who accuses Bolsonaro and Tomaz of conspiring to strip him of a mansion on an island, while Piauí magazine revealed last Thursday that, at the height of the Covid pandemic in 2020, the senator attended a barbecue on a boat with sex workers and lobbyists who were negotiating vaccine purchases with his father’s administration.

Political scientist Manoel Leonardo Santos said he has “no doubt” that Lula will enter the runoff with better chances than he did immediately after Bolsonaro’s first-round victory.

“Whether it will be enough for him to turn it around, we can’t say. But Lula has gained ground while Bolsonaro appears to have stopped growing,” he added.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.title: Hundreds of protests expected across France, with shops, businesses and tourist sites closed – Europe live
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.author: Frances Mao
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.text:
France will deploy 70,000 officers around the country. Protests are also expected in Italy, Spain, Austria, Portugal, Albania and Ireland

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of events in Europe – we will be closely following protests across the continent today.

In France, hundreds of thousands are expected at rallies across the country, with high school students, unionists, “yellow vest” demonstrators and others turning out for a fourth weekend of protests demanding more government funding for schools and measures to help with housing and the cost of living.

Desperate to avoid the looting and property damage seen on the fringes of some protests last weekend, French authorities have ramped up restrictions on where protesters can march and which groups are “authorised” to do so. They’ve increased policing 20%, mobilising 70,000 police officers and soldiers to the streets, including both elite units and trainee officers.

Many of Paris’s metro stations and major museums and tourist sites are shut today, while across the country, shops and businesses have been urged to close their doors. Community tensions are also high following a deadly shooting on Friday west of Paris where the gunman targeted non-white people, killing one person and injuring five others including a child. The French president called it a “racist terrorist attack”.

Meanwhile, Marine Le Pen’s anti-immigration party is also due to hold its national conference in the central city of Orléans. The far-right National Rally’s meeting is expected to draw up to 30,000 counter-demonstrators. Protests are also being held in Italy, Spain, Austria, Portugal, Albania and Ireland today.

The capital’s authorities have shut down the stations in a bid to contain crowds and curb movement throughout the city today. The affected stations are: Argentine, Assemblée Nationale, Bel Air, Champs-Elysées – Clemenceau, Charles de Gaulle – Étoile, Cluny - La Sorbonne, Concorde, Daumesnil, Dugommier, Franklin D. Roosevelt, George V, Mabillon, Maubert – Mutualité, Miromesnil, Odéon, Picpus, Rennes, Rue du Bac, Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Saint-Sulpice, Sèvres - Babylone, Solférino, Tuileries and Varenne.

We’ve seen other attempts by authorities to restrict movement in cities across France for this weekend; Marseille authorities earlier this week said they would suspend public transport services on Saturday; they were forced to reverse the decision following outcry.

In Orléans, which is hosting the far-right National Rally congress, the tram lines are suspended and bike-sharing rentals have been removed from the city centre.

All through the night in neighbourhoods in the centre and east of Paris, the sound of sawing, drilling and hammering rang out as wooden boards were hastily secured into place to cover windows and shop-fronts.

Businesses being boarded up included opticians, supermarkets and pharmacies as well as trainers and handbag stores.

Hundreds of shops were smashed and looted over two nights last weekend in Paris, and thousands more in cities across France, including Marseille and Bordeaux.

At a public meeting at Paris city hall this week, some shop-owners had cried as they spoke of their fears of businesses being smashed and looted again this weekend.

“I’m afraid there isn’t enough wooden board left to protect shops and the demand is making it so expensive to board up shops,” one optician near Châtelet in the city centre said. “We’ll close up and take all our stock of glasses out of the shop.”

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.title: ‘Our third date was at Buckingham Palace’: Marlon James and Nicholas Boggs on life as a literary power couple
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.author: Emma Loffhagen
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.text:
Shortlisted for the Booker and Baillie Gifford prizes respectively, the novelist and biographer talk about working and living together – and giving a voice to Black queer history
