The literary power couple is a historically seductive concept. Two writers sharing a life, their private and creative worlds entwined, each becoming witness to and critic of the other’s work. Think Simone de Beauvoir and Jean-Paul Sartre, Joan Didion and John Gregory Dunne. Or, less auspiciously, Sylvia Plath and Ted Hughes.

Now, into this illustrious company steps a new pair: the novelist Marlon James and the biographer Nicholas Boggs, whose books have each been shortlisted for one of Britain’s most prestigious literary awards – James for the Booker prize and Boggs for the Baillie Gifford prize for nonfiction. Between them, they have produced two formidable books, each the culmination of years of work, and each concerned with the lives of Black queer men whose stories have often been overlooked.

“I’m not sure what to do with it,” James says, when I ask how they feel about the inevitable impending “literary power couple” label. “I have all these romantic notions that we were like Joan Didion and John Gregory Dunne or something – I don’t know. What do you think?” He turns to Boggs, who laughs. “It’s all very new,” he says. “We’re still getting used to it.”

It is a warm October morning in Williamsburg, the fashionable writerly enclave in Brooklyn, and I am sitting across from the pair at their apartment. They are relaxing on a chaise longue, looking comfortable enough to have been there all morning. Their exchanges have the easy rhythm of a long relationship, full of small corrections and private jokes.

James, the 55-year-old Jamaican-born novelist whose 2015 book A Brief History of Seven Killings won the Booker prize, is back on the shortlist this year with The Disappearers, a sprawling, dark reckoning with the brutality of Aids-era gay life and homophobia in Jamaica. Boggs, his 53-year-old partner of nearly nine years, has been shortlisted for the Baillie Gifford prize for his first book, Baldwin: A Love Story, a biography of James Baldwin that draws on two decades of research into the writer’s intimate life and creative relationships.

“The Baillie Gifford’s a prize I know well,” James says. “So when Nick was on the shortlist, I knew what a big deal it was.” Boggs remembers James’s reaction when the nonfiction shortlist was announced on 1 October. “His eyes got very wide. I don’t think I’ve seen his eyes get quite that wide before.”

James had the first taste of the excitement, when the Booker shortlist was announced in September. “You got shortlisted first, so the pressure was on!” Boggs jokes. “No matter how many times you do this, it’s always a great surprise,” James adds.

The pair have been together since 2018 and have lived in this apartment for a little under a year. Its walls form something of a shrine to their work and interests, crowded with art by African American and queer artists, from intimate, often erotic photography to paintings. At one point they rummage beneath the bed to retrieve an original 1938 portrait of James Baldwin by Beauford Delaney, the Harlem renaissance artist who became one of Baldwin’s mentors, and features heavily in Boggs’s book. A monumental horse sculpture dominates the room – or, as Boggs points out with a laugh, “it’s really just the horse’s ass, isn’t it!” Bought by James after his 2015 Booker win and christened “Booker” by Boggs, it stands alongside a similarly imposing gorilla.

Their romance began not in a rarefied literary salon, but through the very ordinary business of a dating app. “I was on the apps and was like, well, I’m only dating in my neighbourhood,” Boggs says. “He was three blocks away, so it was perfect.”

By then, they were both in their 40s. Boggs, who had never been out with a writer before – “it was mostly bartenders”, he jokes – knew of James’s work, but hadn’t read any of his books. James, for his part, didn’t know Boggs was a writer prior to their first meeting.

“It was a very chaste first date,” James says, with a twinkle in his eye. “We were gentlemen.” The relationship developed “healthily slowly” over a summer spent apart while Boggs was teaching in London, until they reunited when James invited Boggs to a Booker anniversary event in the capital. He was keen to set the bar high.

“Our third date was at Buckingham Palace,” James says, with a faux shrug. “I try to keep it classy, you know, gotta impress him. We actually made out in the queen’s bathroom.”

Their relationship may have brought them into the same orbit, but the worlds they each came from – and the experiences that inform their writing – are markedly different.

Growing up in Washington DC, where his father was a civil rights attorney, Boggs read Baldwin from a young age. While studying the writer at college, he came across a reference in a 1966 biography to an out-of-print children’s book by Baldwin, illustrated by a French artist, Yoran Cazac. Boggs had suspicions that there was a love affair behind the collaboration, tried to track down Cazac, but was told he was most likely dead. A few weeks later, the phone rang.

“It was Yoran saying, ‘I’m alive, I’m in Paris, come on over, I have many stories to tell you about Jimmy,’” Boggs recalls. “That was 23 years ago, and it began a realisation that there were these untold stories in Baldwin’s life that needed to be unearthed.”

For James, rampant homophobia shaped his upbringing and his storytelling. Growing up gay and closeted in 1980s Kingston, in the classroom he was “the school homo”; at church, he tried to become straight. He only began to build a more comfortable queer identity after moving to Minneapolis to teach in 2007, away from the scrutiny of family and friends in Jamaica. Unlike Boggs, his queer literary education came late. He picked up Baldwin’s Giovanni’s Room for the first time when he was 50. “The first thing I thought was I could never have read this at 20,” he says. “I was so in the closet.”

Across his fiction, James has repeatedly excavated Jamaica’s histories of violence and political upheaval, from his debut 2005 novel John Crow’s Devil (famously rejected 78 times by publishers), to the gang warfare and state corruption of A Brief History of Seven Killings, which made him the first Jamaican to win the Booker prize. The Disappearers, his sixth novel, grew out of a rumoured homophobic attack in a middle-class area of Kingston in the late 1980s.

“I first heard about it when I was 21,” he says. “I knew it happened, I just couldn’t prove it. It haunted me: the idea that that could happen – and in a posh neighbourhood – was one of the things that certainly pushed me firmly into the closet.”

He was unable to establish exactly what had happened until he began researching the novel, interviewing almost 20 people in Jamaica who helped him piece together the incident over several years. “I wanted to fill in the blanks,” he says. “I wanted to give those guys back some sort of agency and power.”

In different ways, both men are trying to recover Black queer histories that have been marginalised or lost. “We both respond to gaps,” Boggs says.

For James, one such gap became the starting point for The Disappearers. He wanted to build his novel around the production of a play, but couldn’t find one that would fit. The solution came, serendipitously, from Boggs: while researching his biography, he discovered Baldwin directed a 1969 production of John Herbert’s Fortune and Men’s Eyes in Turkey. He suggested James consider it for his novel.

“At first you were like, ‘no’,” Boggs recalls. “And I was like, ‘just read these 60 pages’. And I was right.”

It is no exaggeration to say that the play serves as the novel’s structural and emotional scaffolding, and is central to Boggs’s chapters on Baldwin’s life in Turkey, too. “I like to say I plundered his book with his permission,” James says, smiling. “It’s one way in which our books wouldn’t be possible or wouldn’t have ended up the way they did were we not together.”

On a table in the couple’s living room there sits a 25 September edition of the New York Times. It contains a review now infamous in the literary world, in which the notoriously harsh critic Dwight Garner devoted an almost novella-length appraisal to The Disappearers, hailing it as “a masterpiece, the novel of the decade and possibly of the century”, placing it alongside the work of Salman Rushdie, Toni Morrison and William Faulkner.

“I still don’t quite believe it,” James says. The morning the piece came out, an author friend had emailed to alert him to what he described as a “stonking review” from Garner. “I didn’t know what stonking meant, I thought it was something bad!” he laughs. “So I’m like, ‘God, no. I’m not going to read this.’” But he clicked the link anyway, and saw the word “masterpiece”.

“I went to the newsstand to go find it, because I still didn’t believe it,” he says. “I was like, ‘if I leave this bed, I’m going to wake up.’”

He is wary of the idea that acclaim should ever become an expectation, or success a fait accompli. “There’s a part of me that still thinks I’m this underground, scrapping writer who got lucky,” he says. “For me, it’s still a genuine surprise. It still catches me off guard. I don’t know if I want to get to that point where I start to expect good reviews. I don’t know if I want that level of entitlement.” He laughs. “I know some writers who are like that – I’m not going to name any names,” he adds, with a mischievous look.

Joan Didion once described her collaboration with John Gregory Dunne as a process of creative osmosis: “One of us writes the first draft, and the other functions as really kind of a super-editor and writes the second draft. In the end, you can’t really tell who has done what.”

There is no such blurring of authorship in the James-Boggs household. The pair keep their manuscripts to themselves until the work is finished, even as they discuss the ideas and research behind it.

“People are always surprised to hear that,” Boggs says. “Marlon didn’t read my book until after it was finished, I finished his on the publication date.”

Their working habits are almost opposite, too. James describes himself as a binge writer, while Boggs writes every day and keeps regular hours. James needs music – “lots of free jazz” – while Boggs requires “perfect peace and quiet”. They work on opposite sides of the house, and Boggs also has a separate office a few blocks away. But living with James has helped Boggs reconsider his idea of what writing should feel like.

“Marlon has an incredible work ethic, and it was really a reminder that this is a job,” he says. “That was really helpful. It’s not screaming from the other room in frustration, or complaining about it at dinner every night.”

They insist there is no competition between them. “I think I really worried about that when we first met,” Boggs says. “But we write so differently, even stylistically. And because of the time that we’re living in, getting these stories told is so much more important than any individual anyway.”

Just this month, new research from PEN America found that the US saw almost 12,000 book bans in public schools during the 2025-2026 school year, the highest number in a single year. For James and Boggs, whose work is concerned with recovering the lives and histories that have been overlooked or suppressed, the stakes are difficult to ignore.

James refuses to censor himself in anticipation of a backlash, but he is not oblivious to the risks. “I do sometimes get this fear that the oppressors are coming, because they always burn the books first,” he says. “The forces stacked against me are immense. But then, when have the forces against us not been immense?”

I ask if they have thought about leaving the US altogether. “Yes, 100%,” James says, without skipping a beat. He is uncompromising in his diagnosis of the country’s downward slide. “For me, it’s weird seeing America become the type of country America has spent the past 60 years creating everywhere else. I think we’re becoming a banana republic, which, coming from the Caribbean, I know a lot about.”

He is not, however, a pessimist. “I have to have a pretty big sense of optimism to think that my big-ass books are going to sell,” he says. “Throughout all of this, I’ve never lost faith in the reader. Writing has always been an art form that had to struggle against oppression, that speaks truth to power. If you decide to be a writer, part of it is to say that you’re going to take this on.”

For all their independence on the page, Boggs and James are now embarking on a creative collaboration. Baldwin: A Love Story has been optioned for a film, produced by Barack and Michelle Obama’s production company, Higher Ground. Boggs knew immediately whom he wanted to write the screenplay: James, who has experience writing for the screen, including the television series Get Millie Black.

So far, the process has been seamless. “I think even we are surprised how smooth it’s going,” Boggs says, laughing. “But we’re just so interested in each other’s work and interested in how one another thinks.”

I ask how it feels to be adding to the queer literary canon, in their shared and solo endeavours. They look at each other for a moment before Boggs responds. “Just to be alive is wonderful,” he says. “Something that Marlon and I both share is that when you grow up in the shadow of Aids, you don’t necessarily think that you have a future.”

“We lost so many great artists, gay artists,” Boggs adds. “So there’s a certain kind of responsibility to telling those stories. There are so many that still need to be told.”

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.title: Dónal Lunny, ‘colossus of Irish music’, dies aged 79
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.author: Press Association
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.text:
Founding member of Planxty, Lunny went on to play for bands such as Moving Hearts, the Bothy Band and Coolfin

The Irish traditional musician Dónal Lunny has died at the age of 79 from cancer.

Lunny rose to prominence in the band Rakes of Kildare alongside Christy Moore and his brother Frank. He went on to play in bands such as Planxty, Moving Hearts, the Bothy Band and Coolfin among others and toured the world.

A post on his Facebook page confirmed that Lunny died in St James’s hospital in Dublin on Friday morning.

“We are heartbroken to confirm that our beloved Dónal passed away peacefully this morning in Dublin following a short stay in St James’s hospital,” the post said. “Thank you for helping us to remember and celebrate his immense contribution to music, to culture and to so many people’s lives all over the world.”

The Irish president, Catherine Connolly, expressed her “deepest condolences to the family, friends and many musical collaborators of Dónal Lunny”.

In a statement, she said: “Dónal was one of Ireland’s greatest musical figures, a wonderfully talented musician and producer who was central to so many of the most influential moments of the last 60 years of Irish music.

“Dónal will be particularly remembered for his long partnerships with fellow musicians such as Christy Moore and Andy Irvine and for the innovative music he has left behind both as a musician in groups including Planxty, the Bothy Band and Moving Hearts and also as a renowned producer.

“This rich musical legacy, including his central role in the introduction of the bouzouki into Irish music, was appropriately recognised by his fellow artists in Dónal’s membership of Aosdána, as well as the well-deserved recognition which he received in being awarded a lifetime achievement award at the 2025 RTÉ Radio 1 Irish folk awards.

“Beyond his music, Dónal will be remembered for his warmth and the strong connection which he had with audiences all over Ireland and beyond. He will be deeply missed.”

The post ended in Irish, saying his likes will not be seen again: “Ní bheidh a leithéid arís ann.”

Lunny was born in Tullamore, County Offaly, and was a multi-instrumentalist but was best known for his mastery of the bouzouki. He was a talented melody writer and considered central to the revival of traditional music as he produced 17 albums under his record label Mulligan Records.

Paying tribute to the folk musician, the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said he was “deeply saddened” to hear of his passing. “A colossus of Irish music, as a performer, songwriter and producer,” he wrote in a post on social media.

“Uniquely gifted, Dónal carried traditional and folk music to new audiences through Planxty and his many other endeavours.”

Sinn Féin’s president, Mary Lou McDonald, also paid tribute online, saying: “Deeply saddened to hear of the passing of Dónal Lunny. A giant of Irish traditional music, Dónal helped shape the sound of Irish music for generations, bringing our rich musical heritage to audiences at home and around the world. His contribution to Irish music and culture will never be forgotten.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: ‘Unlike anything we’ve experienced’: fans swarm San Francisco for BTS star’s art exhibition
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Soo Youn
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
K-pop star RM gave a boost to the previously struggling SFMOMA with an exhibition of over 100 pieces from his collection

Two years ago, RM of the wildly popular K-pop boyband BTS was serving as a soldier in the South Korean military when he received an offer from América Castillo, a museum curator in San Francisco: would he consider an exhibition of his private art collection?

“I loved it,” said RM (real name: Kim Namjoon) at the media preview of RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me, a new exhibition that opened in San Francisco earlier this month and is co-curated by SFMOMA’s Castillo and Hyoeun Kim. “There aren’t many things that show a person more honestly than a collection they’ve built over a long period of time.”

The result is a multi-dimensional exhibition of 142 works of RM’s private collection of mostly Korean works, including paintings, calligraphy, sculpture and even a Pokémon animation cel, in conversation with 36 of the museum’s pieces. The show has been a blockbuster success, with over 66,000 tickets sold and advance sales that were six times higher than any previous exhibition at the museum.

RM has been an evangelist for modern Korean art: a song from his 2022 solo album Indigo samples a conversational snippet from the Korean painter Yun Hyong-keun. At the SFMOMA show, Yun’s monochrome Umber-Blue sits juxtaposed next to Mark Rothko’s No. 24 in the show. There’s also an audio guide and playlist by RM.

“I’ve always dreamed of seeing different places, times, boundaries and backgrounds all mixed together in harmony,” RM said at the preview, before adding lightly: “It could be a mess – I never formally studied art history, and I’m not a curator.

While his celebrity looms large over the show, the collection and the curation of the show are formidable. In South Korea, gallery owners and art dealers who have met RM have told me their nickname for him is “bakhsa” (professor) owing to the depth of his knowledge. “It is especially meaningful to bring the depth and richness of his collection to a wider audience,” says Kim, assistant curator of painting and sculpture.

Some of the art is displayed with a scholarly arc, while other curation feels more intuitive. One room is titled “I Don’t Know, But I Like It.”

“I started this with an innocent heart,” RM said at the preview. “I just didn’t know that this innocence would eventually make me write, erase and rewrite hundreds of labels.” His text that accompanies the pieces combines historical context with diaristic personal reflections, in a break from museum convention.

In a placard that accompanies a Lee Ungno painting of the Gwangju uprising in 1980, a brutal crackdown on protesters by a military dictatorship, RM writes: “He painted these crowds until the day he died. Strange, isn’t it. These people are not falling. Arms raised, legs wide, they are dancing.”

Last year, as US museums grappled with the lingering effects of the pandemic on attendance, funding challenges under the current administration and lower tourism rates in many cities, SFMOMA laid off 7.5% of its workforce amid a $5m deficit. Its new director Christopher Bedford wrote that the museum would adjust its programming and budget to reflect “a reduced annual attendance normal in the range of 600,000 visitors”.

Since the RM show opened, the museum has seen an undeniable financial boost. Its success, and whether it ushers in a direction toward celebrity exhibitions, is something officials and other museums seem to already be considering. In 2024, Brooklyn Museum staged a major exhibition showcasing the private collection of Swizz Beatz and Alicia Keys, while other recent shows have focused on art made by musicians like Jack White and Paul McCartney.

Yet the dedication of BTS fans, who call themselves Army, may prove to make this show a one-off. On the day of the media preview and opening reception, a couple hundred fans lined up outside the museum entrance, one holding a sign saying she came from London for RM. Another handed journalists small bags of gifts including custom-made bookmarks, key chains and cake pops along with thank you notes for covering the exhibition.

Exhibition merch available at the SFMOMA Museum Store and web store sold out within three hours. “It’s different in so many ways,” store director Shane Salvata says of the exhibition, adding that it is important for visitors to commemorate “how special it is that he curated this show”.

“It’s unlike anything we’ve ever experienced, and probably will experience ever again,” he says.

For Castillo, who originally conceived the show, success has a different measure. “To actually see it in the galleries … people are crying in front of you,” she says. “You’re never going to expect that. It’s a beautiful surprise.”

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Tinned food, loo roll and power banks: the Brits following advice to stockpile
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Kevin Rawlinson
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Government campaign recommends three days’ worth of stores for emergencies, but some are ahead of the game

Dried foods, bottled water, medicine stocks and backup power banks: it could be the props cupboard on a disaster movie, but instead it is precisely what some UK residents are stockpiling amid official warnings about Russian “state-sponsored terrorism” and the impact of the climate crisis.

The government launched a campaign on Thursday advising people to set aside three days’ worth of stores to deal with a whole range of eventualities, and some are already well under way.

“I’m adding a few extra tinned foods and dried foods to each weekly shop to build up a stockpile over time,” said Lawrence Barratt, from Hythe in Hampshire. “Tinned beans, soups, chilli con carne. Dried noodles, pot noodles, rice. Foods I can cook with bottled water, which I’m also buying gradually – aiming to have enough for two people for three days.”

He added that he was also putting aside a first aid kit, a battery-powered FM radio and a torch. “I have a portable power bank that I’ve used when camping; that should give enough electricity to charge phones, run the TV, even a small fan heater.”

Barratt is not alone. Marco Camurri, from Greenwich in London, said he was collecting pasta, passata and stock cubes as well as tinned foods, bottled water and medicines. And toilet paper, he added. “We remember Covid.”

Camurri said that, with relatives in continental Europe, he and his family could flee temporarily if the UK “entered war and if there was a risk of direct attacks to London”, or if there were “extreme infrastructure failure that would put our jobs at risk”.

He said: “Although I live in London, I have some wood set aside in the back of our small garden in case we need to make fire on the barbecue to boil water. We have power banks that we keep charged, USB rechargeable flashlights, matches and lighters. Although gasoline is expensive, we try to keep the tank over 50% – about 300 miles.”

While the government launched its PR campaign on Thursday, ministers have been making similar noises for several months now – and it had already prompted some to start preparing.

Barratt said a combination of noticing government advice to stockpile online and having been in situations in the past where it would have been useful prompted him to begin about a fortnight ago.

“I took action, I suppose, because I thought back to how scary the initial few days just before and after the first lockdown in 2020 were – remember when you went to the shops and all the pasta, loo roll and tinned stuff would be gone.”

He said he had put that period out of his mind but the government’s Be Ready campaign website made him realise: “I’d be completely unprepared for anything. So I thought I’d better get started.”

Camurri has been setting things aside for himself and his family for much longer. “We started preparing a few months ago when news about potential disruptions to the supply chain caused by El Niño made it into the news. It was an easy decision as we usually eat everything we stocked up, so it was just like doing one extra week of shopping for staples. We are now starting a spreadsheet with the expiry date of all our ‘Doomsday Stash’ items so we can eat them and replace them before they go bad.”

Jack Davenport, from North Shields on the River Tyne, also cited El Niño as a motivation for beginning to stockpile. But he said it was “hard to judge the size” of the multiple threats facing the country.

“From El Niño and other climate-related disasters to Russian shadow threats and AI, as well as interest rate hikes due to energy insecurity. The fact is our physical and technological infrastructure is creaking and outdated.”

He said he thought the government’s goal in highlighting this advice now was to “reduce long-term panic by rolling the pitch that these events are a possibility, and that just because several generations in our country haven’t faced hardship that was common prewar doesn’t mean we won’t”.

But Deirdre O’Sullivan, from Leicester, was less convinced. “This daft advice takes me back to the 1970s when I recall being instructed to hide under the table in the event of a nuclear attack. I didn’t have a table, but somehow made it through.

“In the event of a real emergency, the advice seems totally inadequate. For example, if our drinking water becomes dangerous, I would hope that this could be anticipated a bit more precisely. And we would surely become aware of extreme food shortage within a much longer timeframe.

“The guidance looks like something Yes Minister would come up with to demonstrate that they have a policy in place, even if that policy is clearly totally useless.”

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Caroline Hirons: ‘My celebrity crush? Colin Farrell. I hope he reads this – I hear he likes an older woman’
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Rosanna Greenstreet
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
The beauty entrepreneur on why she wears three wedding rings, her fear of running out of HRT, and what put her off being a midwife

Born in Liverpool, Caroline Hirons, 57, moved to London at 17. In 1997, she joined the Aveda counter in Harvey Nichols and went on to train as an aesthetician. She started a blog in 2010 and, 10 years later, published her first book, which won the nonfiction lifestyle prize at the British Book Awards in 2021. In 2022, she launched the Skin Rocks app and skincare line. Her new book is Skin Rules: Expert Advice That You Can Trust. She is separated with four children, and lives in London.

What is the trait you most deplore in yourself? I can be a tad impatient, and my team would say that’s an understatement.

What is the trait you most deplore in others? I have a long list: misogyny, homophobia, rudeness, greed, arrogance, ignorance.

Aside from a property, what’s the most expensive thing you’ve bought? I do like a handbag. The brand begins with H and ends with èrmes.

What is your most treasured possession? My trio of wedding rings I wear every day – my mum’s, my grandmother’s, mine. I’m separated, but still have the ring because it gave me my kids.

Who is your celebrity crush? Colin Farrell – and I hope he reads this. I hear he likes an older woman.

What do you most dislike about your appearance? I strongly advocate looking at what we like about our appearance rather than what we don’t like.

Who would play you in the film of your life? Queen Latifah, and the menopause years would be played by Denzel Washington.

What is your most unappealing habit? Interrupting people. I have ADHD and I sometimes have to physically bite my tongue and cover my mouth because my instinct is to join in.

What did you want to be when you were growing up? A midwife. And then I had a baby and thought, sod that.

What is the worst thing anyone’s said to you? “I’m very sorry but your mother has passed.”

Have you ever said ‘I love you’ and not meant it? No, I’m very tight with “I love you”.

Which living person do you most despise, and why? So that I can still travel, I would say the majority of old white male politicians.

If you could edit your past, what would you change? In the words of Helen Mirren, I’d tell more people to fuck off.

What do you consider your greatest achievement? Leaving school at 15 and going on to found and run two multimillion-pound businesses.

What keeps you awake at night? Nothing. I’m old, tired and on progesterone so I can sleep.

What is the most important lesson life has taught you? That it’s fucking short. Don’t have any fear. Crack on.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Verse from Qu’ran inspired US man to leap on runaway school bus and halt it
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Ebro Ahmed, who acted after driver’s medical emergency, said he hopes incident will show Eritreans ‘in a good way’

A man who hopped on to a school bus full of terrified children that was careering down a Minnesota street after its driver had a medical emergency and manually halted it says he was motivated to act by a Qu’ran verse about how saving one life is equivalent to saving all of humanity.

“I’m a numbers guy, and those numbers make sense to me,” Ebro Ahmed, 27, said on Friday during an interview about his actions four days earlier in front of his family’s convenience store in Saint Paul, Minnesota. “I didn’t do it for me. It was selflessness in the name of God.”

In a dramatic sequence of events captured on surveillance video by the shop, Ahmed was kicking a soccer ball and scrolling on his cellphone during a break outside his family’s Ya Bricks Snacks and Tobacco store on Monday afternoon when he noticed a yellow school bus passing by with its door flung open.

Ahmed said he deduced something was wrong when he saw the bus driver with foam coming out of his mouth, which can be a symptom of a seizure. He recalled instinctively sprinting to the bus; leaping through the door; and tossing his phone and glasses at two girls in the front to free his hands.

His first thought was to see if he could somehow shift the bus into park. But, with frightened boys and girls screaming all around him, Ahmed said he pulled the emergency brake on the bus, bringing the vehicle to a stop without anyone onboard or on the street being injured.

A statement from Saint Paul’s public school district on Friday confirmed there had been a medical emergency on the bus outside Ahmed’s family store that day that required paramedics to respond. Another bus came to pick up the 19 students onboard and bring them home, the district said.

Meanwhile, the driver was resting at home after being brought to a hospital and discharged.

The National Safety Council estimates that about 20.3 million children ride school buses across the US daily – a number large enough for driver-related emergencies to occasionally occur.

When such emergencies do happen, quick-thinking and -acting bystanders can often help avert disaster.

The local news outlet KTSP obtained and published the surveillance video of Ahmed running on to the runaway bus. That footage went viral alongside an interview that the station did with Ahmed, in which he credited the medical TV drama Grey’s Anatomy with teaching him “what to do in situations that you could never see yourself in”.

Ahmed elaborated with the Guardian on Friday, saying the Qu’ran verse declaring that “whoever saves a life, it will be as if they saved all of humanity” also entered his mind at the moment he decided to intervene on Monday.

Furthermore, he mentioned how challenging it had been for his parents – who are immigrants from the east African country of Eritrea – to run a store in Saint Paul during the mass deportation campaign pursued by Donald Trump during his second presidency.

Ahmed, who said he was US-born, added that business at the store had dropped ever since federal immigration agents at the forefront of that campaign descended on Saint Paul and nearby Minneapolis as part of what the Trump administration dubbed Operation Metro.

But Ahmed described a welcome sense of relief taking the opportunity to – as he called it – portray Eritreans and represent Eritreans and east Africans “in a good way”.

He alluded to a local marketing and media company donating $1,000 to him as a token of appreciation for his bus heroics – a presentation which involved a Superman performer and a novelty check.

Ahmed said he had been invited to speak on at least one panel, and a city council member had contacted him to congratulate him. An uncle in Europe did, too, after learning of what Ahmed had done on the news.

Perhaps most meaningful to Ahmed, he said, was seeing his story trend among Eritrean circles.

“It makes me proud to be able to represent them in a good way,” Ahmed remarked.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Tom Kean had everything going for him. Then the Republican New Jersey congressman disappeared
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ariana Baio in New Jersey
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Even with a multimillion-dollar war chest, the US representative faces a stiff fight for his seat from Democrat Rebecca Bennett

The Republican congressman had a war chest of more than $2.4m in February, an endorsement from Donald Trump and a district whose lines were redrawn in 2022 to benefit his party. He was an established political figure with widespread name recognition, thanks to his father’s stint as a well-regarded governor of New Jersey.

Kean, 58, was not seen in Congress, or public, for more than three months and missed 100 votes without explanation – as Trump’s war on Iran piled pressure on the US economy, and the president threatened fresh tariffs on global imports.

Democrats meanwhile selected a moderate, Rebecca Bennett, to challenge Kean for his seat. Kean, who resurfaced at the end of June, is now in the midst of a tight race in one of the wealthiest districts in the nation.

In an ominous sign for Republicans, the closely watched Cook Political Report moved New Jersey’s seventh congressional district from “toss-up” to “lean Democrat” last month.

Most Republicans fighting for re-election while aligned with Trump are grappling with the impact of the president’s growing unpopularity. His war with Iran has driven the cost of fuel and groceries up, angering the voters who were promised lower prices under his administration.

But Kean has also endured months of discourse – and national headlines – over his prolonged absence, and reserved public appearances. When he returned at the end of June, the congressman said he had been hospitalized for depression.

“I think mental health issues aside, which are serious ... I don’t think he handled the issue very well,” said Albie, a New Jersey voter attending a No Kings protest in New Providence last weekend.

Mike Johnson, the Republican speaker of the House of Representatives, appeared to agree in August. “You know, if it were me, I would have done it a little sooner,” he told the New York Times of Kean’s reluctance to explain his absence.

Johnson, like many, is sympathetic to Kean’s health condition, which affects millions of Americans.

Since his return, Kean has been accused of avoiding the media spotlight. His campaign denied a New York Times reporter entry to an event attended by other media outlets in August; he refused to take questions from reporters after participating in a livestreamed debate against Bennett, his Democratic opponent.

The Guardian sent two emails to Kean’s campaign requesting an interview, or the opportunity to attend a campaign event. They went unanswered.

Harrison Neely, Kean’s campaign manager, did not respond to an initial text message containing the same requests earlier this week. He did, however, respond to a second message asking for a brief interview on Thursday.

“I think the narrative that congressman Kean doesn’t engage with the press is simply false,” said Neely, adding that the campaign prefers to communicate with voters directly. (On Thursday, New York Magazine published an article saying its multiple requests for an interview went ignored.)

Kean does give interviews, mostly to local reporters, and the campaign has invited local outlets to cover events. Neely said the campaign most recently challenged Bennett to a debate on WRNJ, a local radio station. However, the Bennett campaign declined to participate.

“So you know, I think it’s basically fair to say that congressman Kean does more local press engagements than any sitting member of the New Jersey delegation,” Neely said.

Bennett, a political newcomer, is cautiously optimistic that she can flip a battleground district in New Jersey for the Democrats in next month’s midterm.

“We’re going to do everything we can for the next 16 days to flip the seat, but we are feeling good about where we are,” Bennett told reporters after a meet-and-greet with voters in Basking Ridge last Sunday. “We’re seeing a ton of momentum and enthusiasm on the ground.”

Bennett, 39, is a former Navy helicopter pilot and aircraft commander. She’s also a former executive at an online healthcare company.

Democrats in the state are hopeful her moderate stance can appeal to the district’s voters, especially because many 2024 Trump voters have expressed discontent with the economy.

Bennett said she often hears “deeply frustrated” voters bring up Kean’s willingness to let Trump unleash his agenda, such as voting for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, continuing the war with Iran or not doing enough to stop Trump from halting funding for the Gateway Hudson Tunnel Project between New Jersey and New York.

“I understand the challenges that we’re facing because my family is dealing with them too,” said Bennett. “My oldest kid’s in public school. My youngest is in daycare. And so when we talk about the cost-of-living crisis we’re dealing with, this is not abstract talking points on a page – this is my life.”

But nothing is certain in New Jersey’s seventh congressional district, which has seesawed between Republican and Democratic representatives since 2018. The district voted for Trump by a slim majority in 2024, and also elected Mikie Sherrill – its Democratic governor – in 2025.

The Congressional Leadership Fund – the Super Pac dedicated to helping House Republicans – and the Safety and Affordability Pac, affiliated with Trump, have reportedly canceled remaining funding for Kean’s district.

When asked about the pulled funding by the New Jersey Globe, Kean dismissed concerns, pointing to $6.2m in funding from the National Republican Congressional Committee.

Neely also expressed confidence. “If you take a step back and look at the facts, Republicans have outspent Democrats in this district to this point,” he said. “Our campaign is fully funded down the home stretch, and will be matching the Bennett campaign dollar for dollar on the airwaves.”

As Kean’s campaign pushed back against the claim he doesn’t engage with the media, before reaching Neely by phone this week, the Guardian spent time driving around the district one weekend earlier this month.

There appeared to be something in the air: a lack of Tom Kean Jr lawn signs in the Trump-friendly Bedminster area, and an autumnal breeze that appeared more present than his campaign.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘It was so magical’: the 33-year-old who made history swimming the length of California
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Lois Beckett in Los Angeles
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Ultra-endurance swimmer Catherine Breed navigated waves, wildlife and pollution to become the first person to swim from state’s northern-most tip to Mexico border

Nearly four months ago, Catherine Breed, a 33-year-old from the San Francisco Bay Area, set out to become the first person to swim the entire coastline of California – from its northern-most tip to the border with Mexico. She and her support team prepared for encounters with sharks and storms. They hadn’t anticipated completing the marathon swim during a year of historic super El Niño weather.

But after dodging hurricanes, wildlife and 8ft waves in an unusually volatile Pacific Ocean, Breed finally celebrated the end of her journey on a beach in San Diego on Monday.

Breed joins a group of elite ultra-endurance swimmers who continue to set new records for long-distance swims, including swimming the entire coastlines of Ireland and Iceland and one side of New Zealand’s North Island – all journeys of close to 1,000 miles (1,600km).

Breed spoke to the Guardian this week about living onboard the Catalyst, the sailboat that accompanied her, her physical and mental preparations for her 111-day swim, and what she thought about while spending more than 15 weeks in the water. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

On your website, you talk about the desire to be part of “an elite group of humans who have been the first to accomplish a monumental feat”. What does that feel like now that you’ve done it?

It is a little bit of an out-of-body experience. Like, I know I’m the one who did it, but there are parts of me where I feel like I’m along with the audience, watching this thing happen. I think I’m still trying to grasp what I’ve done.

How did you get the idea to swim the full length of California, which no one has ever done before?

Other people showed me that the model was possible. Ross Edgley swam around Great Britain. Sean Conway and Jasmine Harrison swam the length of Britain. [In 2022] I did a swim down the California coast from the Golden Gate Bridge to Half Moon Bay, and it made me realize how much fun I had during that, and I was like: I want to try to do this with the coast.

In college, my coach used to say you only get so many energy units per day. Overthinking or excessive thinking or negative thinking – that can take some of that energy you have. During these marathon swims, I try to keep my thoughts very focused on the task at hand. Coaching myself to get to the next 30 minutes, coaching myself to do the next 2 miles, and kind of like celebrating those little moments. When the conditions were really rough, there was a lot of thought around my technique, because I really had to adjust how I was swimming to not wreck my shoulders in the big waves.

I had earplugs on, so I couldn’t hear the crew. But one thing I could hear very clearly was dolphins. And so there were many occasions where I would hear the dolphins before the crew could see them. And I would look up and I’d be like, you guys, incoming, there’s dolphins.

At points, you were swimming through 6-8ft waves, which you have described as feeling like you were in a washing machine. What is it like to swim in those conditions?

If I’m swimming into the swell, it feels like you’re swimming up a hill. But if it’s behind me, then it’s actually very fun because it feels like I’m surfing. So it really depended on the conditions. When you’ve got a lot of wind and a lot of swell, the waves can crash on you from the back or the side or the front. And it does take a lot of effort to keep my body in the right position. One day a wave picked me up, and I landed on my butt.

I’ve been marathon swimming for 10 years. I grew up swimming, I grew up sailing. So my whole life has been in the ocean. So those moments, they’re difficult, but I’m comfortable. I surf a lot. And so I think surfers are comfortable with waves and they understand kind of just wave mechanics and moving with the ocean.

I think the challenging part of the swell was not so much as swimming, but that there’s no chance of recovery [with living on a boat]. Getting ready to swim is really hard – like you’re trying to make breakfast and you’re falling over, your coffee’s spilling. Even putting my wetsuit on is a challenge in itself.

Yes. Many days. [She laughs.] But for myself, I committed to this goal, and my team committed to being part of it. And so, the days I didn’t want to get in it, it didn’t matter what my emotions were, because this project is bigger than just me.

You swam the English Channel in 2018 and the North Channel crossing between north Ireland and Scotland in 2019. How was preparing for this California challenge different from preparing for those classic marathon swims?

For my other swims, I did follow English Channel rules: it was just one cap, bathing suit, goggles. So that preparation required a lot of cold adaptation, and spending hours in the San Francisco Bay being comfortable to be in those conditions for a long time. In California, I’m wearing a wetsuit, so I didn’t have to focus so much on the cold training. I focused more on putting on muscle, and ensuring my body composition was going to benefit me for the swim. So the training was a little less swimming than my other marathon swims, and more time in the gym.

Swimming down in San Diego by the Imperial Beach and Tijuana River and knowing about the sewage pollution crisis [where billions of gallons of raw sewage and toxic chemicals flow from the river into the ocean] – that was probably the most nerve-wracking, because, though we were 3 miles offshore and I was taking prophylactic antibiotics, I still was so scared about my health. And then, you know, any moments that the team spotted a shark fin.

The team just says: “Shark!” And within five seconds – definitely less than 10 seconds – I’m out of the water. Then we observe the situation. And if we see the shark again, then we were just done for the day. That only happened once in four months. So it really was the most insignificant part of the trip.

Our biggest shark deterrent is the fact that I was swimming right next to a 52ft sailboat. And on the other side of me, I had a tender in the water. Ultimately, the sharks just really weren’t interested in me.

You’ve spoken out on your social media accounts about the assumption that sharks are the biggest threats to your swim. Why do you think that’s the wrong focus?

The pollution definitely made me more uncomfortable than any shark sightings ever did. It’s so interesting how people focus so much on sharks when sharks have been in the water with humans for a really long time. We’re so concerned about them, but we should be more concerned about what damage we’re causing to our planet and our home.

Outside populated cities like San Diego and Los Angeles, we saw trash and plastic pollution every day, all day. It was astounding. I think we picked up over 10 Mylar balloons in one day. I had no idea there were that many in the ocean.

You did not plan to do this swim during a year of extreme super El Niño weather, but that’s what happened. How did that change your experience?

The California coastal current historically goes north to south. That’s why we picked the direction. But with the super El Niño, all of the tropical storms and hurricanes that happened this year, instead we were fighting this insane current that is pushing against us. We had to do a lot of problem-solving and pivoting to make forward progress: some of our sections, we did the opposite way. [Breed swam some daily segments of the journey backwards, south to north, allowing her to go with the current, rather than against it.]

You were swimming down the coast during a summer of massive tropical storms in the Pacific, with giant waves that have wrecked havoc on southern California’s beaches. How did you handle that?

We had some days where we knew there was going to be really bad weather, and so we just didn’t even go out that day. I can think of four or five days where we started to swim – for example, during Hurricane Rachel, we were supposed to be able to swim until 2.30pm. But then the wind went from about 10 knots to 25 knots (11mph to 29mph) in about seven minutes. And so the team was like: we’ve got to get out. We need to get to harbor.

I’ve had manta rays swim around me. In Morro Bay, a humpback whale and her calf swam right next to me. I could see them diving. It was so magical. In Santa Barbara, a pod of bottlenose dolphins came and played with us for about 10 minutes. It really felt like the ocean was welcoming us.

From Humboldt [county] all the way to Point Concepción, we probably saw anywhere from five to 10 whales a day. I think the most we saw on a day maybe was like 50. We would have whales come swim right under the boat.

No, it’s not lonely. It’s absolutely the opposite of a solo expedition. It requires a huge team and it requires a team that I literally trust with my life. Yes, I was in the water for four to five hours a day by myself. But when I got out, I was surrounded by just this incredible team of women. And through the difficult, through the tough, we still found moments to connect with laughter and just bring some lightness to the whole swim.

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: Forget the Live Aid image, Africa is only a broken continent in the minds of the west | Moky Makura
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.author: Moky Makura
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
Innovators and business leaders are driving progress across the continent-wide, but the ‘visibility gap’ prevents the rest of the world from truly seeing it

Thirty years ago, shortly after South Africa emerged from apartheid, I left London for Johannesburg in search of a better life. Not long afterwards, a friend who was preparing to visit from the UK called with an intriguing question: do they have ATMs in South Africa?

After I picked myself off the floor, I explained that not only did South Africa have ATMs, but in many respects its banking system was far more advanced than the one I had left behind in Britain. She was surprised and – dare I say – delighted that she wouldn’t have to lug a wad of cash around South Africa after all.

That moment has stayed with me far longer than it should, because I’ve witnessed too many moments where the continent has persistently surprised and delighted the uninitiated. That’s because, for much of the world, the image of Africa still owes more to Live Aid’s legacy than to the reality.

A study we commissioned by social psychologist Dr Adam Hahn at the University of Bath helps explain why. When people in Britain and the US think about Africa, they disproportionately associate it with economic and political dysfunction, harsh environments and a lack of modernity and culture. Those associations affect whether they want to visit the continent, buy its products or engage with its culture. In their minds, Africa remains a place that is broken, dependent, lacking in agency and apparently in ATMs, too.

Britain may have more ATM’s and higher conventional bank-account ownership, but it was Africa that pioneered one of the biggest innovations in modern finance: mobile money. Kenya showed that millions of people could, in effect leapfrog traditional banking altogether, using their phones to store, send and receive money. Today, sub-Saharan Africa remains the centre of the global mobile-money revolution. And when it comes to new money, Nigeria now ranks third in the world for cryptocurrency adoption, while Britain ranks 17th.

Global investors have noticed the continent’s leadership when it comes to finance and are moving in. We have produced a surprisingly high number of fintech “unicorns” – privately owned startups valued at more than $1bn (£760). Nigeria alone has Flutterwave, OPay, Moniepoint and Interswitch. Investors are not putting billions into African financial technology out of charity; they are backing the entrepreneurs who are not waiting for help to create viable, profitable solutions.

One of those is Aliko Dangote, Africa’s richest man, who has been all over the global media for the world-class refinery he built in Nigeria. The $20bn Dangote refinery is the largest single-train refinery in the world, built in a country that, despite being Africa’s biggest oil producer, spent decades exporting crude oil only to import much of its refined fuel.

Dangote is exceptional in his wealth, the scale of his ambition and visibility he has garnered. But he is not exceptional in spirit. There are thousands of smaller “Dangotes” on the continent: entrepreneurs who see a gap, build something to fill it and, in doing so, move their country forward.

Take Siny Samba, a Senegalese entrepreneur who launched an infant food brand after wondering why virtually all the baby food in her country was imported. She started in her kitchen with banana and millet and in 2018 launched Le Lionceau, creating new markets for local farmers and women’s cooperatives.

In Tanzania, Diana Orembe looked at fruit and vegetables being thrown away and saw fish food. Her company, NovFeed, turns that waste into affordable feed in the agriculture sector and has worked with at least 200 farmers.

In Maiduguri, northern Nigeria, Mustapha Abubakar Gajibo started by converting petrol-powered tricycles to electric. Today his company, African Motor Works, designs and builds electric vehicles, producing about 200 units a month.

Samba, Orembe, Gajibo and thousands like them who are contributing to their countries’ growth, will probably never make international headlines. And that may be one of Africa’s most overlooked challenges: not the absence of progress, but the lack of visibility.

Development experts talk endlessly about Africa’s many gaps – the infrastructure gap, financing gap, skills gap – but perhaps the most consequential gap is the visibility gap: the distance between the Africa today (the one that surprises and delights) and the Africa the world imagines.

Addressing the visibility gap is why the Opportunity Africa initiative was started earlier this year. Its mandate; to make the continent’s progress impossible to overlook by spotlighting the many people – such as Samba, Orembe and Gajibo – the places, the policies and the initiatives moving Africa forward.

Places such as Rwanda, which has rebuilt its reputation around innovation, tourism and digital government. Ethiopia has transformed its agricultural sector and sharply reduced its dependence on imported wheat. Kenya now generates up to 91% of its electricity from renewable sources.

Then there are the policies, the unglamorous government decisions that rarely make headlines: Benin keeping more of its cashews for local processing; Namibia requiring more of its lithium to be processed at home; and Zambia removing fees from state education.

And progress is happening continent-wide through ambitious initiatives. Fifty countries have ratified the African Continental Free Trade Area, making it easier for African businesses to trade with each other. A pan-African payments system now lets them settle transactions in local currencies. And 38 countries have joined the single African air transport market, helping create 108 new intra-African routes since 2022.

And this is just the tip of the iceberg. If my friend was surprised by South Africa 30 years ago, imagine what else has changed and progressed. Through the recent Correct the Map campaign led by Togo, we challenged the world to see Africa differently – quite literally. Now we are asking the world to see us as we truly are.

The #NotWaiting campaign is where you will find the proof point: stories of a continent already building, solving, producing and moving forward.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Medical experts shocked by Tennessee team’s ‘malpractice’ in Christa Pike’s failed execution
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ed Pilkington in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
New details of IV team’s attempts to find a vein shared by Pike’s lawyer ‘shocked and disturbed’ practitioners

Medical experts have expressed shock at the apparent incompetence shown by Tennessee’s execution team during the failed lethal injection of Christa Pike, the prisoner who survived a normally fatal dose of pentobarbital, which they say would be considered medical malpractice in any other setting.

New details emerged on Thursday of how Tennessee’s intravenous (IV) team struggled for almost an hour to set up a line into Pike’s arms through which she would be administered the fatal dose of sedative. A blow-by-blow account was released in legal proceedings from Pike’s lawyer, Randy Spivey, who was present inside the death chamber at her 30 September failed execution.

The technical procedures attempted by the four unidentified members of the IV team as they tried to find a vein, as described by Spivey, provoked alarm among medical experts. They said the standards applied appeared to fall glaringly short of anything that would be deemed acceptable in a medical environment.

“I’m shocked and disturbed by what happened inside the death chamber,” said Jonathan Groner, emeritus professor of clinical surgery at Ohio State University and an expert in execution methods. “The level of incompetence is astounding, and difficult to comprehend.”

Groner, who has written an upcoming book The Hippocratic Paradox that explores the ethical contradictions involved in lethal injections, said that Spivey’s detailed chronology painted a picture in which nobody was in charge and there was no plan in sight.

“What they did to Christa Pike would have been malpractice in a clinical situation. Nobody would infuse a drug like pentobarbital that’s known to cause burns if they were unsure that the IV was actually in place.”

Groner pointed out that the label on a vial of pentobarbital instructs that infusion should cease immediately if the patient complains of pain. Spivey’s account records multiple times in which Pike “grimaced” and said her arm was “really burning”.

Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, when she was 18. Following the failed execution, she spent several days on a ventilator and her lawyers assumed she was brain-dead.

After 10 days in hospital she was returned to her prison cell. She can now talk and walk, but her long-term prospects are not known.

The gruesome nature of Pike’s experiences in the death chamber, which some have likened to torture, have prompted a reckoning on the death penalty nationwide. Tennessee has called off all executions, pending a review.

In Spivey’s detailed account, the IV team used about 10 needles as they repeatedly poked Pike’s arms, failing to secure a line. At several points, team members worried that her veins might have “blown”.

Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology and surgery based in Atlanta, Georgia, who gave expert testimony at legal hearings ahead of Pike’s failed execution, said that the new chronology pointed to several areas of serious concern. “Here we have a poorly written protocol, no one in charge, technology that they may not have had permission to use, and catheters that are far too small for the purpose. We could go on and on …”

Pike’s lawyers, partly on the basis of Zivot’s expert opinion, warned the state on several occasions before the failed execution attempt that the prisoner had exceptionally small and compromised veins.

The Spivey timeline records that at 7.05pm on the evening of the failed execution, about half an hour into the procedure, a member of the IV team asked for a 24-gauge needle “and moved that needle around a lot. Christa continued to grimace.”

Zivot said that a 24-gauge catheter was very small. “That’s the kind of catheter you put in a baby, or a small child.”

He added there was “no way that you can push a 50cc syringe into that small little catheter without it blowing up the vein”. Under Tennessee’s protocol, 50cc of pentobarbital were to be injected into each of Pike’s arms, giving a massive total dose of 5g of the sedative.

The Spivey chronology also reveals that the IV team attempted to find a vein using ultrasound technology. Groner said that from his own personal experience using an ultrasound requires many hours of specialist training and up to 20 actual procedures before an individual can perform the technique smoothly.

“Inserting an IV with ultrasound guidance is a practice-based skill that takes a lot of training. The Tennessee team clearly didn’t know how to use it,” he said.

At 7.23pm in the timeline, the IV team pushed saline through the line they had established “with difficulty”, according to Spivey. That should have been a flashing red light, Groner said.

“No clinician would give a caustic drug through an IV where it didn’t flush easily. That would be malpractice.”

Despite that warning sign, the IV team concluded that the IV was set and that the procedure could commence just a minute later, at 7.24pm.

The medical experts said the timeline underlined fundamental problems with lethal injections, the overwhelmingly dominant form of executions in the US in the modern era. Groner said that it highlighted that lethal injections were a “medical charade. Pike didn’t deserve this. The ultimate penalty in our country, whether one agrees with it or not, is death. It is not torture, then death.”

Zivot said his takeaway was that the execution team pressed on when they should have stopped. “It was clear this was not doable, and yet they kept on doing it anyway.”

He added: “Lethal injection is a theft of a medical procedure, and they stole the wrong part. Medicine is obsessed with safety, accountability and training. You didn’t see any of those things in Pike’s execution chamber.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: New Trump rule allows hunters to bait bears in Alaska with doughnuts, bacon and more
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Tom Perkins
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Critics decry Trump administration rule that lets hunters lure bears with human foods on federal lands in Alaska

A new Trump administration rule allows hunters to bait bears on federal lands in Alaska with bacon, doughnuts, meat scraps or other human foods typically used to help kill the trophy animals at close range.

Opponents say the practice will cause bears to be more aggressive around humans, and allege that the rule change is a political gift to largely rightwing trophy hunters. The rule replaces a 2024 Biden administration rule that banned the practice, and environmental groups criticized the move as “indefensible and inexcusable”.

“We are discouraged to see this rule come back, specifically the bear baiting piece which is cruel and dangerous, not only to wildlife but the public as well,” said Drew Robertson, senior regulatory specialist for Humane World for Animals.

The US interior department on Friday published the rule on the federal register, and it will take effect in mid-November. It marks the latest in a series of rule changes at the state and federal levels since 2023 that allow trophy hunters to use what critics say are barbaric and unethical practices to kill animals.

Doug Burgum, the secretary of the interior, wrote in a press release that the latest rule was developed in response to demands by Alaska residents and it was a “commonsense framework and gives Alaskans a stronger voice in decisions affecting the lands, wildlife and traditions they know best”.

The federal rule does not list specific foods that are allowed, but it defers to state rules, which allow for baiting, and hunters typically use “the cheapest and most effective food, which is high fat and high sugar”, said Nicholas Arrivo, a managing attorney at Animal Protection Law. Hunters typically put food in a steel drum or garbage can, monitor the bait, then set up from a nearby blind from which they kill the bear at short range, Arrivo said.

The practice raises broader ethical questions around the spirit and intent of sport hunting.

“It is a more extreme practice than the hunting traditions that people think of, and many hunters would not see this as a fair chase,” Robertson said.

The move comes after Alaska and federal officials in recent years started allowing sport hunters to hunt big game with controversial practices, like shooting bears from helicopters, shooting swimming caribou from motor boats, killing wolf pups in their dens and using artificial lights to draw bears out of the dens to kill them. The bear baiting is not highly unusual as about a dozen states allow similar practices, but more do not.

The rule change came at the direction of Donald Trump in an executive order, called Unleashing Alaska’s Extraordinary Resource Potential, which was issued in his second administration’s early days.

“It was a priority for the president … and he included direction to reissue this rule, which says that there is a political motivation, not something that seems to be derived from careful consideration,” Robertson said.

This baiting rule has a long history. A ban was first put in place by Barack Obama’s administration, then undone by the first Trump administration. Litigation upheld the Obama rule and overturned the Trump rule. The Biden administration then reimplemented the rule in 2024, largely because science shows that the practice will make bears more aggressive, and put park visitors’ lives at risk.

Though the Trump administration has said the rule was designed to give the state more control over the land, the lands are federal and Congress created the federal land program to give the federal government decision-making power, not state governments, Arrivo said. He said it “is anathema to federal land management goals … of preserving wildlife diversity”.

Though no decision has yet been made about a lawsuit, Arrivo said the interior department’s decision to fully scrap the 2024 rule that underwent a more robust scientific process “doesn’t smell right and raises questions about the legality of this rule”.

https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/.title: Lime bike jousts? Why youth culture is embracing the medieval era
https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/.author: Ellie Violet Bramley
https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/.text:
From chainmail-wearing pop stars to high-fashion catwalks, the spirit of the middle ages is erupting into the zeitgeist

Medieval knights used to joust on warhorses with wooden lances, but this week in east London, two men jousted on Lime bikes with PVC pipes. This contemporary spin on a medieval spectacle is just one example of the spirit of the middle ages erupting into the zeitgeist.

As part of Frieze art fair, the artist Corbin Shaw staged a show called Feast of Fools. The “‘anti-Frieze” Frieze show took inspiration from a medieval festival where, as Shaw put it to GQ, “the peasant class could insult the rich”. In the video for Troye Sivan’s latest song, Party, the Australian pop star postures as a medieval knight.

On catwalks at Givenchy, Louis Vuitton and Max Mara, from wimples to chainmail, it’s been called “medievalcore”. In the new film The Uprising, actor Andrew Garfield has been leading the rabble in Paul Greengrass’s retelling of the Peasants’ Revolt. Sports Banger, the political collective that makes punchy T-shirts, has offerings that read: “Peasants’ Revolt 1381. Let’s finish the job”.

Why is the medieval era being mined by contemporary culture? Simon Trafford, a senior lecturer in medieval history at the University of London Institute of Historical Research, says “it’s always there”, but it’s more “a matter of which particular bit of it we decide to borrow from at any one time”.

“Some of the way modern artists and fashion designers are using the medieval is focused on joy and playfulness,” says Marion Turner, a professor of English literature and language at the University of Oxford. They’re not, she adds, “saying: ‘This is what I actually think the medieval world was like.’”

Bridget Dalton, a semiotician and cultural analyst at Truth Consulting, says: “It’s fun. It can be camp and it can be macho and it can be sexy as well.” In the video for Party, a victorious, post-battle Sivan gallops to celebrate with a hedonistic, homoerotic knees-up in a castle. In one piece of choreography, Sivan is used like a battering ram.

Dalton describes another emerging medieval strand as “wenchcore”, which offers “a more acceptable voracious sexuality, the ribald, singing, dancing, drinking, doesn’t-need-to-be-perfect idea of womanhood and of masculinity … more of just whatever goes”. It could be seen as the perfect, medieval-inflected answer to Brat. The middle ages, says Trafford, “gives us a sort of fantasy other space”.

Many buzzy modern ideas feel medieval-tinged: seasonality, an emphasis on nature, folklore and locality, which take on different emphases in our technological, globalised times. Community, is a focal point in much of this contemporary medievalism. The joust in London was geared towards accessibility in the week that Frieze, described by 24-year-old jousting artist Jack Lowden as “expensive and inaccessible”, took place. “So many members of the community came out,” he says.

There’s also an anti-authoritarian streak in medievalism, from Shaw to The Uprising in which a Ploughman takes his grievances to London in a move to restore egalitarianism to 14th-century England. With its own “no kings” moment, Garfield told the Washington Post recently he saw it as “prescient and kind of predictive” of the No Kings movement in the US.

There is, says Turner, an “interesting parallel” in the pandemic. “After the plague swept across Europe, there was massive social change, prompted by population decline, wage rises and new social mobility.” The peasants’ revolt “is absolutely that generation after the plague”. In the UK, in the post-Covid era, “people feel like they just don’t want to put up with what they used to put up with before the pandemic”.

Another parallel could be the advent of printing then versus the advent of the internet and AI now. For Turner, “AI is more extreme in its negative effects, but again there are parallels with the squashing of individual creativity by big technology”.

While rightwing politics often looks back to the middle ages for its own ends, within today’s youth-centric medievalism there’s a reclamation of the symbols of Englishness. As Shaw, whose cult-favourite T-shirt reads “Eng ‘lish’”, told GQ: “I hate the ruling classes of England, but there’s a lot of reasons to be proud to be English, we have to take these symbols back.”

According to Dalton, “watching youth culture embrace the medieval is a way to talk about Britain without flying a St George. It’s a very interesting route to reparative ideas about what it means to be British.”

For Trafford, “you will always be able to cherrypick … the little bits that play to your cause.” Marine Le Pen might be drawing on Joan of Arc as “this massively militant Christian figure”, while “you can definitely find that more friendly, more conducive society if you happen to be a leftwing person.” There’s a medievalism for everyone.

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: The Stone Roses showed me the power of being an introvert
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.author: Henry Yates
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
At boarding school in the early 90s, quietness was seen as weakness. But then I saw the band’s guitarist John Squire making a vast noise while hiding behind a fringe – and learned the strength of understatement

In September 1991, I had just been thrown into the meat-grinder of a Midlands boarding school. In this bear pit, there were predators and there was prey. You were either the swaggering rugby alpha, whipping a wet towel at pale bodies in the eight-boy dormitory; or the homesick ghost, keeping your guard up, endlessly braced for your toilet cubicle to be kicked open or your washbag chucked off the fire escape.

My mind had always been loud, racing with opinions, stories, jokes. But by the time I adequately considered a thought, the conversation had raced on without me. Suddenly, under 24/7 social scrutiny in a world where bullhorn confidence is king, I felt dismissed.

Up to that point, music hadn’t helped. Every rock star I had ever seen – Elton John, Freddie Mercury, Mick Jagger – was a showboating peacock, all hips, handclaps and absurd glasses, seeming to whisper in my ear: “This isn’t for you, bookworm.” But that September, I stumbled across the Stone Roses’ self-titled 1989 debut album. I must have seen John Squire’s genius before I heard it, on his paint-splashed, lemon-drizzled sleeve art.

Hearing his cascading, iridescent guitar solos, I assumed Squire must be an extrovert axe hero: foot on the monitor, diamante codpiece, the works. But there he was on the CD inlay: pipecleaner-skinny, dressed in Manchester streetwear and inscrutable beneath a bird’s-nest fringe (until the mid-90s, I genuinely wasn’t sure if Squire had eyes), slinging a Gretsch Country Gentleman guitar but not treating it like a penis extension.

Years before YouTube, it wasn’t easy to find out more. But when I dug up back issues of NME, I went from fan to disciple. A sometime model-maker who once worked on The Wind in the Willows – but also a child of 70s punk – Squire was enigmatic and otherworldly, softly spoken yet intense as a laser-cutter. Asked by one interviewer what the Roses were all about, his answer was the perfect collision of sky-scraping ambition and bone-dry Britishness: “Love and hate. War and peace. Morecambe and Wise …”

In those formative weeks, for the first time, I realised that “quiet” could also mean charismatic, insolent, snarky, simmering with latent attitude and temperamentally suited for a life in the arts. Through Squire, I discovered painting (Jackson Pollock’s “drip and splash” influence was all over his sleeves and guitars), modern history (the Paris riots of May 68 referenced on Bye Bye Badman), fashion and even religion (you only had to read his lyric to 1994’s Love Spreads, a take on the Passion, with Jesus imagined as a Black woman, to sense the iconoclast claws below the still waters).

Hearing the Roses at school, meanwhile, was my ticket into a secret society of indie kids that I hadn’t known existed, all swapping albums, making mixtapes, easy in each other’s company, building each other’s confidence. I picked up the guitar that same year, too, went on to write about it for the music press – and now play so loud in my own band that I can drown out a thousand braying show-offs.

Squire doesn’t do many interviews, and when I drove to his Cheshire farmhouse for Guitarist Magazine, I was worried he wouldn’t actually speak. But perhaps he recognised a kindred spirit. Over an hour’s encounter in his studio, the musician who had meant so much to me proved thoughtful, witty and profound, signed the schoolboy-era guitar I’d flecked Pollock-style with paint, and even gave me a parting hug.

John Squire didn’t change me; he stopped me fighting myself. Under his influence, I stopped trying to turn up the volume, accepted being an introvert and held him in mind whenever anyone equated quietness with dullness. Fast-forward 35 years – to a time when influencers squeal and preen, flogging every last grain of themselves to the attention economy – and the Roses guitarist seems a few degrees cooler for existing on his own terms, leaving something to the imagination, and treating Jonathan Ross with chilly disdain. Perhaps we could all stand to be a little more Squire?

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: Vance front and center in Republican midterms push – is this a dry run for a White House bid?
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: Robert Tait
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
Vice-president’s visibility has risen as Trump’s popularity wanes, but path to inherit Maga throne is more complicated than it may seem

A day after JD Vance suggested Donald Trump would endorse him if he runs for president, the vice-president shifted awkwardly in the Oval Office as his boss was asked about the remark.

“He’s a very talented person, and he’s a very good person,” Trump said of the man standing behind him, with a forced smile this week. “But we’ve literally – I don’t think we’ve ever talked about,” the president claimed, leaving the assertion unconfirmed.

As the campaign for the congressional midterms has intensified, the vice-president’s visibility has risen. If Trump and Vance truly have yet to discuss his presidential prospects, they are firmly in the minority in Washington.

While many aspects of this political era remain extraordinary, the core question hanging over Vance is one that has been asked for decades: is the vice-presidency a platform, or a poisoned chalice, for those who dare to dream of higher office?

Having spent only two years as a US senator before Trump tapped him in 2024 as his running mate, Vance has hit the campaign trail in recent weeks like a seasoned veteran – making stump speeches on behalf of Republican candidates as the party struggles to retain its grip on the US Senate and House of Representatives amid Trump’s plunging approval ratings.

He has held rallies in states such as Iowa, Florida, Texas, Alaska, Georgia, Michigan and his native Ohio in a criss-crossing odyssey that compares to that of Trump, who has told voters to behave as though he were on the ballot.

With secretary of state Marco Rubio – widely seen as his main rival for the next Republican nomination – focused on fighting the fires sparked by Trump’s global agenda, analysts believe Vance’s campaigning roadshow is intended as a dry run for a 2028 presidential bid. Each stop enables him to build contacts and goodwill, which he can call on in the likely event of him seeking the nomination in less than two years’ time.

Matthew Dallek, a political historian at George Washington University, said Vance was trying to “build up chits” aimed at making Trump’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement “remember that he was a good soldier”.

“He is trying to do what a lot of smart vice-presidents have done throughout history, and that’s to earn some credit out there with state and and congressional candidates,” said Rick Wilson, a former Republican strategist who now runs the anti-Trump Lincoln Project, “so that when he kicks up a campaign machine in two years, people owe him something”.

Time and again over the past two years Vance has slipped into “explainer-in-chief” mode, providing a more palatable narrative in the wake of Trump’s more extreme statements, impulses or policy decisions.
